ian-smith: Ian Douglas Smith was born on 8 April 1919 in Selukwe, a mining and farming town in Southern Rhodesia, to British settler parents. His father had grown up in Scotland and emigrated to Southern Rhodesia in 1898, building interests in farming, mining and livestock. Smith was studying at Rhodes University College in South Africa when the Second World War began, and he enlisted in the Royal Air Force in September 1941 as a fighter pilot. After demobilisation in 1945 he completed a Bachelor of Commerce degree, studied agriculture near Salisbury, and farmed cattle and tobacco at Gwenoro, near Selukwe. He was elected to the Southern Rhodesian Legislative Assembly in November 1948.

Smith favoured Southern Rhodesian independence and doubted that the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, formed in 1953, would advance it. He sat in the Federal Assembly from 1953 and was Chief Whip of the United Federal Party from 1958. As Britain moved towards majority rule in Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia, he founded the Rhodesian Reform Party in December 1961, and he co-founded the Rhodesian Front in 1962. After its victory in December 1962, Winston Field made him deputy prime minister and Minister of the Treasury, and he succeeded Field as prime minister in April 1964.

Britain required guarantees of progress towards majority rule, which Smith's government did not accept. On 11 November 1965 it issued the Unilateral Declaration of Independence. Britain answered with economic and financial sanctions but ruled out military intervention. Talks with Prime Minister Harold Wilson on HMS Tiger in December 1966 and HMS Fearless in October 1968 failed. Rhodesia declared itself a republic in 1970. The Bush War against ZANU and ZAPU intensified from December 1972. In 1978 Smith negotiated the Internal Settlement with several black nationalist leaders, which led to Zimbabwe Rhodesia in 1979 with Abel Muzorewa as prime minister, but excluded ZANU and ZAPU and won no international recognition.

Smith took part in the Lancaster House negotiations, which led to British-supervised elections and internationally recognised independence as Zimbabwe in April 1980. He sat in the Zimbabwean parliament until 1987 and was Leader of the Opposition at its opening in May 1980. His autobiography, The Great Betrayal, appeared in 1997. He died in Cape Town on 20 November 2007, aged 88, and his ashes were scattered at Gwenoro. Historian Mordechai Tamarkin called him a symbol and father figure of white Rhodesia. His supporters credited him with defending Rhodesia against communism, while critics held him responsible for prolonging white-minority rule and the conflict before independence.
ibadan: Ibadan is the capital of Oyo State, about 120 kilometres inland northeast of Lagos. Its name is said to come from Eba-Odan, meaning by the edge of the meadow. The site is a forest of several ranges of hills between 160 and 275 metres high, which offered strategic defence, and its position at the fringe of the forest made it a trading point between forest and grassland. The principal inhabitants are Yoruba, with communities from other parts of Nigeria. Parts of the city's old protective walls still stand.

Ibadan came into existence in 1829, during a period of turmoil in Yorubaland in which older cities such as Old Oyo, Ijaye and Owu disappeared and newer ones such as Abeokuta, New Oyo and Ibadan arose. According to local historians Lagelu founded it, at first as a war camp for warriors from Oyo, Ifẹ and Ijebu. It began as a military state and kept that character until the last decade of the 19th century. Historians have called it a military republic, unlike most Yoruba cities with hereditary kingship; four chiefs governed it, three of whose offices were open to all freeborn males and one reserved for women.

Warriors were the dominant class and military success offered a path of advancement, which earned it the derision of other Yoruba. Between the 1860s and 1890s it was the centre of an empire over much of northern and eastern Yorubaland, nicknamed idi-Ibon, gun base.

Refugees came in large numbers from northern Oyo after raids by Fula warriors, and in 1840 Ibadan's armies decisively defeated an attempt by the Sokoto Caliphate to expand southwards. David and Anna Hinderer of the Church Missionary Society arrived in 1853 and founded a mission and the city's first Western schools. In 1893 the area became a British protectorate after a treaty signed by Fijabi, the Baale of Ibadan, with the acting Governor of Lagos Colony, George C. Denton, on 15 August. After a small rubber boom from 1901 to 1913, cocoa became the main product. Ibadan was made headquarters of the Western Provinces in 1939.

At independence in 1960 Ibadan was the most populous city in Nigeria and the second most populous in Africa after Cairo. Its metropolitan area now has some four million people. The University of Ibadan was founded in 1948 as a college of the University of London and became autonomous in 1962. The University College Hospital was the first teaching hospital in Nigeria. Western Nigeria Television, begun at Ibadan in 1959, was the first television station in Africa. Cocoa House at Dugbe was the first skyscraper in West Africa, and Bower's Tower, built in 1936, stands on Oke Aàre.
iban-people: The Iban are a Dayak people native to north-western Borneo, found mainly in Sarawak, Brunei and parts of West Kalimantan. They trace their origins to the Kapuas basin in West Kalimantan, specifically its Ketungau tributary, from which they moved into what is now Sarawak from the middle of the 16th century, driven by tribal conflict, territorial expansion and the search for fertile land. Iban oral tradition holds that Tembawai Tampun Juah, in the Segumon region of Sanggau, was their first settlement. Before the Raj of Sarawak was founded in 1841, Iban was an exonym used by neighbours, and the Iban named themselves by the rivers they lived on, such as Kami Saribas, we of the Saribas River.

Their history is preserved in oral literature and in writing on wooden plaques called papan turai. In the 19th century, under the Brooke family's Raj of Sarawak, large-scale migration consolidated the Iban as one of the dominant ethnic groups in Sarawak. They met hunting and gathering societies and some agricultural communities, some of which were assimilated or displaced, while others were destroyed or driven from their lands.

The first direct encounter between the Iban and James Brooke came in 1843, when his forces attacked the Batang Saribas region; the peace treaty drawn up at Nagna Sebuloh to end piracy and headhunting was refused by the people there. The Iban served as soldiers under the Brooke family. Migrations continued in the 20th century, including settlement of the Baleh tributary of the Rejang in 1922 and a government-supported move to Lundu in 1955.

Iban live in longhouses, communal dwellings for extended families, and traditionally practised shifting cultivation of hill rice once a year in twenty-seven stages, as Derek Freeman described. Weaving was the women's warpath, as headhunting, called kayau, was the men's; pua kumbu blankets carry ritual motifs such as the Brooding Elephant and the Shrine. Iban music is percussion-oriented, using agung ensembles of gongs and drums.

The language, jaku Iban, belongs to the Malayic branch of the Austronesian family. Most Iban are now Christian, though many still observe traditional ceremonies at weddings and festivals. They make up 28.8 percent of the population of Sarawak.
ibaraki-prefecture: Ibaraki lies on Japan's eastern Pacific coast and borders Fukushima Prefecture to the north, Tochigi to the north-west, Saitama to the south-west and Chiba to the south. Its northern third is mountainous, with the Tsukuba Mountains at the centre, but most of it is a flat plain with many lakes, part of the Kantō Plain. It has Lake Kasumigaura, the second-largest lake in Japan, and the Tone River, the second longest in the country. In the 17th century the Tokugawa shogunate diverted the Edo River's source to the Tone to protect Edo from flooding.

Humans are believed to have lived in the area around the time of the ash deposit from the Aira Caldera about 24,000 years ago. During the Asuka period the provinces of Hitachi and Fusa were created, and Fusa was later divided, among others, into Shimōsa Province. In the 14th century Kitabatake Chikafusa made Oda Castle his field headquarters for over a year and wrote the Jinnō Shōtōki there.

In the Edo period one of the three Tokugawa houses descended from Tokugawa Ieyasu settled in the Mito Domain, in Hitachi Province, and became known as the Mito Tokugawa. In 1657 Tokugawa Mitsukuni, head of the domain, commissioned the Dai Nihonshi, a history of Japan, and the Mito school of learning grew from it. In 1833 Tokugawa Nariaki began breeding black cattle at Mito. During the Meiji Restoration the old provinces were converted or merged into prefectures: the province became Ibaraki in 1871, and in 1875 the prefecture reached its present size by taking in districts of the former Shimōsa Province.

Mito is the capital and largest city, and other major cities are Tsukuba, Hitachi and Hitachinaka. The prefecture has 2,828,086 people in 2023. Hitachi, Ltd. was founded at Sukegawa, in Hitachi, in 1910, and Tsukuba is a research and academic city with dozens of institutes. Agriculture is important, with melons, pears and peppers among its products, and Mito is known for nattō and for Kairakuen, one of the Three Great Gardens of Japan, with over 3,000 plum trees. Morihei Ueshiba, founder of Aikido, spent the later part of his life at Iwama, now part of Kasama, where his shrine and dojo remain.
ibbi-sin: Ibbi-Sin was king of Sumer and Akkad and the last king of the Ur III dynasty, reigning c. 2028–2004 BCE by the Middle chronology. During his reign Amorites attacked the empire repeatedly. His father Shu-Sin had built a wall, the wall of Martu, across Mesopotamia against Amorite incursions, but they penetrated it early in the reign. His 17th year was nevertheless officially named for the Amorites submitting to him. As faith in his leadership failed, Elam declared its independence and began to raid as well. He ordered fortifications built at Ur and Nippur, but they did not stop the raids or keep the empire unified.

Scholars have suggested that the kingdom was already in decline through long-term drought, the same drought that may have helped bring down Akkad c. 2193 BCE, and studies of Persian Gulf sediments indicate that the Tigris and Euphrates ran very low around 2100–2000 BCE. In years seven and eight of his reign the price of grain rose to 60 times the norm, which suggests that the success of the Amorites owed something to attacks on the agricultural and irrigation systems. Cities fell away from a king who could not protect them, notably Isin under the Amorite ruler Ishbi-Erra. By the end Ibbi-Sin held only the city of Ur.

The attacks brought famine and economic collapse, paving the way for Elam under Kindattu to strike at Ur and capture the king. Elam, with tribesmen from the region of Shimashki in the Zagros Mountains, sacked Ur and took Ibbi-Sin captive to Elam, where he was imprisoned and died at an unknown date. The Lament for Sumer and Ur tells that the gods An, Enlil, Enki and Ninhursaja decided its fate and that Ibbi-Sin was taken in fetters to Elam, never to return to his city. All of his year names are known and document the major events of his reign, among them the destruction of Simurrum and the building of the great walls of Nippur and Ur.
iberia: The Iberian Peninsula is the westernmost of the three major southern European peninsulas, with the Italian and Balkan peninsulas. The Pyrenees separate it from the rest of continental Europe, and the Strait of Gibraltar divides its southern tip at Tarifa from the northwest coast of Africa. Its area is about 583,254 square kilometres, and its major rivers, the Ebro, Douro, Tagus, Guadiana and Guadalquivir, flow through wide valleys between mountain systems.

The name goes back to the River Ebro, called Ibēros in Greek and Hiberus in Latin. The Ebro Treaty of 226 BCE between Rome and Carthage set the limit of Carthaginian interest at that river. Greek geographers used Iberia for the land this side of it, and Roman writers used Hispania and Hiberia as synonyms. The modern phrase Iberian Peninsula was coined in 1823 by the French geographer Jean-Baptiste Bory de Saint-Vincent.

People of the genus Homo have lived on the peninsula for at least 1.2 million years, as remains at the Atapuerca sites show. Around 2800 to 2700 BCE the Beaker culture probably arose among copper-using communities of the Tagus estuary and spread through western Europe. Bronze Age cultures such as Los Millares and El Argar developed from about 1800 BCE. By the Iron Age the peninsula held Celtic and pre-Celtic peoples, the Iberians of the east and south, and the Aquitanian cultures in the west of the Pyrenees. Phoenician merchants from Tyre founded the trading colony of Gadir, and they traded with the metal-rich community known as Tartessos.

Roman troops first occupied the peninsula in 218 BCE, during the Second Punic War against the Carthaginians, and after 197 BCE the Romans divided the Mediterranean coast and the Guadalquivir valley into Hispania Ulterior and Hispania Citerior. Celtiberian and Lusitanian resistance led to wars in the 2nd century BCE. In the early 5th century the Suebi, Vandals and Alans occupied the peninsula, and the Visigoths then took all of it, absorbing the Suebi kingdom in 584–585. Umayyad conquest followed.

In the 15th and 16th centuries Iberian expansion began a new age. The Portuguese established routes to Asia, and Spain created a vast empire in the Americas, with Seville at the centre of the transatlantic bullion trade. Jews and Moriscos were banished, and roughly 300,000 Moriscos were expelled from Spain in 1609–1614.

The peninsula is divided between most of Spain and Portugal, the microstate of Andorra, the British territory of Gibraltar and a small part of France. Its population is roughly 53 million, and its largest cities are Madrid, Barcelona and Lisbon. Apart from Basque, which is of unknown origin, all its languages descend from Vulgar Latin.
iberian-union: The Battle of Alcácer Quibir in 1578 killed the young King Sebastian of Portugal. His granduncle and successor, Cardinal Henry, was 66, and his death was followed by a succession crisis in which three grandchildren of Manuel I claimed the throne: Infanta Catarina, Duchess of Braganza, António, Prior of Crato, and King Philip II of Spain. António was acclaimed king at Santarém on 24 July 1580 and then in many other towns, but members of the Council of Governors who backed Philip fled to Spain and declared him the legal successor.

Philip marched into Portugal and defeated the troops loyal to António at the Battle of Alcântara. The Duke of Alba imposed Philip's rule on the provinces before entering Lisbon, where he seized a great treasure and let his soldiers sack the surroundings. The Cortes of Tomar recognised Philip as king in 1581, and he left for Madrid in 1583, naming his nephew Albert of Austria viceroy. Under the pledges made at Tomar, Portugal kept its own law, currency and government, and offices at home and overseas were reserved for Portuguese subjects. A Council of Portugal advised the king in Madrid. In the sixty years of the union the country had 13 viceroys and four regency councils.

The union brought Portugal into Spain's wars. The Dutch treated it as a reason to attack Portuguese colonies, and the loss of Hormuz followed the war with England. The Dutch invaded parts of Asia, including Portuguese Ceylon, and in Brazil they took Recife and Olinda in 1630. John Maurice of Nassau-Siegen, governor of the Dutch possessions from 1637, also took Elmina Castle, São Tomé and Luanda. The Dutch occupation of Brazil ended after the Second Battle of Guararapes.

Under Philip III of Portugal, taxes fell mainly on Portuguese merchants, Spaniards took government posts and the nobility lost influence. The Count-Duke of Olivares pressed for uniformity and for Portugal to share Castile's military burdens. On 1 December 1640 the Forty Conspirators killed the Secretary of State Miguel de Vasconcelos, imprisoned the vicereine Margaret of Savoy and acclaimed John, 8th Duke of Braganza, as John IV.

The Restoration War that followed consisted mainly of skirmishes near the border, with Portuguese victories at Elvas in 1659, Ameixial in 1663, Castelo Rodrigo in 1664 and Montes Claros in 1665. Spain recognised Portuguese sovereignty and made peace on 13 February 1668. The city of Ceuta, once Portuguese, stayed with Spain, and its coat of arms is nearly identical to that of the Kingdom of Portugal.
iberians: Greek and Roman writers, among them Hecataeus of Miletus, Herodotus and Strabo, describe the Iberians, and Roman sources also call them Hispani. The ancient authors used the name in two senses: generally, for all the peoples of the Iberian Peninsula, and in the narrower ethnic sense used here, for the people of the eastern and southern coasts. By the 6th century BCE they had absorbed influences from the Phoenicians, Carthaginians and Greeks.

They lived in villages and oppida, or fortified settlements, in tribal communities, and those in the Spanish Levant were more urbanised than the peoples of the centre and northwest, who spoke Celtic dialects. In the late 5th and early 4th centuries BCE an aristocracy consolidated, and the oppidum became the political centre of the landscape.

The Iberians traded widely, and their pottery and metalwork have been found in France, Italy and North Africa. They had extensive contact with Greek colonists at Emporion and with Phoenician colonies in the south such as Gadir. Sculptures such as the Lady of Baza and the Lady of Elche are thought to be the work of Iberians fairly well acquainted with Greek art. From the 5th century BCE Iberian soldiers were often sent to fight in Italy, Greece and especially Sicily.

After the First Punic War, Carthage expanded in the peninsula under Hamilcar Barca, Hasdrubal the Fair and Hannibal, who besieged Saguntum and so began the Second Punic War. Many Iberian warriors fought on both sides, though most tribes sided with Carthage. Rome sent Gnaeus and Publius Cornelius Scipio, and after Scipio Africanus arrived in 210 BCE it took Carthago Nova and won the Battle of Ilipa. The conquered lands became Hispania Ulterior and Hispania Citerior, and fighting in the north continued until 16 BCE.

Iberian society had kings or chieftains, nobles, priests, artisans and slaves; the nobles met in a council that ancient sources call a senate. The Iberians adopted wine and olives from the Greeks, bred horses, mined silver, iron, tin and copper, and made iron weapons such as the falcata. They produced sculpture in stone and bronze, and their religion was polytheistic and influenced by Greek, Carthaginian and Phoenician practice. They cremated their dead. They wrote in three scripts, and their language, unclassified and non-Indo-European, became extinct by the 1st or 2nd century CE as Latin replaced it.
ibibio-people: The Ibibio, also known as the Ibom, are found mostly in Akwa Ibom, Cross River and the eastern part of Abia State. Their related groups are the Annang, Ekid, Oron and Ibeno, who share names, culture and traditions and speak closely related, more or less mutually intelligible varieties of Ibibio. The Ibibio themselves are divided into the Eastern Ibibio or Ibibio Proper, the Western Ibibio or Annang, the Northern Ibibio or Enyong, the Southern Ibibio or Eket and the Riverine Ibibio or Uruan.

Where they came from is not settled. They are reputed to be among the earliest peoples of southern Nigeria. Some scholars see a link with the central Benue Valley and the Jukun, and the most widely accepted account, drawn partly from oral testimony, traces the core Ibibio of the Afaha lineage to Usak Edet in Cameroon. The traditions tell of a first settlement at Uruan and of clashes with the Igbo moving south, after which the Ibibio spread through their present lands.

Traditionally Ibibio society was made up of communities of large related families, each led by a constitutional and religious head, the Obong Ikpaisong. He ruled with the heads of the families, the Mbong Ekpuk, and the heads of the cults and societies, together forming a traditional council. The Ekpo society enforced his decisions: masked members acted as messengers of the spirits and as the community's military and police. Putting on an Ekpo mask meant surrendering earthly identity and assuming an ancestral one. Before the British began to abolish slavery in the mid-1880s, society ranked people as freeborn, strangers or later immigrants, and slaves.

The Ibibio are known for woodcarving, raffia weaving and pottery, and many carvers of Ekpo masks live at Ikot Ekpene. Ibibio masks play with proportion, and contrast dark male masks with light female ones. Body art, including painting, hairdressing and modification, marks occasions such as marriage and childbirth, and the dot is regarded as the mark of beauty. Traditional religion centred on Abasi Enyong, the God of Heaven, Abasi Isong, the God of the Earth, and Abasi Ibom, the Supreme Being.

Before Nigeria existed the Ibibio governed themselves. They and the Annang, Oron and Eket were part of the Bight of Biafra before the British created Eastern Nigeria, and they became part of it under colonial rule. Christianity came through nineteenth-century missionaries, and Samuel Bill began work at Ibeno and founded the Qua Iboe Church. Akwa Ibom State was carved out of Cross River State on 23 September 1987, and a 1961 plebiscite divided the Ibibio and Annang between Nigeria and Cameroon. The first Ibibio Bible translation was presented at Uyo on 27 August 2020.
ibn-arabi: Ibn Arabi was born in the Taifa of Murcia, in what is now south-eastern Spain, in 1165, and was named Muhammad. His father served in the army of Ibn Mardanish, ruler of Murcia. After Murcia fell to the Almohad Caliphate in 1172 and Ibn Mardanish was killed in battle, the father pledged allegiance to the Almohad caliph, and the family moved to Seville to serve the new ruler. Ibn Arabi grew up at the ruling court and received military training.

As a teenager he had a first vision, and the philosopher and judge Ibn Rushd, Averroes, asked to meet him. Ibn Arabi said that he learned from this meeting to tell formal knowledge from the unveiling of insight into the nature of things, and he then took up Sufism.

He left al-Andalus for the first time at 28, reaching Tunis in 1193, and crossed from Gibraltar for the last time in 1200, after a vision that told him to go east. He reached Mecca for the pilgrimage in 1202 and lived there three years, beginning there his largest work, the Meccan Illuminations. He then travelled through Syria, Palestine, Iraq and Anatolia, entering Baghdad in 1205.

In 1223 he chose Damascus as his final home and spent his last years teaching and writing there. He composed The Bezels of Wisdom in 1229 and finished two drafts of the Meccan Illuminations, in 1231 and 1238. About 850 works are attributed to him, of which around 700 are thought authentic and over 400 survive.

Ibn Arabi is known as the first to set out explicitly the doctrine of waḥdat al-wujūd, the unity of being, which holds that everything in the universe manifests a single reality, which he called Absolute Being. He distinguished rational knowledge, which he held to be fallible, from experiential knowledge, which he called dhawq, and from divine knowledge, which he believed was given to prophets and their spiritual heirs.

He died on 16 November 1240 and was buried on Qasiyun Hill in Damascus. His teaching spread quickly through the Islamic world, carried by the Sufi orders and by works in Persian, Turkish and Urdu, and he came to be called Shaykh al-Akbar.
ibn-battuta: All that is known of Ibn Battuta's life comes from the account of his travels. It records that he was of Arabised Berber descent and was born into a family of Islamic legal scholars, known as qadis, in Tangier on 24 February 1304, under the Marinid dynasty. His family belonged to a Berber clan called the Lawata. As a young man he probably studied at a Sunni Maliki school, the dominant form of education in North Africa at the time.

On 14 June 1325, aged 21, he set out from Tangier on the hajj to Mecca, a journey that would ordinarily take sixteen months. He did not return to Morocco for 24 years. He travelled overland along the North African coast through Tlemcen, Béjaïa and Tunis, usually joining a caravan for safety, and reached Alexandria in the early spring of 1326. After his third pilgrimage to Mecca he decided to seek employment with Muhammad bin Tughluq, the Sultan of Delhi, and went by way of Anatolia, where members of the fityan associations of young artisans welcomed him in more than 25 towns.

He left Quanzhou in 1346 and reached Damascus in 1348, where he learned that his father had died 15 years earlier. He saw the Black Death in Syria, Palestine and Egypt, and he was back in Tangier in 1349, only to find that his mother had also died. In 1350 he went to al-Andalus, and in 1352 he crossed the Sahara by caravan from Sijilmasa, by way of the salt mines of Taghaza, to Oualata, which had recently become part of the Mali Empire.

After he came home in 1354, the Marinid ruler Abu Inan Faris suggested that he dictate an account of his journeys, which he did in Arabic to the scholar Ibn Juzayy. It is known as the Rihla and is the only source for his travels. He seems to have kept no notes, and Ibn Juzayy copied descriptions of Damascus, Mecca, Medina and Palestine from earlier travellers without acknowledging them. Modern scholars doubt that Ibn Battuta visited every place he describes. In 2010 Tim Mackintosh-Smith reported manuscripts of Islamic law at Al-Azhar University copied by Ibn Battuta in Damascus in 1326, which support the Rihla's date for his stay in Syria.
ibn-hajar-al-asqalani: Ibn Hajar was born into an Arab Kinani family in Cairo in 1372, the son of the Shafi'i scholar and poet Nur ad-Din Ali. His parents came from Alexandria, and the family originally hailed from Ascalon, which gave him the name al-Asqalani. Ibn Hajar was the nickname of an ancestor, extended to his descendants. Both parents died in his infancy, and he and his sister became wards of Zaki ad-Din al-Kharrubi, who enrolled him in Qur'anic studies at five. He memorised the whole Qur'an by the age of nine, and at twelve, accompanying al-Kharrubi to Mecca, he was thought competent to lead the Tarawih prayers.

After his guardian died in 1386, the hadith scholar Shams ad-Din ibn al-Qattan guided his education in Egypt. He studied Shafi'i jurisprudence under Sirajud-Din al-Bulqini and Ibn al-Mulaqqin and hadith under Zain al-Din al-Iraqi, then travelled to Damascus and Jerusalem and visited Mecca, Medina and Yemen before returning to Egypt. He had 628 teachers, 55 of them women. In 1397 he married the hadith expert Uns Khatun, and he had five daughters by her and one by a later wife, all of whom died in his lifetime. He was appointed Egyptian qadi, or chief judge, several times, and had a scholarly rivalry with the Hanafi scholar Badr al-Din al-Ayni.

He wrote some 150 works on hadith, its terminology, biographical evaluation, history, tafsir, poetry and Shafi'i jurisprudence, though he wished to revise many of them. His student al-Sakhawi recorded that he thought only a few complete and polished, among them the Fath al-Bari, Tahdhib al-Tahdhib and Lisan al-Mizan. Other works include al-Isabah, a dictionary of the Companions of the Prophet, the biographical dictionary al-Durar al-Kaminah, a discussion of the Black Death called Merits of the Plague, and Bulugh al-Maram.

The Fath al-Bari, his commentary on the Sahih of al-Bukhari, became his best-known work. The historian Ibn Iyas described the celebrations near Cairo on its publication in December 1428, with many of Egypt's leading dignitaries present, readings by Ibn Hajar, eulogies by poets and gold distributed, as the finest of the age. He died on 2 February 1449, aged 79, and the funeral prayer was led by the Abbasid caliph. An estimated 50,000 people attended, among them Sultan Jaqmaq, and he was buried in the cemetery of Karafat al-Sughra. He is regarded as the foremost scholar of the fifteenth century in Islamic law, and his work is called the final summation of the science of hadith.
ibn-hawqal: Muhammad Abu'l-Qasim Ibn Hawqal, also called Abu al-Qasim ibn Ali Ibn Hawqal al-Nasibi, was a 10th-century Arab Muslim writer, geographer and chronicler born in Nisibis in Upper Mesopotamia. He travelled in various countries from 943 to 969. What is known of his life is extrapolated from his own book, which shows that he died after 978. One journey took him 20 degrees south of the equator along the East African coast, where he found large populations in regions that ancient Greek writers had judged uninhabitable.

His major work, written in 977, is the Surat al-Ard, the face of the earth. It revises and enlarges the Masalik al-Mamalik of Istakhri, written in 951, which was itself a revised edition of the Suwar al-aqalim of Ahmed ibn Sahl al-Balkhi. Ibn Hawqal was more than an editor: he wrote as a travel writer, drawing on the reports of merchants and travellers. His account of Sicily under the Kalbid-Fatimid dynasty introduces humour, and as a primary source his geography tends to exaggerate, as in its picture of the barbaric and uncivilised Christians of Palermo, which reflects the attitudes of his time. Medieval Arab travellers nevertheless relied on his accounts of his own journeys.

The chapters on al-Andalus, Sicily and the cultivated area of Fraxinet describe innovations practised by Muslim farmers and fishermen. The chapter on the Byzantine Empire records his observation of 360 languages spoken in the Caucasus, with Arabic and Persian as the lingua franca. He also published a map of Sindh with accounts of its geography and culture and of the Indus River.

An anonymous epitome of the book was written in 1233. In the 1870s the Dutch orientalist Michael Jan de Goeje edited a selection of Arabic geographers, published by Brill in Leiden. Ibn Hawqal's text was the second volume, published in 1873 under the Latin title Viae et Regna.
ibn-khaldun: Abd al-Rahman ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis in 1332 into an upper-class Andalusian family of Yemeni Arab descent, the Banu Khaldun, whose eponymous ancestor had settled first in Carmona and then in Seville. His first and most influential teacher was his father, under whom he studied the Islamic and the rational sciences. He also learned from Moroccan and Tunisian scholars and from Andalusian exiles in Tunis, studying Quranic recitation, Maliki law, hadith and poetry, and while still young he became a hafiz. His autobiography is described as the most detailed in medieval Muslim literature, though it lacks many personal details.

At 20 Ibn Khaldun began his political career in the chancellery of the Tunisian ruler Ibn Tafrakin as seal-bearer. Unhappy with this politically meaningless position, he followed his teacher al-Abili to Fez, where the Marinid sultan Abu Inan Fares I made him a writer of royal proclamations. He schemed against his employer and in 1357 received a prison sentence of 22 months, which ended with Abu Inan's death in 1358. He travelled through Fez, Granada and Tlemcen, repeatedly changing roles, and arrived in Cairo in 1380.

In 1384 the sultan Barquq made him professor of the Qamhiyyah Madrasah and grand qadi of the Maliki school. His efforts to reform abuses in the administration of justice met resistance, and within a year he resigned. A ship carrying his wife and children sank off Alexandria that year. He was called to the Maliki judgeship six times and never held it long.

His best-known book is the Muqaddimah, the Introduction, which he says he wrote in six months. It is the first book of the Kitab al-Ibar, begun as a history of the Berbers and expanded into a universal history in seven books. He departed from the classical style of Arab historians by synthesising multiple, sometimes contradictory sources without citations. His method had very few followers in his own time, but Ottoman historians such as Katip Celebi took up his theory of the rise and fall of empires in the 17th century. Europe first learned of him in 1697 through a biography in d'Herbelot's Bibliothèque Orientale, and the complete Arabic edition of the Muqaddimah appeared in 1858.
ibn-rusta: Ahmad ibn Rusta Isfahani, known as Ibn Rusta, was a Muslim Persian explorer and geographer of the 10th century, born in Rosta, Isfahan, in the Abbasid Caliphate. He wrote a geographical compendium known as the Kitāb al-A'lāq al-Nafīsa, the Book of Precious Records. His information on Isfahan is especially extensive. He states that for other lands he had to depend on second-hand reports, often acquired with great difficulty and with no means of checking, while for Isfahan he could use his own observation or statements from reliable people.

His account of Isfahan describes the twenty districts, called rostaqs, with details found in no other geographer's work, and says the town was perfectly circular, half a parasang round, with walls defended by a hundred towers and four gates. His information on the non-Islamic peoples of Europe and Inner Asia makes him a useful source for these obscure regions, and for the prehistory of the Turks and other steppe peoples; he knew of the British Isles and the Heptarchy of Anglo-Saxon England. He travelled to Novgorod with the Rus' and compiled books on his own travels and on what he learned second-hand of the Khazars, Magyars, Slavs and Bulgars.

He described the Rus' as living on an island that takes three days to walk round, raiding the Slavs by ship and selling them as slaves. A Russian translation by Daniel Chwolson rendered his remark on their clothes as clean, though later editions note that the Arabic original says the opposite. Of Croatia's ruler he wrote that he was called sacred king, and of a king of the Caucasus that he prayed with Muslims on Fridays, with Jews on Saturdays and with Christians on Sundays. He also travelled in Arabia and described Sanaa as a populous city of fine dwellings.
ibn-saud: Ibn Saud was born in Riyadh, the fourth child and third son of Abdul Rahman bin Faisal, one of the last rulers of the Emirate of Nejd, the second Saudi state, a tribal sheikhdom centred on Riyadh. The Al Saud family had been a power in central Arabia for about 130 years. The family's long-term rivals, led by Muhammad bin Abdullah Al Rashid, conquered Riyadh when Ibn Saud was a boy, and the family took refuge with the Al Murrah, a Bedouin tribe, and then settled in Kuwait for nearly a decade, where he developed a rapport with the ruler Mubarak Al Sabah. His paternal aunt, Jawhara bint Faisal, told him of his ancestors' deeds and helped persuade him to return to Nejd.

He reconquered Riyadh in 1902, and many former supporters of the House of Saud rallied to him. Over the next two years his forces recaptured almost half of Nejd from the Rashidis. On 15 June 1904 combined Ottoman and Rashidi forces defeated him heavily, but he waged a guerrilla war on the Ottomans and in February 1905 they named him qaimmaqam of southern Nejd. His victory at Rawdat Muhanna ended the Ottoman presence in Nejd and Qassim by the end of October 1906.

Over three decades his conquests made him ruler of nearly all of central and northern Arabia. He consolidated control over Najd in 1921 and conquered the Hejaz in 1925, and in 1932 his dominions became the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. He signed a friendship and cooperation pact with Britain in 1915. In the Saudi-Yemeni War of 1934 the Treaty of Taif confirmed his sovereignty over Asir, Jazan and Najran. Oil was discovered in 1938, after he granted a concession in 1933.

He kept Saudi Arabia neutral in the Second World War. On 14 February 1945 he met the American president Franklin D. Roosevelt aboard USS Quincy on the Great Bitter Lake, a meeting that laid the basis of later relations between the two countries. He fathered almost one hundred children, including 45 sons. He died in his sleep at Shubra Palace in Ta'if on 9 November 1953, with Prince Faisal at his side, and was buried in Riyadh next to his sister Noura. His sons have succeeded him as kings.
ibn-taymiyya: Ibn Taymiyya was born on 22 January 1263 in Harran, to a family of Hanbali scholars. His father held the Hanbali chair in Harran and later at the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus. In 1269, aged seven, he left Harran with his father and three brothers, and the city was destroyed in the Mongol invasion that followed. The family settled in Damascus, under Mamluk rule. After his father died in 1284 he took over the Sukkariyya madrasa and began to lecture on hadith.

During the Mongol invasions of Syria, from 1299 to 1303, Ibn Taymiyya declared the Ilkhanid regime unbelieving because it ruled by the Mongol Yassa code rather than sharia. He urged resistance in Damascus, rebuked those who fled, and issued fatwas making jihad against the Mongols a duty. His third fatwa, of 1303, is sometimes called his best known. He also issued a ruling for jihad against the Shia of Kisrawan.

He was imprisoned several times for conflicts with the jurists and theologians of his day. His creedal work Al-Aqidah Al-Waasitiyyah, which held that God should be described as the Qur'an and hadith describe him, drew four hearings in 1305-1306. After a debate at the Citadel of Cairo on 8 April 1306 he was jailed on the charge of anthropomorphism until 25 September 1307. He returned to Damascus on 28 February 1313, where he taught Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya.

His treatise on journeys to the tombs of prophets and saints condemned the cult of saints. For it he was imprisoned in the Citadel of Damascus on 18 July 1326, and the sultan forbade him to issue fatwas. He fell ill in early September 1328 and died on 26 September, aged 65. Thousands came to pay their respects, and he was buried in the cemetery of the Sufis. Many hold that portrayals of him as hostile to Sufism are inaccurate, since he praised many Sufi masters and belonged to the Qadiriyya order.

His writings influenced Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and the Salafi movement, and in the 20th century his anti-Mongol fatwas were taken up by Islamist thinkers such as Sayyid Qutb, who applied them to the governments of their own day.
ibn-tufayl: Ibn Tufayl was born in Guadix, near Granada, and was educated by the scholar Ibn Bajjah, known in Latin as Avempace. His family belonged to the Arab Qays tribe. He worked as a secretary to several leaders: the Almohad governor of Granada, and in 1154 the rulers of Ceuta and Tangier, one of whom was Abu Saʿid ʿUthman, a son of ʿAbd al-Mu'min. He then entered the service of Abu Yaʿqub Yusuf, who was a prince at the time and became the second Almohad caliph. Ibn Tufayl served him as vizier and physician.

In 1169 he recommended Ibn Rushd, known as Averroes, to the caliph as his own future successor. Ibn Rushd later recalled that Ibn Tufayl had told him of the caliph's complaint that Aristotle's expression, or his translators', was disjointed and obscure. Ibn Tufayl urged him to summarise and clarify the books, saying that only his great age and the cares of his office kept him from doing it himself. Ibn Rushd succeeded him when he retired in 1182, and Ibn Tufayl died in Morocco in 1185. The astronomer Nur ed-Din al-Bitruji was among his disciples.

Ibn Tufayl's best-known work is Hayy ibn Yaqzan, which means Alive, son of Awake and is also known in Latin as Philosophus Autodidactus. It is a philosophical romance, inspired by Avicennism and Sufism, about a feral child raised by a gazelle on a desert island who discovers ultimate truth through reasoned inquiry. Hayy meets a castaway named Absal and comes into contact with civilisation and religion. He concludes that imagery and material goods in religion are necessary for the multitude to live decent lives, but are distractions from the truth for those whose reason recognises this. The names of the characters and the title come from tales by Ibn Sina. The work was written as a response to al-Ghazali's The Incoherence of the Philosophers.
He also wrote a long poem in the rajaz metre on medicine, describing how to diagnose illnesses and find their cures, and he was an early supporter of dissection and autopsy.

Ibn al-Nafis answered Hayy ibn Yaqzan in the 13th century with a work known in the West as Theologus Autodidactus. Edward Pococke the Younger published a Latin translation in 1671, and Simon Ockley's English translation followed in 1708. The book became a best-seller in Western Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries. It may have inspired Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe, and it is thought to have influenced John Locke's idea of the tabula rasa in An Essay Concerning Human Understanding of 1690.
ibn-tumart: Many details of Ibn Tumart's life were recorded by hagiographers, whose accounts probably blend in elements of Almohad doctrine. He was born between 1078 and 1082 in the village of Igiliz in the Sous region of southern Morocco, a member of the Hargha, a Berber tribe of the Anti-Atlas belonging to the Masmuda confederation. His family was humble, and his father was a lamplighter at a mosque. He and his followers asserted that he descended from Idris I and so from al-Hasan ibn Ali, a claim that modern scholars widely dispute. About 1106 he went to Córdoba to study under al-Turtushi, and then east, where he came under the influence of al-Ghazali's ideas.

His main principle was a rigid unitarianism, tawhid, which denied that God has attributes as incompatible with his unity. He opposed the Almoravid sponsorship of the Maliki school, accusing it of neglecting the Sunnah and hadith, and objected to the public sale of wine and pork. His followers took the name al-Muwwahidun, those who affirm the unity of God, which Spanish authors rendered Almohades. He returned to the Maghreb in 1117/18, preaching a puritan Islam from town to town, and about 1119 set up camp at Mellala, near Bejaia, where his first followers joined him, among them al-Bashir and Abd al-Mu'min.

In 1120 he went to Fez and then to Marrakesh, where he confronted the Almoravid emir Ali ibn Yusuf and was expelled after a flogging of fourteen lashes. He returned to Igiliz and lived in a nearby cave. Towards the end of Ramadan in late 1121 he declared himself the Mahdi, the expected divinely guided justicer, which was effectively a declaration of war on the Almoravid state. In 1122 or shortly after he founded a ribat at Tinmel in the High Atlas as the spiritual centre and military headquarters of the revolt.

For eight years the Almohad revolt was largely a guerrilla war in the Atlas ravines and peaks. In early 1130 the Almohads besieged Marrakesh and were crushed by the Almoravids at the Battle of al-Buhayra, with huge losses; al-Bashir was killed. Ibn Tumart died in August 1130. He had organised the Almohad commune as a pyramidal hierarchy of fourteen grades, with a Council of Ten and a wider Council of Fifty of Masmuda sheikhs. After a probable struggle for the succession, Abd al-Mu'min, a Zenata Berber, was chosen, and led a seven-year campaign of conquest of Morocco that culminated in the fall of Marrakesh in 1147.
ibrahim-lodi: Ibrahim Lodi, the eldest son of Sikandar Lodi, ascended the throne without opposition after his father's death in late 1517. Early in his reign he tried a power-sharing arrangement by installing his brother Jalal Lodi as autonomous governor of Jaunpur. When Jalal began to assert independence, Ibrahim reversed the decision on the counsel of senior courtiers. He summoned Jalal to Delhi and, when Jalal refused, secretly told provincial governors and nobles to withhold recognition, forcing Jalal back to Kalpi.

Jalal won the backing of the noble Azam Humayun Sarwani and seized Awadh, but Azam went over to the Sultan when Ibrahim advanced with a large force. A truce let Jalal keep Kalpi, but it was short-lived. Ibrahim pursued him to Gwalior, Malwa and the Gonds, who betrayed him; he was captured on his way to Hansi and quietly executed on Ibrahim's orders. Ibrahim then sent an expedition of 30,000 cavalry and 300 elephants, led by Azam Humayun, against Gwalior, which fell in 1518 with the surrender of Vikramaditya Tomar. A further army sent against Rana Sanga of Mewar was defeated, a blow to his military reputation.

Jalal's revolt deepened Ibrahim's mistrust of his Afghan and Turkish nobles. He tightened court protocol and arrested prominent figures, among them Azam Humayun Sarwani and Mian Bhuwah. Azam's son Islam Sarwani raised about 40,000 men with the support of Lodi chiefs to demand his father's release; Ibrahim refused and crushed the rebellion in an engagement that killed around 10,000. He had Mian Bhuwah executed, Azam Humayun died in captivity, and Mian Husain Farmuli was murdered at Chanderi by Ibrahim's agents. Nobles in the eastern provinces began fortifying their positions, and Bahar Lodi proclaimed independence on the death of his father Darya Lohani.

Daulat Lodi, governor of Punjab, sent his son to Kabul to enlist Babur's support, and Ibrahim's uncle Alam also sought Babur's aid. In 1524 Babur seized Lahore and took control of the Punjab. By early 1526 he launched a full invasion, and at the First Battle of Panipat in April 1526 Ibrahim's larger army was defeated by Babur's tactics and superior cavalry. Ibrahim died on the field, ending Lodi rule in Delhi and the independent Delhi Sultanate and opening the way for the Mughal Empire.

His tomb is often mistaken for the Shisha Gumbad in Lodi Gardens, Delhi; it stands near the tehsil office in Panipat, and in 1866 the British moved and renovated it during the building of the Grand Trunk Road.
ibrahim-pasha-of-egypt: Ibrahim was the first-born son of Muhammad Ali and Amina Hanim, the widow of an Ottoman official. He was born in the village of Nusratli, near Drama in the Ottoman province of Rumelia, and was of Albanian origin through his father. In 1805, at sixteen, he was sent as a hostage to the Ottoman Kapudan Pasha during his father's struggle to establish himself in Egypt, and he returned once his father was recognised as Wāli. From 1811 to 1816 he was Prince of Upper Egypt, with his seat at Girga, and in 1816 he succeeded his brother Tusun Pasha in command of the Egyptian forces in Arabia.

His campaign in Arabia lasted two years and ended in the destruction of the House of Saud as a political power. He followed the Saudis into the desert of Nejd, and by the end of September 1818 he had forced their leader Abdullah bin Saud to surrender and had taken and sacked Diriyah. He entered Cairo in triumph on 11 December 1819. In 1824 he sailed for the Morea with 17,000 men to help Sultan Mahmud II against the Greek Revolution, landing at Modon on 26 February 1825.

He brought the siege of Missolonghi to an end on 24 April 1826, but was defeated three times in Mani. In reprisal against Greek guerrillas he devastated the country and sent thousands of inhabitants into slavery in Egypt, which aroused indignation in Europe. After the Battle of Navarino on 20 October 1827 he evacuated the Morea under the capitulation of 1 October 1828.

In 1831 he was sent to conquer Ottoman Syria. He took Acre on 27 May 1832, defeated Ottoman armies at Homs and Beilan, and routed the Grand Vizier Reşid Mehmed Pasha at Konya on 21 December. He stayed on as governor, but intensified taxation, conscription, disarmament and forced labour provoked revolts from 1834. In that year he besieged Al-Karak for 17 days and destroyed the town. After his last victory at Nezib on 24 June 1839, the United Kingdom and Austria intervened, and he was compelled to evacuate Syria in February 1841.

Ibrahim spent his last years in peace, but his health was ruined. He visited Western Europe in 1846, and when his father became senile he was appointed regent, holding the office from July until his death on 10 November 1848. In 1872 the Khedive Ismail commissioned a large statue of him by Charles Cordier, but the Ottomans objected to two reliefs showing their defeats, so it was first erected without them. On the centenary of his death in 1948 the reliefs were rebuilt, and the complete statue stands in a square in Cairo.
ibycus: Ibycus was an ancient Greek lyric poet, a citizen of Rhegium in Magna Graecia, active in the second half of the 6th century BCE and probably at Samos during the reign of the tyrant Polycrates. Few biographical facts are known and the testimonia are difficult to interpret.

The Byzantine encyclopaedia Suda gives his father as Phytius, Polyzelus or Cerdas, and says he went from Rhegium to Samos in the 54th Olympiad; its chronology has been dismissed as muddled, and Eusebius's date for the poet's first fame, between 542 and 537 BCE, fits Polycrates' reign better. A proverb tells that he refused the chance to become tyrant of Rhegium to pursue poetry. Some scholars think he spent time at Sicyon, and possibly in Sparta, before Samos.

Hellenistic scholars at Alexandria counted him among the nine canonical lyric poets. He was remembered mainly for love poetry, but he also composed narratives on mythological themes in the manner of Stesichorus, and structured his verses in triads. The scholars compiled only seven books of his work, numbered, not titled. His surviving verse is a blend of the public choral style of Stesichorus and the private style of the Lesbian poets, in a literary language largely Epic with Doric touches.

Until the 1920s only two fairly large fragments and about fifty lines from commentaries were known; papyrus finds since then added forty-eight lines addressed to Polycrates. Athenaeus quotes a fragment in which love, like the Thracian north wind ablaze with lightning, shakes the poet from the roots, in contrast with the calm of spring.

The Suda says he was captured by bandits in a deserted place and declared that cranes flying overhead would avenge him; later one of the bandits saw cranes in the city and cried out, and the crime was confessed. This gave the proverb the cranes of Ibycus.

The story is also found in Plutarch and Antipater of Sidon and inspired Friedrich Schiller's ballad Die Kraniche des Ibykus of 1797, though it may derive from a play on his name and the Greek word for a bird. An anonymous poem in the Palatine Anthology names Rhegium as his resting place. Ancient scholars said that Ibycus first told that Achilles would marry Medea in the Elysian Fields.
idar-oberstein: Idar-Oberstein lies on the southern edge of the Hunsrück on both sides of the river Nahe, in the Birkenfeld district, and is the largest town in the Hunsrück. The present town is the product of two rounds of administrative reform, in 1933 and 1969, which joined many municipalities into one. Nine villages, among them Enzweiler, Göttschied, Weierbach and Nahbollenbach, were added in 1969 and 1970. The districts have kept their own identities, and Idar and Oberstein are the more urban ones, the others recalling their past as rural villages.

Before the French period the area was split among many lordly domains. Oberstein grew out of the Imperially immediate Lordship of Oberstein, whose Herren vom Stein, the Lords of the Stone, are first mentioned in 1075. They sat at Castle Bosselstein, above the cliff where the Felsenkirche, or Rock Church, was later built, and after 1323 called themselves von Daun-Oberstein. Oberstein took on the character of a town without ever gaining the legal status of a market town, and its old town wall was built about 1410. The lordship passed to the Counts of Leiningen-Heidesheim in 1682, to the Counts of Limburg-Styrum in 1766 and to the Margraves of Baden in 1776.

The French reorganised the territory from 1794, and until 1814 it lay in the arrondissement of Birkenfeld. The Code civil and the abolition of noble and clerical privilege made French rule popular, though taxes and conscription weighed heavily. After the Congress of Vienna the Nahe became a border, and the centres on its north bank joined the Principality of Birkenfeld, an exclave of the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg. At the end of the First World War Grand Duke Friedrich August abdicated, and the French occupied the area on 4 December 1918 and stayed until 30 June 1930. Since 1938 the town has been a garrison town and later the site of the Bundeswehr artillery school.

Idar-Oberstein is known as a gemstone town. Until the 18th century the area was a source of agate and jasper, and cheap labour and the free water power of the Nahe, which drove the mills with cutting and polishing machines, helped the industry flourish. The Felsenkirche, built in 1482 by Wirich IV of Daun-Oberstein on the foundations of an older refuge castle in a great cave, is the town's defining landmark. The German Gemstone Museum stands in Idar, and a gemstone mine, the Steinkaulenberg, is open to visitors.
idi-amin: Idi Amin was born to a Kakwa father and a Lugbara mother. Virtually all retellings of his early life are contradictory, since he wrote no autobiography and never authorised an account of his life, and no records were kept for native Ugandans at the time. In 1940 he was rejected when he tried to register for primary school, reportedly because of his paternal Nubian heritage. He joined the King's African Rifles in 1946 as an assistant cook and received military training until 1947. He served in Kenya, was sent against Somali rebels in 1949 and against the Mau Mau rebels in 1952, and was promoted to sergeant in 1953.

After Uganda's independence in 1962 Amin was promoted to captain and then to major in 1963, and in 1964 he became Deputy Commander of the Army. A rift with President Milton Obote grew from Amin's support within the army, recruited from his home region of West Nile, and in October 1970 Obote took control of the armed forces. Having learned that Obote planned to arrest him for misappropriating army funds, Amin seized power on 25 January 1971 while Obote was at the Commonwealth summit in Singapore, and he declared himself president on 2 February.

Amin ruled by decree, placed military tribunals above the civil law and replaced the General Service Unit with the State Research Bureau, whose headquarters in Nakasero became a scene of torture and capital punishment. Lango and Acholi soldiers were massacred in the barracks at Jinja and Mbarara in July 1971, and bodies were often dumped in the River Nile. The killings continued throughout his eight years in power, and the exact number of dead is unknown, with estimates differing widely.

He expelled Asians, mostly Indian-Ugandans, in 1972, and India broke off diplomatic relations. In 1977 the United Kingdom broke off relations and he added CBE, for Conqueror of the British Empire, to his titles. His attempt to annex Tanzania's Kagera Region in 1978 led President Julius Nyerere to order an invasion, and Tanzanian and rebel forces took Kampala in 1979. Amin fled to Libya, then to Iraq, and finally to Saudi Arabia. He died in Jeddah on 16 August 2003.
idomeneus: In Greek mythology Idomeneus was a Cretan king and commander who led the Cretan armies to the Trojan War in eighty black ships. He was also one of the suitors of Helen and a comrade of the Telamonian Ajax, and Meriones was his charioteer and brother-in-arms. He was the son of Deucalion and Cleopatra and the grandson of King Minos of Crete and Queen Pasiphaë, so his line ran back to the sun god Helios. His wife Meda bore him Orsilochus, Cleisithyra, Iphiclus and Lycus. The chronicler Malalas described him as above average height, dark-skinned, with a thick beard and curly hair, and a berserker when fighting.

In Homer's Iliad Idomeneus stands in the first rank of the Greek generals, leads his troops against the enemy head-on and escapes serious injury. He is one of Agamemnon's trusted advisors and one of the main defenders when most of the other Achaean heroes are wounded, and he fights Hector briefly and repulses his attack. He is alive at the close of the story and is among those who enter the Trojan Horse. He is said to have killed twenty men and at least three Amazon women, including Bremusa.

A later tradition, kept by the grammarian Servius in his commentary on Virgil's Aeneid, tells of his return. A terrible storm struck his ship, and he promised Poseidon to sacrifice the first living thing he saw at home if the god saved ship and crew. It was his son, whom he sacrificed. The angry gods sent a plague to Crete, and the Cretans exiled him to Calabria and then to Colophon in Asia Minor, where he died. Apollodorus tells it differently: his foster son Leucus drove him out after seducing and killing Meda and seizing the throne, and Porphyry says Idomeneus sacked Lyctus and other cities Leucus had taken.

Varro held that the Salentini descended from Idomeneus, who sailed from Crete to Illyria and then with Illyrians and Locrians to Salento. The story was also told by the French writer François Fénelon in the seventeenth century. Mozart's opera seria Idomeneo of 1781 is based on the tale of his return to Crete, but in it Poseidon, called Neptune, spares Idomeneo's son Idamante on condition that Idomeneo hands his throne to the new generation.
idrija: Idrija lies in the Idrija Basin, surrounded by the Idrija Hills, in the traditional region of Inner Carniola, though its inhabitants now mostly consider it part of the Slovene Littoral. The Idrijca River runs through the town. Under Austrian rule the town was known as Idria.

In the Middle Ages Idrija was managed by the Patriarchate of Aquileia and the Counts of Gorizia. Mercury was discovered in the late 15th century, with various sources citing 1490, 1492 and 1497. According to legend, a bucket maker working at a local spring saw a small amount of liquid mercury in 1490. Idrija is one of the few places where mercury occurs both in its native state and as cinnabar ore. The Republic of Venice occupied the town for one year, in 1508, but it was otherwise governed by the House of Habsburg. The mine owners built Gewerkenegg Castle between 1522 and 1533, and the government took over the mining in 1580.

Idrija was a cornerstone of the global supply of mercury, and it supplied the silver mines of the Spanish Empire when other mines faltered in their deliveries. The mineral idrialite, found there in 1832, is named after the town. In the later 19th century lace-making became a source of international trade, and by 1905 lace was exported to Europe, America and Egypt. Idrija passed to Italy in 1920 under the Treaty of Rapallo and in September 1943 came under Nazi Germany. After the war it formed part of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia within Yugoslavia, and in June 1991 it became a town in independent Slovenia.

The mercury mine, with its stores and infrastructure, the miners' living quarters and a miners' theatre, forms a World Heritage Site together with the Spanish mine at Almadén, inscribed in 2012. Visitors can tour the upper levels through Anthony's Shaft, while the lower levels, which reach almost 400 metres below the surface, are no longer worked. Idrija lace is a bobbin tape lace with protected geographical indication.
idris-i-of-morocco: Idris ibn Abd Allah, also called Idris the Elder, was a Hasanid, a great-grandchild of Hasan, the son of Fatima and Ali and grandson of Muhammad. He was born and raised in Arabia. His paternal half-brothers Muhammad al-Nafs al-Zakiyya and Ibrahim had been killed by the Abbasids during an abortive rebellion, and his brother Yahya, who rose in revolt in Daylam, was forced to surrender and was afterwards persecuted and repeatedly imprisoned by Caliph Harun al-Rashid.

Idris himself took part, with Yahya, in the Alid uprising of 786 under al-Husayn ibn Ali al-Abid. After the revolt's defeat at the Battle of Fakhkh he escaped and hid, then moved to Egypt, where Wadih, the local head of the caliphal postal system, helped him reach the Maghreb.

In 789 Idris arrived in Tangier and went on to Walīlī, the site of the Roman Volubilis. Recent excavations by the Moroccan Institute of Archaeology and University College London have found his headquarters just outside the walls of the Roman town, which the Berber tribe of the Awraba, under Ishaq ibn Muhammad, then occupied. He married Kenza of the Awraba and fathered a son, Idris II. This is regarded as the consolidation and birth of the Idrisid dynasty, the fourth Muslim state in Morocco after Nekor, Barghawata and Midrar. Idris conquered large parts of northern Morocco, founded the city of Fez, and captured Tlemcen from the Sufrite Ifranid Abu Qurra.

These successes prompted Harun al-Rashid to send emissaries to kill him. Idris died in 791 at Walīlī, allegedly poisoned by the caliph's agents. His son Idris II was born a few months later and brought up by the Awraba under the regency of Rashid, his father's freedman and adviser; he left Walīlī for Fez in 808 and consolidated the Idrisid state. Idris I was buried on a hill not far from Walīlī, and the site grew into the village of Moulay Idriss Zerhoun, where a zawiya centred on his mausoleum developed over the centuries and remains an important religious site in Morocco. He is regarded as the founding father of Morocco.
idris-of-libya: Idris was born at Al-Jaghbub, the headquarters of the Senussi movement, the son of Sayyid Muhammad al-Mahdi al-Senussi and his third wife. His grandfather, Sayyid Muhammad ibn Ali as-Senussi, founded the Senussi Sufi order, a revivalist Sunni movement based largely in Cyrenaica. By the end of the 19th century the order had set up a government in Cyrenaica that united its tribes, controlled its pilgrimage and trade routes and collected taxes. In 1916 Idris became head of the order when his cousin Ahmed Sharif as-Senussi abdicated.

Ahmed Sharif had attacked British forces in Egypt under Ottoman pressure. Idris stopped the attacks and made a tacit alliance with the British Empire that lasted half a century. Through British intermediaries he negotiated with the Italians, who had invaded Cyrenaica in 1913, and agreements at al-Zuwaytina and Akrama left most of inland Cyrenaica under the Senussi. In 1920 the Accord of al-Rajma made him Emir of Cyrenaica with autonomy over several oases. In 1922 Tripolitanian leaders asked him to extend the emirate into Tripolitania, and he agreed in November. Fearing Italian retaliation under Mussolini, he went into exile in Egypt in December 1922.

The Italian reconquest followed. Cyrenaica's livestock was decimated, much of its population was interned in camps, and an estimated 12,000 Cyrenaicans were executed in 1930 and 1931. In the Second World War Idris supported the United Kingdom, and a Libyan Arab Force of volunteers served in support and gendarmerie roles. After the war British and French forces governed Libya. The United Nations General Assembly resolved in November 1949 that Libya should become a single independent state under Idris as king by January 1952.

Idris proclaimed the United Kingdom of Libya from Benghazi on 24 December 1951. The country had about one million people and was one of the poorest in the world, with an illiteracy rate of 94 percent. It was federal, with Benghazi and Tripoli as joint capitals. Idris banned political parties, and from 1952 all candidates were government nominees. In 1963 he abolished the federal system and the country became the Kingdom of Libya. He allowed British and American air bases in return for aid. Large oil reserves found in 1959 raised per capita income from $25 to $35 in 1951 to $2,000 by 1969, and Libya joined OPEC in 1962.

Idris was deposed on 1 September 1969, while in Turkey for medical treatment, by army officers under Muammar Gaddafi; the coup came a day before his intended abdication. He went into exile in Egypt and was sentenced to death in absentia in November 1971. He died in Cairo in 1983 and was buried at Medina. He had married five times, and none of his children survived childhood.
ifat-sultanate: The Sultanate of Ifat, called Wafāt or Awfāt in Arabic texts and also the Kingdom of Zeila, was a Sunni Muslim state of the eastern Horn of Africa. It formed around eastern Shewa in present-day Ethiopia and stretched from Zequalla to the port of Zeila, which gave it a trade outlet and an entry point for Islam into Ethiopian lands. According to al-Maqrizi, the Walashma ruling class claimed Arab descent from the Hejaz and from Aqil ibn Abi Talib, but scholars hold this claim was probably fictitious and that the dynasty was of local origin.

Ifat arose when Umar ibn Dunya-huz, later called Sultan Umar Walasma, carved out a kingdom and conquered the Sultanate of Shewa. In 1288 Sultan Wali Asma imposed his rule on Hubat, Zeila and other Muslim states. Taddesse Tamrat compares this effort to unite Muslim lands with the one Emperor Yekuno Amlak was making among the Christian highlands.

In 1320 a conflict began between the Christian monarchy and Ifat. Emperor Amda Seyon I had warned the Mamluk sultan Al-Nasir Muhammad to stop persecuting Copts, and Sultan Haqq ad-Din I responded by invading Amhara, burning churches and forcing conversions. He also seized the emperor's envoy and killed him when he would not convert. Amda Seyon raided Shewa and Ifat in return. In early 1332 Sabr ad-Din rebelled, aiming, according to the emperor's chronicle, to become king of all Ethiopia. Amda Seyon destroyed Ifat's capital, took Sabr ad-Din prisoner and appointed his brother Jamal ad-Din I in his place.

Fighting continued under the emperor's successors. Haqq ad-Din II moved the capital towards the Harar plateau and Zeila, and is regarded by some as the true founder of the Adal Sultanate. According to al-Maqrizi, he fought the emperor in over twenty battles and died in 1376. His successor Sa'ad ad-Din II raided Ethiopian lands. In the early fifteenth century an Ethiopian emperor invaded Ifat and its troops were defeated in 1403 on the Harar plateau. Sa'ad ad-Din fled to Zeila, where he died. The sources disagree on which emperor led the campaign, and on whether he died in 1403 or 1410.

The Muslims were harassed for over twenty years after the defeat, according to al-Maqrizi, who wrote around 1435. Adal, with its capital at Harar, emerged as the leading Muslim principality in the later fifteenth century, and small territories were ruled by Walasma groups until the eighteenth century. Harari tradition holds that the Argobba fled Ifat for the Harar area during the fifteenth-century conflict. Ifat's infantry consisted of Argobba, and its people included Somalis, Afars, Warjih, Silte and Hararis, speaking Cushitic and Ethio-Semitic languages with Arabic as the common tongue. The name survives in the Ethiopian district of Yifat in North Shewa.
ife: Ife lies in Osun State in south-western Nigeria, about 218 kilometres north-east of Lagos, in a mixed rural and urban landscape within the tropical savanna climate zone. Roads link it to Ibadan, to the west, and to Osogbo, 40 kilometres away. The city is said to have been founded sometime between 1000 BCE and 500 BCE, and by 900 CE it had become an important West African emporium producing sophisticated art. By the 1100s it had entered a classical period and become the capital of a significant regional empire. The name Ife means "expansion".

In Yoruba tradition the supreme god Olodumare ordered Obatala to create the earth, but Obatala became drunk on palm wine on the way. Oduduwa took the items of creation, descended on a chain and cast earth on the primordial ocean, so that it rose as a mound called Oke Ora; a five-toed cockerel scattered the earth. Oduduwa planted a palm nut that grew into a tree with sixteen branches, which stands for the sixteen clans of the early Ife confederation. The rivalry of Oduduwa and Obatala is still re-enacted at the Itapa festival.

The sons, daughters and grandchildren of Oduduwa are held to have founded other kingdoms, among them Ila Orangun, Owu, Ketu, Sabe, Egba, Popo, Ilesha and Oyo. Oranmiyan served in Benin and left behind a son, Eweka, who became the first Oba of the second Edo dynasty; Oranmiyan later founded Oyo.

Ife is known for its naturalistic bronze, stone and terracotta sculpture, which reached its peak between 1200 and 1400. Around 1300 artists developed a refined naturalistic tradition, many works apparently made under the patronage of King Obalufon II, who is said to have invented bronze casting. Production declined as political and economic power shifted to Benin. Excavations at the grove of Igbo Olokun show glass bead making from between the 11th and 15th centuries, one of the earliest known glass workshops in West Africa, and the beads have been found as far away as Mali, Mauritania and Ghana.

Ife is called the city of 401 deities, and festivals of the orisha are held through the year, among them Olojo and Itapa. Its sacred sites include the shrine and grove of Oduduwa, the Agbonniregun Temple, grove of Orunmila, and Igbo Olokun.
ifriqiya: Ifriqiya, Arabic for Africa, was an Arabic derivation from the Latin Africa. Some Arabic sources gave it mythical origins, deriving it from a king of Yemen named Ifriqis or Ifriqish who conquered the Maghreb in ancient times, or from a son of Abraham named Ifriq. The region lay between the sea and the edges of the Sahara and included all of the former Byzantine province of Africa Proconsularis and more, though not the Mauretanias.

Its boundaries changed between authors and periods. The Mediterranean and the Saharan border areas were normally the northern and southern limits, and the east usually lay between Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, which was attached administratively to Egypt in the early Islamic period. The western boundary varied most. Al-Bakri thought Ifriqiya nearly equivalent to the whole Maghreb up to Morocco, but most writers placed it in northeastern Algeria and divided the Maghreb into three parts: the Far West, the Middle West and Ifriqiya. For most of its early history the capital was Qayrawan (Kairouan). It moved to Mahdiya in some periods and later remained at Tunis.

The Umayyads created the province in 703 when they seized North Africa from the Byzantine Empire. Religious tension and conflict between the invading Arabs and the native Berbers continued, most sharply between coastal cities and villages. After the Umayyads collapsed, the Aghlabids governed as agents of the Abbasids in Baghdad. The Fatimids overthrew them in 909, taking their capital of Raqqada. As the Fatimid regents, the Zirids, became more autonomous, they separated fully in the mid-11th century.

Religious divisions helped the Almohads take western Ifriqiya in 1147 and all of it by 1160. Their empire lasted into the early 13th century, when the Hafsids, a clan that supplied many of its governors, replaced it. In 1229 they declared independence under Abu Zakariya, who built the Hafsid state around its new capital, Tunis. The Black Death reached the Maghreb through Europe in the 14th century. Maghreb and Ifriqiya were largely under Ottoman rule between the 16th and 18th centuries.
iga-province: Iga lay in what is today the western part of Mie Prefecture. It bordered Ise to the east and south, Ōmi to the north, Yamato to the west and south, and Yamashiro Province to the northwest. It roughly coincides with the modern municipalities of Iga and Nabari in Mie and Yagyu in Nara Prefecture. Surrounded by mountains, it was historically rather inaccessible because of extremely poor roads. Under the Engishiki classification it ranked as an inferior country and a near country, and it was counted among the provinces of the Tōkaidō. It was divided into four districts and 197 villages, with an assessed value of 110,843 koku.

Iga was separated from Ise Province around 680 CE, in the Asuka period. The provincial capital stood in what is now part of the city of Iga, where the ruins of the Iga Kokubun-ji remain, and the province's Ichinomiya is the Aekuni Shrine. Little is known of the Heian and Kamakura periods. By the middle of the Muromachi period Iga had become effectively independent of its nominal feudal rulers and formed a confederacy, the Iga Sokoku Ikki. It was then known as a centre of ninja activity, and with Kōka in what is now Shiga Prefecture it claims to be one of the birthplaces of the ninja clans and ninjutsu.

In 1581, two years after a failed invasion led by his son, Oda Nobunaga attacked Iga from six directions with 40,000 to 60,000 men, which effectively destroyed the political power of the ninja (the Tenshō Iga War). After the Tokugawa shogunate was established, Iga was briefly under the Iga-Ueno Domain of 200,000 koku, ruled from 1600 to 1608 by Tsutsui Sadatsugu, a former retainer of Toyotomi Hideyoshi. The Tsutsui were dispossessed in 1608, and the territory went to Tōdō Takatora, daimyō of Tsu Domain, to which it belonged until the Meiji Restoration. Iga Ueno Castle remained a secondary administrative centre of the domain.

After the abolition of the han in July 1871 Tsu Domain became Tsu Prefecture, which later became part of Mie Prefecture. In 1896 the four districts were merged into two, Ayama and Naga. The province was the home of the samurai Hattori Hanzō and the haiku poet Matsuo Bashō. The area is now relatively easy to reach from Nara, Kyoto, Osaka and Nagoya.
igbo-people: The Igbo homeland straddles the lower Niger River, east and south of the Edoid and Idomoid groups and west of the Ibibioid cluster. The Igbo language belongs to the Niger-Congo family. Evidence of early iron smelting has been excavated in the Nsukka region, dated to 750 BCE at Opi and 2,000 BCE at Lejja. Igbo-Ukwu, in what is now Anambra State, has yielded more than 600 prestige objects, including cast copper-alloy sculptures and over 165,000 glass and carnelian beads, dated to the 9th and 10th centuries. They may be associated with the Kingdom of Nri and its priest-king, the Eze Nri, whose traditions trace the people back to a figure named Eri.

Traditional Igbo government was in most places a consultative one. Communities were governed by councils of elders and assemblies of the common people, and many towns were also partly governed by the Ozo society, whose titles could be earned or inherited. A few places had kings, such as Onitsha with its Obi, or priest-kings, such as Nri and Arochukwu, and the spiritual though not political authority of the king of Nri was recognised across Igboland. Igbo unity as one identity is comparatively recent, and the novelist Chinua Achebe placed it somewhere between a tribe and a nation.

Many of the people taken across the Atlantic from the Bight of Biafra were probably Igbo, usually sold to Europeans by the Aro Confederacy. Enslaved Igbo were known to planters as outspoken and rebellious, and were dispersed to colonies including Jamaica, Cuba, Saint-Domingue and Trinidad. British colonial rule, which depended on appointed warrant chiefs, did not suit Igbo decentralised government, and the period was marked by conflicts. The Igbo embraced Christianity and Western-style education.

After ethnic clashes in 1966 and 1967, General Emeka Odumegwu-Ojukwu proclaimed the Republic of Biafra on 30 May 1967, beginning the Nigerian Civil War of 1967 to 1970. Millions of Biafran civilians died of starvation under a blockade by the Nigerian military, and Biafra was defeated and reintegrated.

The traditional Igbo religion is Odinani, whose supreme deity is Chukwu, the "great spirit", who created the world. Christianity and Odinani are now the major religions, with Islamic minorities. Yam is the staple crop, cultivated mostly by men. Traditional compounds group several houses around a central courtyard, built of mud, clay, wood and thatch. Instruments include the udu, a clay jug, the ekwe, a hollowed log, and the ogene, an iron bell.
ignacy-krasicki: Ignacy Krasicki was born on 3 February 1735 in Dubiecko, on the San River in southern Poland, into a noble family that bore the title of Imperial Count. He attended a Jesuit school in Lwów, studied at a Catholic seminary in Warsaw and took holy orders in 1759.

On returning to Poland he became secretary to the Primate and formed a friendship with the future King Stanisław August Poniatowski. When Poniatowski was elected king in 1764, Krasicki became his chaplain and helped found the Monitor, the leading periodical of the Polish Enlightenment, which the king sponsored.

In 1766 Krasicki, after serving that year as coadjutor, became Prince-Bishop of Warmia, with a seat in the Senate of the Commonwealth. The cathedral chapter received him coolly, and Prussia was applying growing pressure in preparation for taking Warmia in the First Partition. Krasicki protested publicly against outside intervention. In 1772 the partition made him a Prussian subject, though he did not pay homage to his new ruler, Frederick II.

He nevertheless cultivated an acquaintance with Frederick and visited Berlin, Potsdam and Sanssouci often. He officiated at the opening of St Hedwig's Cathedral in Berlin in 1773 and was called to the Prussian Academy of Sciences in 1786. In 1795 he became Archbishop of Gniezno and Primate of Poland.

Krasicki began as a poet late, nearing forty, with the hymn Święta miłości kochanej ojczyzny, published in 1774, which later served for many years as a national anthem. His novel Mikołaja Doświadczyńskiego przypadki of 1776 is the first modern Polish novel and combines the satirical, adventure, utopian and didactic strands of the Enlightenment novel. Tradition holds that his mock-heroic poem Monachomachia, published in 1778, grew from a conversation with Frederick II at Sanssouci. Its publication caused a public scandal.

His most lasting works are the Fables and Parables and the Satires, both of 1779. The fables usually place their moral in the last line, so that even a reader who could not read well could take it in. He also wrote the epic Wojna chocimska and a two-volume encyclopedia of 1781–83. He died in Berlin in 1801, and in 1829 his remains were moved from St Hedwig's Cathedral to Gniezno Cathedral.
ignalina-nuclear-power-plant: The Soviet Union intended the Ignalina plant as a symbol of its technological progress. Preparations began in 1974 and fieldwork three years later. The plant had two RBMK-1500 reactors, water-cooled and graphite-moderated, each with two turbines built by the Kharkiv turbine plant. After the Chernobyl disaster of April 1986 the reactors were de-rated to 1,360 MW. Unit 1 came online in December 1983 and Unit 2 in August 1987, a year later than planned because of Chernobyl.

The town of Visaginas was built for the workers, about 5,000 of whom staffed the plant. It produced 70 percent of the electricity of the Lithuanian S.S.R. and exported power elsewhere in the Soviet Union. Cooling water came from Lake Drūkšiai, the largest lake in Lithuania.

When Unit 1 came online in December 1983 a design flaw of the RBMK was noticed for the first time: graphite-displacer tips on the control rods caused a power excursion when they were inserted. The problem was not addressed until a similar surge partly caused the Chernobyl disaster, and the modifications that followed were tested at Ignalina in 1987 and 1988.

In 1999 Lithuania agreed to close the units as a condition of joining the European Union, citing the lack of a containment building as a high risk.
