The European Union agreed to pay 820 million euros towards decommissioning and compensation. Closure met fierce opposition because the plant gave income to most local residents. A 2008 referendum on keeping Unit 2 open until a replacement was built won 1,155,192 votes but failed to reach the required 50 percent turnout, and President Valdas Adamkus opposed it on the grounds of Lithuania's international commitments. Unit 1 closed on 31 December 2004 and Unit 2 on 31 December 2009.

The plant had accounted for 25 percent of Lithuania's generating capacity and supplied about 70 percent of its electrical demand. Decommissioning was funded about 95 percent by the international community, through the European Union and a fund set up in 2001 under the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, and 5 percent by Lithuania. The first phase ran from 2004 to 2013, and a second was scheduled for 2014 to 2029, so that the site could be reused by 2030.

A new plant at the site was discussed. Parliament passed a law in 2007 and the power companies of Lithuania, Estonia, Latvia and Poland agreed in 2008 to form a company for it, but the project stopped after a 2012 referendum gave no mandate to continue. Ignalina also served as a filming location for the 2019 television series Chernobyl.
ignatius-of-loyola: Ignatius was born Íñigo López de Oñaz y Loyola, probably on 23 October 1491, in the castle of Loyola in Azpeitia, Gipuzkoa. He was the youngest of thirteen children of parents from the minor nobility, and his mother died soon after his birth. He became a page in the household of Juan Velázquez de Cuéllar, treasurer of the kingdom of Castile, and in 1509 entered the service of Antonio Manrique de Lara, Duke of Nájera. On 20 May 1521, at the Battle of Pamplona, a cannonball ricocheting off a wall broke his right leg. Several operations left it shorter than the other, and he limped for the rest of his life.

While recovering he asked for romances of chivalry, but the castle had none, and his sister-in-law Magdalena de Araoz brought him lives of Christ and the saints. Ludolph of Saxony's De Vita Christi struck him most, and its method of imagining oneself at a Gospel scene shaped his later meditation. In March 1522 he visited Montserrat and hung his sword and dagger at the Virgin's altar. He then lived for about a year at Manresa, begging and praying in a cave, where he formulated the basis of his Spiritual Exercises. In September 1523 he reached the Holy Land, but the Franciscans sent him back.

He studied at Alcalá in 1526-1527, where the Inquisition questioned him because he preached without a degree in theology, and then at the University of Paris, adopting the name Ignatius. There six fellow students joined him, among them Francis Xavier, Diego Laynez and Peter Faber. With them he founded the Society of Jesus and became its first Superior General. He aimed it at missionary work and teaching and added a fourth vow of obedience to the Pope to the usual vows of chastity, obedience and poverty.

Ignatius died on 31 July 1556. His method of spiritual formation, recorded in the Spiritual Exercises of 1548, became known as Ignatian spirituality. The Jesuits were instrumental in leading the Counter-Reformation. He was beatified in 1609 and canonised on 12 March 1622, and his feast day is 31 July. He is patron saint of the Basque provinces of Gipuzkoa and Biscay and of the Society of Jesus, and in 1922 Pope Pius XI declared him patron of all spiritual retreats.
ignaz-semmelweis: Ignaz Semmelweis was born on 1 July 1818 in the Tabán neighbourhood of Buda, the fifth of ten children of a prosperous grocer family. His father József Semmelweis ran a wholesale business for spices and consumer goods, and his mother was Teréz Müller. Ignaz began studying law at the University of Vienna in the autumn of 1837 but switched to medicine and received his doctorate in 1844. Having failed to win a post in internal medicine, he specialised in obstetrics.

On 1 July 1846 Semmelweis became assistant to Professor Johann Klein in the First Obstetrical Clinic of the Vienna General Hospital. Its maternal mortality from puerperal fever was about 10 per cent, against under 4 per cent in the Second Clinic, and women begged not to be admitted to the First. His breakthrough came in 1847 after the death of his friend Jakob Kolletschka, who was pricked by a student's scalpel during an autopsy and showed a pathology like that of the dying women. Semmelweis concluded that he and his students carried cadaverous particles on their hands from the autopsy room to patients, and he introduced hand washing in chlorinated lime solutions.

Klein did not extend his term, and Semmelweis had to leave the clinic on 20 March 1849. On 20 May 1851 he took an unpaid post heading the obstetric ward of the Szent Rókus Hospital in Pest, where from 1851 to 1855 only eight of 933 mothers died of childbed fever. His book Etiology, Concept and Prophylaxis of Childbed Fever appeared in 1861.

His claim that the disease had a single cause, a lack of cleanliness, ran against the doctrine of the four humours, and he could not give a theoretical explanation. Some doctors were offended by the suggestion that their hands were unclean. After unfavourable reviews of his book he wrote open letters that were polemical and offensive. In 1865 he was committed to the provincial asylum at Döbling and died there on 13 August 1865, 14 days later, of septic shock, possibly after a beating by guards.
His practice won wide acceptance only years later, when Louis Pasteur's germ theory gave it an explanation and Joseph Lister developed antiseptic surgery. He is called the saviour of mothers.
igor-of-kiev: Almost everything known of Igor comes from the Primary Chronicle, which names him as the son of Rurik, who had established himself at Novgorod. According to the chronicle, Rurik on his deathbed left his realm to Oleg, a man of his kin, and entrusted the young Igor to him. Oleg then led warriors drawn from the Varangians, Chuds, Slavs, Merians and Krivichians down the river route, took Smolensk and Lyubech, and came to the hills of Kiev. There he lured out Askold and Dir, who ruled the town, and presented the child Igor as Rurik's son. Askold and Dir were killed.

Little is known of Igor between 912 and 941, because the chronicle has a gap for those years. It tells that he twice besieged Constantinople, in 941 and 944. Greek fire destroyed part of his fleet, but he concluded a favourable treaty with the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII in 945, and the chronicle has preserved its text. Rus' raids on Arab lands in the Caspian Sea are recorded for 913 and 944, but it is unclear whether Igor had any part in them.

Igor was killed in 945 while collecting tribute from the Drevlians. The Byzantine historian Leo the Deacon, who was born around 950, describes how the Drevlians bent two birch trees down to the prince's feet, tied them to his legs and let the trees spring up, tearing his body apart. The Primary Chronicle blames his greed, saying that he tried to collect tribute for a second time in a month.

His widow Olga avenged his death by punishing the Drevlians. She also changed the system of gathering tribute, called poliudie, in what may be regarded as the first legal reform recorded in Eastern Europe.
ijssel: The IJssel is a Dutch distributary of the Rhine that flows northward and discharges into the IJsselmeer, which was known as the Zuiderzee before the Afsluitdijk was completed in 1932. It is sometimes called the Gelderse IJssel to distinguish it from the Hollandse IJssel, and it runs through the provinces of Gelderland and Overijssel, the latter named after the river. It starts at Westervoort, on the east side of Arnhem. The Rhine feeds it through the Pannerdens Kanaal, which it shares with the Nederrijn.

The Romans knew the river as Isala. Its two earliest Old Dutch attestations, from 797 and 814, give the name as Hisla. The name is thought to derive either from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to move quickly or from an older European source.

Most of the IJssel was originally the lower part of the small river Oude IJssel, which rises in Germany near Borken and joins the IJssel at Doesburg. The connection between the Rhine and the IJssel was probably artificial and is allegedly dug by men under the Roman general Nero Claudius Drusus around 12 BCE, as a defence against Germanic tribes and to let Roman ships carry troops.

The river served as a natural barrier, and in April 1945 Allied assault troops stormed it while liberating the Netherlands from German occupation. Near Kampen the river forms a small delta, whose branches include the Keteldiep and Kattendiep, and the whole delta was prone to flooding when northwestern gales pushed saline Zuiderzee water back into it. Most of the damming of the branches was done before 1932.

Man has cut off some bends, near Rheden and Doesburg, which reduced the river's length from 146 kilometres to 125. Its average daily discharge is about 300 cubic metres per second, and weirs west of Arnhem control how much water enters from the Rhine. Besides the Oude IJssel, the Berkel and Schipbeek streams are among its tributaries, and canals such as the Twentekanaal and Apeldoorns Kanaal join it. The river passes Zutphen, Deventer, Zwolle and Kampen on its way north.
ikaria: Ikaria lies 19 km south-west of Samos and covers 255 square kilometres, with a population of 8,312 in 2021. The Aitheras mountain range runs east–west across it, rising to 1,037 metres. The north is greener and the south rockier and drier. In antiquity the island was called Icaria, because Icarus was believed to have fallen into the sea nearby, though the name may instead come from a Phoenician word for fish or sheep.

The island has been inhabited since at least 7000 BCE. Greeks from Miletus settled it around 750 BCE near present-day Kampos, which became the ancient capital Oenoe. Ikaria was part of the sea empire of Polycrates of Samos in the 6th century BCE, and Oenoe and Thermae belonged to the Delian League in the 5th century BCE. A temple of Artemis Tauropolos stood at the cove of Nas from about the 6th century BCE; its marble was taken by villagers for a church in the mid-19th century. Under the Byzantine Empire the islanders moved inland because of piracy, and Koskinas castle was built in the 10th century. The Genoese took the island in 1362 and withdrew in 1481, when the Knights Hospitaller took it.

The Ottomans conquered it from the Knights Hospitaller in 1521. The islanders hid their villages in the highlands and abandoned the coast, a period of about 80 years called the Century of Invisibility, which protected them from corsairs such as Hayreddin Barbarossa. The Ottomans sent no officials for several centuries. Joseph Georgirenes, bishop of Samos, described almost 1,000 inhabitants in 1677, poor and long-lived.

Ikaria broke away in 1827 during the Greek War of Independence but was left outside the new Greek state. On 17 July 1912 the locals expelled the Turkish garrison, and on 18 July they declared the Free State of Ikaria, with Ioannis Malachias as its only president. It had its own flag, stamps and anthem for five months and joined Greece on 4 November 1912; the Treaty of London of 1913 confirmed this. During the Second World War the island suffered under Italian and then German occupation, and in the Greek Civil War about 13,000 people were exiled there.

The principal town and port is Agios Kirykos; Evdilos is the historic main town. The island forms a municipality within the North Aegean region, formed in 2011 from Agios Kirykos, Evdilos and Raches. An airport was built in the 1990s. Its traditional festivals, the panigyria, are among the largest in the Aegean. Ikaria is counted among the world's blue zones, areas where people often live to advanced ages, and a study published in 2011 examined the reasons.
ikskile: Ikšķile, in German Üxküll or Uexküll, is a town in Ogre Municipality in the Vidzeme region of Latvia, on the right bank of the Daugava River, 28 kilometres from Riga and 7 kilometres from Ogre. Mounds and ancient burial grounds in the surrounding rural area show that it is one of the oldest inhabited regions of Latvia, and by the 9th to 12th centuries there was already a Liv village on the Daugava waterway. According to Urmas Sutrop's research, the name comes from a Livonian term for the ford or islets belonging to the son of a local ruler named Ike, whose family controlled military and trade traffic across the river.

The Livonian Chronicle of Henry, written by an eyewitness, tells of Meinhard, a canon of the Augustinian monastery of Segeberg in Holstein, who went to the Daugava to convert the Livs and Letts. He built a church in the village and baptised some Livonians, but it was vulnerable to attacks, mainly by Lithuanian pagan inhabitants; after a winter raid Meinhard and the local people hid in the forests. According to the chronicle he told the Livonians they were foolish to have no fortifications and promised to build castles if they converted.

In 1185 stonemasons from Gotland built the castle of Ikšķile with a chapel or church, the oldest stone castle in Latvia and the oldest stone building in the Eastern Baltic. In 1186 the Archbishop of Bremen appointed Meinhard first bishop of Ikšķile. The second bishop, Berthold of Hanover, a Cistercian abbot of Loccum, followed him, and both were buried in the church, though Meinhard was later reburied in the Dome Church in Riga. The third bishop, Albert of Buxhovden, judged the diocese too far from the river mouth to be effective in battle and moved its centre to Riga in 1201. The castle was attacked repeatedly by Semigallian troops, and in 1203 and 1206 Prince Vladimir of Polotsk tried to capture it.

The original castle was destroyed in the 17th century, and the often rebuilt church was destroyed by German artillery in 1916. Ikšķile became an urban-type settlement in 1968 and received full town rights in 1992. In the 1970s the reservoir of the Riga Hydroelectric Power Plant flooded the ruins of the castle and manor, but the ruins of the first stone church were preserved on an artificially raised and fortified island.
ilanz: Ilanz, called Glion in Romansh, lies in the district of Surselva in the Swiss canton of the Grisons. It is the first town on the Rhine, where the headwaters gather to form the valley of the Vorderrhein. The town stands at a fork between the Surselva and the Vrin and Vals valley, which is divided by Piz Mundaun, and the villages of Ruschein, Ladir, Vrin, Vals and Obersaxen are reached from it. It has served as the market town of the surrounding area and has the main railway station and nearest hospital of the region. The old town covers 4.7 square kilometres, about half of it forest.

Ilanz was first mentioned in 765 as Iliande. In 1395 it became the capital of the newly formed Grey League, the second of the Three Leagues that eventually formed the canton of the Grisons. Johannes von Ilanz, the Abbot of Disentis, was one of the three nobles who helped to create this eternal alliance.

The town has a special place in the history of the Protestant Reformation. In the 1520s the Diet of Ilanz declared that citizens of the Three Leagues should be free to choose between Catholicism and the Protestant forms of Christianity then rising. The Ilanz Reformation of 1526 was another shock to the Catholic Church, which had come under attack in Zürich in 1523. These and other events led to a counter-reformation within the Swiss Confederation that reversed many of the Reformation's gains in Switzerland.

Near the ruins of Grüneck Castle, destroyed before 1544, two ornately decorated Carolingian salt containers and coins were found in 1811. One, a T-shaped container of antler, is now in the British Museum. In 1904 a hoard of forty Carolingian gold coins, with Lombard and Arab coins, known as the Ilanz Hoard, was found there too. About 142 coins from the finds are kept at the Rätisches Museum in Chur.

The former municipality of Strada joined Ilanz on 1 January 1978, and on 1 January 2014 Ilanz and twelve surrounding municipalities merged into the new municipality of Ilanz/Glion. The Church of St Margreta and the Church of St Martin are listed as Swiss heritage sites of national significance. At the census of 2000 German was the most widely spoken language and Romansh the second, and a majority of residents were Roman Catholic, with a large Swiss Reformed minority.
ile-de-france: The Île-de-France lies in the north-central part of France and covers 12,012 square kilometres, about 2 per cent of metropolitan French territory. The Seine flows through the middle of the region, with tributaries including the Marne, the Oise and the Epte, and the outer parts remain largely rural. Despite the name, which means Island of France, the region is not an island. The island may be the land between the Oise, the Marne and the Seine, or the Île de la Cité, where the royal palace and cathedral stood, or the lands under the direct rule of the kings of the Capetian dynasty, an island in a sea of feudal territories.

The Parisii, a sub-tribe of the Celtic Senones, inhabited the area from about the middle of the 3rd century BCE, and the Romans conquered it in 52 BCE. Saint Denis, the first Bishop of Paris, introduced Christianity in the middle of the 3rd century CE; according to legend he was beheaded on the hill later called Montmartre. Clovis, the first Merovingian king, made Paris his capital in 508. Vikings sacked the Île de la Cité in 845, but the successful defence of Paris in the siege of 885-86 established its strategic importance. In 987 Hugh Capet, Count of Paris, was elected King of the Franks.

The kings hunted in the game-filled forests of the region and built palaces, most notably Fontainebleau and Versailles, which from the time of Louis XIV to the French Revolution was the official residence of the kings and the seat of government. The name Île-de-France came to mean the territory of Paris and the surrounding province, administered directly by the king. The revolution abolished the royal provinces and divided them into departments. In 1959, under President Charles de Gaulle, a new region of six departments, roughly the historic one, was created, and on 6 May 1976 it was renamed Île-de-France.

Île-de-France is the most populous of France's eighteen regions, with over 12 million residents, and contains the capital, Paris. It is made up of eight departments: Paris, Essonne, Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis, Seine-et-Marne, Val-de-Marne, Val-d'Oise and Yvelines. Beyond Paris it holds historic sites including the palaces of Versailles and Fontainebleau.
ile-de-la-cite: The Île de la Cité is one of two natural islands in the Seine in central Paris, the other being Île Saint-Louis. It covers 22.5 hectares. Bridges once ran on both sides of it, and it was the most convenient place to cross the river. The Parisii, a small Gallic tribe and known river traders, lived nearby, and their coins of about 100 BCE have been found across France and Europe. A Gallic settlement called Lutetia may have stood on the island since the 3rd century BCE, though no significant traces earlier than the 1st century CE have been found there.

In the 4th century the island held the fortress of the Roman governor of the area. In 508 Clovis I, the first king of the Franks, set up his castle there, and an early cathedral, Saint-Étienne, was built in the Romanesque style. In 1160 Bishop Maurice de Sully began a new Gothic cathedral, Notre-Dame de Paris, whose first stones were laid by Pope Alexander III in 1163. It was largely complete by 1345. Louis IX built the Sainte-Chapelle to house relics of the Crucifixion, among them the Crown of Thorns, which he bought in 1239 from the Emperor of Constantinople; it was consecrated in 1248.

Crowding and bad conditions led the kings to leave. After the Parisian rebellion of 1358 led by Étienne Marcel, Charles V moved first to the Hôtel Saint-Pol, then to the Bastille and finally to the Louvre. The island remained a centre of justice, and in 1302 the first meeting of the Parlement of Paris was held in the old palace. In the French Revolution the Conciergerie held Marie-Antoinette, who was sentenced to the guillotine in 1793, and later Robespierre, arrested there on 27 July 1794.

In the mid-19th century, after cholera epidemics in 1832 and 1849, Napoleon III ordered the old streets pulled down and wide avenues opened; in 1867 he demolished the medieval Hôtel-Dieu and replaced it with the present hospital. Henry IV had built the Pont Neuf, finished in 1606, and the triangular Place Dauphine from 1609.

Notre-Dame stands at the eastern end with the Place Jean-Paul-II before it. Its spire and much of the roof were destroyed by fire on 15 April 2019, and the cathedral reopened on 7 December 2024. The Sainte-Chapelle, the Conciergerie and the Palais de Justice lie along the Quai de l'Horloge, and the Préfecture de Police, the Tribunal de commerce and the Hôtel-Dieu, reputed to be the oldest functioning hospital in the world, are also on the island. The Mémorial des Martyrs de la Déportation, dedicated in 1962, commemorates the 200,000 people deported to Nazi camps from France.
ilheus: Ilhéus lies in the southern coastal region of Bahia, 211 kilometres south of Salvador, the state capital. Its downtown is 1 kilometre from the Atlantic Ocean, and the municipality has an area of 1,850 square kilometres and 159,923 inhabitants. The municipality holds a small part of the Una Wildlife Refuge, 15 per cent of the Serra do Conduru State Park, created in 1997, and part of the Lagoa Encantada e Rio Almada Environmental Protection Area, created in 1993. Water pollution threatens the protected area, because most of the communities have no sanitation, and squatters, irregular fishing, deforestation, fires, hunting and the illegal trade in wild animals are other threats.

The town was founded as the Vila de São Jorge dos Ilhéus. It was once one of the biggest exporters of cocoa beans, and the port of Ilhéus carried the trade. The cocoa economy shaped the writer Jorge Amado, who was born there and wrote more than 25 novels, translated into 48 languages. Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon and Dona Flor and Her Two Husbands portray life and customs in north-eastern Brazil. Their plots largely treat the lives of poor urban and rural black and mulatto communities of Bahia, and the land wars that raged in Ilhéus, where cocoa barons killed each other for power and for cocoa plantations.

Ilhéus is known as one of the most important tourism centres of north-eastern Brazil. Its economy rests mainly on tourism, drawn by its beaches and its cultural heritage, which includes early Portuguese buildings, history and local cooking. The road BR-101 connects it to Itabuna and beyond, and the city has a port and an airport, Ilhéus Jorge Amado Airport. A proposed new deep-water port has been opposed by environmental activists but accepted by the government as important for the economy.
ili-river: The Ili is a river of north-western China and south-eastern Kazakhstan, 1,439 kilometres long including its source river the Tekes, of which 815 kilometres are in Kazakhstan. It rises from the Tekes and Künes rivers in the eastern Tian Shan and drains the basin between the Tian Shan and the Borohoro Mountains. It ends in Lake Balkhash, where it forms a large delta of about 8,000 square kilometres between the Saryesik-Atyrau and Taukum deserts. The name is usually taken from the Mongolian il, meaning open or clear, in reference to the river's wide central valley, although other derivations from Persian and Uyghur have been proposed.

The river appears in the Turkic dictionary of Mahmud al-Kashgari, written in 1072-74, which says that the Turkic tribes of the Yaghma, Tokhsi and Chiglig lived on its banks and that Turkic countries regarded it as their Jayhoun, their Amu Darya. In 638 the Ili River treaty formalised the division of the Western Turkic Kaganate (552-638) into the Nushibi and the Dulu and made the river the border between the two states.

The upper valley, on the Chinese side, was the stronghold of the Qing administration in Xinjiang in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Russia occupied it from 1871, after the rebellion of Yaqub Beg, until the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1881. Its main city, Yining, was long known by the river's name, written Ili, until the early 1900s. The Xibe people, many of whom live in the Qapqal county on the southern bank, resettled there in the eighteenth century as part of the Manchu garrison.

On the Kazakh side the region drained by the river is known as Zhetysu in Kazakh and Semirechye in Russian, both meaning Seven Rivers. Twenty kilometres downstream stands Tamgaly-Tas, a protected site of rock drawings, and the Kapshagay hydroelectric power plant was built near Kapchagay between 1965 and 1970. An area of 9,766 square kilometres in the delta is a Ramsar site, with 427 species of plants and 345 species of animals. Until 1948 the delta was a refuge of the Caspian tiger.
iliad: The Iliad is one of two major surviving ancient Greek epic poems attributed to Homer, the other being the Odyssey. It is divided into 24 books, is written in dactylic hexameter and has 15,693 lines in its standard edition. It was likely composed in Homeric Greek, a literary mixture of Ionic Greek and other dialects, in the late 8th or early 7th century BCE, and its reflection in art and literature shows that it existed before 630 BCE. Its composition, historicity and authorship are extensively debated as the Homeric Question, as is whether the poems were composed independently and whether they survived through an oral or also a written tradition.

The poem is set towards the end of the Trojan War, a ten-year siege of Troy by a coalition of Mycenaean Greek states, and centres on Achilles, whose wrath, mēnis, the poem's first word, drives the narrative. After nine years of fighting, Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, takes the captive Chryseis, and Achilles takes Briseis. Agamemnon's refusal to return Chryseis to her father, a priest of Apollo, brings a plague on the Achaeans, and when Agamemnon seizes Briseis, Achilles withdraws from the fighting.

Patroclus then fights in Achilles's armour and is killed, and Achilles returns to battle and kills the Trojan prince Hector. The poem does not depict the fall of Troy or mention the Trojan Horse, which come from later sources. The Olympian gods aid favoured warriors and cities and intervene in personal disputes, and its themes include glory, fate and pride. In the last book Achilles and Priam share food and grief and agree a truce of twelve days for Hector's burial.

The ancient Greeks esteemed the Iliad highly and used it and the Odyssey as the basis of education. Professional reciters known as rhapsodes performed it at festivals such as the Panathenaia. By the end of the fifth century BCE both poems were widely known, and in the late fifth century it was the sign of a man of standing to be able to recite them by heart.

Later writers drew on it: Shakespeare used it as a source for Troilus and Cressida, and George Chapman published his English translation in instalments from 1598, in a long-line ballad metre that quickly became a classic of English poetry. More than 2,000 manuscripts of Homer survive.
ilinden-preobrazhenie-uprising: Competition for control between national groups in the Ottoman Empire was fought largely through propaganda, conducted through churches and schools. The Internal Macedonian-Adrianopolitan Revolutionary Organization (IMARO) was founded in Thessaloniki in 1893. It was predominantly Bulgarian and sought autonomy for Macedonia and the Adrianople region within the Ottoman state, under the motto Macedonia for the Macedonians.

The Ilinden Uprising began on 2 August in the Manastir vilayet, chosen because it lay farthest from Bulgaria, to show the Great Powers that the revolt was of a Macedonian character. Telegraph lines to Bitola were cut, and the town of Kruševo was captured by 800 rebels led by Nikola Karev and Pitu Guli. On 4 August a local administration, the Kruševo Republic, was set up, and Ottoman troops twice failed to retake the town.

On 19 August a revolt began in the Adrianople province. Its commanders included Mihail Gerdzhikov and Lazar Madzharov, and the insurgents proclaimed a Republic of Strandzha. According to Khadzhiev, its main aim was to engage Ottoman troops and prevent their movement into Macedonia, and a region of Strandzha was held for about twenty days. In mid-August some 40 battalions were sent to reinforce Ottoman forces in Macedonia, and on 24 August Nasir Pasha launched a massive offensive in five detachments, systematically burning Christian villages. The Kruševo Republic had by then been overrun after ten days. On 9 September the uprising's staff appealed to the Bulgarian government for armed intervention, but the Great Powers kept to their policy.

The revolutionaries kept up a guerrilla campaign for almost three months before the uprising was suppressed. It failed for lack of outside support, preparation and weapons. An IMARO memorandum of 1904 estimated 5,000 casualties, 205 villages burned, 70,000 homeless and 30,000 refugees to Bulgaria and the United States, while Georgi Khadzhiev counted 4,694 killed and 201 villages burned. Its greater effect was to persuade the European powers to press the sultan to take a more conciliatory attitude toward his Christian subjects in Europe. Under an agreement of 1904, Bulgaria committed not to support the revolutionary movement and the Ottomans to carry out the Mürzsteg Reforms, though neither happened.

The uprising is commemorated in both Bulgaria and North Macedonia as the peak of their nations' struggle against Ottoman rule. In Bulgaria it is seen as a general rebellion with the goal of autonomy and later unification with Bulgaria, while North Macedonia acknowledges only the Ilinden Uprising, which it sees as exclusively Macedonian.
ilkhanate: The Ilkhanate arose in the south-western territories of the Mongol Empire and was known to the Mongols as the Hülegü Ulus, the people or state of Hülegü. Its realm was officially called the Land of Iran, Irān-zamin. After Genghis Khan declared war on the Anushtegin dynasty of Khwarazm in 1219, the Mongols overran Iran, and by 1231 an army under Chormaqan, sent by the Great Khan Ögedei, had crushed Jalal al-Din Mangburni.

Hülegü, a son of Tolui, a grandson of Genghis Khan and a brother of Möngke and Kublai, was given a fifth of the Mongol army to conquer the Abbasid Caliphate. He destroyed the Nizari Ismaili state in 1256 and the Abbasid Caliphate in 1258, and inherited the West Asian part of the empire after Möngke died in 1259.

Hülegü advanced as far as Gaza and took Aleppo in 1260, but Möngke's death forced him to return to Mongolia for the kuriltai. The small force he left in Palestine was defeated at Ain Jalut by the Mamluks of Egypt. His successor Abaqa beat back an invasion by Berke of the Golden Horde and one by Ghiyas-ud-din Baraq of the Chagatai Khanate. The Mamluks defeated the Mongols at Elbistan in 1277 and again at Homs in 1281.

Under Gaykhatu the realm's finances were ruined, and his vizier's attempt to introduce paper money on the Yuan model largely failed. After Gaykhatu was overthrown in 1295 and his cousin Baydu removed within a year, Ghazan took the throne and was the first ilkhan to convert to Islam. Under Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan, enthroned in 1316, the realm faced rebellions and invasions. In the 1330s the Black Death ravaged it, and Abu Sa'id, the last ilkhan, died of the plague in 1335. Short-lived khans followed, and in 1357 Jani Beg of the Golden Horde took Tabriz, ending what remained.

Unlike the Yuan dynasty in China, which excluded the native population from high office, the Ilkhanids governed through a Central Asian and Persian administration working with Turco-Mongol military officers. Not every administrator was Muslim or from the old families: the vizier from 1288 to 1291, Sa'ad al-Dawla, was a Jew, and Rashid al-Din Hamadani was a Jewish convert to Islam. Persian bureaucrats promoted the idea of kingship over the Land of Iran, and historians presented the Mongols as heirs of the Sasanian Empire.

The period produced many works of history, the best known being Rashid al-Din's Jami' al-tawarikh, commissioned by Ghazan and presented to Öljeitü in 1307. Hülegü's astronomers built an observatory at Maragheh. Western European courts repeatedly sought an alliance against the Mamluks but never concluded a formal one.
ille-et-vilaine: Ille-et-Vilaine lies in Upper Brittany in the north-west of France and is named after its two main rivers, the Ille and the Vilaine, whose confluence is in Rennes. It is one of the original 83 departments created during the French Revolution on 4 March 1790, formed from part of the province of Brittany. It is bordered by the departments of Manche to the north-east, Mayenne to the east, Maine-et-Loire to the south-east, Loire-Atlantique to the south, Morbihan to the south-west and Côtes-d'Armor to the west and north-west, and by the English Channel to the north. Its boundary with Côtes-d'Armor, 19 metres long, is the shortest of any department of France.

The land is moderately high, with many hills. A dense network of tributaries drains the large basin of Rennes, whose rich farmland is ringed by hills with old forests worked for timber. The Rance forms part of the north-western border and flows into the Channel along the Côte d'Émeraude between Dinard and Saint-Malo. The Couesnon marks the eastern end of the coast, in the flat Bay of Mont Saint-Michel. In the south the Vilaine near Redon has often flooded, partly because the farmland round Rennes was drained too intensively, and some fields there are now left to flood while works regulate the water.

Rennes is the prefecture of the department and the capital of the region of Brittany, and the subprefectures are Fougères, Redon and Saint-Malo. Gallo, a historic minority language of eastern Brittany, is spoken here. Breton was little spoken in this part of Brittany and disappeared for many centuries, but it is taught again today, and both languages are studied at the University of Rennes. The population has grown steadily since the 1960s.
illinois: Illinois lies in the Midwest and is one of the eight states of the Great Lakes region. Most of its western border with Missouri and Iowa is the Mississippi River, the Wabash River forms part of the eastern border with Indiana, the Ohio River marks the southern border with Kentucky, and the northeast reaches into Lake Michigan. The state lies entirely in the Interior Plains, with a small unglaciated area, the Driftless Area, in the extreme north-west, where Charles Mound, at 376 metres, is the highest natural point. The Illinois River bisects the state from north-east to south-west.

The name is the modern spelling of what early French missionaries and explorers called the Illinois Native Americans. It derives from the Miami-Illinois verb irenwe·wa, 'he speaks the regular way', which passed into Ojibwe and then French. The older explanation that it means 'men' is not supported by the Illinois language, and the spelling Illinois began to appear in the early 1670s.

American Indians of successive cultures lived along the waterways for thousands of years; the Koster Site shows 7,000 years of continuous habitation. Cahokia, the largest chiefdom and urban centre of the pre-Columbian Mississippian culture, stood near present-day Collinsville. It had more than 100 platform and burial mounds, a large plaza and a woodhenge of sacred cedar, and its Monks Mound, 30 metres high, is the largest pre-Columbian structure north of the Valley of Mexico.

The French were the first Europeans to arrive, settling near the Mississippi and Illinois rivers in the 17th-century Illinois Country of New France. After American independence in 1783 made the Mississippi the national boundary, settlers arrived from Kentucky by the Ohio River. Illinois became part of the Northwest Territory and achieved statehood in 1818. John Deere's self-scouring steel plow turned the prairie into productive farmland. In the mid-19th century the Illinois and Michigan Canal and a large railroad network made the state a transportation hub, and Chicago became the world's fastest-growing city by the late 19th century. By 1900 industrial and coal-mining jobs had attracted immigrants from Eastern and Southern Europe, and the Great Migration from the South established a large black community.

Springfield is the capital and Chicago the largest city, and the Chicago metropolitan area holds about three-quarters of the state's 12.8 million residents. Two World Heritage Sites lie in Illinois: the Cahokia Mounds and part of the Wright architecture site. Illinois honours Abraham Lincoln with its slogan Land of Lincoln, and the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum is in Springfield.
illyria: Illyria was a region in the western part of the Balkan Peninsula, named for the Illyrians, a group of Indo-European speaking peoples who inhabited it. The Greeks first used Illyris for roughly northern and central present-day Albania, down to the valley of the Aoös, the modern Vjosa, and the Bay of Vlorë, neighbouring Macedonia and Epirus. In Roman times Illyria, Illyris and Illyricum came to mean a broader region reaching from the south-eastern Adriatic coast, modern Albania and Montenegro, and its hinterland to the whole eastern Adriatic and the Danube.

The earliest recorded Illyrian kingdom was that of the Enchele in the 8th century BCE, and the era of other kingdoms runs from about 400 BCE. The Autariatae under Pleurias, in 337 BCE, are counted as one. The most notable were those of Bardyllis of the Dardani and of Agron of the Ardiaei, who created the last and best-known Illyrian kingdom. The kingdoms were small and covered only parts of Illyria. Polybius describes peasant infantry fighting under aristocrats, each holding a town, and the monarchy passed by descent, with marriages used as alliances. In the south the kingdoms imitated their Greek neighbours.

Rome defeated Queen Teuta in the First Illyrian War. She withdrew to the Bay of Kotor, and in 228 BCE Rome imposed a protectorate on Issa and Corcyra and on Epidamnos, Apollonia and Oricum. Macedon tried without success to take the southern Illyrian ports as bases for an attack upon the Italian Peninsula. In 168 BCE the Romans defeated Gentius, the last king, at Scodra, and took him to Rome in 165 BCE. Four client republics were set up, and the region was later governed directly as a province with Scodra as its capital.

The Roman province of Illyricum stretched from the river Drilon in Albania to Istria and the river Sava, with its capital at Salona, near modern Split. After a revolt of Pannonians and Daesitiates the province was divided in 10 CE between Pannonia in the north and Dalmatia in the south, but the name Illyria stayed in use in Late Latin and through the medieval period. In the Late Roman Empire it named a praetorian prefecture.

Church history kept the name too. The bishops of Thessalonica appointed papal vicars for Illyricum, and in 515 forty Illyrian bishops renewed their loyalty to Rome under Pope Hormisdas; in the 8th century the patriarchs of Constantinople brought Illyria under their jurisdiction. Jewish communities are attested at Salona, Narona and Sirmium, known from menorahs and inscriptions.
illyrian-provinces: The Illyrian Provinces were created by the Treaty of Schönbrunn on 14 October 1809, after the Austrian defeat at Wagram, when the Austrian Empire ceded western Carinthia with Lienz, Carniola, Gorizia and Gradisca, Trieste, the March of Istria and the Croatian lands southwest of the Sava. These territories were joined with the former Venetian Dalmatia and Istria and the former Republic of Ragusa to form provinces technically part of France. The name Illyrian was probably suggested by Auguste de Marmont, who wanted to support a sense of commonality among the peoples, and alluded to the ancient Illyria.

The capital was Ljubljana, called Laybach, which was the seat of the governor-general. By a decree of 15 April 1811 the central government consisted of the governor-general, an intendant of finance and a commissioner of the judiciary. The governors-general were Auguste de Marmont, Henri-Gatien Bertrand, Jean-Andoche Junot and Joseph Fouché. Illyrian offices answered to ministries in Paris, and the inhabitants had Illyrian nationality. In 1811 the population of four intendancies, Ljubljana, Karlovac, Trieste and Zara, was given as 1,504,258.

The French introduced the Napoleonic Code, equality before the law, compulsory military service, a uniform tax system and the separation of church and state, with civil registration of births and weddings, and they nationalised the judiciary. A decree emancipated the Jews and abolished a Habsburg-era regulation that had forbidden Jews to settle within Carniola. At first French, Italian and German were the official languages; Croatian and Slovenian were added in 1811, and Slovene became official for the first time. A decree of 4 July 1810 created écoles centrales at Ljubljana and Zara, and it is now considered the charter of the University of Ljubljana.

After the Treaty of Tilsit the Royal Navy blockaded the Adriatic, bringing merchant shipping to a standstill. In August 1813 Austria again declared war. Austrian troops took Trieste on 29 October, Zara surrendered on 6 December after a 34-day siege, and the French garrisons at Kotor and Dubrovnik surrendered on 3 and 27 January 1814, effectively ending French rule. The Treaty of Paris of 30 May 1814 reduced France to its 1792 borders. The permission to use Slovene in schools won the sympathy of members of the Slovene National Awakening, and Valentin Vodnik wrote school books that made Slovene teaching possible.
illyrians: The Illyrians spoke an Indo-European language and, with the Thracians and Greeks, were one of the three main Paleo-Balkan populations. Later Greek and Roman writers called their territory Illyria and placed it between the Adriatic Sea, the Drava and Morava rivers and the Ceraunian Mountains. The first known mention is in fragments of Hecataeus of Miletus, in the late 6th and early 5th century BCE, who calls them a barbarian people. It has been suggested that the tribes never called themselves Illyrians collectively, and that the Greeks applied the name of one tribe to all people with similar language and customs. According to the archaeological account, they emerged from the fusion of Yamnaya-related movements around 2500 BCE with the Balkan Neolithic population.

Organised realms formed earlier in southern Illyria than elsewhere. One of the oldest kingdoms was that of the Enchelei, at its height in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, and its place was taken by the Dassaretii. Many scholars hold that the dynasty of Bardylis, the first attested Illyrian dynasty, was Dassaretan. Illyrian society consisted of numerous tribes and small realms ruled by warrior elites. According to Pseudo-Scymnus, some were governed by hereditary kings, some by elected chieftains and some by autonomous communities under their own tribal laws.

The Illyrians were notorious as seafarers, with a reputation for piracy that was especially strong under King Agron and later Queen Teuta. They used fast ships of the types called lembus and liburna, later adopted by the Macedonians and Romans. The Roman Republic fought a series of Illyrian Wars from 229 BCE until 168 BCE, when the Romans defeated Gentius at Scodra. In the 1st century CE the Great Illyrian Uprising in the Roman province of Illyricum was led by Bato the Breucian and Bato the Daesitiate. The name last appears in the 7th century, for a Byzantine garrison in the former province of Illyricum.

Their languages are extinct and poorly attested, and it is not clear whether they belonged to the centum or the satem group. The Illyrians were subject to varying degrees of Celticization, Hellenization, Romanization and later Slavicization.Messapic, once spoken in Apulia, is often considered a dialect or sister language of Illyrian. What happened to the Illyrians afterwards is debated, and a hypothesis that the Albanian language descends from an Illyrian language is often supported but not proven. The idea of continuity between Illyrians and Albanians has played a significant role in Albanian nationalism since the 19th century. In 1809 to 1814 Napoleon named conquered South Slavic lands after Illyrian provinces, and from 1835 a Croatian national revival called itself the Illyrian movement.
illyricum-roman-province: Illyricum took in the Illyrian lands in the south, along the east coast of the Adriatic Sea and its inland mountains, and the plains of Pannonia in the north. The southern part stretched from the River Drin in what is now northern Albania to Istria and the River Sava. Pannonia lay north of the mountains, up to the westward bend of the River Danube, and included present-day Vojvodina, northern Croatia and western Hungary. As the province developed, Salona, near modern Split, became its capital.

The region was a valuable source of soldiers for the empire. Its native peoples had a reputation for fighting ability, and from the 3rd to the 6th century some of the most useful Roman troops were recruited from Pannonia, Dalmatia, Moesia and Thrace. Several emperors of the Crisis of the Third Century, among them Claudius II and Aurelian, were born at Sirmium, and Diocletian was born at Salona.

Rome fought three Illyrian wars between 229 and 168 BCE. The first, in 229–228 BCE, followed attacks by Illyrian pirates on the ships of Rome's Italian allies and the growing power of the Ardiaei, a tribe of what is now Montenegro and northern Albania. The second, in 219–18 BCE, was also won by Rome. In 168 BCE the Ardiaei joined Macedon against Rome in the Third Macedonian War and were quickly defeated. In 59 BCE the lex Vatinia gave Julius Caesar the governorship of Gallia Cisalpina and Illyricum, with three legions based at Aquileia, for five years.

Between 35 and 33 BCE Octavian campaigned in Illyricum, partly because of raids on north-eastern Italy and piracy in the Adriatic. Illyricum became a formal province in 27 BCE, at first under the senate, and in 11 BCE it became an imperial province under Publius Cornelius Dolabella. Rebellions in southern Pannonia and northern Dalmatia from 14 to 10 BCE, known as the Pannonian war, are poorly recorded, mostly in brief accounts by Cassius Dio.

The Batonian War of 6–9 CE began when native auxiliaries gathered for a campaign against the Marcomanni rebelled under Bato the Daesitiate. Bato the Breucian led the Breuci of southern Pannonia, and the two leaders joined forces on Mount Alma. Tiberius took command of the Roman army and met their guerrilla tactics with counterinsurgency operations. Paul, writing to the Romans in the winter of 57–58 CE, names Illyricum as the westernmost point of his missionary travels so far.
ilocos: The region was originally inhabited by Negritos as early as 30,000 BCE, who were displaced over time by successive waves of Austronesian migrants arriving along the narrow coast in traditional boats. The first wave, some 10,000 to 7,000 years ago, brought the ancestors of the indigenous groups of the Cordillera Central, and later migrations introduced agriculture. Before colonial rule, the Ilocanos, then known as Samtoy, traded with local and foreign merchants at coastal hubs such as Vigan, Candon and Lingayen, which were visited by Austronesian, Arab, Indian, Chinese and Japanese ships. Gold from the Cordillera, porcelain, silk, cotton, beeswax and stoneware jars were among the goods exchanged. In the south the polity of Caboloan lay in the Agno River basin.

A year after Miguel López de Legazpi declared Manila the capital on 24 June 1571, Spanish colonization expanded to northern Luzon. Martín de Goiti began the conquest of Pangasinan and founded settlements between 1571 and 1573, and in 1572 Juan de Salcedo landed at the mouth of the Agno River with eight armed boats and 80 men. In 1574 the Chinese pirate Limahong fled to Pangasinan after being driven from Manila, but an army led by Salcedo chased him out after a seven-month siege.

American forces landed in the region on 18 November 1899 in pursuit of Emilio Aguinaldo, and guerrillas under Gen. Manuel Tinio kept fighting in the countryside. At the Battle of Tirad Pass on 2 December 1899, Gen. Gregorio del Pilar and about 60 soldiers faced over 300 American troops and lost their position. Japanese forces landed at Vigan on 10 December 1941 and took it the next day.

The Ilocos Region, designated Region I, lies in north-western Luzon between the Cordillera and the West Philippine Sea. It has four provinces, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union and Pangasinan, and the city of San Fernando in La Union is its regional centre. Pangasinan was transferred to it from Central Luzon by a decree of 1973, and Abra, Mountain Province and Benguet were moved to the Cordillera Administrative Region in 1987. The 2020 census counted 5,292,297 people, mostly Ilocanos, with Pangasinans the second largest group.

Ilocano is the main language, and the epic Biag ni Lam-ang belongs to its literary tradition. Two UNESCO World Heritage sites stand here: the Baroque churches of Paoay and Santa Maria, and the colonial city of Vigan. Pangasinan is known for milkfish farming and salt production, and the region's crafts include inabel weaving and damili, red clay pottery.
iloilo-city: Iloilo City lies on the southern shore of Panay, facing the Iloilo Strait and the island of Guimaras, which together form a natural harbour and a safe anchorage for ships. The Iloilo and Batiano rivers flow through its districts into the strait. The name derives from the older Irong-irong, meaning nose-like, which referred to the promontory between the two rivers where Fort San Pedro and the 17th-century Spanish port stood. The city is a conglomeration of former towns, now seven districts: the City Proper, Jaro, Molo, Mandurriao, La Paz, Arevalo and Lapuz. In 1930 the architect Juan Arellano drew a plan for it based on Ebenezer Howard's Garden City concept.

The earliest written reference to Iloilo appears in Yuan dynasty records of the 1300s, which identify Oton, west of the city, as a bustling trade outpost in the Visayas. In 1565 Miguel López de Legazpi sent his grandson Felipe de Salcedo and Augustinian missionaries, among them Martín de Rada, to explore the Visayas for resources, and they set up a temporary settlement at Araut on Panay to secure food supplies. In 1566 the Spanish settled in the area, which became the second Spanish colonial centre in the Philippines after Cebu. Mexican soldiers from Latin America reinforced the garrison in 1603, 1636, 1670 and 1672.

Queen Regent Maria Christina of Austria gave the city the title La Muy Leal y Noble Ciudad, Most Loyal and Noble City, in recognition of its loyalty to the Spanish crown during the Philippine Revolution. Iloilo served as the last capital of the Spanish Empire in Asia and the Pacific before the Philippines was ceded to the United States in 1898. By 1900 it was widely known as the Queen City of the South, and it was considered the second most important city in the Philippines after Manila. Japanese forces invaded Panay in 1942. A fire in 1966 destroyed nearly three quarters of the downtown area.

Iloilo City is the regional centre of Western Visayas and the capital of Iloilo Province, though it is administered independently of the province. It had 473,728 inhabitants in the 2024 census, and Hiligaynon is the predominant language. The Calle Real Heritage Zone preserves buildings of the Spanish and American periods. The city is the centre of devotion to Nuestra Señora de la Candelaria de Jaro, and holds the Dinagyang Festival every January. UNESCO recognises it as a Creative City of Gastronomy, known for dishes such as La Paz batchoy and pancit Molo.
ilorin: Ilorin lies where Nigeria's northern savanna meets the southwestern forest belt, in the transitional Middle Belt, about 300 kilometres north-northeast of Lagos. The Asa is the longest of the rivers that drain the area. Its people speak mainly Yoruba, in a local dialect known as Ilorin Yoruba, while the ruling dynasty is of Fulani origin and its titles, festivals and Islamic scholarship tie it closely to the Hausa–Fulani north. Scholars therefore describe it as a meeting point of north and south.

Oral tradition holds that the area was settled for many centuries by successive groups. Tradition credits Ojo Isekuse, a hunter and blacksmith, as one of the early founders, and traces the city's name to okuta ilọ irin, the stone for sharpening iron. By the 18th century Ilorin was a border settlement of the Oyo Empire with a mainly Yoruba population and growing numbers of Hausa and Fulani immigrants.

In the early 19th century Afonja, the Oyo field marshal (Aare Ona Kakanfo) stationed at Ilorin, rebelled against the Alaafin with the support of the Fulani scholar Shehu Alimi. Their alliance collapsed in a struggle for power and Afonja was killed. Alimi's eldest son Abd al-Salam became the first Emir of Ilorin, receiving a flag from Sokoto and bringing Ilorin into the Sokoto Caliphate as an emirate, traditionally dated between 1823 and 1831.

Ilorin repelled an Oyo-led coalition at the Battle of Ilorin, around 1835, an event that hastened the collapse of Old Oyo. The army of Ibadan halted its southward expansion at Osogbo in 1840. Through the century it was a major trading node between the Hausa–Fulani north and the Yoruba south and a centre of Islamic learning.

Ilorin resisted British rule but was occupied by the Royal Niger Company in 1897 and incorporated into the Northern Nigeria Protectorate in 1900. In 1967 it became the capital of the newly created Kwara State.

Ilorin is the capital of Kwara State and the seat of the Ilorin Emirate, ruled by eleven emirs, all from the house of Shehu Alimi. Islam is the majority religion, though Christianity is widely practised. The Ilorin Central Mosque, begun in 1977 and opened in 1981, has 99 domes and four minarets. Its Durbar, a procession of decorated horses and riders led by the Emir, is held a day or two after Eid al-Adha. The city has some of the largest traditional pottery workshops in Nigeria and produces hand-woven aso-oke textiles.
iltutmish: Iltutmish was born into a well-off family; his father Ilam Khan led the Ilbari Turkic tribe. According to Minhaj's Tabaqat-i Nasiri, his jealous brothers sold him to a slave dealer at a horse show, a story that seems modelled on the Quranic account of Yusuf. He spent his early life in Bukhara and Ghazni under several masters. In about 1197 the Ghurid slave-commander Qutb al-Din Aibak bought him in Delhi for 100,000 jitals, making him the slave of a slave.

He became head of Aibak's bodyguard and was later given the important iqta of Badaun. His campaigns against the Khokhar rebels in 1205–1206 won the notice of Muhammad of Ghor, who freed him before Aibak himself was freed.

After Aibak died in 1210, the nobles at Lahore appointed Aram Shah as his successor. Nobles elsewhere, led by the military justiciar Ali-yi Ismail, proposed Iltutmish instead, since Aibak had called him a son. He marched to Delhi, defeated Aram Shah's forces and set up his capital there. Some nobles rebelled, and he had many of them beheaded. He then brought Badaun, Awadh, Banaras and Siwalik back under Delhi's control and faced rival former Ghurid slaves, among them Taj al-Din Yildiz and Nasir ad-Din Qabacha.

In 1228–1229 he invaded Qabacha's territory, which the Mongols and the Khwarazmians had weakened, and annexed large parts of Punjab and Sindh. On 18 February 1229 an embassy from the Abbasid caliph al-Mustansir reached Delhi with a deed of investiture and the titles Yamin Khalifat Allah and Nasir Amir al-Mu'minin. In 1230 he defeated Malik Balkha Khalji in Bengal, and in 1231 he besieged Gwalior, which fell on 12 December 1232. He died in Delhi on 30 April 1236.

Iltutmish freed the sultanate from a subordinate position to Ghazni. He introduced the silver tanka and the copper jital, the basic coins of the later sultanate, and the iqta system, which assigned the revenues of a region to officers in return for military service. He is probably the first ruler of the sultanate to organise a centrally recruited and paid army.

Delhi became a centre of Islamic power and culture under him; he patronised the historian Minhaj-i-Siraj and the Sufi Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki. He completed the Qutb Minar, built the Hauz-i-Shamsi reservoir and in 1231 raised the Sultan Ghari tomb for his eldest son, the first Islamic mausoleum in Delhi.
ilya-muromets: Ilya Muromets, also called Ilya of Murom, is a bogatyr, or hero, of the Russian byliny, a type of oral epic poem set in the time of Kievan Rus' and collected as folklore in the 18th and 19th centuries. He often appears with the bogatyrs Dobrynya Nikitich and Alyosha Popovich, the three being known in Russian culture as the three bogatyrs. Attempts have been made to find a historical nucleus for him. The main candidate is Ilya Pechersky, a 12th-century monk of the Kiev Pechersk Lavra who was canonized in 1643 and whose relics are kept in the monastery. His character probably does not represent a single historical person but a fusion of several real or fictional heroes of different epochs.

In the byliny Ilya is the son of a peasant, born in the village of Karacharovo near Murom. A serious illness left him unable to walk until the age of 33, lying on a Russian stove until two pilgrims miraculously healed him. A dying knight, Svyatogor, gave him superhuman strength, and he set out to free Kiev from Idolishche and to serve Vladimir I of Kiev. On the way he defended Chernigov from a nomadic invasion, possibly by the Polovtsi, and declined the local ruler's offer of knighthood. In the forests of Bryansk he killed the monster Nightingale the Robber, who murdered travellers with his whistle.

In Kiev Vladimir made him chief bogatyr, and he defended the land from attacks from the Pontic–Caspian steppe, traditionally personified as Kalin-tsar of the Tatars. Generous and simple-minded but also temperamental, he once destroyed all the church steeples of Kiev after Vladimir failed to invite him to a celebration, and was soon appeased. The cycle of tales has its own type, SUS -650C*, in the East Slavic Folktale Classification, with variants from Russian, Belarusian and Ukrainian sources.

Ilya Pechersky is said by hagiography to have been a warrior known for his strength before taking monastic vows, nicknamed Chobotok, small boot. In 1988 Soviet archaeologists exhumed his remains and reported a tall man whose bones showed signs of spinal disease at an early age and the marks of many wounds, one fatal. The hero has inspired Catterino Cavos's opera of 1807, Viktor Vasnetsov's painting Bogatyrs of 1898, Reinhold Glière's Symphony No. 3 of 1911 and Aleksandr Ptushko's film Ilya Muromets of 1956.
imad-al-din-zengi: Zengi's father, Aq Sunqur al-Hajib, was the Turkic governor of Aleppo under the Seljuk ruler Malik-Shah I and was beheaded for treason in 1094, when Zengi was about ten. Zengi was raised by Kerbogha, the governor of Mosul, and served the governors of Mosul, then entered the service of the Seljuk ruler Mahmud in 1118. In 1122 he received his first major command, an expedition against the Banu Mazyad leader Dubays ibn Sadaqa, and was granted the governorship of Wasit. He added Basra in 1124 and Baghdad in April 1126, which put him in control of Seljuk Iraq.

Zengi became governor of Mosul in 1127, after the assassination of Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi, and atabeg of Aleppo in 1128, uniting the two cities under his personal rule. In 1130 he allied with Taj al-Mulk Buri of Damascus against the Crusaders, only to seize Hama from Buri's son. Damascus remained his goal, and he besieged it several times without success, while the Damascenes under Mu'in al-Din Unur allied with the Kingdom of Jerusalem. In 1137 he defeated King Fulk of Jerusalem at the Battle of Ba'rin, and in 1138 his forces turned back the Byzantine emperor John II Comnenus and the Crusader princes at Shaizar.

In 1139 he took Baalbek by promising its defenders safe passage and then broke his word, having the governor flayed and the rest hanged, according to Ibn al-'Adim. He granted the town to his lieutenant Najm al-Din Ayyub, father of Saladin. In 1144 he captured Edessa on 24 December after a siege of four months.

The County of Edessa was the first of the Crusader states to be created and the first to fall. Its loss led to the Second Crusade, and later Muslim chroniclers noted it as the start of the jihad against the Crusader states. Zengi was killed in September 1146. Islamic sources say a Frankish slave named Yarankash assassinated him, while western sources blame his own court officials. He founded the Zengid dynasty. His eldest son Sayf al-Din Ghazi I succeeded him in Mosul and his second son Nur al-Din in Aleppo, and Qutb al-Din Mawdud followed Sayf in Mosul in 1149.
imagawa-yoshimoto: Imagawa Yoshimoto was born in 1519, the third son of Imagawa Ujichika of the Imagawa clan, which claimed descent from Emperor Seiwa. As a younger son he was sent to a temple, where he was named Baigaku Shōhō. In 1536 his elder brother Ujiteru died suddenly and a succession dispute followed. His half-brother Genkō Etan sought the lordship, and the clan split. Yoshimoto's faction argued that his mother, Jukei-ni, had been Ujichika's consort. With help from Hōjō Ujitsuna of Sagami and the support of Takeda Nobutora of Kai, the other faction was eliminated in the Hanagura Disturbance, and Yoshimoto took his name and the headship.

Yoshimoto married a sister of Takeda Shingen, which sealed an alliance with the Takeda, and in 1540 he helped Shingen imprison Nobutora. He defeated an invasion of Suruga by the Later Hōjō clan. His advance into Mikawa met a defeat at the 1542 Battle of Azukizaka, but in 1548 he beat Oda Nobuhide in the Second Battle of Azukizaka and gained Suruga, Tōtōmi and Mikawa. Marriages tied him to the Takeda and the Hōjō, and a peace with the Hōjō followed in 1554. He was known as the number one archer in the Tōkaidō. Later he left the clan's political affairs to his son Imagawa Ujizane to concentrate on the advance westward into Mikawa and Owari.

In the summer of 1560 Yoshimoto marched towards the capital with Matsudaira Motoyasu, later known as Tokugawa Ieyasu, in the vanguard. He had a force of 25,000 but announced 40,000, and some sources support the larger figure. After taking several Oda castles his army feasted with song and sake. Following a downpour, Oda Nobunaga attacked by surprise with 3,000 men. Two Oda samurai, Mōri Shinsuke and Hattori Koheita, killed Yoshimoto at Dengakuhazama on 12 June. Ujizane succeeded him, but the Imagawa fell from power. Yoshimoto's body is buried at the Daisei-ji temple in Toyokawa, in modern Aichi Prefecture.
imam-shamil: Shamil was born on 26 June 1797 into an Avar Muslim family in the small village of Gimry, in present-day Dagestan. He was first named Ali, but after an illness his name was changed to Shamuyil, which is pronounced Shamil in the Caucasus. His father, Dengau, was a landlord, and this let Shamil and his friend Ghazi Muhammad study Arabic and logic. He grew up while the Russian Empire expanded into Ottoman and Qajar lands, and many Caucasian peoples united in resistance in what became known as the Caucasian War, which lasted from 1817 to 1864. Shamil became the disciple and counsellor of Ghazi Mollah, the earlier leader of the resistance.

Ghazi Mollah died at the battle of Gimry in 1832, and Shamil was one of only two murids to escape, badly wounded by a bayonet. He rejoined the murids under the second Imam, Hamzat Bek, and when Hamzat Bek was killed in 1834 he became the leader of the resistance. In 1839 he and about 4,000 followers, men, women and children, were besieged by General Pavel Grabbe in the stronghold of Akhoulgo. He refused Grabbe's demand to surrender and accept exile. The Russians stormed the stronghold; Shamil escaped on the first night, and many Dagestani and Chechen chieftains declared loyalty to the Tsar. He then fled to Chechnya and extended his influence over the clans there.

He united quarrelsome peoples through charisma, piety and fairness in applying sharia law, and used guerrilla tactics against the larger Russian army. In 1845 his forces surrounded and destroyed a column of 8,000 to 10,000 men under Count Mikhail Vorontsov in the forests of Chechnya. Shamil hoped for help from Britain, France or the Ottoman Empire, which never came. After the Crimean War Russia redoubled its efforts, and in September 1859 Shamil surrendered.

Shamil was sent to meet Tsar Alexander II and was then exiled to Kaluga. In December 1868 he was allowed to move to Kyiv, where he was given a mansion. In 1869 he received permission to make the Hajj. Sultan Abdulaziz received him at Istanbul, and at Mecca he met Emir Abdelkader. He died in Medina in 1871 and was buried in the Jannatul Baqi.

Peoples of the Northern Caucasus regard him as a hero. Russians came to respect him despite the bloody conquest of Chechnya and Dagestan, and Alexander II is said to have admired his resistance. His grandson Said Shamil was one of the founders of the Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus, set up in 1917 and conquered by Soviet Russia in 1920.
imbros: Imbros, officially Gökçeada since 29 July 1970, is the largest island of Turkey, in Çanakkale Province. It lies in the north-northeastern Aegean Sea at the entrance of Saros Bay, and Cape İncirburnu is the westernmost point of Turkey. The island has an area of 286.8 square kilometres and some wooded areas. It is mainly of volcanic origin, and its highest peak, İlyas Dağ, is an extinct stratovolcano. It lies just south of the North Anatolian Fault, and a severe earthquake struck it on 21 August 1859.

Herodotus records Pelasgians as the original inhabitants, who worshipped the Cabeiri and Hermes. Imbros and Lemnos were sacred to Hephaestus, and an ithyphallic Hephaestus appears on the island's ancient coins. In classical antiquity Imbros was an Athenian cleruchy, a colony whose settlers kept Athenian citizenship. The Iliad mentions the island and a lord of Imbros named Eëtion. The island was primarily inhabited by ethnic Greeks from the Iron Age until about the 1960s.

After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 the Byzantine forces left, and the Ottomans took the island not by force but by a policy of conciliation. Michael Critoboulos, a leading Imbriot and later a chronicler of Mehmet II, arranged its peaceful surrender. In return for taxes and loyalty the island kept a degree of autonomy under a local administrator, and in 1479 it came under definitive Ottoman rule. The islanders lived in relative peace and prosperity until the 20th century and took no part in upheavals such as the Greek War of Independence.

In 1915 Imbros was a staging post for the Allied Mediterranean Expeditionary Force during the Gallipoli campaign, with a field hospital and an airfield, and General Ian Hamilton had his headquarters there. A naval action, the Battle of Imbros, was fought nearby on 20 January 1918. From November 1912 to September 1923 the island was under Greek naval administration. Article 14 of the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 exempted Imbros and Tenedos from the population exchange between Greece and Turkey.

After Turkish authorities took over in October 1923 the elected island government was dismissed. Law 1151 of 25 June 1927 abolished local administration and closed the Greek schools. Many Greeks left from the 1960s, and settlers from the mainland now make up most of the population. A Greek school reopened in September 2015. The main industries are fishing and tourism. Çınarlı is the only town, and the island is one of Turkey's cittaslow towns.
imhotep: Imhotep, whose name means the one who comes in peace, was chancellor to King Djoser, a possible architect of his step pyramid and high priest of the sun god Ra at Heliopolis. Little is known of him as a historical figure. Two contemporary inscriptions on the base of one of Djoser's statues establish him as chancellor, and a graffito on the enclosure wall of Sekhemkhet's unfinished step pyramid suggests that he outlived Djoser by a few years and worked on that king's pyramid, which was abandoned because Sekhemkhet reigned briefly.

He held the unique title bity sensen, literally the King of Lower Egypt, the two brothers, which has been read as meaning he was the king's twin; with no comparable holders the reading remains speculative. If not a relative, he may have been the king's confidant or childhood friend.

Egyptologists, following much later legends, credit Imhotep with the design and building of the Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara, built during the 3rd Dynasty. He may also have been responsible for the first known use of stone columns to support a building. Stone had appeared sporadically in the Archaic Period, but nothing as large as the step pyramid had been built wholly of stone; earlier kings were buried in mastaba tombs. The ancient Egyptians themselves never credited him as designer of the step pyramid or inventor of stone architecture. Manetho, in the Ptolemaic period, credited him with inventing the method of dressed-stone building under Djoser.

The location of his tomb is unknown. No text from his lifetime mentions skill in medicine or wisdom writing, and none names him for 1,200 years after his death. The first surviving text to name him dates to the time of Amenhotep III and mentions libations poured to him, and his cult in the New Kingdom was distinct from offerings to other commoners. Imhotep is one of fewer than a dozen non-royal Egyptians deified after death, with his cult centred at Memphis.

Healing powers are first attached to him from the Thirtieth Dynasty, about 2,200 years after his death, and the Greeks equated him with Asklepios. The Famine Stela of the Ptolemaic period credits him with ending a seven-year famine under Djoser. A demotic papyrus of the 2nd century CE from Tebtunis tells a long story of him that includes a magical duel with an Assyrian sorceress.
imjin-war: Ming China and Joseon Korea both emerged in the fourteenth century after the fall of the Yuan dynasty and faced similar threats from Jurchen raiders and the wokou. By the last decade of the sixteenth century Toyotomi Hideyoshi had unified Japan. A man of relatively humble origins who owed his position to his military might, he sought military power to legitimise his rule. It has also been suggested that he meant to fulfil the dreams of his late lord Oda Nobunaga and to keep the new state united against a common enemy, easing the threat of disorder from idle samurai and ambitious daimyos.

Japanese tanegashima matchlock arquebuses proved effective in land combat and sieges, while Korea was a manufacturing hub for cannons and ships, so Japanese strength lay on land and Korean strength at sea.

On 23 May 1592 about 7,000 men of the First Division under Konishi Yukinaga reached Busan from Tsushima. After the fall of Busan and the fortress of Dongnae, where about 3,000 were killed and the Japanese took no prisoners, they advanced north. Koreans were enraged rather than cowed and raised militias called righteous armies; by summer 1592 about 22,200 guerrillas tied up much of the Japanese force. At sea, Yi Sun-sin destroyed Japanese ships carrying troops and supplies, and Japan, short of arms and men, changed its aim from conquering China to occupying Korea.

Ming forces under Li Rusong, with 43,000 Chinese alongside Koreans, guerrillas and warrior monks, retook Pyongyang. In July 1593 Ukita Hideie led 90,000 Japanese troops against Jinju, the largest force of the war for a single operation. After talks the Japanese withdrew to the Busan area and a ceasefire followed, with little fighting for three years.

Hideyoshi launched a second invasion in 1597, no longer aiming at China. The Japanese were again halted in the south. Hideyoshi died in 1598, the Council of Five Elders ordered the withdrawal, and the Japanese fleet was attacked at the Battle of Noryang on 16 December 1598, the final, largest and bloodiest battle of the war.

These were East Asia's first regional wars of massed armies with modern weapons, with Japanese armies of up to 200,000 and Ming armies of 80,000. Hideyoshi's order for the second invasion called for everyone to be mown down, young or old, and the heads sent to Japan. The war weakened the Toyotomi clan and, since the forces came mostly from western daimyos, strengthened Tokugawa Ieyasu, who became shogun in 1603 after the Battle of Sekigahara. Later Japanese leaders cited the invasions to justify the annexation of Korea.
immanuel-kant: Immanuel Kant was born Emanuel on 22 April 1724 in Königsberg, East Prussia, into a Lutheran family. His father, Johann Georg Kant, was a harness-maker from Memel, and his mother was Anna Regina Reuter. He was the fourth of nine children, six of whom reached adulthood. The household stressed Pietist values of religious devotion, humility and a literal reading of the Bible, and his early schooling was strict, with an emphasis on Latin and religious instruction. He changed the spelling of his name to Immanuel after learning Hebrew.

Kant received a licence to lecture at Königsberg in 1755 and taught mathematics, physics, logic and metaphysics. In 1757 he began lecturing on geography, one of the first to teach it as a subject of its own. His Universal Natural History and Theory of the Heavens (1755) set out the nebular hypothesis, in which the Solar System formed from a cloud of gas. He also suggested that other distant nebulae might be other galaxies. In 1756 he published three papers on the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, among the first systematic attempts to explain earthquakes in natural terms. He became a professor in 1770.

The Critique of Pure Reason appeared in 1781, with a heavily revised second edition in 1787. The Critique of Practical Reason followed in 1788 and the Critique of the Power of Judgment in 1790. In 1792 the King's censorship commission opposed the publication of part of his work on religion. He published the book through the University of Jena, which earned him a royal reprimand, and a royal order later required him never to publish or speak publicly about religion. He died in Königsberg on 12 February 1804, saying Es ist gut, 'It is good'.

In the Critique of Pure Reason Kant argues for transcendental idealism: space and time are forms of intuition that structure all experience, and we know only appearances, not things in themselves. He compared this to a Copernican Revolution, proposing that objects of experience conform to the mind's forms of intuition and categories, not the reverse. His aim was to secure both knowledge and morality against scepticism and determinism, and he wrote that he had to deny knowledge in order to make room for faith.
imola: Imola is a city and comune in the Metropolitan City of Bologna, on the river Santerno in the Emilia-Romagna region. It is traditionally considered the western entrance to the historical region of Romagna. Its Roman name was Forum Cornelii, the Forum of Cornelius, after the dictator Sulla, who founded the city around 82 BCE. It was an agricultural and trading centre, notable for its ceramics. The name Imola was first used in the 7th century by the Lombards, who applied it to the fortress now known as the Castellaccio.

According to Paul the Deacon, Imola was in 412 the scene of the marriage of Ataulf, king of the Visigoths, to Galla Placidia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius the Great. With the exarchate of Ravenna it passed under papal authority. In the 10th century and after, it saw incessant wars against Ravenna, Faenza and Bologna, and out of these conflicts came the city's republican constitution. In the contest between pope and emperor it was generally Ghibelline. Pope Benedict XII made Lippo II Alidosi pontifical vicar, and his family held power until 1424, when the condottiero Angelo della Pergola gained the upper hand.

In 1426 the city was restored to the Holy See, and it was conferred on the Sforza, dukes of Milan, in 1434, 1438 and 1470. It was later bestowed as a dowry on Caterina Sforza, bride of Girolamo Riario, nephew of Pope Sixtus IV, and under the Riarii it was embellished with palaces and works of art. Pope Alexander VI deprived Girolamo's son Ottaviano of power, and on 25 November 1499 the city surrendered to Cesare Borgia. In 1504 Imola submitted to Pope Julius II. It remained papal, apart from the years after 1797, until it joined the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1860.

Imola is best known for the Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari, opened in the 1950s. Among its older buildings are the Rocca Sforzesca, built under Girolamo Riario and Caterina Sforza, the cathedral dedicated to San Cassiano, erected between 1187 and 1271, and Palazzo Tozzoni, built between 1726 and 1738 and since 1981 a civic art museum.
imperial-examination: Tests of skill such as archery contests existed from the Zhou dynasty, and the Confucian character of the later examinations owed much to the reign of Emperor Wu of Han. Before the Sui dynasty most official posts were filled through recommendation, based on qualities such as social status, morals and ability. The original purpose of the examinations under the Sui was to strike a blow against the hereditary aristocracy, whose power in the period of Northern and Southern dynasties had seriously constrained the emperor, and to centralise power around him.

In 622 the first Tang emperor let men nominate themselves, and throughout the Tang the vast majority of males were eligible. Oral interviews were meant to be unbiased but in practice favoured candidates from the elite clans of Chang'an and Luoyang. Empress Wu Zetian created military examinations in 702.

Under the Song dynasty the examinations became the primary method of recruiting officials and took the form of a rough ladder of local, provincial and court examinations. By the mid-12th century 100,000 candidates registered for the prefectural examinations each year, and by the mid-13th more than 400,000. The Liao and Jin dynasties held examinations for their Han subjects, while the Yuan ended them after the defeat of the Song in 1279, since Kublai Khan believed that Confucian learning was not needed for government posts. The Ming retained and expanded the system. In 1370 the Hongwu Emperor declared that the examinations would follow the Neo-Confucian canon of Zhu Xi, and the first palace examination of the dynasty was held in 1385.

From the 1830s and 1840s officials proposed adding Western technology, and in 1888 international commerce was added. The system lasted about 1,300 years until its abolition in the late Qing reforms in 1905.

By the Ming the degrees formed a ladder of success, with the jinshi, awarded at the palace level, regarded as the mark of success. Candidates spent up to three days and two nights in an isolated cell, writing eight-legged essays; guards searched them for hidden texts. The passing rate among the two or three million annual applicants was about 1%. The top three palace graduates were appointed directly to the Hanlin Academy.
