The exams were written in Classical Chinese, which spread as an educational standard to Japan, Korea and Vietnam.

The problem of surplus graduates became acute from the 18th century, when a long peace let many candidates prepare and examiners found their papers of similar quality. Reformers charged that the eight-legged essay stifled original thought. European missionaries and diplomats described the system, and in 1855 Britain adopted a similar testing system for its civil servants.
imphal: Imphal lies in the Imphal Valley in the extreme east of India, surrounded by nine ranges of hills, at an average elevation of 786 metres. Its climate is humid subtropical, with cool, dry winters and a slightly hot monsoon season. The name comes from two Meitei words, yum, meaning house, and phāl, meaning plenty or beautiful.

Tradition holds that King Pakhangba established Kangla Fort, once the capital of Manipur, in 33 CE. The kingdom had earlier been ruled by kings of the Khaba clan; the Ningthouja dynasty began to rule after the ascension of Nongda Lairen Pakhangba and came to dominate the region in politics and war. Kangla Palace was built by King Khagemba and his son Khunjaoba. In the reign of Maharaja Bhagyachandra there were a number of Burmese invasions, and the kingdom survived with the help of Maharaj Gambhir Singh.

Imphal remained peaceful until 1891, when disputes within the royal family led the British to send J. W. Quinton, and an order to arrest the prince Senapati Tikendrajit angered the people. The resulting Anglo-Manipur War was won by the British. The king, Maharaja Kulachandra, was sentenced to imprisonment and sent to the Cellular Jail in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and Tikendrajit and Thangal General were hanged. The British destroyed Kangla Palace in the war. The region merged with India in 1949.
The Battle of Imphal was fought between March and July 1944. The Japanese had invaded in order to destroy the Allied forces and then invade India, but were defeated and forced to retreat.

Imphal is the capital of the Indian state of Manipur, with a population of 277,196 at the 2011 census; most people speak Manipuri. Hinduism is the majority religion and Sanamahism the second largest, and the Pakhangba temple stands within Kangla Fort, whose ruins are surrounded by a moat. The Ima Keithel, or Mothers' Market, was established in the 16th century and is run by women vendors. The Imphal War Cemetery commemorates Indian and British soldiers who died in 1944.
impressionism: In the middle of the 19th century, as Napoleon III rebuilt Paris, the Académie des Beaux-Arts dominated French art. It valued historical and religious subjects and portraits, and preferred carefully finished pictures whose brush strokes were blended to hide the artist's hand. Its annual juried show, the Salon de Paris, decided prizes and commissions. By the 1850s some artists, notably Gustave Courbet, had drawn attention and censure by depicting contemporary realities without idealisation. The Impressionists also learned from painters such as Eugène Boudin and Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot, who worked from nature in a direct and spontaneous style, and followed Eugène Delacroix and J. M. W. Turner in letting freely brushed colour take precedence over line.

Impressionism began with a group of Paris-based artists whose independent exhibitions brought them to prominence in the 1870s and 1880s. They painted outdoors, en plein air, to capture the momentary effects of sunlight, and portrayed overall visual effects rather than details. They used short, broken strokes of colour set side by side with as little mixing as possible, and placed wet paint into wet paint.

They chose subjects such as middle-class leisure, cafés, theatres, train stations and the widened avenues of Paris, and included factories in their landscapes. Among the central figures were Claude Monet, Camille Pissarro, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Alfred Sisley, Edgar Degas, Berthe Morisot and Mary Cassatt; Pissarro was the only one to take part in all eight Impressionist exhibitions. Women were excluded from much of the social life of the boulevard and café where ideas were shared.

The name comes from Monet's Impression, Sunrise. The critic Louis Leroy coined it in a mocking review of the First Impressionist Exhibition of 1874 in Le Charivari, writing that wallpaper in its embryonic state was more finished than that seascape. The artists earned little from the exhibitions, but the dealer Paul Durand-Ruel kept their work before the public and arranged shows in London and New York. Renoir had a great Salon success in 1879, Monet became financially secure in the early 1880s and Pissarro by the early 1890s, while Sisley died in poverty in 1899.

The style spread to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia and the Netherlands, and analogous movements arose in music and literature. In the 1880s Vincent van Gogh, Paul Gauguin, Georges Seurat and Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec developed different ideas of colour and form, and their work is called post-Impressionism.
imre-nagy: Imre Nagy was born on 7 June 1896 in Kaposvár, in the Kingdom of Hungary, to a family of peasant origin. His father was a carriage driver and later an unskilled worker. After a poor record at the gymnasium he trained as a locksmith and metal fitter.

Conscripted into the Austro-Hungarian Army in 1914, he was wounded on the Italian Front and again on the Eastern Front, where Russian forces took him prisoner in July 1916. In Siberia he joined a Marxist discussion group, and in 1918 he joined the Communist Party of the Foreign Workers of Siberia and fought in the Red Army in the Russian Civil War. He joined the Russian Communist Party in 1920.

Sent by the Hungarian Communist Party to Hungary in 1921, Nagy worked on underground networks and was arrested several times. From 1930 he lived in the Soviet Union, where he did agricultural research and, from 1933 to 1941, served the NKVD as an informer under the codename Volodia.

After the Second World War he returned to Hungary and was Minister of Agriculture, distributing land to the peasants, then Interior Minister. As prime minister from 1953 to 1955 he promoted his New Course, easing the harshest parts of Mátyás Rákosi's Stalinist regime, but Rákosi's influence prevailed and he was dismissed on 18 April 1955, losing his party posts.

After Nikita Khrushchev's Secret Speech of February 1956, criticism of Rákosi grew, and he was forced out in July. On 23 October a student demonstration in Budapest called for Nagy's return, and the revolt began. Nagy was named prime minister on 24 October. On 28 October he negotiated a ceasefire with Soviet representatives and announced the dissolution of the ÁVH secret police.

By 30 October he promised a multi-party system, and on 1 November he announced Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact and appealed to the UN for recognition of its neutrality. Soviet forces attacked Budapest on 4 November, and Nagy took refuge in the Yugoslav Embassy.

Despite János Kádár's written safe conduct, he was arrested on 22 November as he left the embassy and taken to Romania. He was secretly tried in Hungary for treason and the organisation of the overthrow of the republic, and hanged on 16 June 1958; his burial was in an unmarked grave in the prison yard. In June 1989 he and other figures of the revolution were rehabilitated and reburied with full honours, an event that played a key part in the fall of the Hungarian Socialist Workers' Party regime.
imre-thokoly: Imre Thököly was born in Késmárk, now Kežmarok in Slovakia, on 25 September 1657, the fifth son of Count István Thököly and the only one to survive childhood. His father was among the wealthiest nobles of Upper Hungary. He studied at the Lutheran lyceum in Eperjes from 1668. In 1670 his father was accused of joining the aristocrats' conspiracy against Leopold I and died during the siege of Árva Castle on 4 December; accounts differ on how the son got away to Transylvania.

His estates in Hungary were confiscated, but he kept his Transylvanian lands and continued his studies at the Reformed college of Nagyenyed. Meanwhile Leopold I appointed a Directorium in 1673 that pursued a violent anti-Protestant policy, and refugees, called kuruc, raided the borderlands of Royal Hungary.

The princely council appointed him to command the Kuruc army on 26 September 1677, after a treaty at Warsaw in which Louis XIV promised an annual subsidy. He joined the Kuruc at Derecske on 27 November. In 1678 he captured Szendrő and Murány and the mining towns of the Garam valley, and he kept control of thirteen counties of Royal Hungary after a defeat at Barsszentkereszt. Reinforced in 1681, he forced the emperor to grant an armistice. In June 1682 he married Ilona Zrínyi, widow of Francis I Rákóczi.

Sultan Mehmed IV gave him the title King of Upper Hungary on condition of an annual tribute of 40,000 thalers. He assisted the Turks at the Battle of Vienna in 1683, and the grand vizier blamed him for the defeat. In 1685 he was defeated at Prešov, and the Turks seized him at Nagyvárad and sent him in chains to Edirne. Released in 1686, he was imprisoned a second time before the Turks sent him into Transylvania in 1690. He won at Zărneşti and was elected prince of Transylvania, but left in 1691.

Thököly led the Turkish cavalry at Slankamen and distinguished himself at Zenta in 1697. The Treaty of Karlowitz of 26 January 1699 excluded him by name from its amnesty. After another failed attempt on Transylvania in 1700 he settled at Galata with his wife, holding estates from Sultan Mustafa II and the title of count of Widdin. He died in 1705 in İzmit and is buried at Kežmarok. His statue stands on Heroes' Square in Budapest, and a street and a memorial in İzmit commemorate him.
imru-al-qais: Imru' al-Qais was a poet from Najd in the late fifth and early sixth centuries and the last king of Kinda. Tradition makes his father Hujr, regent of the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan, and his mother Fatimah bint Rabi'ah al-Taghlibi. The Kinda had migrated north from South Arabia, and his grandfather al-Harith was said to be the most powerful of their kings. Historians are divided on his birth year; one estimate is about 526 CE. Because early Arabia relied on oral transmission, the details of his life are hard to fix, and later biographers' stories have to be set against clues in the poems.

Tradition says he was the youngest son and began composing verse as a child, which his father disliked as unfit for a prince. Stories tell of drinking parties, many love affairs and a scandal with his cousin 'Unayzah, and say Hujr expelled him. He then wandered from oasis to oasis with friends, drinking and reciting poetry.

When the tribe of Asad killed Hujr, Imru' al-Qais was, in the most popular account, still in exile. Ibn al-Kalbi, who died in 826, says that on hearing the news he declared, 'Today is for drink, and tomorrow for serious matters.' Of his brothers he alone took on the duty of vengeance. Bakr and Taghlib supported him against Asad until they judged enough blood had been shed.

He then travelled across the Arabian peninsula and the Levant, seeking support to regain his father's kingship, and finally went to Constantinople to appeal to Emperor Justinian I, sponsored by the Ghassanid prince al-Harith ibn Jabalah. Most accounts say he won some promise of help. He fell ill near Ankara and died there, probably between 561 and 565. One story says Justinian sent him a poisoned jacket, but most historians favour death from a chronic skin disease mentioned in one of his poems. He was called the Lost King because he never recovered the throne.

His long poem beginning 'Let us stop and weep' (qifa nabki) is one of the seven Mu'allaqat, poems prized as the best pre-Islamic Arabian verse, and he is sometimes called the father of Arabic poetry. His lovers appear throughout his verse, which praises their graces and laments their cruelty and their absence. Another poem attributed to him mourns the princes of his family led away to slaughter, who died far from water, their skulls spattered with blood.
inanna: Inanna was worshipped in Sumer as early as the Uruk period, about 4000 to 3100 BCE. Her main cult centre was the Eanna temple at Uruk, whose name means House of Heaven; in archaic Uruk she was worshipped as morning Inanna, evening Inanna and princely Inanna. Scholars have proposed that she arose from the merging of several unrelated Sumerian deities, or that she was a Semitic deity who entered a Sumerian pantheon already fully structured and took on the roles not yet assigned.

Scholars believe that Inanna and Ishtar were originally separate, unrelated deities, conflated during the reign of Sargon of Akkad until they were regarded as one goddess under two names. Her worship was relatively localised before Sargon's conquest. Afterwards she became one of the most widely venerated deities of the Sumerian pantheon, with temples across Mesopotamia, and the Assyrians raised her to the highest place in their pantheon after their national god Ashur.

Her most common symbol was the eight-pointed star, which by the Old Babylonian period was specifically associated with the planet Venus; she was also shown with the lion. Her husband was the god Dumuzid, later known as Tammuz, and her attendant was the goddess Ninshubur. Her twin brother Utu, later Shamash, was the god of the sun and justice, and the two were regarded as dispensers of divine justice.

The Sumerians worshipped her as the goddess of both warfare and love. Her stories describe her moving from conquest to conquest, young and impetuous and always seeking more power than she had been allotted. She was not the goddess of marriage and was never viewed as a mother goddess. She appears in more myths than any other Sumerian deity and has an unusually large number of epithets.

Her best-known myth tells of her descent into the underworld ruled by her older sister Ereshkigal. Two versions survive: a Sumerian one dating to the Third Dynasty of Ur and a derivative Akkadian one of the early second millennium BCE. In the poem Inanna and Enki she takes the sacred mes, the powers behind the parts of civilisation, from the god Enki. In the Akkadian Epic of Gilgamesh, Ishtar asks Gilgamesh to be her consort and sends the Bull of Heaven against him when he refuses.

The Queen of Heaven mentioned in the Book of Jeremiah is probably a blend of Inanna or Ishtar and the West Semitic goddess Astarte, and Astarte may in turn have influenced the Greek goddess Aphrodite. Her worship declined gradually between the first and sixth centuries CE with the spread of Christianity.
inca-garcilaso-de-la-vega: He was born Gómez Suárez de Figueroa on 12 April 1539 in Cuzco. His father was the Spanish captain Sebastián Garcilaso de la Vega y Vargas and his mother the Inca ñusta Palla Chimpu Ocllo, a granddaughter of Huayna Capac. Because his parents were not married in the Church, he was considered illegitimate and was given only his mother's surname. His first language was Quechua. After ten years with his mother's family his father took him into his household and gave him an education under Juan de Cuéllar, a canon of the Cathedral of Cusco. In 1554 he became secretary to his father, then corregidor of Cusco. After his father's death in 1559 he left Peru at the age of 21.

In Spain he went to Montilla, where his father's brother Alonso de Vargas became his protector, and then to Madrid to seek acknowledgement from the Crown as his father's son. He was allowed to take the name Garcilaso de la Vega, which helped him enter Spanish society, and he was known as El Inca. He received an informal education and never returned to Peru. He entered Spanish military service in 1570, fought in the Alpujarras against the Moors after the Morisco Revolt, and received the rank of captain. He had at least two sons by servants; one, Diego de Vargas, born in 1590, helped him copy the Royal Commentaries.

His first work, La Florida del Inca, was published in Lisbon in 1605. It describes Hernando de Soto's expedition in Florida and defends both Spanish sovereignty and the dignity and rationality of Native Americans. Historians such as Jerald T. Milanich and Charles M. Hudson note serious problems with its sequence of events and the locations of towns.

His best-known work, the Comentarios Reales de los Incas, was published in Lisbon in 1609, with a second part on the conquest of Peru published in 1617. It rests mostly on what his Inca relatives told him in childhood and partly on the history of Blas Valera. He portrays the Incas as benevolent rulers of a well-fed country, describes their system of tribute and labour, and does not discuss human sacrifice. In the 1780s Charles III of Spain banned its publication in Quechua in Lima, and the book was not reprinted in the Americas until 1918. It was first published in English in 1685. Nineteenth-century Peruvian scholars treated it more sceptically. He died in Córdoba, recorded as 23 April 1616.
incandescent-light-bulb: In 1761 Ebenezer Kinnersley demonstrated heating a wire to incandescence, but such wires melted or oxidised very quickly in air. The British physicist and chemist Joseph Swan began working with carbonised paper filaments in an evacuated glass bulb in 1850, and by 1860 he could show a working device. Without a good vacuum and an adequate supply of electricity, however, the bulb lasted only a short time and gave an inefficient light. By the mid-1870s better pumps had become available, and Swan returned to his experiments.

The bulb is an airtight glass envelope, either evacuated or filled with an inert gas, around a filament through which current is passed. The first commercially successful filaments were made from carbonised paper or bamboo. Carbon tended to sublimate and blacken the glass, and its resistance falls as it heats, which made lamps sensitive to the power supply. Modern bulbs use tungsten wire, usually a coiled coil, which runs hotter and evaporates more slowly. A bulb's life is a trade-off between efficiency and longevity: general lamps are set for 1,000 to 2,000 hours, while theatre and projection lamps may last only a few hours.

Historians Robert Friedel and Paul Israel conclude that Edison's version was the first practical implementation because of four factors: an effective filament material, a higher vacuum, a high resistance that made distribution from a central source economically viable, and the development of the components of a large-scale lighting system. Swan's bulb was nonetheless in daily use in London in 1881. Thomas Hughes attributes Edison's business success to his integrated system of electric lighting.

Early bulbs were blown by hand by teams of three workers, and Corning Glass Works made about 150 an hour in the 1880s. Libbey's Westlake machine went into production in 1910, and Corning's Ribbon Machine, installed in 1926, was making 1,000 bulbs per minute by 1939. Less than 5 per cent of the energy a bulb uses becomes visible light, the rest being released as heat.
incense: The word incense comes from the Latin incendere, to burn. The earliest documented use is associated with ancient Nubia: excavations at Qustul in Lower Nubia, in present-day Sudan, found one of the earliest known incense burners, of ceramic, dating to the A-Group culture of about 3300 to 3000 BCE, before Egypt's Early Dynastic period. Its decoration, including processional imagery read by some scholars as royal, suggests that incense already had ritual and political meaning.

In ancient Egypt it was burned to mask unpleasant odours, repel malevolent spirits and honour the gods, and resin balls in prehistoric tombs at El Mahasna show its early place in funerary practice. Reliefs at Deir el-Bahari depict expeditions to obtain incense and aromatic resins. The Babylonians used it in prayers and offerings to oracles, and its use passed from Mesopotamia to Greece and Rome.

Incense is aromatic plant material that releases fragrant smoke when burnt, made from local ingredients: sage and cedar among the indigenous peoples of North America, agarwood and sandalwood in China and Japan. It comes in two main kinds. Indirect-burning incense, such as the resins frankincense and myrrh, needs a separate heat source such as charcoal.

Direct-burning incense is a paste of ground fragrant material and an odourless binder, shaped into sticks, coils or cones, which smoulders once lit. Coils burn for hours or days and are common in Chinese cultures, while cones were invented in Japan in the 1800s. Trade in incense materials formed a major part of commerce along the Silk Road and the Incense Route.

Incense has served practical, aesthetic and religious ends. Its strong scent covered the smell of decay in funerals. It is offered to deities in Jewish, Christian, Taoist and Buddhist worship, and many cultures have seen the rising smoke as prayer directed to a deity on high. The incense of the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem, called ketoret, is stated in the Book of Exodus to be a mixture of stacte, onycha, galbanum and frankincense.

In China, calibrated incense sticks and incense clocks came with Buddhism, and the poet Yu Jianwu (487–551) wrote of telling the night's hours by burning incense. In Japan the art of incense appreciation is called kōdō, and in many Arab countries scented chips called bakhoor are burned to welcome guests.
incheon: Incheon has been inhabited since the Neolithic. The first historical record of the area dates from 475 CE, in the reign of King Jangsu of Goguryeo, under the name Michuhol, which is supposed to have stood on the modern Munhak Hill. The area changed names with successive kingdoms. In the Goryeo era it was called Gyeongwon or Inju, and the present name dates from 1413. Old Incheon had its centre at Gwangyo-dong, where the prefecture office and the local academy stood.

Only 4,700 people lived there when it became an international port in 1883. The other historical name, Jemulpo or Chemulpo, came into wide use only with the opening of the port, and the city centre moved from Gwangyo to Jemulpo. During Japanese rule it was internationally known as Jinsen, from the Japanese pronunciation of its Sino-Korean name. In 1914 the Japanese colonial government merged its outer parts with Bupyeong County to form Bucheon County, and between 1936 and 1940 part of that county was recombined into Incheon. The first shots of the Russo-Japanese War were fired at the Battle of Chemulpo Bay.

North Korean troops occupied Incheon on 4 July 1950. In the Battle of Inchon UN troops landed to relieve pressure on the Pusan Perimeter and to launch an offensive northward, a decisive UN victory, and the city was recaptured on 19 September 1950. The USS Inchon was named after it. Incheon was separated from Gyeonggi Province as a Directly Governed (now Metropolitan) City on 1 July 1981, and neighbouring islands and parts of Gimpo County and Ganghwa were added in 1989 and 1995. It was spelled Inchon until South Korea adopted a new Romanization system in 2000. Pro-democracy protests took place there before and during the June Democratic Movement of 1987.

Incheon is a city in north-western South Korea, bordering Seoul and Gyeonggi Province to the east, and part of the Seoul Metropolitan Area. About 3 million people live there. It is a major transportation hub in northeast Asia, with Incheon International Airport and Incheon Port. In 2003 it was designated South Korea's first free economic zone, and it hosted the Asian Games in 2014.
independent-social-democratic-party-of-g: The Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD) officially supported the war bonds for World War I in 1914. Fourteen of its 110 Reichstag members, among them Karl Liebknecht and Hugo Haase, had spoken against them but bowed to party discipline. In December 1914 Liebknecht was the only member to vote against further bonds, and in December 1915 eighteen members voted with him and Otto Rühle. Liebknecht was expelled from the parliamentary group on 12 January 1916 and the eighteen on 24 March; they formed the Social Democratic Working Group. On 18 January 1917 Friedrich Ebert had the group and the Spartacus League expelled from the party.

The USPD was founded at Gotha from 6 to 8 April 1917, with 124 delegates. Hugo Haase and Georg Ledebour were elected chairmen. It was heterogeneous, uniting traditionalists such as Haase, revisionist opponents of the war such as Kurt Eisner and Eduard Bernstein, the theorist Karl Kautsky, and the Spartacus Group, which joined as a bloc on condition of complete political independence. The party agitated against the war and welcomed the Russian Revolution. In July 1917 it voted against the Reichstag Peace Resolution as ambiguous.

When the revolution broke out in 1918, the USPD leadership was caught off guard. After the Majority Social Democrats offered a joint government, USPD members joined the Council of the People's Deputies but resigned after less than two months, as the USPD favoured a council republic and the SPD a parliamentary one. In the election of 19 January 1919 it won only 7.6 percent of the vote. At a Leipzig congress in November 1919 it adopted a programme calling for political workers' councils, with Ernst Däumig and Arthur Crispien as chairmen.

In October 1920 a party convention at Halle voted 236 to 156 to join the Comintern. The party split, and on 4 December 1920 the Left USPD, with about 400,000 members, merged into the Communist Party, while the Right USPD, with about 340,000, continued. After the murder of Walther Rathenau in June 1922 the remainder rejoined the SPD that September, though a shrunken USPD continued until 1931.
index-librorum-prohibitorum: After Gutenberg's press of about 1440, books could be mass-produced, and in the 16th century churches and governments across Europe tried to control printing. The first lists of prohibited books were not Roman: the Catholic Netherlands issued one in 1529, Venice in 1543 and Paris in 1551. A first Roman Index was printed in 1557 under Pope Paul IV and then withdrawn for unclear reasons.

In 1559 a new Index banned the entire works of some 550 authors as well as individual titles, on the view that an author's religious convictions contaminated all his writing. After the Council of Trent authorised a revised list under Pope Pius IV, the Tridentine Index of 1564 was issued, and it remained the basis of all later lists until Leo XIII published his Index Leonianus in 1897.

In 1571 a Sacred Congregation of the Index was created to examine writings denounced in Rome, to keep the list up to date and to list corrections where a work needed only amending. Such a work carried a clause such as donec corrigatur, forbidden until corrected, or donec expurgetur, forbidden until purged. The pope had to approve any addition or removal. The Index was enforceable in the Papal States but elsewhere only where civil powers adopted it, as several Italian states did. In France officials decided what was banned and the Index was not recognised, and Spain kept its own Index Librorum Prohibitorum et Expurgatorum.

The Index condemned religious and secular works alike, among them theologians such as Robert Bellarmine, Kepler's Epitome astronomiae Copernicanae (on it from 1621 to 1835), Kant's Critique of Pure Reason and unapproved Bible editions. Works by Protestant authors were barred even on subjects outside doctrine, among them Conrad Gesner's Historiae animalium and anything by Martin Luther, John Calvin or Philipp Melanchthon. Schopenhauer and Nietzsche were not named, since works contradicting dogma were forbidden anyway.

The Congregation of the Index was merged with the Holy Office in 1917. The last edition, the twentieth, appeared in 1948 with 4,000 titles. Hitler's Mein Kampf was studied for three years but not placed on it, according to the church historian Hubert Wolf, because its author was a head of state. In 1965 the Holy Office was reorganised and the Index was not listed among the new congregation's duties. A notification of June 1966 declared that the Index kept its moral force as a warning to the conscience but no longer had the force of ecclesiastical law with its penalties.
india: Modern humans reached the Indian subcontinent from Africa by about 55,000 years ago. Neolithic and chalcolithic cultures arose around Mehrgarh after 7000 BCE and gradually evolved into the Indus Valley Civilisation, which flourished during 2500 to 1900 BCE around cities such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa and Dholavira. Between 1500 and 1200 BCE an archaic form of Sanskrit diffused into India from the northwest, and its evidence is found in the Rig Veda. By the middle of the first millennium BCE caste, or varna, had emerged in the cities of the central Ganges plain, and Jainism and Buddhism arose, both stressing non-violence and rejecting birth into a fixed hereditary varna.

The Maurya Empire followed, and under Ashoka (ca. 268 to 232 BCE) it briefly controlled the major urban hubs of the subcontinent, except in the deep south. Early in the 2nd millennium Muslim armies from Central Asia intermittently overran the northern plains, eventually establishing the Delhi Sultanate. Sikhism emerged in the Punjab, and the Mughal Empire brought two centuries of economic expansion and relative peace. The British East India Company consolidated territorial control, and crown rule, the British Raj, began in 1858. A nationalist movement, noted for nonviolent resistance after 1920, was a major factor in ending British rule. In 1947 the British Indian Empire was partitioned into the dominions of India and Pakistan, a partition that brought large-scale loss of life and unprecedented migration.

The Constitution of India, drafted between 1946 and 1949, took effect on 26 January 1950 and made India a federal republic with a democratic parliamentary system. It makes untouchability illegal. The Lok Sabha, the lower house, has 543 elected members. The reorganisation of states in 1956 followed linguistic lines. India's population was 361 million in 1951. Economic reforms of the 1990s reopened the economy to the world. India has 45 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
indian-institute-of-science: The idea began with a chance meeting in 1893 between Jamsetji Tata and Swami Vivekananda on a ship, where they discussed Tata's plan to bring the steel industry to India. Five years later Tata wrote to Vivekananda of his scheme for a research institute of science for India. Interested in education and the skills needed for industrial projects such as steelmaking, he had sent his associate Burjorji Padshah on a world tour in 1896 to examine research institutions, and Padshah produced a guiding document, An Institute of Scientific Research for India, in 1898.

Tata formed a provisional committee, which presented a draft proposal to Viceroy George Curzon on 31 December 1898. The Nobel laureate Sir William Ramsay was asked to propose a suitable place and suggested Bangalore.

The land and other facilities were donated by Maharaja Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV and by Tata. The maharaja gave about 371 acres (150 ha) and also granted Rs 500,000 towards capital expenditure and Rs 50,000 for annual expenses, while Tata gave several buildings. Nizam Osman Ali Khan also contributed around Rs 300,000 over 31 years. The vesting order that allowed the institute to function was signed on 27 May 1909. Early in 1911 the maharaja laid the foundation stone, and on 24 July the first students were admitted to the departments of General and Applied Chemistry under Norman Rudolf and of Electro-Technology under Alfred Hay. The Department of Organic Chemistry opened within two months.

Morris Travers, a co-worker of Ramsay in the discovery of the noble gases, who had played a part in the founding, became the first director. The first Indian director was the Nobel laureate Sir C. V. Raman. The institute was the first in India to introduce master's programmes in engineering, and it was deemed a university by the University Grants Commission in 1958.

The main campus is fully residential and spreads over about 400 acres in the north of Bengaluru. Its Main Building, designed by C. F. Stevens and Company of Bombay in 1912–13, is classical in style and fronted by a grey tower, and in front of it stands a monument by Gilbert Bayes in memory of J. N. Tata. Departments and centres belong either to the Science Faculty or to the Engineering Faculty. Research students make up more than 60 per cent of those on campus, and an undergraduate programme in science, begun during the centenary celebrations in 2009, admitted its first students in 2011.
indian-institutes-of-technology: In the late 1940s a 22-member committee headed by Nalini Ranjan Sarkar recommended founding such institutions in various parts of India, along the lines of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The first was set up at the site of the Hijli Detention Camp in Kharagpur, West Bengal, and formally inaugurated by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad on 18 August 1951. Jawaharlal Nehru said at its first convocation in 1956 that a monument of India's future stood where the detention camp had been. On 15 September 1956 Parliament declared the Kharagpur institute an Institute of National Importance. On the Sarkar Committee's recommendation four more campuses followed, at Bombay in 1958, Madras and Kanpur in 1959 and Delhi in 1961, scattered across India to prevent regional imbalance.

The Institutes of Technology Act, notified as Act Number 59 of 1961 and in force from 1 April 1962, gave the IITs legal status and degree-granting powers. Each IIT is autonomous, and all are linked through the IIT Council, with the president of India as ex officio visitor. Under each board of governors is a director, the chief academic and executive officer.

The Bachelor of Technology is the most common undergraduate degree, a four-year programme with eight semesters, and the first year is often common to all students. The IITs also offer dual degrees, master's degrees and doctorates, and they subsidize undergraduate fees by approximately 80%. All provide on-campus residential facilities, and students live in hostels throughout their stay.

Until the liberalisation of the early 1990s India experienced large-scale emigration of IIT graduates to developed countries, especially the United States. Since 1953 nearly twenty-five thousand have settled there. Critics call this a brain drain at the cost of Indian taxpayers, while others argue that the money graduates sent home helped to expand India's foreign exchange reserves.

The relationship between caste, reservation and academic merit has been contested since the institutions were established. Ajantha Subramanian argues that the IITs gained a distinctive status partly through exemption from reservation policies, with the Joint Entrance Examination as the symbol of merit. Reservation of 22.5% of seats for SC and ST students came in 1973, and 27% for Other Backward Classes in 2006.
indian-national-army: Before the Second World War, Japan and South-East Asia were refuges for exiled Indian nationalists. Japan sent intelligence missions into South Asia, notably under Major Iwaichi Fujiwara, whose F Kikan made contact with Indian nationalists in Thailand and Malaya. About 70,000 Indian troops, mostly Sikhs, were stationed in Malaya, and in the Malayan Campaign many were captured, nearly 45,000 after the fall of Singapore alone. From these prisoners the first Indian National Army was formed under Captain Mohan Singh. He refused to align it with the Japanese and resigned after ordering it to disband, which ended the first INA.

Subhas Chandra Bose reached Singapore from Nazi Germany in May 1943, and on 4 July he took over the Indian Independence League and the Second INA. Around 18,000 Indian civilians in the region also enlisted. On 23 October 1943 Azad Hind declared war on Britain and the United States. Bose insisted that the INA should rank as an allied army in the Japanese offensive towards Manipur rather than serve only for espionage and propaganda. Its 1st Division, under Shah Nawaz Khan, advanced through Tamu towards Imphal and Kohima, but the offensive was halted, and in the withdrawal many INA soldiers died of starvation.

In 1945 the INA took part in the defence of Burma, and surviving units surrendered at various places in early April. Nearly 6,000 troops under A. D. Loganathan remained in Rangoon and surrendered as the city fell. The INA has been described as a collaborationist force, and its battlefield performance was poor.

Of the INA's 43,000 recruits, 16,000 were captured, and the British charged 300 officers with treason. Between November 1945 and May 1946 about ten courts-martial were held in public at the Red Fort in Delhi. Claude Auchinleck hoped they would turn opinion against the INA, but the first accused, Prem Sahgal, Gurubaksh Singh Dhillon and Shah Nawaz Khan, a Hindu, a Muslim and a Sikh, were acclaimed by many Indians as patriots. Philip Mason wrote that in a matter of weeks the INA were acclaimed as heroes who fought for the freedom of India. The Indian National Congress and the Muslim League both made the release of the prisoners a political issue.

Several INA veterans later held public office: Mohan Singh sat in the Rajya Sabha, Shah Nawaz Khan was Minister of State for Rail in the first Indian cabinet, and Lakshmi Sahgal, Minister for Women's Affairs in the Azad Hind government, became a public figure in India.
indian-national-congress: During the later 1870s Indians made concerted efforts to found a pan-Indian organisation with nationalist political influence. In 1883 Allan Octavian Hume, a retired British civil servant known for his pro-Indian activities, set out the idea of a body representing Indian interests in an open letter to graduates of the University of Calcutta. Its aim was to win a greater share in government for educated Indians. A meeting planned for Poona was moved to Bombay because of a cholera outbreak, and the first session of the Congress was held there from 28 to 31 December 1885. Hume organised it with the approval of the Viceroy, Lord Dufferin, and served as general secretary.

From its start the Congress was led by Moderates influenced by Western liberalism, who demanded the rule of law and equality regardless of caste, creed or sex. By 1905 it had divided in two. The Moderates, among them Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale, sought self-government by peaceful, constitutional means within the British Empire. The Extremists, led by Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal and Bal Gangadhar Tilak, favoured a more confrontational course.

Mahatma Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and joined the Congress. After the First World War the party came to be associated with him as its unofficial spiritual leader. In 1920 he allied with the Khilafat Movement against British rule, using civil disobedience, or satyagraha, as his tool, and in 1922 he suspended the agitation after policemen were killed at Chauri Chaura.

After independence in 1947 the Congress dominated Indian politics. In the first general election of 1952 it won 364 of 479 contested seats, and it held power nationally until 1977. Its first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, led it to support a mixed economy, the Planning Commission and Five-Year Plans. In 1969 the party split, and from 1975 to 1977 Indira Gandhi declared a state of emergency.

The party has governed India for more than 54 years, with six prime ministers from its ranks, the first being Nehru. Under Nehru it oversaw the founding of institutions such as the Indian Institutes of Technology and the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, and it helped shape India's non-aligned foreign policy during the Cold War.
indian-ocean: The Indian Ocean covers 70,560,000 km2, about 20% of the water area of the Earth's surface, with an average depth of 3,741 m. It is bounded by Asia to the north, Africa to the west and Australia to the east, and to the south by the Southern Ocean or Antarctica, depending on the definition in use. Its large marginal seas include the Andaman Sea, the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal and the Laccadive Sea. In 1953 the International Hydrographic Organization drew its borders to include the Southern Ocean; in 2002 it delimited the Southern Ocean separately.

Unlike the Atlantic and Pacific, the Indian Ocean is enclosed by major landmasses on three sides and does not stretch from pole to pole. Its climate is governed by the monsoon, the strongest on Earth. Strong north-east winds blow from October until April, and from May until October south and west winds prevail. The monsoon reverses the large seasonal currents, including the Somali Current.

The Indian Ocean, together with the Mediterranean, has connected people since ancient times, whereas the Atlantic and Pacific long acted as barriers. The ocean is named after India, which projects into it, and has been known by its present name since at least 1515, when the Latin form Oceanus Orientalis Indicus is attested. Ancient Greek geography called the part known to the Greeks the Erythraean Sea. Chinese explorers of the 15th century, such as Zheng He of the Ming dynasty, called it the Western Oceans.

The written history of the ocean has been largely Eurocentric, because it depends on the sources of the European colonial era. It is often divided into an ancient period and an Islamic period, followed by Portuguese, Dutch, French and British periods. A concept of an Indian Ocean World, based on the monsoon that linked Asia, China, India and Mesopotamia, is sometimes called the first global economy. It developed independently of European trade in the Mediterranean and Atlantic and remained largely independent of it until the colonial dominance of the 19th century. The first human settlement around its shores dates to the Pleistocene, with fossils of Homo erectus found in India.
indian-rebellion-of-1857: The East India Company had been in India since 1612, but its victory at the Battle of Plassey in 1757 began its firm foothold in eastern India. In 1764 it defeated the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II at the Battle of Buxar and gained the right to collect revenue in Bengal, and the Anglo-Mysore and Anglo-Maratha Wars brought more territory under its control.

The rising had no single cause. Resentment grew over invasive British-style social reforms, harsh land taxes, the summary treatment of some landowners and princes, and doubts about British claims of material improvement. The Bengal Army, which recruited heavily among high-status Hindus and comparatively wealthy Muslims, was the largest of the Company's three armies. The immediate flashpoint is often linked to the Pattern 1853 Enfield rifle-musket, whose greased paper cartridges were opened with the teeth. In early 1857 a rumour spread that the grease was cow tallow, offensive to Hindus, and pig lard, offensive to Muslims.

The rebellion began on 10 May 1857 with a mutiny of sepoys at Meerut, 40 miles northeast of Delhi. Early on 11 May the 3rd Cavalry reached Delhi and called on the 81-year-old Mughal ruler Bahadur Shah II to lead them, and he was proclaimed Emperor. Most accounts hold that he was coerced. His adhesion turned the Sikhs of the Punjab away from the rebellion, and the large princely states, including Hyderabad, Mysore, Travancore and Kashmir, did not join it.

Rebels took large parts of the North-Western Provinces and Awadh. At Lucknow, Sir Henry Lawrence fortified the Residency, and after 90 days of siege the defenders were reduced to 300 loyal sepoys, 350 British soldiers and 550 non-combatants. Rani Lakshmi Bai of Jhansi, whose state had been annexed under the doctrine of lapse, became a centre of revolt. British forces retook Kanpur by mid-July and Delhi by the end of September 1857, and the rebels were defeated at Gwalior on 20 June 1858.

Both sides committed atrocities against civilians. Rebels killed British officers and civilians, including women and children, and British reprisals fell on rebels and their supporters, sometimes entire villages. Some estimates put the toll in Awadh alone at 150,000 Indians killed, 100,000 of them civilians. Bahadur Shah II was tried for treason and exiled to Rangoon, where he died in 1862, ending the Mughal dynasty.

The Government of India Act 1858 dissolved the East India Company and placed India under the Crown. The Bengal Army was scaled back and recruitment in the Punjab increased. The name remains contested: Indian Mutiny, Revolt of 1857 and First War of Independence are all used.
indian-subcontinent: The Indian subcontinent is a physiographic region of Asia that takes in most of the Himalayas and the land south of them, projecting into the Indian Ocean between the Bay of Bengal to the east and the Arabian Sea to the west. Politically it is divided among Bangladesh, India and Pakistan, whose territories were part of historical and British India before the partition of 1947. The term is more geophysical than South Asia, which is more geopolitical and which also includes Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

The Indian plate rifted from Gondwana and drifted north towards Eurasia. Its collision with Eurasia closed the Neo-Tethys Ocean, and the suture zone that marks India's welding to Eurasia, the Indus-Yarlung suture zone, lies north of the Himalayas. The headwaters of the Indus and of the Yarlung Tsangpo, later the Brahmaputra, flow along it, and the two rivers define the western and eastern limits of the Himalayan range.

The region around and southeast of the Indus River was often called simply India in historical sources, and historians still use India for the whole subcontinent when discussing the time before the British Raj. The use of subcontinent in this sense is attested from the early twentieth century, when most of the territory was part of the British Empire or allied with it, as a convenient term for British India and the princely states together. Since the partition of British India, many in Pakistan and Bangladesh have found the name offensive, because India is placed first in it.

Four religions originated in the subcontinent: Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism and Sikhism. They share terminology, concepts and goals, and spread from South Asia into East and Southeast Asia. Early Christianity and Islam were brought to the coastal regions by merchants who settled among the local people. Sindh, Balochistan and parts of the Punjab later came under conquest by the Arab caliphates, with an influx of Muslims from Persia and Central Asia, and under the Islamic sultanates and the Mughal Empire Islam spread more widely across South Asia.
indian-territory: Indian Territory and the Indian Territories described an evolving area that the United States government set aside for the relocation of Native Americans, a policy that grew out of the Indian removal of the 18th and 19th centuries. It was not the traditional territory of the tribes settled on it. Its general borders were set by the Indian Intercourse Act of 1834, and it was the successor to the remainder of the Missouri Territory. Congress never passed an Organic Act for it, so it was never an organized territory. Treaties restricted entry by non-Indians, and the tribes were largely self-governing, with established governments, until after the Civil War.

The idea descended from the British Indian Reserve, set up by the Royal Proclamation of 1763. The Five Civilized Tribes, the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee Creek and Seminole, ceded most of their southeastern lands between 1814 and 1840. The Indian Removal Act of 1830, pursued aggressively by Andrew Jackson, sent them to what became Oklahoma, a relocation known as the Trail of Tears during the Choctaw removals that began in 1831. The tribes established capitals at Tahlequah, Tishomingo, Tuskahoma, Okmulgee and Wewoka. The territory's size shrank as Wisconsin, Iowa, Minnesota and Dakota territories were formed, and by the Civil War it was essentially the present boundaries of Oklahoma.

Most of the Five Civilized Tribes signed treaties with the Confederacy, and Stand Watie, a Cherokee brigadier general, was the last Confederate general to surrender, on 23 June 1865. After the war the 1866 treaties reduced the tribes' lands and made room for Plains Indians and Midwestern tribes. The Organic Act of 1890 reduced Indian Territory to the lands of the Five Civilized Tribes and the Quapaw Agency tribes and created Oklahoma Territory from the west. In 1905 the people of the territory sought admission as the State of Sequoyah but were rebuffed, and the Oklahoma Enabling Act, signed on 16 June 1906, joined the two territories, effectively extinguishing Indian Territory with statehood in November 1907.

In 2020 the Supreme Court's decision in McGirt v. Oklahoma prompted a review of tribal lands, and almost the entire eastern half of Oklahoma was subsequently found to have remained Indian country. The population of Indian Territory was estimated at 94,860 in 1838 and 82,334 in 1884.
indira-gandhi: Indira Nehru was born on 19 November 1917 in Allahabad, into a Kashmiri Pandit family. Her father, Jawaharlal Nehru, was a leading figure in the movement for independence from British rule. She was her parents' only surviving child and grew up with her mother, Kamala Nehru, at the Anand Bhavan estate. Her childhood was lonely: her father was often away or in prison, and her mother, frequently ill, died of tuberculosis in February 1936. She studied in India and Switzerland and at Santiniketan, founded by Rabindranath Tagore, and married Feroze Gandhi, with whom she had two sons, Rajiv and Sanjay.

In 1959, as president of the Indian National Congress, she played a part in the dissolution of the communist-led Kerala government. Lal Bahadur Shastri made her minister of information and broadcasting in 1964, and after his death in January 1966 she defeated Morarji Desai in the party's leadership election. Party bosses and the press at first called her a dumb doll, Goongi goodiya in Hindi. The Congress expelled her in 1969, and her faction, the INC (R), won a landslide in 1971 under the slogan Garibi Hatao (Remove Poverty), an answer to the opposition's Indira Hatao.

In 1969 she nationalised fourteen major commercial banks. In December 1971 India intervened in the war in East Pakistan, where the Pakistani army's repression had sent about ten million refugees across the border; it ended in Indian victory and the independence of Bangladesh. India tested a nuclear device in 1974, and Sikkim joined the Indian Union in 1975. After extending the state of emergency twice, she called elections in 1977 and lost her seat as Congress fell from 350 seats to 153. Congress returned in January 1980, and Sanjay died in a plane crash on 23 June.

In Punjab the preacher Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, whom Congress had helped to prominence, moved into a guest house near the Golden Temple in 1982 with about 200 armed followers. Indira Gandhi was assassinated on 31 October 1984, while chairing the Non-Aligned Movement. World leaders mourned her, and Margaret Thatcher travelled to New Delhi for the funeral. She had received the Bharat Ratna in 1971, and Henry Kissinger's phrase iron lady became her nickname.
indo-european-languages: The Indo-European family is native to the north of the Indian subcontinent, most of Europe and Greater Iran, with further branches in Armenia and parts of the southern subcontinent. Historically its languages were also spoken in Anatolia and north-western China. Eight branches are still spoken: four by hundreds of millions of native speakers each (Indo-Iranian, Italic, Germanic and Balto-Slavic) and four by fewer than fifteen million each (Hellenic, Albanoid, Armenian and Celtic). Two major branches, Anatolian and Tocharian, are extinct.

Over 3.4 billion people speak an Indo-European language as a first language, the most of any language family. Ethnologue estimates about 446 living languages, of which 313 belong to the Indo-Iranian branch. Several European languages, among them English, French, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish and Dutch, spread through colonialism in the modern period.

All Indo-European languages descend from a single prehistoric language, reconstructed as Proto-Indo-European and spoken sometime in the Neolithic or early Bronze Age. Its homeland is the subject of competing hypotheses. The academic consensus supports the Kurgan hypothesis, which places it on the Pontic–Caspian steppe, in what is now Ukraine and southern Russia, in association with the Yamnaya culture.

The oldest records are isolated Hittite words and names in Assyrian texts from Kültepe in eastern Anatolia, dating to the 20th century BCE. The Anitta text, in Hittite, dated to 1700 BCE, is the oldest known text in an Indo-European language, and fragmentary Mycenaean Greek records date from between 1450 and 1350 BCE. How the parent language split into its branches is not attested, and the timeline is disputed: David Anthony places Pre-Anatolian at about 4200 BCE and Proto-Indo-Iranian at about 2200 BCE.

European visitors to the Indian subcontinent began to notice similarities among Indo-Aryan, Iranian and European languages in the 16th century. In 1583 the Jesuit Thomas Stephens wrote from Goa of likenesses between North Indian languages and Greek and Latin, and in 1585 the merchant Filippo Sassetti compared Sanskrit and Italian words, such as sapta and sette for seven. Neither led to further inquiry. In 1647 the Dutch scholar Marcus Zuerius van Boxhorn proposed a common ancestor that he called Scythian.

In 1786 Sir William Jones told the Asiatic Society of Bengal that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin bore a stronger affinity than could have arisen by accident and had sprung from some common source which perhaps no longer existed. The analysis of these relationships and the reconstruction of their common source were central to the development of historical linguistics as a discipline in the 19th century. The current consensus accepts no genetic link between the family and any other language family.
indo-greek-kingdom: After Alexander's death in 323 BCE, Bactria came under Seleucus I Nicator, and the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom arose when its satrap Diodotus I seceded from the Seleucid Empire, in about 255 or 246 BCE, since the sources disagree. In India the Maurya dynasty was overthrown in about 185 BCE by Pushyamitra Shunga, who founded the Shunga Empire, and this is thought to have encouraged Greek expansion. Demetrius I, son of Euthydemus, is generally considered the Greco-Bactrian king who first launched it, and so the founder of the Indo-Greek realm. His father was a Magnesian Greek according to Polybius.

The name Indo-Greek Kingdom loosely covers a number of Hellenistic states ruling from regional capitals such as Taxila, Sagala, Pushkalavati and Bagram. No narrative history survives for India; the main Greco-Roman source is Justin's anthology of Pompeius Trogus. The most successful king was Menander I, who expanded the kingdom to its widest extent; his coins are the most numerous and widespread, and his capital was at Sakala in the Punjab. Buddhist literature remembers him as Milinda, a convert to Buddhism. After his death most of his empire splintered, and new kingdoms and republics east of the Ravi began to mint their own coins.

In about 115 BCE Heliodorus came as ambassador of King Antialkidas to the Shunga king Bhagabhadra at Vidisha and set up a pillar dedicated to Vāsudeva, showing that the Indo-Greeks readily followed Indian religions. Through the 1st century BCE they lost ground to Indians in the east and to the Scythians, Yuezhi and Parthians in the west. About twenty kings are known from this period, down to Strato II and Strato III, who ruled in the Punjab until about 10 CE, when the Indo-Scythians ended the kingdom as a political entity.

The Indo-Greek kings combined Greek and Indian languages and symbols on bilingual coins, struck to both the Greek round and the Indian square standard, and their coinage is considered some of the most artistically brilliant of antiquity. They also struck the first known cupro-nickel coins. Their own art is poorly documented, and most Gandharan Hellenistic works are attributed to their successors, the Indo-Scythians, Indo-Parthians and Kushans. Pockets of Greek population probably remained for centuries under later rulers.
indo-pakistani-war-of-1965: Since the partition of British India in August 1947 the two states had contended over Kashmir and over other borders, notably the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, a dispute that arose in 1956 and ended with India regaining control. Pakistan had signed a defence agreement with the United States in 1954 and in the 1960s received 700 million dollars of military aid. After India's defeat in the Sino-Indian War of 1962, its army was being reorganised and re-equipped. Pakistan's forces were smaller but had an edge in air power and armour, which Pakistan wished to use before India completed its build-up.

On 5 August 1965 Pakistani soldiers dressed as Kashmiri locals crossed the Line of Control in Operation Gibraltar, intending to start an insurgency. Indian forces, tipped off by local people, captured several of them, and the operation failed. India took the Haji Pir pass, 8 km inside Pakistan administered Kashmir, by 28 August. On 1 September Pakistan launched Operation Grand Slam to capture Akhnoor in Jammu and cut Indian supply lines. On 6 September India crossed the international border in the west, and President Ayub Khan declared a state of emergency, proclaiming that Pakistan was at war.

The fighting included large armoured battles. In the Sialkot sector India's 1st Armoured Division met Pakistan's 6th Armoured Division at Phillora after 9 September, and Pakistan lost 66 tanks to India's 6 before falling back on Chawinda. At Asal Uttar, Pakistan's 1st Armoured Division pushed towards Khem Karan to threaten Amritsar, but India breached the Madhupur canal on 11 September and the offensive was halted. The war was a stalemate, with both sides holding the other's territory. About 3,000 Indian and 3,800 Pakistani soldiers were killed. The air forces of both countries fought each other for the first time since independence.

On 20 September the United Nations Security Council passed a resolution demanding an unconditional ceasefire within 48 hours. India accepted at once and Pakistan on 23 September. The Soviet Union under Premier Alexei Kosygin hosted talks at Tashkent, where Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri and President Ayub Khan signed the Tashkent Declaration on 10 January 1966, agreeing to withdraw to the lines held before August by 25 February 1966. Shastri died of a heart attack on 11 January.

Many Pakistanis criticised the ceasefire, having been told in official reports that the army was doing well, and student riots followed. In India Shastri was hailed as a national hero, and the outcome was widely viewed as a political and strategic victory, given the failure of the insurgency in Kashmir. Pakistan's forces, in this view, had to turn to the defence of Lahore.
indo-scythians: The Indo-Scythians, also called Indo-Sakas, were nomadic people of Iranian Scythian origin. Saka is more a generic term than the name of one state: Saka tribes were part of a cultural continuum of early nomads across the steppe, Iranian-speaking horse nomads who buried their dead in mound tombs called kurgans. Chinese sources record that after the Xiongnu defeated the Yuezhi, the Yuezhi moved west and displaced the Saka, who migrated south toward Bactria and present-day Afghanistan. Many settled in Drangiana, later called Sakastan or Sistan, from which the Indo-Scythian kingdom and its vassal states arose.

Maues is the first Saka king in the Indian subcontinent. Petroglyphs at river crossings in Chilas and on the Sacred Rock of Hunza mark the route across the Karakoram that he used to capture Taxila from the Indo-Greek king Apollodotus II. In 55 BCE Azes I took control of north-western India after his victory over Hippostratos. In the east the Indo-Scythians held Mathura from about 60 BCE under satraps such as Hagamasha, Hagana and Rajuvula, called the Northern Satraps. After Azes, the Indo-Parthian ruler Gondophares ended Indo-Scythian rule in the north-west, and the Kushans later regained the region, taking the Mathura area about 100 CE.

The Western Satraps ruled Kathiawar and Gujarat until the fifth century. Rudradaman I is known from the Junagadh rock inscription, which records his conquest of the Yaudheyas and his defeat of the Satavahana empire. The last Western Satrap, Rudrasimha III, was defeated by the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II in 395 CE.

Indo-Scythian coinage is generally of high quality, between Indo-Greek and Kushan work, and may have benefited from Greek coin-makers. The coins use the Greek alphabet on the obverse and Kharoshthi on the reverse, show the king on horseback or seated cross-legged, and often show Greek gods on the reverse. The Indo-Scythians seem to have supported Buddhism. Kharahostes and Rajuvula are named on the Mathura lion capital, which records the gift of a stupa with a relic of the Buddha, and coins of Azes were found in the Bimaran casket, one of the earliest representations of the Buddha. Indian texts such as the Mahabharata name them Shakas and list them among warlike tribes of the north-west.
indonesia: Indonesia is an equatorial archipelago of coastal plains, mountains and volcanic islands, extending 5,120 kilometres from east to west across three time zones and 1,760 kilometres from north to south. Published counts of its islands range from 13,000 to 25,000, and the most widely cited official count is 17,508, with about 6,000 inhabited.

Its five main islands are Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi, Borneo and New Guinea. Strategic shipping routes between the Indian and Pacific oceans run through the Malacca, Sunda and Lombok straits. The country lies on a complex plate-boundary zone, with at least 127 active volcanoes and a high exposure to earthquakes and tsunamis; the Toba super-eruption about 74,000 years ago was one of the largest known.

Java has yielded hominin fossils generally attributed to Homo erectus, and narrative cave art in Sulawesi has been dated to a minimum age of 51,200 years. From the third millennium BCE Austronesian-speaking communities moved south from Taiwan through the Philippines into the archipelago, and from around 500 BCE regional trading networks connected it with South and East Asia.

In the early centuries CE some coastal communities in Borneo, Sumatra and Java developed into trading ports, and Indian merchants and religious specialists brought Sanskrit literacy, Hindu and Buddhist practices and models of kingship that local rulers adopted. Srivijaya, founded in southeastern Sumatra in the late 7th century, became a maritime trading polity and a centre of Buddhist learning.

Rulers in central Java supported the building of Borobudur and Prambanan between the 8th and 10th centuries. Majapahit emerged in eastern Java in the late 13th century after Raden Wijaya used a Mongol expedition to defeat his rivals and then forced the Mongols to withdraw.

Its rulers claimed suzerainty over ports across the archipelago, although beyond Java this authority was often exercised indirectly through tributary, ritual and commercial relationships. Islamic states grew from the late medieval period, and European powers competed to monopolise trade in the Spice Islands of Maluku. Dutch commercial and colonial control expanded from the 17th century and covered most of the archipelago by the early 20th century.

Indonesia proclaimed its independence in the aftermath of World War II. After the fall of Suharto in 1998, decentralisation transferred substantial lawmaking powers to provincial, regency and city governments, and constitutional amendments between 1999 and 2002 introduced direct presidential elections, which began in 2004. The country is a presidential republic of 38 provinces.

The Javanese are the largest ethnic group, at about 40%. More than 700 languages are spoken, and Indonesian, a standardised variety of Malay adopted as a language of unity through the 1928 Youth Pledge, is the official language. Its motto, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, comes from the 14th-century poem Sutasoma.
indonesia-raya: While living in Jakarta, Wage Rudolf Supratman, a musician and young reporter, read an essay in Timbul magazine that challenged Indonesian music experts to compose a future national anthem. He took up the challenge, and the song, titled Indonesia, was completed in Bandung in 1924. According to Tempo the words were revised after Supratman was reportedly inspired by Tan Malaka's book Massa Actie, published in 1926, and the song went through several revisions before reaching its final form in 1928.

That year youths from across Indonesia held the first Indonesian Youth Congress to push for independence. Supratman asked the organisers for access to report on it, and they asked him not to publish, for fear that the Dutch authorities would ban the event. Encouraged by the leader Sugondo Djojopuspito, he played the song on the violin on 28 October 1928, at the Second Indonesian Youth Congress, hoping it would one day become the national anthem.

After the congress many political and student organisations distributed the text, and the press played a key part. The daily Soeloeh Ra'jat Indonesia published the words on 7 November 1928, and the Chinese Indonesian weekly Sin Po followed on 10 November, an act of defiance towards the Dutch. In 1929 Supratman retitled the song Indonesia Raya, Great Indonesia, and printed pamphlets himself; all one thousand copies sold quickly. The businessman Tio Tek Hong issued the first records that year, but in 1930 the Dutch colonial authorities banned the song and confiscated the unsold records.

The first stanza was chosen as the national anthem when independence was proclaimed on 17 August 1945, and the constitution and a state gazette of 1958 confirm that only that stanza serves as the anthem. It is played at flag-raising ceremonies in schools every Monday, and at the main ceremony on 17 August each year.

The song marked the birth of the archipelago nationalist movement that aimed to end Dutch colonial rule. Because there was no orchestral version, the Indonesian government asked the Dutch arranger Jozef Cleber in 1950 for a symphonic one. President Sukarno found his first recording too frilly and wanted something solemn like the Dutch Wilhelmus. Cleber considered that impossible, saw some of the character of the Marseillaise in the tune, and made a second arrangement marked maestoso con bravura, which Sukarno approved. It remained in use for 47 years, until a remastered version by Addie MS in 1998.

Supratman died in 1938, and his four surviving sisters inherited the rights. The state became owner when the song became the national anthem, and in 1958 the government obtained the sole right from his family, rewarding each sister with 250,000 rupiah in 1960.
indonesian-national-armed-forces: Before the Republic of Indonesia existed, military authority in the Dutch East Indies lay with the Royal Dutch East Indies Army and the Royal Netherlands Navy. They did not directly form the later Indonesian forces and were mainly the enemy during the Indonesian National Revolution of 1945 to 1949, but the Army had given military training to some future officers. It recruited Ambonese, Kai Islanders, Timorese and Minahasan people, and in 1940 it opened to large intakes of Javanese, among them the future officers Suharto and Abdul Haris Nasution.

The forces themselves were formed during the Revolution, when they fought a guerrilla war alongside informal militia. They began as the People's Security Agency on 22 August 1945, became the People's Security Forces on 5 October 1945 and then the Armed Forces of the Republic of Indonesia in January 1946. The name Tentara Nasional Indonesia was first used on 3 June 1947. Later names included the War Forces of the Republic of Indonesia (1950 to 1962) and the Armed Forces of the Republic of Indonesia, ABRI (1962 to 1999). The name Tentara Nasional Indonesia was restored on 1 April 1999.

The Army, Navy and Air Force have long been organised along territorial commands, a legacy of the guerrilla war and of the need for internal security. Seven commands were established by 1958, and no central reserve formation existed until 1961. Only after the attempted coup of 1 October 1965 and General Suharto's rise to the presidency did it become possible to integrate the services and develop a joint operations structure. A 1985 reorganisation separated the Ministry of Defense and Security from the ABRI headquarters, leaving the commander in chief in command of the forces and a member of the cabinet.

The military philosophy is civilian-military defence, called Total People's Defence. It foresees three stages: a short period in which an invader defeats the conventional army, a long period of territorial guerrilla warfare, and a final expulsion, with the army as a rallying point from village level upwards. The Armed Forces Enters the Village programme, begun in 1983, is held three times a year to build civilian projects. Indonesia has also sent forces to UN peacekeeping missions, including in Lebanon and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The President of Indonesia is Supreme Commander. Each service has a chief of staff, but only the commander of the armed forces holds command authority over all three. Special forces include the army's Kopassus and the navy's Kopaska. After the Surabaya bombings of 2018 President Joko Widodo agreed to revive a joint special operations command, and in July 2019 he formed the Armed Forces Special Operations Command. In January 2021 a regulation created a reserve component, with voluntary membership.
indonesian-national-revolution: Indonesian nationalism grew rapidly in the first half of the 20th century. The independence movement is dated to 20 May 1908, commemorated as the Day of National Awakening. Budi Utomo, Sarekat Islam, the Indonesian National Party and the Indonesian Communist Party took different paths, some cooperating with the Volksraad in hope of self-rule, others refusing to cooperate.

The Japanese occupation of three and a half years during the Second World War was a crucial factor. The Netherlands could hardly defend its colony, and within three months the Japanese held it. In Java and, to a lesser extent, Sumatra they encouraged nationalist sentiment for their own advantage, elevated leaders such as Sukarno and destroyed much of the infrastructure built by the Dutch.

Japan surrendered on 15 August 1945, and radical youth groups, the pemuda, pressed Sukarno and Hatta to proclaim independence on 17 August. The next day Sukarno was elected president and Hatta vice-president. The Netherlands, weakened by the war, did not return as a significant military force until early 1946, and Allied forces under British command acted as caretakers in the interval.

In November 1946 the British brokered the Linggadjati Agreement, under which the Netherlands recognised the Republic as the de facto authority over Java, Madura and Sumatra. Neither party was satisfied. At midnight on 20 July 1947 the Dutch launched Operatie Product, a major offensive to regain economically valuable areas, which they described as police actions. Republican forces were confined to the Yogyakarta region. Alongside the war came social revolutions against aristocrats and village heads, and in East Sumatra the sultanates were overthrown and many aristocrats killed.

Resistance and diplomacy turned world opinion against the Dutch, and the second police action was a diplomatic disaster for them. The United States, threatening to cut off economic aid, pushed the Netherlands into negotiations. At the Round Table Conference at The Hague, from 23 August to 2 November 1949, the Netherlands agreed to recognise a federal United States of Indonesia over all the former Dutch East Indies except Dutch New Guinea, and Indonesia took on a colonial debt of 4.5 billion guilders. Sovereignty was transferred on 27 December 1949.

Estimates of Indonesian deaths in fighting and among civilians range from 97,421 to 100,000, and more than 4,000 Dutch soldiers died. The revolution ended Dutch colonial administration and reduced the power of many local rulers, but did not significantly improve the fortunes of most of the population.
indra: Indra is of ancient but unclear origin, and the roots of his name have been contested among scholars since the 19th century. Aspects of him resemble other Indo-European thunder gods, such as Zeus, Thor and Perun, who are linked to rain and thunder and share parts of his heroic mythology. A tablet from Boghaz-köi, dated to about 1400 BCE, records a treaty that names Mitra, Varuna, Indra and Nasatya among its gods. Modern scholarship suggests that the name arose at the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex, where the Aryans lived before settling in India.

More than a quarter of the 1,028 hymns of the Rigveda mention Indra, which makes him the deity referred to most often. The commonest theme is his killing, with his thunderbolt, of the serpent Vritra, which held back the rains; the rivers are thereby released. In the Rigveda he is armed with a thunderbolt, the vajra, rides a chariot and has golden hair. In later art he rides a four-tusked white elephant, Airavata, and the rainbow is called his bow. His abode is Amaravati, the capital of Svarga.

In post-Vedic texts his importance declines and he is shown as an intoxicated, hedonistic god, a minor figure beside Vishnu, Shiva or Devi. The Puranas, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata make him a son of the sage Kashyapa and of Aditi, and husband of Shachi. According to the Vishnu Purana, Indra is a title borne by the king of the gods, which changes with each Manvantara, a cyclic period of time in Hindu cosmology.

In Buddhism Indra, called Śakra or Sakka, rules over the Trāyastriṃśa heaven above Mount Sumeru, one of the realms of rebirth, and Buddhist texts reduce him to a figurehead who himself suffers rebirth. In Jainism he is not the king of the gods but the king of superhumans in Svarga-Loka, and Jain literature knows sixty-four Indras who attend the five auspicious events in the life of a Tirthankara. In Iranian religion the roles were reversed, and the Vendidad names Indra as a relatively minor demon. Tamil Sangam literature describes a month-long festival for Indra, the Indra Vila, held for want of rain.
indus: The Indus is 3,180 kilometres long. It rises in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China, where it is known as Sengge Zangbo, flows northwest through Ladakh and Gilgit-Baltistan, and bends sharply to the left after the Nanga Parbat massif. It then runs south-by-southwest through Pakistan and empties into the Arabian Sea near Karachi. Its left-bank tributary on the plains is the Panjnad, formed by the successive confluences of the five Punjab rivers: the Chenab, Jhelum, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. Its principal right-bank tributaries are the Shyok, Gilgit, Kabul, Kurram and Gomal.

Its headwaters, with those of the Yarlung Tsangpo to the east, follow the suture where the Indian plate collided with the Eurasian plate about 50 million years ago. Its traditional name in Sanskrit and Tibetan is Sindhu, a word for river, and the English name derives through Greek and Old Persian from the same root, as do Hindustan and India.

The cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, date back to around 3300 BCE and were among the largest human settlements of the ancient world. The civilisation reached from northeast Afghanistan to Pakistan and northwest India, and over 1,052 cities and settlements have been found, mainly around the Ghaggar-Hakra River and its tributaries; only about 40 sites lie on the Indus and its tributaries. Its people were the first to build irrigation canals in the valley, and the Kushan and Mughal empires later built canals too.

In the 2nd millennium BCE the Punjab was called Sapta Sindhu in the Rigveda and Hapta Həndu in the Avesta, both meaning seven rivers. Early kingdoms of the valley included Gandhāra and Sindhu-Sauvīra. The river became known to the western world when King Darius of Persia sent his Greek subject Scylax of Caryanda to explore it, about 515 BCE. In 1850 the British East India Company introduced modern irrigation and restored old canals, and the British supervised the building of one of the most complex irrigation networks in the world.

The Indus is the chief supplier of water to the plains of Punjab and Sindh, where rainfall is meagre, and it is the backbone of agriculture in Pakistan. The river is sacred to Hindus, and the Sindhu Darshan Festival is held on its banks at Leh. The Indus River dolphin is found only in this river.
indus-script: Early examples of the script come from pottery inscriptions and clay impressions of inscribed seals dated to about 2800–2600 BCE, in the Early Harappan period, where they appear alongside administrative objects such as seals and standardised weights. Excavations at Harappa show that some symbols developed from potters' marks and graffiti of the earlier Ravi phase, about 3500–2800 BCE. In the Mature Harappan period, from about 2600 to 1900 BCE, strings of signs are common on flat rectangular stamp seals and on pottery, tools, tablets and ornaments. At Harappa the use of the script largely ceased around 1900 BCE as inscribed seals went out of use, though it may have lasted longer in other regions, for example at Rangpur in Gujarat.

The signs are largely pictorial, depicting objects of the Harappan world and of nature, though many abstract signs have also been identified. Some are compounds of simpler signs, and some resemble tally marks and are often interpreted as numerals. The number of principal signs is over 400, which is considered too many for each to stand for a single sound, so the script is generally believed to be logo-syllabic. Iravatham Mahadevan listed 419 distinct signs in the 1970s, while in 2015 Bryan Wells estimated around 694. Just 67 signs account for 80 per cent of usage.

Most scholars agree that the script was generally read from right to left, though exceptions are known. The direction has been deduced from external evidence, such as signs crowded on the left side as if the writer were running out of space at the end of a row. Seals were small, mostly 2–3 centimetres on a side, and animals such as bulls and elephants often accompany the text.

The first publication of a seal with Harappan symbols dates to 1875, in a drawing by Alexander Cunningham. By 1992 about 4,000 inscribed objects had been found, some as far away as Mesopotamia. The script has not been deciphered. The inscriptions are very short, averaging around five signs, no bilingual text like the Rosetta Stone has been found, and the language is unknown. Over 100 mutually exclusive attempts at decipherment have been published since the 1920s, without scholarly consensus. Some scholars, among them Asko Parpola and Iravatham Mahadevan, argue that the language was Dravidian, while others propose an Indo-Aryan or Munda language. Steve Farmer, Richard Sproat and Michael Witzel argued in 2004 that the signs were nonlinguistic, a view Parpola disputed.
