indus-valley-civilisation: The civilisation lasted from 3300 BCE to 1300 BCE, and in its mature form from 2600 BCE to 1900 BCE, across much of Pakistan, north-western India and north-eastern Afghanistan. Its area was larger than ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia combined. It is called Harappan after Harappa, the first site excavated, in the 1920s. The early Harappan cultures grew out of Neolithic cultures, of which the best known is at Mehrgarh in Balochistan, one of the earliest sites of farming and herding in South Asia. A gradual drying of the region during the third millennium BCE may have stimulated urbanisation, and flood-supported farming produced surpluses that supported cities.

Over a thousand Mature Harappan sites have been reported, but there are only five major urban centres: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Ganeriwala, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi. Mohenjo-daro and Harappa probably held 30,000 to 60,000 people each. The cities were noted for grid planning, baked-brick houses, covered drains and water supply, and merchants traded by caravan with Central Asia and the Iranian plateau.

Around 1900 BCE signs of decline appeared, and by about 1700 BCE most cities were abandoned. In 1953 Sir Mortimer Wheeler proposed that Aryan invaders caused the end, but scholars rejected this because the skeletons he cited belonged to a later period. Many now point to drought, a weakening monsoon and a decline in trade with Egypt and Mesopotamia. After 1900 BCE the number of sites in India rose from 218 to 853, as people moved east.

Archaeology gives no direct answer about who ruled the cities. The consistency of weights and measures and the uniform planning suggest some central authority, and theories range from a single state to self-governing city states. An ivory scale from Lothal has a smallest division of about 1.704 millimetres. Craftsmen worked copper and bronze alloyed with tin, arsenic and lead. Between 400 and 600 distinct symbols of the undeciphered Indus script are known, and typical inscriptions are about five characters long. Interpretations of Indus religion are largely speculative. Mohenjo-daro was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980 and Dholavira in 2021.
industrial-revolution: Several factors enabled industrialisation: high agricultural productivity, as in the British Agricultural Revolution, which supplied surplus labour and food; managerial and entrepreneurial skills; ports, rivers, canals and roads that moved raw materials and goods cheaply; natural resources such as coal, iron and waterfalls; political stability and a legal system that supported business; and capital available to invest. Innovations such as Jethro Tull's seed drill of 1701 and Andrew Meikle's threshing machine of 1784 cut the labour that farming required. Before the change, most manufacturing took place in China and India, and India, China and parts of the Middle East produced most of the world's cotton cloth.

The textile industry was the first to use modern production methods. In 1750 Britain imported 2.5 million pounds of raw cotton, mostly spun and woven by hand in Lancashire homes and workshops. By 1787 raw cotton consumption was 22 million pounds, most of it spun on machines, and in 1800 the industry used 52 million pounds. Mechanised spinning powered by water and later steam raised output per worker by a factor of around 500, and the power loom by a factor of 40.

Coke replaced charcoal in iron making: in 1720 Britain made 20,500 tons of charcoal iron and 400 tons with coke, and in 1806 coke cast iron reached 250,000 tons. John Roebuck's lead chamber process of 1746 began large-scale chemical production. Steam supplied an estimated 10,000 horsepower in Britain by 1800 and 210,000 by 1815, though water and wind supplied most industrial power early on. William Murdoch's gas lighting reached London between 1812 and 1820, and steam locomotives came in the early 19th century. Mechanised production spread to continental Europe and the United States by about 1840.

Historians debate the precise start and end of the Industrial Revolution and the pace of its changes. Growth slowed from the late 1830s as markets for the early innovations matured, and revived after 1870 with the steel-making, assembly-line and electrical innovations of the Second Industrial Revolution. The earliest recorded use of the term Industrial Revolution was in 1799, by the French envoy Louis-Guillaume Otto, and Arnold Toynbee's lectures of 1881 are credited with popularising it.

Output and population grew at unprecedented rates. Visible poverty, a growing population and new wealth caused tensions between rich and poor, which led to ideas such as socialism, communism and anarchism. Children as young as eight worked in textile mills. Economists such as Robert Lucas Jr. hold that for the first time the living standards of ordinary people began sustained growth, while others say they did not improve meaningfully until the 20th century. After the Industrial Revolution most manufacturing took place in North America and Western Europe.
inferno-dante: Dante probably began work on the Comedy around 1306, although some modern scholars argue that the composition of the Inferno began as late as 1313, and early commentators proposed start dates before 1302. He had been exiled from Florence in 1302 after his faction, the pro-empire White Guelphs, was defeated by the pro-papal Black Guelphs, and he spent nearly all of the last fifteen years of his life on the Comedy. Many scholars agree that the Inferno was begun in 1306–1307 and completed in 1309–1310, though revisions probably continued. Giovanni Boccaccio and some other early commentators held that Dante composed the first seven cantos before his exile.

The poem describes the journey of a fictionalised Dante through Hell, guided by the ancient Roman poet Virgil. Hell is depicted as nine concentric circles of torment within the Earth, culminating at the centre, where Satan is held in bondage. As an allegory, the Divine Comedy represents the journey of the soul toward God, and the Inferno the recognition and rejection of sin. Each punishment is a contrapasso, a symbolic instance of poetic justice: fortune-tellers, for example, must walk with their heads on backward because they tried to see the future by forbidden means.

The poem begins on the night of Maundy Thursday in 1300, when Dante, aged 35 and "midway in the journey of our life", finds himself lost in a dark wood. His way is blocked by three beasts, a leopard, a lion and a she-wolf. Virgil explains that he has been sent by Beatrice, and the two enter the gate of Hell, which bears the inscription ending "Abandon all hope, ye who enter here".

The circles are Limbo, for the unbaptised and the virtuous pagans; lust; gluttony; greed; wrath; heresy; violence; fraud; and treachery. The eighth circle, Malebolge, is a funnel of stone with ten concentric ditches, and the ninth is a frozen lake, Cocytus, where traitors are held in ice according to their guilt. Among the damned are historical persons and figures of Dante's own Florence, such as the Ghibelline leader Farinata degli Uberti and Emperor Frederick II, both in flaming tombs among the heretics.
ingelheim-am-rhein: Ingelheim lies on the left bank of the Rhine in the north of Rhenish Hesse, in the bend of the river west of Mainz. The Rhine forms its northern limit, and to the south the town stretches into the valley of the Selz, which flows into the Rhine at Frei-Weinheim. The ending -heim in the name probably goes back to Frankish times, as far as the fifth or sixth century. The name is recorded as Ingilinhaim in 782, and since 1269 a distinction has been made between Nieder-Ingelheim and Ober-Ingelheim, Lower and Upper Ingelheim.

The area was settled in prehistoric times, but it became important only under Charlemagne and his successors. Charlemagne had the Ingelheim Imperial Palace built after 785, and in the time that followed synods and imperial diets were held there. The palace served emperors and kings as lodging and ruling seat until the eleventh century. Charlemagne held court at Ingelheim in 807, and his son and successor Emperor Louis the Pious died there on 20 June 840, in a summer tent on an island in the Rhine off the town.

In the High and Late Middle Ages the importance of the Palatinate, and with it Ingelheim, shrank. The Ingelheimer Oberhof, the Ingelheim Upper Court, is of particular importance in German legal history, since a unique collection of its judgments from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries has survived. The Dutch writer Multatuli, Eduard Douwes Dekker, lived in Ingelheim in the late nineteenth century. In 1939 the formerly self-governing municipalities of Nieder-Ingelheim, Ober-Ingelheim and Frei-Weinheim were merged into the town of Ingelheim am Rhein.

Ingelheim is the seat of the Mainz-Bingen district in Rhineland-Palatinate. Remnants of the Imperial Palace can be seen beside the Museum bei der Kaiserpfalz, which has an exhibit on the palace, with archaeological finds, architectural sculpture and a model of the building. A golden solidus found in 1996 is so far the only gold coin known to have been struck with Charlemagne's effigy. The town also has a Carolingian aqueduct and the Ohrenbrücker Tor, a gate of the town wall first mentioned in the thirteenth century.
ingolstadt: Ingolstadt is an independent city on the Danube in Upper Bavaria. The old town stands about 374 metres above sea level in a wide, flat basin, where the river Schutter reaches the Danube from the west. The Ingolstadt basin borders the foothills of the Franconian Jura, and lowland forests of the Danube reach into the urban area. The river there is between 80 and 100 metres wide and flows from west to east past the old town.

The place was first mentioned in a document of Charlemagne of 6 February 806 as Ingoldes stat, the place of a person named Ingold. It was granted city status around 1250. In the late Middle Ages it was one of the capitals of the Bavarian duchies, alongside Munich, Landshut and Straubing. Louis VII, Duke of Bavaria ordered the building of the New Castle and of the Church of Our Lady, a Gothic hall church begun in 1425 as the intended burial place of the dukes of Bavaria-Ingolstadt.

The university founded in 1472 became an influential defender of the Catholic Church in the Reformation era, led by scholars such as Johann Eck. In 1516 William IV, Duke of Bavaria wrote and signed the Bavarian Reinheitsgebot in the city. On 30 April 1632 the German field marshal Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly died there during a Swedish siege. Ingolstadt was the first fortress in Germany to hold out for the whole length of a Swedish siege, and the Swedes withdrew. A cannon inside the fortress shot the horse from under King Gustavus Adolphus, and its remains are kept in the city museum.

Adam Weishaupt, who founded the Order of Illuminati in the city in 1776, was born there in 1748. After the French invasion of 1799 the fortress was demolished and the university was moved to Landshut. The Bavarian fortress, in use from 1537 to 1930, held the future French president Charles de Gaulle as a prisoner of war during the First World War. In 1945 the car maker Auto Union arrived, and it was formally re-founded in Ingolstadt in 1949, with Marshall Plan aid. It became the modern Audi company after Volkswagen took it over in 1964.

The historic old town has been preserved, with Gothic buildings such as the old ducal castle of about 1255, the Kreuztor of 1385 and the Old City Hall. The New Castle and the Tilly redoubt house the Bavarian Army Museum, the oldest museum in the city. The Old Anatomy building of 1723 to 1736 holds the German Museum of Medical History, and Mary Shelley set part of Frankenstein in the city. The city has two universities and Audi is the largest employer in the region.
ingria: Ingria, also called Ingermanland, takes in the area around the Neva River, the south-eastern shore of the Gulf of Finland and the south-western shore of Lake Ladoga. Its historical boundaries reached the Narva River in the west and the Sestra River in the north. The Votians and Izhorians, both Baltic Finnic peoples, are among its indigenous peoples. The origin of the name is uncertain. One explanation derives it from the River Inger, a tributary of the Neva; another from Eymund's saga, which says that the Swedish princess Ingegerd Olofsdotter received Ladoga and its lands from Yaroslav the Wise on her marriage in 1019, so that the region became Ingegerd's land.

From the 750s Ladoga served as a bridgehead on the Varangian trade route to Eastern Europe. In the 12th century western Ingria was absorbed by the Novgorod Republic, and centuries of wars followed, chiefly between Novgorod and Sweden. Ingria became a Swedish dominion in the 1580s and was returned to Russia by the Treaty of Teusina in 1595. Russia ceded it to Sweden in the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617, after the Ingrian War of 1610 to 1617. Sweden valued it as a buffer for the Karelian Isthmus and Finland and as a toll on Russian Baltic trade.

Under Swedish rule the province remained sparsely populated, about 15,000 in 1664. Efforts to introduce Lutheranism met repugnance among the Orthodox peasantry, but Lutheran Finns from Savonia and Karelia settled voluntarily, and they made up 73.8 per cent of the population in 1695. Russia reconquered the region in the Great Northern War and founded Saint Petersburg in 1703 near Nyen. Sweden formally ceded it in the Treaty of Nystad in 1721. In 1919 and 1920 the short-lived Republic of North Ingria held a small area near the Finnish border, returned to Soviet Russia by the Treaty of Tartu in 1920.

Historic Ingria covers about the same area as the city of Saint Petersburg and seven districts of Leningrad Oblast. Under the Soviet Union the Ingrian Finns were deported and dispersed from the late 1920s, and both they and the Izhorians all but disappeared from the region, outnumbered by Russian immigration. The 1926 census recorded 114,831 Ingrian Finns, and the Soviet census of 1989 counted 829 Izhorians.
ingrian-finns: Ingria is the historical region that corresponds to the central part of today's Leningrad Oblast. During Swedish rule in 1617 to 1703 its population changed drastically. After the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617, and especially after the War of Rupture of 1656 to 1658, much of the Orthodox population fled to Russia, largely in response to heavy taxation and to Swedish pressure to convert to Lutheranism. Lutheran migrants from Finland settled the empty lands, mainly the Äyrämöiset from the Karelian Isthmus and the Savakot from Savo. For many the region was a frontier that offered an escape from taxes and military service. The movement was mostly voluntary, though some Forest Finns from Närke were forced to move.
Finns made up 41.1 percent of the population in 1656 and 73.8 percent in 1695, and by the end of the century they were about three quarters of a rural population of some 60,000.

Russia conquered Ingria in 1702 to 1703 and founded Saint Petersburg in 1703. Under Russian rule the Ingrian Finns became serfs, forbidden to move, but they kept their Lutheranism while Orthodox Christianity became dominant among a growing Russian population. After serfdom ended in 1861 many became independent peasants. The Kolppana seminary for teachers and cantors was founded in 1863, a first library opened in 1850 and the first Finnish-language newspaper, Pietarin Sanomat, began in 1870. There were 130,413 Ingrian Finns in 1897 and more than 140,000 by 1917.

After the 1917 revolution Ingrian Finns on the southern Karelian Isthmus seceded from Soviet Russia and formed the Republic of North Ingria with Finnish backing. The Treaty of Tartu of 14 October 1920 returned it to Soviet Russia. From 1928 to 1939 North Ingria's Finns formed the Kuivaisi National District, with Finnish as its official language.

Collectivisation began in 1928, and between 1929 and 1931 18,000 people from North Ingria were deported to East Karelia, the Kola Peninsula and Central Asia. Further deportations followed in 1935 and 1936 as the Soviet Union planned border zones free of the Finnic peoples, whom it considered politically unreliable. In 1941 Moscow decided that Ingrian Finns were unreliable, and in 1942 most of those left in Ingria were relocated to Siberia. After the Continuation War, most of those evacuated to Finland were returned to the Soviet Union and dispersed in Central Russia, though nearly 4,000 stayed in Finland.

From 1991 to 2010 about 25,000 Ingrian Finns moved to Finland under its Law of Return, which the government stopped applying in 2010. Many Ingrian Finns in Russia belong to the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Ingria.
ingush-people: The Ingush call themselves Ghalghai, a name most often linked to the word ghāla, tower or fortress, so that it means people of towers. Georgian sources knew them as Gligvi and Dzurdzuks, and Russian sources as Kists. Their ethnonym Ingush comes from the medieval village of Angusht, which by the end of the 17th century was a large settlement in the Tarskoye Valley.

In the early Bronze Age the territory of Ingushetia lay where the Maykop and Kuro-Araxes cultures met, and the Koban culture, dated from the 12th to the 4th century BCE, is usually tied to the origins of the proto-Ingush. Late in the 1st millennium BCE Koban tribes formed a large union known as Malkh or, in Georgian sources, Dzurdzuketi, which controlled the Darial Gorge. It was defeated at the beginning of the 2nd century BCE by the Seleucid king Antiochus III.

From the late 9th to the early 13th century the Ingush belonged to the kingdom of the Alans, and some Ingush researchers place its capital, Magas, on the territory of present-day Ingushetia. On 4 to 6 March 1770, 24 Ingush elders swore an oath of allegiance to the Russian Empire at Barta-Bos, near Angusht, although each side treated such oaths as a union treaty and relations stayed much the same.

In the 19th century the Ingush resisted Russian expansion in the Caucasian War and were considered half-conquered. In 1860 their lands formed the Ingushskiy Okrug of the Terek Oblast, and the 1897 census counted 47,409 Ingush in the empire.

In the Soviet period an Ingush alphabet based on the Latin script was introduced in 1923 and the first newspaper in the language, Serdalo, appeared that year. The 1939 census counted 92,120 Ingush. They were exiled en masse in 1944. In 1992 the Republic of Ingushetia was formed within the Russian Federation, and armed clashes with Ossetians over the Prigorodny district of North Ossetia killed 583 people according to the Russian prosecutor's office. The capital Magas was founded in 1995.

The Ingush are predominantly Sunni Muslims and speak the Ingush language. Their society was traditionally classless, built on clans and unwritten law, with about 350 clans in Ingushetia today. Villages were governed by senior family members and acted together only in great danger, and the Ingush had no titles giving civil authority over others. Their stone architecture is tied to life in the mountains: a family had a tower, a church and a necropolis. Combat towers usually had five or six levels and a stepped pyramidal roof, with the entrance on the second floor.
inhambane: Inhambane, also known as Terra de Boa Gente, 'Land of the Good People', lies on Inhambane Bay, 470 km north-east of Maputo. The settlement owes its existence to a deep inlet into which the small Mutamba River flows. Two protective sandy headlands shelter the harbour and form a sandbank. The sister town of Maxixe stands across the bay, and motor and dhow taxis sail between the two. Inhambane has one of the largest working fleets of dhows on the Swahili Coast.

Inhambane is one of the oldest settlements on Mozambique's eastern coast. It is recorded as a city-state that submitted to successive powers, beginning with the Kilwa Sultanate, then the Gaza Empire, and finally Portuguese Mozambique. Dhows traded here as early as the 11th century, and Muslim and Persian traders, the first outsiders to arrive by sea, dealt in pearls and ambergris. The area was known for cotton spinning and production by the Bitonga. Before the Portuguese came, the Karanga had invaded and formed a number of local chiefdoms, dominating the Tonga cotton workers and profiting from the trade with Muslim merchants.

Vasco da Gama put in to replenish stocks and explore, and named the place Terra de Boa Gente. In 1505 a ship sent by Francisco de Almeida was wrecked south of the town, and the Portuguese gained a first meeting with the Karanga chiefs. They established a permanent trading post in 1534, and in 1560 Inhambane was chosen as the first Jesuit mission to Southeast Africa. The port grew as an ivory and slave trading centre, particularly in the 18th century under mostly Indian control.

Soshangane destroyed it in 1834, but it grew rapidly in the second half of the century as a town of Portuguese East Africa, and the old cathedral and old mosque were built in that period. In the 20th century its standing declined, as Maputo, called Lourenço Marques before 1975, became the main centre.

Inhambane is the capital of Inhambane Province. The census of 2017 gave it a population of 79,724, up from 54,157 in 1997. The Cathedral of Our Lady of Conception, about 170 years old, stands in the old quarter, and the city has a museum and a central market, the Mercado Central, on its main boulevard. The beaches of Tofo and Barra lie nearby.
inigo-arista: Íñigo Arista, Eneko in Basque, was a Basque chieftain and the first king of Pamplona. His origin is obscure, and even his father's name is disputed: a charter preserved at Leyre calls him Íñigo son of Jimeno, another document Íñigo Garcés, commonly called Arista, while the chroniclers Ibn Hayyan and Al-Udri indicate that his father was also named Íñigo. The nickname Arista appears as early as the 10th century and may come from the Basque Aritza, the oak, or the Latin Aresta. His mother married the muwallad lord Musa ibn Fortun, bearing Musa ibn Musa, who became head of the Banu Qasi and ruler of Tudela. Because of this kinship Íñigo and his kin often acted in alliance with Musa.

The family rose through struggles over Frankish and Córdoban influence. In 816, according to Ibn Hayyan, a Córdoban campaign routed the pro-Frankish Velasco the Gascon, lord of Pamplona, and killed him, which appears to have allowed the anti-Frankish Íñigo to come to power. In 820 he is said to have ejected the Frankish vassal Aznar I Galíndez from the County of Aragon in favour of García Galíndez, who became his son-in-law.

In 824 a Carolingian force under the counts Aeblus and Aznar Sánchez was defeated at the second battle of Roncesvalles. Tradition has this crown Íñigo as king, though there is no direct evidence of his part in the battle, and Arab chroniclers give him the same title of lord of Pamplona as Velasco.

In 840 an attack by Abd Allah ibn Kulayb, wali of Zaragoza, drove Musa ibn Musa to rebel against the Emirate of Córdoba, and Íñigo's son García, as regent, and Íñigo's brother Fortún Íñiguez joined him. Abd-ar-Rahman II launched reprisals. In 843 Fortún was killed, and the next year Íñigo's son Galindo went over to Córdoba. A peace followed in 845, and in 850 Musa rebelled again with Pamplona's support.

Íñigo died after a long illness, during which his son García Íñiguez was already governing, and was reported buried at the monastery of Leyre, which he is said to have granted the town of Yesa in 842, though the grant's authenticity is disputed. The dynasty he founded reigned for about 80 years until a rival dynasty supplanted it in 905. Because of intermarriage, later kings of Navarre descended from him, and he is remembered as the founder of Navarre.
inle-lake: Inle Lake lies in the Nyaungshwe Township of Shan State, in the Shan Hills. It is the second largest lake in Myanmar, with an estimated surface area of 116 square kilometres, and one of the country's highest, at 880 metres. The average water depth in the dry season is 2.1 metres, and the deepest point is 3.7 metres. The lake drains through the Nam Pilu at its southern end. Large sections are covered by floating plants, and its clear waters hold more than 35 native fish species, 17 of them endemic. The climate is tropical monsoon, with a rainy season from June to October.

The people of the lake, the Intha, live in four towns bordering it, in small villages along its shores and on the water itself. Most are devout Buddhists and live in houses of wood and woven bamboo on stilts, and are largely self-sufficient farmers. Fishermen are known for a distinctive rowing style, standing at the stern on one leg with the other leg wrapped round the oar. It arose because the reeds and floating plants made it hard to see ahead from a seat, and only men practise it.

The lake dwellers also grow vegetables and fruit in gardens floating on the surface. Farmers gather weeds from the lake bottom and make them into beds anchored by bamboo poles. The gardens rise and fall with the water level, so are resistant to flooding. Between 1935 and 2000 the open water shrank by 32.4 per cent, and about 93 per cent of the loss is thought to be due to floating-garden agriculture, a practice introduced in the 1960s.

The lake area has an established weaving industry. It produces hand-woven silk fabrics known as Inle longyi, and a lotus silk made only at Inle Lake and in Cambodia, which was used for robes for the Buddha. The Hpaung Daw U Festival, which lasts 18 days, falls between August and October, and its boat races, with teams of leg-rowers in Shan dress, are among the most anticipated events. In 2015 the lake became Myanmar's first biosphere reserve, and since 2018 it has been a Ramsar site.
inn-river: The Inn is a right tributary of the Danube and its third largest by discharge. It rises in the Swiss Alps, west of St. Moritz in the Engadine, a valley named after the river and the only Swiss valley whose waters end in the Black Sea. Soon after its source the river passes through its largest lakes, Lake Sils and Lake Silvaplana. It runs north-eastwards into Austria and from Landeck eastwards through Tyrol and its capital Innsbruck, then crosses into Bavaria near Kufstein. There it passes Rosenheim and Wasserburg am Inn, turns east at Mühldorf, and takes in the Alz and the Salzach. From there to Passau it forms the border between Bavaria and Upper Austria, passing Braunau am Inn and Schärding.

At Passau, where the Ilz also joins, the Inn enters the Danube. Its average flow at the mouth is 735 cubic metres a second, greater than the Danube's at that point, and its watershed holds Piz Bernina, the highest point in the Danube basin. It is still counted as the tributary because the Danube is longer, drains a larger area and flows more evenly.

The name comes from old Celtic words, en and enios, meaning water. The first written mention, in a Roman text of the years 105 to 109, speaks of Sextilius Felix being sent to seize the banks of the Aenus, which flows between the Rhaetian and the Noric peoples. Greek and Latin authors called it Ainos or Aenus, and medieval Latin wrote Enus or Oenus; the Old Bavarian change from e to i turned Enus into In. The double n appeared in the 16th century, as in the Tyrolian Landreim of 1557. The Tyrolean section was first called Aenus by Venantius Fortunatus in the 6th century.
Since at least the 16th century the source has been placed uniformly in the lakes by the Maloja Pass, though it was once believed to lie near the Reschen Pass.

The river is also known for floods. On 3 June 2013 its discharge at Passau reached 6,820 cubic metres a second and its level 12.85 metres, the highest recorded flood level there since 1501, and the old centre of Passau was severely flooded. Today 24 hydroelectric power plants stand on the Inn.
inner-hebrides: The Inner Hebrides lie off the west coast of mainland Scotland, to the south east of the Outer Hebrides, and have a mild oceanic climate. They comprise 35 inhabited islands and 44 uninhabited islands of more than 30 hectares, covering about 4,130 km2. Skye, Mull and Islay are the largest, with Skye alone covering 1,656 km2. Skye and Mull are mountainous, and the Cuillins of Skye are the highest mountains, while Tiree is low-lying. Strong tides sweep many of the islands, and the Corryvreckan tide race between Scarba and Jura is among the largest whirlpools in the world.

The islands were first settled in the Mesolithic. A flint arrowhead from Islay has been dated to 10,800 BCE, and at Staosnaig on Colonsay hundreds of thousands of burned hazelnut shells, dated to about 7000 BCE, record a communal harvest. Hearths on Jura dated to 6000 BCE are the earliest stone-built structures found so far in Scotland. Pliny the Elder gives the earliest written reference, naming 30 Hebudes. In the 6th century the kingdom of Dál Riata was founded, covering roughly Argyll and Bute, Lochaber and County Antrim. Columba founded a monastery on Iona, which made Dál Riata important in the spread of Christianity in northern Britain.

Viking raids on the British Isles are recorded from 793. Iona was sacked in 802 and 806. Norse rulers held the islands as the kingdom of the Suðreyjar for more than 400 years. After Somerled, who styled himself Lord of Argyle, died in 1164, his sons divided the southern isles. Haakon Haakonarson of Norway led an expedition, fought the stalemate of the Battle of Largs and died in Orkney in 1263. The Hebrides passed to the Kingdom of Scotland by the Treaty of Perth in 1266.

The Lords of the Isles, a title first recorded in 1336, ruled the Inner Hebrides as subjects of the King of Scots. John MacDonald, the fourth lord, made a secret treaty with Edward IV of England in 1462, and James IV forfeited the lordship for the last time in 1493. In the 19th century the Highland Clearances evicted many people and replaced them with sheep farms, and emigration became widespread. The Crofters' Act of 1886 followed years of disturbance.

The islands had 18,948 inhabitants in 2011, and Scottish Gaelic is spoken by about 4,000. The south forms part of the Argyll and Bute council area and the north of the Highland Council area. Tourism, crofting, fishing and whisky distilling are the main commercial activities. Sea transport is essential, with ferries running to the mainland and between the islands.
inner-mongolia: Inner Mongolia is a long, narrow region along the north of China. It borders eight provincial-level divisions and shares two-thirds of the length of China's border with the country of Mongolia, as well as a small section with Russia. Because it stretches so far from east to west, its eastern part is often counted with Northeastern China and its western part with North China. The winters are very long, cold and dry, the springs arid with large sandstorms, and the summers warm to hot. The terms Inner and Outer Mongolia in Chinese derive from the Manchu words dorgi and tulergi.

Before the rise of the Mongols in the 13th century, the central and western parts, especially the Hetao region, passed back and forth between Chinese farming communities in the south and northern peoples including the Xiongnu, Xianbei, Khitan, Jurchen and Tujue. The history of the east is mostly one of alternating Tungusic and Mongol tribes. After Genghis Khan unified the Mongol tribes in 1206, the Western Xia was conquered in 1227 and the Jin dynasty fell in 1234. Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271, and his summer capital Shangdu (Xanadu) stood near present-day Dolonnor.

After the Ming overthrew the Yuan in 1368, they took parts of the region and rebuilt the Great Wall roughly along its present southern edge. After the Tumu incident of 1449, when the Oirat ruler Esen taishi captured the Chinese emperor, Mongols moved south from Outer Mongolia, and until 1635 Inner Mongolia was the political and cultural centre of the Mongols of the Northern Yuan. The Manchus gained far-reaching control of its tribes in 1635, when Ligden Khan's son surrendered the Chakhar Mongols, and the Qing dynasty administered the Mongolian Plateau differently in each region.

Outer Mongolia gained independence from the Qing in 1911, and almost all banners of Inner Mongolia recognised the Bogd Khan as supreme ruler of the Mongols, though internal strife prevented unification. The Republic of China suppressed the Mongol rebellions and reorganised the region into provinces, among them Rehe and Chahar. After the Second World War the Chinese Communists, with Soviet support, established the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region in 1947. It first covered only the Hulunbuir region and was expanded westwards over the next decade into its present elongated shape under its leader Ulanhu.

The Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region has Hohhot as its capital, with Baotou, Chifeng, Tongliao and Ordos among its other major cities. Han Chinese form the majority of the population, and the region has the largest Mongol population in the world, with over 4 million people. Mongolian is written in the traditional Mongolian script. Herding is the traditional subsistence of the grasslands, and Buddhist temples such as Dazhao, built in 1580, survive in Hohhot.
innsbruck: Innsbruck stands on the River Inn at its junction with the Wipp Valley, which gives access to the Brenner Pass 30 kilometres to the south. It lies in a broad valley between high mountains, the Karwendel Alps to the north and the Patscherkofel and the Serles to the south. The name means bridge over the Inn, and the town began in the Middle Ages as a strategic crossing of the river.

In the 4th century the Romans set up an army station, Veldidena, at Oenipons, as Innsbruck was then called, to guard the commercial road from Verona over the Brenner to Augsburg in their province of Raetia. The name Veldidena survives in the district of Wilten. In 1363 Innsbruck came under Habsburg control, and in 1429 it became the capital of all Tyrol.

In the 1490s Emperor Maximilian I also resided in the city, and it became a centre of European politics and culture. A regular postal service between Innsbruck and Mechelen was set up in 1490. The Golden Roof was completed around 1500, and the Court Church holds a funeral monument for Maximilian, partly erected by his successors, with a cenotaph and bronze statues of real and mythical ancestors of the emperor. After the Treaty of Pressburg the city was for a time part of Bavaria, and it returned to Austria after the Congress of Vienna.
Austria was annexed by Nazi Germany in 1938. Innsbruck held two subcamps of the Dachau concentration camp, and between 1943 and April 1945 it suffered twenty-two air raids and heavy damage.

Innsbruck is the capital of the Austrian state of Tyrol and the fifth-largest city in Austria, with 132,188 inhabitants. It hosted the Winter Olympics in 1964 and 1976 and the Winter Paralympics in 1984 and 1988. Among its modern buildings is the Bergisel ski jump, designed by Zaha Hadid and completed in 2002.
innu: The ancestors of the Innu lived on these lands as hunter-gatherers for many thousands of years. They call their homeland Nitassinan, meaning "our land", or Innu-assi, "Innu land". Innu means "people" in their language, Innu-aimun, which belongs to the Cree–Montagnais–Naskapi dialect continuum and is unrelated to the Inuit languages of nearby peoples. The Innu are broadly divided into the Montagnais in the forested south and the Naskapi in the north, who differ in dialect and partly in way of life. Since about 1990 the Montagnais have generally chosen to be called Innu, while the Naskapi have kept the name Naskapi.

Scholars do not describe the Innu as a warlike people, though they at times clashed with the Inuit, the Haudenosaunee, the Mi'kmaq and the Abenaki, and some of these hostilities were a side effect of European contact. Around Tadoussac they were military allies of the French in their wars with the British and their Indigenous allies, and the Haudenosaunee raided into Innu territory during the Iroquois Wars of the 17th century. In June 1609 Samuel de Champlain set out with a party of Wendat, Algonquin and Montagnais warriors and reached the lake later named after him.

Innu oral tradition records two versions of how the French came to settle at Uepishtikueiau, which became Quebec City. In one, gifts of food and goods made the Innu dependent, and the French then turned to trade for furs. In the other, more widespread, the Innu taught the French to survive, conflict followed, and the Innu, outnumbered and outarmed, withdrew from the area. In 1976 the Labrador Innu organised the Naskapi Montagnais Innu Association, renamed the Innu Nation in 1990, and they have never ceded their territory by treaty.

All Innu groups were traditionally nomadic. The Montagnais moved within the forested south of the peninsula, the Naskapi over the barren lands of the north. They hunted caribou in the east and north and moose in the west, and also took beaver, bear, fish, salmon and seals, and gathered berries and maple sap. They lived in wigwams covered with birchbark in the south and caribou hide in the north, and travelled by canoe in summer and by snowshoe and toboggan in winter. Women prepared the hides and made much of the clothing.

Pre-colonial belief encouraged respect for animals. The caribou was the most revered, shamans performed shaking tent rites, and hunters placed bones and skulls in trees or on raised platforms. About 28,960 people of Innu origin live in settlements and reserves in Quebec and Labrador. At its own request the Davis Inlet community was relocated to a mainland site, Natuashish, and the Innu of Labrador won recognition as status Indians in 2002.
innviertel: The Innviertel, officially the Innkreis, is the north-western of the four traditional quarters of Upper Austria, the others being the Hausruckviertel, Mühlviertel and Traunviertel. It includes the districts of Braunau am Inn, Ried im Innkreis and Schärding and covers about 2,250 square kilometres. The landscape is a fertile, flat to hilly part of the Alpine foothills between the Salzach, Inn and Danube and the Hausruck hills. Its main towns are Braunau am Inn, Ried im Innkreis and Schärding, which is known as a tourist centre for its baroque town centre. Since the formation of political districts in 1868 the quarters have had no legal basis and are purely regional names.

From the sixth century most of the Innviertel was part of the Mattiggau region of the stem duchy of Bavaria, with ducal courts at Ranshofen and Mattighofen. In 1507 it became part of the Rentamt of Burghausen. For centuries the area served Bavaria as an eastern defence line against the rising Archduchy of Austria and as arable land. During the Bavarian uprising of 1705 to 1706 against Habsburg occupation, Braunau was the seat of the short-lived Bavarian State Defence Congress in December 1705, called the Braunau Parliament.

The death in 1777 of the childless Bavarian elector Maximilian III Joseph, which ended the Bavarian line of the Wittelsbachs, led to the War of the Bavarian Succession. With the Treaty of Teschen the Innviertel became part of Upper Austria in 1779. At first it was called the Fünfte Viertel, the Fifth Quarter, and before that it had been known as Innbaiern. The population was not content under Habsburg rule, and the cry Lieber bayrisch sterben als kaiserlich verderben, better to die Bavarian than suffer imperial ruin, was long in circulation. After the Treaty of Schönbrunn of 1809 Bavaria took the Innviertel again in 1810. The Treaty of Munich returned it to Austria on 1 May 1816.

The people of the Innviertel kept their Bavarian dialect, a West Central Austro-Bavarian variety, despite adopting much Austrian standard vocabulary. The colourful house facades of the Inn-Salzach style in its towns recall Bavarian tradition. Rivalry with the rest of Upper Austria lasted into the twentieth century, and today the inhabitants identify more closely with their region than those of the other quarters. Franz Xaver Gruber, composer of Silent Night, the Schwanthaler family of sculptors, the conscientious objector Franz Jägerstätter and the physicist Anton Zeilinger were born there.
institutional-revolutionary-party: The party was founded on 4 March 1929 as the National Revolutionary Party (Partido Nacional Revolucionario) by Plutarco Elías Calles, president from 1924 to 1928 and self-proclaimed Jefe Máximo of the Mexican Revolution. It answered the political crisis caused by the assassination of president-elect Álvaro Obregón in July 1928, which had shown that presidential succession had no institutional structure. Before then parties were not generally the route to the presidency. Calles meant the party to give all the surviving leaders and combatants of the Revolution a shared political space.

In 1938 Lázaro Cárdenas, known for expropriating foreign oil interests that year, reorganised it as the Party of the Mexican Revolution, aiming at a democracy of workers and socialism, which was never achieved. The name changed again in 1946, in the last year of Manuel Ávila Camacho's term, to Institutional Revolutionary Party. Observers have noted that the name sounds like a paradox, since revolution can imply destroying institutions; Rubén Gallo reads it as a sign of the party's corporatist nature, which absorbed the Revolution's disruptive energy by bringing its enemies into the party's bureaucracy.

For most of the twentieth century the PRI governed Mexico as a de facto one-party state. All presidents belonged to it, all senators until 1976 and all state governors until 1989. The president stood at the apex of the system, and the practice of the dedazo, by which he pointed to his successor, lasted until the 1990s. The party relied on corporatism, co-option, electoral fraud and political repression. From the administration of Miguel Alemán (1946–1952) to 1970 Mexico enjoyed sustained growth known as the Mexican Miracle, when GDP rose sixfold while population doubled.

Discontent grew. In 1968 the army killed hundreds of unarmed demonstrators in the Tlatelolco massacre in Mexico City, and economic crises began in the 1970s. In 1988 Carlos Salinas de Gortari won an election over Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, who had left the party, by 50.89 per cent in the official figures, after a delayed count. The PRI lost its absolute majority in the federal congress in 1997 and lost the presidency in 2000, after 71 years. Under Enrique Peña Nieto it won the presidency again in 2012.

Over nine decades the party has represented a wide range of ideologies, usually following the policies of the sitting president. It began as a social democratic party, moved left under Cárdenas and moved gradually right from 1940. Its supporters are called priistas, and it is nicknamed El tricolor after the colours of the Mexican flag. In 1990 the writer Mario Vargas Llosa described Mexico under the PRI as the perfect dictatorship, a phrase that became popular in Mexico.
insulin: In 1869 Paul Langerhans, a medical student in Berlin, noticed clumps of tissue scattered through the pancreas, later called the islets of Langerhans. In 1889 Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering removed the pancreas from a healthy dog and found sugar in its urine, establishing for the first time a link between the pancreas and diabetes. In 1901 Eugene Lindsay Opie showed that the disease arose from destruction of the islets.

In October 1920 Frederick Banting concluded that digestive secretions were breaking down the islet secretion and making extraction impossible. As a surgeon he knew that blocking the pancreatic duct would make most of the pancreas atrophy while leaving the islets intact, and he reasoned that a relatively pure extract could then be made. He and Charles Best, working in John Macleod's laboratory at the University of Toronto, were the first to isolate insulin from dog pancreas in 1921.

Insulin is a peptide hormone made by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets, and its name comes from the Latin for island. It regulates the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats and protein by promoting the absorption of glucose from the blood into the liver, fat and skeletal muscle. Decreased or absent insulin activity results in diabetes. In type 1 diabetes an autoimmune reaction destroys the beta cells, and in type 2 the tissues become resistant to insulin. Human insulin has 51 amino acids, arranged in an A-chain and a B-chain joined by disulfide bonds.

Tensions arose among the four co-discoverers in January 1922, and James Collip briefly threatened to patent his purification process separately. John G. FitzGerald, director of Connaught Laboratories, made an agreement on 25 January 1922 that none of them would patent the work with a commercial pharmaceutical firm. The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine of 1923 went to Banting and Macleod. Banting, incensed that Best was not mentioned, shared his prize with him, and Macleod shared his with Collip. The patent was sold to the University of Toronto for one dollar.

Insulin was the first peptide hormone discovered. Frederick Sanger determined its amino acid structure in 1951, making it the first protein fully sequenced, and Dorothy Hodgkin determined its three-dimensional structure in 1969. Sanger won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1958 and Rosalyn Sussman Yalow the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1977, for work on insulin.
intef-i: Intef I was a local nomarch at Thebes during the early First Intermediate Period, and later a pharaoh. He was the elder brother of Intef II, who succeeded him. He was the first member of the 11th Dynasty to claim a Horus name, Sehertawy, variously rendered as Maker of peace in the two lands, He who has brought calm to the two Lands, and Pacifier of the two lands.

By taking a Horus name with both crowns, Intef declared himself ruler of all Egypt. His authority was contested by the other nomarchs, chief among them the rulers of the 10th Dynasty at Herakleopolis Magna, who also claimed the title of pharaoh, and their powerful ally Ankhtifi, nomarch of Hierakonpolis. On his accession Intef probably ruled only the Theban nome, the fourth. It is conjectured that after defeating Ankhtifi or one of his successors he gained the three nomes to the south of Thebes, down to Elephantine, though this may instead have been achieved by his predecessor Mentuhotep I; both hypotheses remain conjectural, given the scarcity of records.

Intef was rapidly involved in a war with his northern neighbours. A graffito found at Gebel Tjauti, northwest of Thebes, reports the presence of the assault troops of the son of Ra, Intef. It has been proposed that this refers to Intef I, whose soldiers were fighting the Coptite nomarch Tjauti, although Intef II has also been proposed. A nearby stele erected by Tjauti records the building of a road across the desert which the ruler of another nome had sealed off in order to fight his nome. The defeat of Tjauti put Coptos, Dendera and the three nomes of Hierakonpolis under Theban control, extending the Theban kingdom 250 km northward to a border near Abydos.

No contemporary monument can be positively attributed to Intef I. He is known for certain from only one near-contemporary source, two inscribed blocks from the temple of Montu at Tod, erected in the reign of Mentuhotep II, which show Mentuhotep II facing the names of three ancestors, Intef I Sehertawy, Intef II Wahankh and Intef III Nakht-neb-tep-nefer. The relief establishes the succession of the kings of the 11th Dynasty.

His tomb is thought to be the Saff el-Dawaba at El-Tarif, a funerary complex dug into a hillside. It has no inscriptions but yielded the earliest type of pottery found at El-Tarif, so it is most often assigned to him. Today it lies beneath the buildings of a village.
intef-ii: Wahankh Intef II, also written Inyotef II or Antef II, was the third ruler of the Eleventh Dynasty. During the First Intermediate Period, from about 2181 to about 2055 BCE, rule of Egypt was decentralised and split between several dynasties based in different cities, and his capital was Thebes. His parents were Mentuhotep I and Neferu I. His predecessor Intef I may have been his brother, and he was succeeded by his son Intef III.

After the death of the nomarch Ankhtifi, Intef united all the southern nomes down to the First Cataract. He then clashed with his main rivals, the kings of Herakleopolis Magna, over Abydos. The city changed hands several times, but Intef II was eventually victorious and extended his rule north to the thirteenth nome. After these wars the rest of his reign was peaceful. A statue of Intef II in a sed festival robe, found at Elephantine, suggests that his authority reached the First Cataract and perhaps part of Lower Nubia. At his death he left a strong government in Thebes that controlled the whole of Upper Egypt, with a border just south of Asyut.

He never held the full fivefold titulary of the Old Kingdom pharaohs. He did claim the dual kingship nswt bity and the title son of Ra, which emphasises the divine nature of kingship, and on accession he added the Horus name Wahankh, enduring of life, to his birth name. The earliest dated mention of the god Amun at Karnak is from his reign.

The earliest surviving fragment of royal construction at Karnak is an octagonal column bearing his name, and he was the first ruler to build chapels for Satet and Khnum on the island of Elephantine. He started a tradition of royal building in the provincial temples of Upper Egypt that lasted through the Middle Kingdom. His tomb at El-Tarif is a saff tomb, with a double row of columns in front of a large trapezoidal courtyard. In the reign of Ramses IX a royal commission, recorded in the Abbott Papyrus, found his pyramid-tomb intact. No remains of the pyramid have yet been found, and the tomb lies beneath the buildings of a village.
integrated-circuit: A precursor of the integrated circuit was the micromodule, a small ceramic substrate holding a single miniaturised component, which could be assembled with others into a compact grid. Jack Kilby proposed the idea to the United States Army in 1957, which led to the short-lived Micromodule Program. As that project gained traction, Kilby devised a fundamentally new approach. Newly employed by Texas Instruments, he recorded his first ideas in July 1958, and in his patent application of 6 February 1959 he described a body of semiconductor material in which all the components of the circuit are completely integrated. The first customer was the United States Air Force. Kilby won the 2000 Nobel Prize in physics for his part in the invention.

In its strict sense the term means a monolithic circuit built on a single piece of silicon, though it is also applied to hybrid and multi-chip constructions. Chips are made by a planar process of photolithography, deposition and etching, and printed as a unit rather than built one transistor at a time. This makes them small, cheap and fast, but designing a complex chip costs many tens of millions of dollars and the factories are enormously expensive, so chips pay only where production volumes are high.

Most modern ones rest on the metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor, developed at Bell Labs between 1955 and 1960. Fred Heiman and Steven Hofstein built the earliest experimental MOS chip, with 16 transistors, at RCA in 1962, and General Microelectronics introduced the first commercial MOS circuit in 1964.

Aerospace projects helped inspire the technology. The Minuteman missile and the Apollo programme both needed lightweight digital computers for inertial guidance. The Apollo Guidance Computer motivated the technology, but it was the Minuteman missile that forced it into mass production. Minuteman and other United States Navy programmes accounted for the whole 4 million dollar integrated circuit market in 1962, and in 1968 government spending on space and defence still made up 37 per cent of a 312 million dollar market.

Complexity then rose by stages, from hundreds of transistors per chip in the late 1960s to tens of thousands by the mid-1970s. One-megabit memory chips, with over a million transistors, appeared in 1986, and microprocessors passed the million mark in 1989 and the billion mark in 2005.
intercession-of-the-theotokos: According to Eastern Orthodox Sacred Tradition, the apparition took place in the tenth century at the Blachernae church in Constantinople, where relics of the Virgin Mary, her robe, her veil and part of her belt, were kept. At four in the morning on Sunday, 1 October, Saint Andrew the Blessed, a Fool-for-Christ and a Slav by birth, saw the dome of the church open and the Virgin enter, surrounded by angels and saints. She prayed with tears for all faithful Christians, then spread her veil over everyone in the church as a protection. Andrew asked his disciple Epiphanius whether he saw it, and Epiphanius said that he did.

The Primary Chronicle of Nestor the Chronicler tells another story: the people of Constantinople called on the Mother of God to protect them from a large Rus' army, then still pagan, and the feast celebrates the destruction of that fleet in the ninth century.

The Slavonic name Pokrov and the Greek Sképē mean a cloak or shroud as well as protection or intercession. The feast falls on 14 October or 1 October and is served as an all-night vigil, but without an afterfeast. Veneration of the Pokrov in Rus' dates to the twelfth century. In the Slavic Orthodox Churches it ranks as the most important solemnity after the Twelve Great Feasts and Pascha, though the Oriental Orthodox Churches do not keep it.
Its icon, not found in Byzantine art, shows the Virgin in a luminous aureole holding a veil in her outstretched arms, with saints and angels on either side and Andrew and Epiphanius below.

In Ukraine the Intercession became the third most important holiday after Easter and Christmas, linked to the Ukrainian Cossacks, whose Zaporozhian Host took the Virgin as patroness. A presidential decree of 1999 made the day Ukrainian Cossack Day, and on 14 October 2014 another decree made it Defenders of Ukraine Day.

Many churches carry the name, among them Saint Basil's Cathedral in Moscow, officially the Church of the Intercession on the Moat, and the Church of the Intercession on the Nerl near Vladimir. Both are on the World Heritage List.
internal-combustion-engine: Various scientists and engineers contributed to the engine's development. In 1791 John Barber developed a gas turbine, and Robert Street's patent of 1794 described an engine that was also the first to use liquid fuel. In 1798 John Stevens built the first American internal combustion engine. In 1807 the Swiss engineer François Isaac de Rivaz invented a hydrogen-based engine ignited by an electric spark, and in 1808 he fitted it to a primitive working vehicle. In 1823 Samuel Brown patented the first internal combustion engine applied industrially. The first such engines did not compress the mixture, and these attempts to imitate the steam engine were very inefficient.

An internal combustion engine burns fuel with an oxidiser, usually air, in a combustion chamber that is part of the engine's working fluid flow circuit, and the expanding gases act directly on parts of the engine. The term usually means engines with intermittent combustion, such as the two-stroke and four-stroke piston engines and the Wankel rotary engine. A second class uses continuous combustion: gas turbines, jet engines and most rocket engines. In external combustion engines, such as steam engines, the working fluid is kept separate from the combustion products. Engines are usually run on hydrocarbon fuels such as gasoline, diesel fuel or natural gas, and as early as 1900 Rudolf Diesel was using peanut oil.

Most internal combustion engines serve in mobile applications and are the primary power supply of cars, aircraft and boats. Reciprocating piston engines are by far the most common power source for land and water vehicles, including automobiles, motorcycles, ships and, to a lesser extent, locomotives. The first engines were started by turning the flywheel, and the Daimler Reitwagen was started with a hand crank. All automobiles with such engines were started this way until Charles Kettering developed the electric starter.
internal-macedonian-revolutionary-organi: The Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization, IMRO, was a secret revolutionary society founded in Salonica in 1893. It sought autonomy for Macedonia and the Adrianople region within the Ottoman Empire. Its founders were Hristo Tatarchev, Dame Gruev, Petar Pop-Arsov, Andon Dimitrov, Hristo Batandzhiev and Ivan Hadzhinikolov, all connected with the Bulgarian Men's High School of Thessaloniki. They modelled it on Vasil Levski's earlier Bulgarian revolutionary organisation and took its motto, Freedom or Death. Its first statute of 1894 reserved membership for Bulgarians, but Gotse Delchev had it opened to all inhabitants of European Turkey and sought autonomy under the slogan Macedonia for the Macedonians.

The organisation remained divided over aims from the start. Some members saw autonomy leading to an independent Macedonia within a Balkan federation, others to union with Bulgaria. In practice its base stayed among Slavic speakers, primarily Bulgarian Exarchists, and it was often called the Bulgarian Committee.

After a Foreign Representation was set up in Sofia in 1896, the organisation fought the Ottomans with guerrilla tactics, in places running a state within a state with its own tax collectors. The Ottoman discovery of an ammunition depot in 1897, the Vinitsa Affair, led to wide repression and turned it into a militant guerrilla force whose bands were called chetas. In 1903 the struggle escalated into the Ilinden-Preobrazhenie Uprising, in which about 15,000 irregulars faced about 40,000 Ottoman soldiers for over seven weeks. The Ottomans destroyed some 100 villages, and afterwards IMRO turned to more systematic terrorism against civilians.

The defeat split it into a left-wing federalist faction, led by Yane Sandanski, who favoured autonomy and a Balkan Federation, and a right-wing centralist faction, led by figures such as Ivan Garvanov and Boris Sarafov, who favoured union with Bulgaria. Fighting between the factions reached assassinations: in 1907 Todor Panitsa, on Sandanski's instructions, killed Sarafov and Garvanov. In the Balkan Wars and the First World War the organisation supported the Bulgarian army. After the Treaty of Neuilly the movement separated into Macedonian and Thracian organisations.

Both Bulgaria and Yugoslavia claimed the heroes of the early IMRO, above all Delchev and Sandanski, and from 1948 to 1989 disputes over Macedonian history between them followed their political relations. Both states called the interwar leaders Todor Aleksandrov and Ivan Mihailov fascist. A new party using the name, VMRO-DPMNE, was founded in Skopje on 17 June 1990 and claims descent from the old organisation, though there is no real connection between them. A separate party, VMRO, was also revived in Bulgaria after 1989.
international-committee-of-the-red-cross: Until the middle of the 19th century armies had no organised nursing systems for their casualties and no safe institutions in which to treat the wounded. In June 1859 the Swiss businessman Henry Dunant reached Solferino on the evening of 24 June and saw the aftermath of the Battle of Solferino, in which about 40,000 soldiers died or were left wounded in a single day. Shocked by the suffering and the near-total lack of medical care, he spent several days helping to treat the wounded, organising local people to give aid without discrimination.

Back in Geneva he wrote A Memory of Solferino, published at his own expense in 1862 and sent to leading figures across Europe. It called for national voluntary relief organisations to nurse wounded soldiers and for international treaties guaranteeing the neutrality and protection of the wounded and of medics. The first Geneva Convention was signed in 1864 by 16 countries.

On 15 October 1914, soon after the First World War began, the Committee set up an International Prisoners-of-War Agency. By the war's end the Agency had handled about 20 million letters and messages and 1.9 million parcels, and its intervention led to the exchange of about 200,000 prisoners. Its card index grew to about 7 million records and led to the identification of about 2 million prisoners. In the Chaco War of 1932 the Committee visited 18,000 Bolivian prisoners and 2,500 Paraguayan detainees.

In 1995 its president, Cornelio Sommaruga, took part in the ceremony marking the liberation of Auschwitz and publicly regretted the past mistakes and shortcomings of the Red Cross towards the victims of the concentration camps.

Its operations rest on international humanitarian law: the four Geneva Conventions of 1949, the Additional Protocols of 1977 and 2005, and its own statutes. Its tasks include monitoring compliance with the Conventions, supervising the treatment of prisoners of war, tracing missing persons and acting as a neutral intermediary between warring parties. It prefers low-key confidential negotiation to public pressure, reasoning that this gains greater access; in apartheid South Africa it was granted access to prisoners such as Nelson Mandela, who later praised it. Its motto is Inter Arma Caritas, amidst war, charity.

The Assembly, of at most twenty-five Swiss citizens, sets policy, and the Directorate manages daily affairs. The Committee had only twelve employees in 1914. In 2005 it adopted the Red Crystal as a protective symbol, and Magen David Adom, which uses the Star of David, was accepted into the Movement in 2006.
international-court-of-justice: The first permanent institution for settling international disputes was the Permanent Court of Arbitration, created by the Hague Peace Conference of 1899, which was initiated by Tsar Nicholas II. It was established in 1900 and began proceedings in 1902. After the First World War the League of Nations Covenant called for a Permanent Court of International Justice, which the League established in 1920. Following a peak of activity in 1933 the court declined amid growing international tension, and the Second World War effectively ended it: it held its last public session in December 1939 and issued its last orders in February 1940.

In 1942 the United States and the United Kingdom jointly declared support for an international court after the war, and in 1943 the United Kingdom chaired a panel of jurists, the Inter-Allied Committee. Its 1944 report recommended that a new court's statute be based on that of the earlier court, that it keep an advisory jurisdiction and that acceptance of its jurisdiction be voluntary. The Charter of the United Nations established the International Court of Justice in June 1945, and it began work in April 1946.

The court has fifteen judges, elected for nine-year terms by the UN General Assembly and Security Council, with five elected every three years; no two may be nationals of the same country, and together they are to represent the main forms of civilization and the principal legal systems of the world. A party to a case that has no judge of its nationality may choose an additional ad hoc judge. Nominations come from national groups of members of the Permanent Court of Arbitration. The court sits in the Peace Palace in The Hague, its working languages are English and French, and a Registry serves as its permanent secretariat.

Its jurisdiction in contentious cases rests on consent, and only states may be parties. It also gives advisory opinions requested by the General Assembly, the Security Council or other authorised UN bodies. It applies international conventions, custom and the general principles of law, and its decision binds only the parties to the case. No appeal is possible.

Among the contentious cases are a complaint by the United States in 1980 over the detention of its diplomats in Tehran, a dispute of 1984 over the maritime boundary in the Gulf of Maine and a complaint by Iran in 1989 after the shooting down of Iran Air Flight 655. After the court ruled in Nicaragua v. United States that the American covert war against Nicaragua violated international law, the United States withdrew in 1986 from the court's compulsory jurisdiction. Rulings are binding, but the court has no formal enforcement mechanism, and enforcement rests with the Security Council, where the five permanent members hold a veto.
international-monetary-fund: During the Great Depression countries sharply raised barriers to trade in an attempt to improve their failing economies. This led to the devaluation of national currencies and a decline in world trade, and the breakdown of international monetary cooperation created a need for oversight. Representatives of 45 governments met at the Bretton Woods Conference in the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, to discuss a framework for postwar international economic cooperation and how to rebuild Europe. The Fund was established there in July 1944, on the ideas of Harry Dexter White and John Maynard Keynes.

For its first three decades the Fund oversaw the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rate arrangements. Countries that joined between 1945 and 1971 agreed to keep their exchange rates at levels that could be adjusted only to correct a fundamental disequilibrium in the balance of payments, and only with the Fund's agreement. Special drawing rights, created in 1969, were each worth 0.888671 grams of gold, roughly one US dollar at the time.

After the Bretton Woods agreement was terminated in 1971, the Fund redefined the unit in 1973 as the value of a selection of world currencies, and its role shifted to managing balance-of-payments difficulties and international financial crises. In the early 2000s it provided two major lending packages, to Argentina and to Uruguay.

The Fund is a specialised agency of the United Nations, headquartered in Washington, D.C., and acts as a lender of last resort to members facing balance of payments crises. Through a quota system, countries contribute funds to a pool from which they can borrow, and a country's quota also determines its voting power. Each member has basic votes equal to 5.502% of the total, plus one additional vote for each 100,000 special drawing rights of its quota.

A managing director, who has historically been European, leads the staff, and the first deputy has by convention been a citizen of the United States. Conditionality, the policies the Fund requires in exchange for its financial resources, was introduced in a 1952 decision of the Executive Board. Critics argue that these conditions impose austerity and limit the economic sovereignty of borrowing nations, and that the Fund's governance is dominated by Western countries.
international-security-assistance-force: The International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) was established by United Nations Security Council Resolution 1386, under the Bonn Agreement, which outlined the creation of a permanent Afghan government after the United States invasion of October 2001. Its first mandate was to secure Kabul and its surroundings so that the Afghan Transitional Administration headed by Hamid Karzai could form. The first headquarters was based on the British 3rd Mechanised Division under Major General John McColl and arrived in December 2001. Turkey took command in June 2002. Under the resolution, participating states bore the costs through a trust fund to which all United Nations member states were encouraged to contribute.

For almost two years the mandate did not go beyond Kabul. NATO took command on 11 August 2003 at the request of the United Nations and the Afghan government, its first deployment outside Europe and North America. On 13 October 2003 Resolution 1510 opened the way to a wider role, and the German Bundestag voted on 24 October to send troops to Kunduz, the first ISAF soldiers outside Kabul.

ISAF then grew in four stages: to the north, completed in October 2004, to the west in 2005 and 2006, to the south on 31 July 2006, and to the east on 5 October 2006, when it took responsibility for the whole country. Its strength rose from about 5,000 in 2003 to some 31,000 in October 2006. After 2006 the Taliban insurgency intensified, especially in the south, and British, Dutch, Canadian and Danish soldiers in Helmand, Uruzgan and Kandahar came under almost daily attack. A tactical directive of General Stanley A. McChrystal in July 2009 ordered steps to minimize civilian casualties.

At its peak, between 2010 and 2012, ISAF had 400 military bases and roughly 130,000 troops, and forty-two countries contributed, including all 30 members of NATO. By 2010 the United States provided most of the troops, followed by the United Kingdom, Turkey, Germany, France and Italy. Its aim was to transfer security responsibility to Afghan forces, and it ceased combat operations and was disbanded in December 2014. Some troops stayed in a supporting and advisory role in its successor, the Resolute Support Mission.
international-workingmens-association: In 1844 the Fraternal Democrats were founded in London by political refugees and Chartist leaders, and their structure served as a model for the later International. A new generation of British trade union leaders, known as the Junta, organised solidarity with Garibaldi, with Poland against Russian repression and with the Union side in the American Civil War. Contacts between British and French workers' leaders at the London International Exhibition of 1862 led to a meeting in London in July 1863.

The founding meeting was held at St Martin's Hall on 28 September 1864, with some 2,000 workers, and resolved to found an international organisation with a General Council in London. A committee of twenty-one was elected to draft its rules, including George Odger, the French delegates Henri Tolain and Eugène Varlin, and Karl Marx. Marx drafted the Inaugural Address and the Provisional Rules, after earlier drafts by Mazzinists and Owenites were rejected. The Preamble stated that the emancipation of the working classes must be achieved by the workers themselves.

The Association brought together socialists, communists and anarchists, and its history was one of factional struggle. The French members were at first dominated by the followers of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, who opposed political action, strikes and collective ownership. They were largely defeated at the Geneva Congress of 1866, and the Brussels Congress of 1868 declared that mines, railways and arable land should become common property. From 1868 the Russian Mikhail Bakunin led an anti-statist opposition that wanted the state abolished.

The International reached its peak after the Paris Commune of 1871, in which around a third of the members of the Commune's council belonged to it. Marx defended the Commune in The Civil War in France, but its suppression brought harsh repression, including a ban on the International in France. Modern research puts membership at its peak at around 150,000. At the Hague Congress in September 1872, Bakunin and James Guillaume were expelled, and on a proposal of Engels the General Council's seat was moved to New York. The anarchist wing formed a rival International at St. Imier, which disintegrated by 1877. The Association was officially disbanded at Philadelphia on 15 July 1876.

The First International did not achieve a social revolution, but it was the first mass international movement of the working class. It established the foundations of revolutionary communism, moderate socialism and anarchism as the three trends of the workers' movement, and its experience prepared the way for the Second International of 1889.
inti: Inti, from the Quechua word for sun, was the national patron of the Inca state. He is better viewed as a cluster of solar aspects than as a single god, since the Incas divided his identity according to the stages of the sun. Pachacuti is often linked to the origin and expansion of the Inca Sun Cult. The most common belief was that Inti was born of Viracocha, the God of Creation, though in another myth he is the son of the Earth goddess Pachamama and the sky god. Manco Cápac, the founding Inca ancestor, was thought to be the son of Inti, although another legend names Viracocha as his father.

The Inca ruler was considered the living representative of Inti, and the emperor and his family were believed to be descended from him. The high priest of the Sun, the Willaq Umu, was the second most powerful person in the kingdom. Each conquered province was supposed to dedicate a third of its lands and herds to Inti, and each major province had a Sun Temple served by priests and priestesses. The chief temple was the Qurikancha in Cusco, where the bodies of earlier rulers were displayed in wall niches.

Inti Raymi, the sun festival, was held at the winter solstice, around 24 June. It began with a three-day fast without fires, lasted nine days, and included sacrifices on the first day. Offerings to Inti included prayers, food, coca leaves, woven cloth, animals, blood and human beings. Scholars regard the growth of the cult as a use of religion for political purposes, since the king was increasingly identified with the sun god.

Sun symbolism predates the Inca; the Sun Gate at Tiwanaku shows the sun's position on solstices and equinoxes. The sun appears on the coats of arms of Bolivia and Ecuador and on the historical flag of Peru, and the highest honour of the Peruvian state, the Order of the Sun, recalls Inti.
inti-raymi: Inti Raymi, Quechua for festival of Inti, honoured Inti, the sun and the most venerated deity of Inca religion. It marked the winter solstice, the shortest day of the year in the southern hemisphere, and the Inca New Year, when the hours of light begin to lengthen again. According to the chronicler Garcilaso de la Vega, who calls it the most important festival of the empire, Sapa Inca Pachacuti created it. It took place in the Haukaypata, the main square of Cusco.

The ceremony lasted nine days, with dances, processions and animal sacrifices to thank Pachamama and ensure a good harvest. The last Inti Raymi attended by the Inca emperor was held in 1535, after which Spanish colonists and Catholic priests banned it with other Inca religious practices.

In 1944 a historical reconstruction was directed by Faustino Espinoza Navarro with indigenous actors, based largely on the chronicles of Garcilaso de la Vega and covering only the religious ceremony. Since then a yearly theatrical staging has taken place at Saksaywaman, two kilometres from the original site, drawing thousands of visitors.

Over 800 performers take part in three settings. The ceremony begins at the temple of Qorikancha, historically the main site of sun worship. In the Plaza de Armas the Inca meets the city's mayor and exchanges the khipu that stands for munay (to want), yachay (to know) and llankay (to work). The central ceremony at Sacsayhuamán includes a report from the four suyus, rites of chicha, sacred fire and holy bread, a llama sacrifice with omens, and dances.

Inti Raymi is still observed in indigenous cultures throughout the Andes, with music, colourful costumes, among them the woven Aya Huma mask, and shared food. In many places it has been connected with the Catholic festival of Saint John the Baptist on 24 June, a few days after the southern winter solstice.
inuit: Inuit are the descendants of the Thule people, who emerged from the Bering Strait and western Alaska around 1000 CE. Anthropologists hold that they had split from the related Aleut group about 4,000 years earlier. They spread eastward across the Arctic and displaced the related Dorset culture, called the Tuniit in Inuktitut. Inuit legends describe the Tuniit as giants, taller and stronger than Inuit. Researchers believe that Inuit society had advantages in having adapted to using dogs as transport animals and in developing larger weapons and other technologies. The Aleut and Yupik peoples generally do not identify as Inuit, and many people once called Eskimo find that term offensive.

The lives of the Paleo-Eskimos of the far north were largely unaffected by visiting Norsemen except for mutual trade. By the mid-16th century Basque whalers and fishermen worked the coast of Labrador and had set up whaling stations on land, such as the one excavated at Red Bay. Inuit do not appear to have interfered with their operations, but raided the stations in winter, taking tools and worked iron.

During the 19th century the Western Arctic lost close to 90 per cent of its population to new diseases, among them tuberculosis, measles, influenza and smallpox. Canadian churches and the federal government later ran the earliest health facilities for Inuit, which involved the forced removal of patients from their communities. In the 19th and 20th centuries Christian missionaries forbade many cultural practices, among them Indigenous languages, dances and tattoos.

Inuit speak Inupiaq, Inuinnaqtun, Inuktitut, Inuvialuktun and the Greenlandic languages. They have traditionally been fishermen and hunters of whales, seals, caribou and other animals. They hunted at sea from the qajaq, a single-passenger boat covered in sealskin that could be righted by a seated person, the design from which the kayak takes its name, and carried people, goods and dogs in the larger umiaq. In winter they watched an aglu, a breathing hole in the ice, for seals. Their industry relied on hides, driftwood and bones, with walrus ivory essential for knives. Labour was divided by gender, but not absolutely. Inuit relied on the angakkuq, or shaman, for spiritual interpretation.
inukai-tsuyoshi: Inukai was born on 4 June 1855 in Bitchū Province, the second son of a samurai who served as a district magistrate. In 1876 he went to Tokyo and graduated from Keio Gijuku, specialising in Chinese studies, and then worked as a journalist, going to the front with the Imperial Japanese Army as a reporter during the Satsuma Rebellion. In 1882 Ōkuma Shigenobu invited him to help form the Rikken Kaishintō, which opposed the domination of the government by the former Chōshū and Satsuma domains and called for a British-style constitutional monarchy. First elected to the Lower House of the Imperial Diet in 1890, he was reelected 17 times and held the same seat for 42 years until his death.

He was briefly Minister of Education in 1898, for eleven days, and Minister of Communications in 1923–1924. He supported the Chinese republican movement and aided Sun Yat-sen during the Xinhai Revolution of 1911. After Tanaka Giichi died in 1929, he became president of the Rikken Seiyūkai.

After the Wakatsuki administration resigned, the genrō Saionji Kinmochi asked Inukai to form a government in 1931. His cabinet was divided between factions, from the Army Minister Sadao Araki on the right to the Finance Minister Takahashi Korekiyo, a liberal. He took Japan off the gold standard, which devalued the yen and raised exports. He was forced to accede to the Army's request to send more troops to Manchuria and Tianjin, and fighting spread to Shanghai from January to March 1932. His efforts to limit deployments and to settle the Shanghai Incident by negotiation drew the anger of militarists. When Manchukuo was proclaimed on 1 March 1932, Inukai withheld formal recognition.
