Inukai was shot by eleven junior Navy officers in the Prime Minister's residence in Tokyo during the May 15 Incident of 1932. His last words were roughly 'If we could talk, you would understand', and his killers replied 'Dialogue is useless'. The conspirators also attacked the residence of Makino Nobuaki, Saionji's residence and the headquarters of the Rikken Seiyukai. The original plan included killing the film star Charlie Chaplin, who was Inukai's guest, but he was watching sumo wrestling with the prime minister's son that day. The murderers received only light sentences. The incident effectively marked the end of civilian political control over government decisions until after the Second World War.
inverness: Inverness stands at the mouth of the River Ness, which flows from Loch Ness, at the south-western extremity of the Moray Firth. The city lies at the northern end of the Great Glen, where the Caledonian Canal connects Loch Ness, Loch Oich and Loch Lochy. It is the northernmost city in the United Kingdom. Long regarded as the de facto capital of the Scottish Highlands, it is the administrative centre of the Highland Council region and serves the wider Highlands and Islands, with around half a million people.

Human settlement in the area dates back to around 7000 BCE. Inverness was one of the chief strongholds of the Picts. In 569 Saint Columba visited it to convert the Pictish king Brude, who is supposed to have lived in the vitrified fort on Craig Phadrig on the city's western edge. In the 11th century Macbeth held a castle in the city as Mormaer of Moray and Ross. King David I granted the first royal charter in the 12th century, around 1160.

In 1562 Mary, Queen of Scots, was refused admittance to Inverness Castle by its governor, a follower of the Earl of Huntly, whom she afterwards had hanged. In 1715 the Jacobites occupied the fortress as a barracks, and the government built the first Fort George there in 1727. It surrendered to the Jacobites in 1746 and was blown up. Culloden Moor nearby saw the Battle of Culloden in 1746, the last pitched battle fought in the United Kingdom. The area was solidly Gaelic-speaking until the late 19th century, and the railway reached Inverness in 1855.

Inverness was granted city status in 2000 as a Millennium City. It was the county town of Inverness-shire before becoming the headquarters of the Highland Council. The old urban core west of the A9 had 48,248 people in 2022. The powerful Clan Mackintosh, Clan Fraser and Clan MacKenzie are closely linked to the surrounding country.
investiture-controversy: After the decline of the Western Roman Empire, investiture of bishops and abbots was usually performed by the ruling nobility, known as lay investiture, although it was theoretically a task of the church. Many bishops and abbots came from noble families, and offices carried wealth and land, so the sale of church offices, known as simony, was an important source of income. German bishops and the soldiers their dioceses provided were the main source of the empire's military strength. The controversy was sparked when Emperor Henry III appointed and dismissed three popes in quick succession in the mid-11th century. In 1059 Pope Nicholas II made cardinals the electors of the pope and banned lay investiture.

In 1075 Pope Gregory VII drew up the Dictatus papae, which asserted that the pope alone could depose an emperor. Henry IV continued to appoint his own bishops, and sent Gregory a letter headed "Henry, king not through usurpation but through the holy ordination of God, to Hildebrand, at present not pope but false monk". Gregory excommunicated Henry, which temporarily disabled his military regime. Each successive pope then tried to diminish imperial power by stirring revolt in Germany, and on 31 December 1105 Henry IV was forced to abdicate in favour of his son Henry V, who had rebelled for the papacy.

A separate dispute between Pope Paschal II and Henry I of England ended with the Concordat of London in 1107. Henry I gave up the right to invest bishops and abbots while keeping the custom of requiring homage for their temporalities, the landed properties tied to the episcopate. On the mainland the fighting lasted about 50 years, until Pope Callixtus II and Emperor Henry V agreed on the Concordat of Worms on 23 September 1122.

The Concordat of Worms ended lay investiture while leaving secular leaders some unofficial influence. In Germany the election of bishops and abbots was to take place in the emperor's presence, or his legate's, as a judge between disputing parties. Without a dispute the cathedral canons chose the bishop and the monks the abbot. In Burgundy and Italy the church handled elections without imperial interference. The emperor kept some power over imperial churches but lost the religious authority that had belonged to the king's office, and the historian Davis argues that the rifts left in Germany and Italy delayed nation-states there until the 19th century.
ioannina: Ioannina lies about 500 metres above sea level on the western shore of Lake Pamvotis, and is the capital of the Ioannina regional unit and of the region of Epirus. Its climate is borderline between hot-summer Mediterranean and humid subtropical, with hot, moderately dry summers and wet winters that bring frequent frosts. The name is probably a corruption of Agioannina or Agioanneia, place of St. John, linked to a monastery dedicated to Saint John the Baptist around which the settlement grew near the present castle. Another theory ties it to Ioannina, a daughter of Belisarius, the general of Justinian.

Tradition ascribes the foundation to the Byzantine Emperor Justinian in the 6th century, but archaeology has found Hellenistic settlements. Human presence in the basin goes back to the Paleolithic, about 24,000 years ago, and in antiquity the Molossians had four settlements there. After the Roman conquest of 167 BCE settlement continued, but no longer in an urban pattern. The city flourished in the late Byzantine period. After the Fourth Crusade, Michael I of Epirus enlarged and refortified it and settled refugees from Constantinople there, turning a small town into a fortress that John Apokaukos called an ark of salvation. Local people tried in 1232 to expel the refugees but failed.

Ioannina surrendered to the Ottomans in 1430 and remained an administrative centre, at first as the seat of a sanjak and until 1867 of the Ioannina Eyalet, and a power base for Ali Pasha. The first Ottoman tax register, of 1564, records 50 Muslim households and 1,250 Christian ones. Between the 18th and 19th centuries it was a major centre of the modern Greek Enlightenment. A great fire in 1820 destroyed many buildings. Greek forces took the city after the Battle of Bizani on 21 February 1913, and after the exchange of populations following the Treaty of Lausanne its Muslim population was replaced by Greek refugees from Asia Minor.

The city had 64,896 inhabitants in the 2021 census, and its municipality 113,978. It is the seat of the University of Ioannina, founded in 1964. Ioannina Castle, on a rocky peninsula of the lake, was the administrative heart of the Despotate of Epirus and later of the Ottoman province. It holds the Fethiye Mosque, the tomb of Ali Pasha and the Old Synagogue of 1829, one of the oldest and largest of its type in Greece. On an island in the lake stands the monastery of St Panteleimon, where Ali Pasha spent his last days. The city is known for its silverwork.
ioannis-kapodistrias: Ioannis Kapodistrias was born about 10 February 1776 in Corfu, then under Venetian rule, into a noble family. His father, Antonios Maria Kapodistrias, was a nobleman, artist and politician, and the family's title of count was inscribed in the Libro d'Oro of Corfu nobility in 1679. The family had come from Capodistria, now Koper, and had moved to Corfu in the 13th century, where they became Orthodox and fully hellenised. His mother, Adamantine Gonemis, belonged to a family that had fled Cyprus and Crete before settling in Corfu.

In 1799 Russia and the Ottoman Empire drove the French from the seven Ionian Islands and organised them as the Septinsular Republic, ruled by its nobles. Kapodistrias, substituting for his father, became one of its two ministers at the age of 25. He was later appointed Chief Minister of State by the Ionian Senate, which passed a more liberal constitution in December 1803, and he put emphasis on education. The French dissolved the republic in 1807. In 1809 he entered the service of Alexander I of Russia and in 1813 worked as unofficial Russian ambassador to Switzerland, where he helped secure its unity, independence and neutrality and drafted parts of a federal constitution.

At the Congress of Vienna in 1815 he counterbalanced the Austrian minister Prince Metternich, who wrote in 1819 that Kapodistrias was a perfect miracle of wrong-headedness. Alexander I appointed him joint foreign minister of Russia with Karl Robert Nesselrode. He held the post from 1816 until 1822, when he became increasingly active in supporting the Greek War of Independence.

In 1827 the Greek National Assembly at Troezen elected him the first head of state of liberated Greece, with the title Kyvernetes, or governor, for a seven-year term, and he served from 1828 to 1831. He launched a programme of reform and modernisation, working from 5 am until 10 pm. He distrusted the leaders of the war of independence and held that the Greeks were not ready for democracy, saying it would be like giving a boy a razor, and that they first needed an enlightened autocracy.

By 1831 his government was hated, chiefly by the Maniates and by merchant families of Hydra, Spetses and Psara. On 27 September 1831 Konstantis and Georgios Mavromichalis, relatives of the imprisoned Petrobey Mavromichalis, killed him outside the Church of Saint Spyridon in Nafplio.
ioannis-metaxas: Ioannis Metaxas was born in 1871 at Vathy on the island of Ithaca, into a family that claimed descent from Byzantine nobility. He enrolled at the Hellenic Military Academy in 1885 and fought in the Greco-Turkish War of 1897 on the staff of Crown Prince Constantine, who became his patron. From 1899 to 1903 he studied at the Berlin War Academy, where an instructor called him a little Moltke, and he came home an admirer of Prussian militarism. He wrote in 1900 that he rejected any opposition to the king and the intemperate parliamentarism of Greece.

During the First World War Metaxas was a monarchist in the National Schism. He opposed Eleftherios Venizelos and Greek entry into the war, and he led monarchist forces in the Noemvriana. When Venizelos returned to power in 1917 he was exiled to Corsica, and in January 1920 he was sentenced to death in absentia. After his return in November 1920 he opposed the continuing campaign in Asia Minor on logistical grounds and retired from the army. He founded the Freethinkers' Party in October 1922, and it won 52 seats in 1926.

King George II returned in 1935 after a plebiscite whose figures were widely regarded as rigged, and appointed Metaxas prime minister in April 1936. After four months of constitutional government, Metaxas and the king began the 4th of August Regime. He banned political parties, prohibited strikes and introduced widespread censorship. His Minister of Security, Konstantinos Maniadakis, practically dissolved the Communist Party of Greece. There were book burnings, and Metaxas rewrote school texts when he became Minister of Education in 1938. He also introduced the eight-hour day and the Social Insurance Institute.

Historians describe the system as a form of fascism, a conventional authoritarian-conservative dictatorship or a regime with a strong fascist component. Greece remained a close ally of Britain, and on 28 October 1940 Metaxas rejected an Italian ultimatum, committing Greece to the Allies in the Second World War.

Metaxas died at his home in Kifissia on 29 January 1941, aged 69, from an infection of the throat, before the German invasion. Alexandros Koryzis succeeded him. Greeks celebrate Ohi Day on 28 October in memory of his refusal, and the fortifications he built along the Bulgarian border became known as the Metaxas Line. Until the military junta of 1967 to 1974 he was honoured as a patriot and war leader. Afterwards, writers and film-makers connected his regime with the junta and with fascism.
ion-antonescu: Ion Antonescu was born on 14 June 1882 in Pitești, into an upper-middle-class Romanian Orthodox family with some military tradition. His father, an army officer, sent him to the Infantry and Cavalry School in Craiova. He made his name as an army officer in the peasants' revolt of 1907 and in the Romanian campaign of the First World War, when he served as chief of staff to General Constantin Prezan. Between the wars he was military attaché to France and later Chief of the General Staff, and he served as Defence Minister in the cabinet of Octavian Goga and the first Cristea cabinet. His sympathy with far-right politics brought him into conflict with King Carol II and led to his detention.

In the crisis of 1940 Romania ceded Southern Dobruja to Bulgaria and Northern Transylvania to Hungary under Axis pressure, and Carol's popularity collapsed. Antonescu left his assigned residence and negotiated with Iuliu Maniu. The National Legionary State, proclaimed on 14 September 1940, made the Iron Guard the only legal party, with Antonescu as Prime Minister and Conducător and Horia Sima as his deputy. After Hitler told him in January 1941 of the plan to invade the Soviet Union, and judged him the more competent leader, Antonescu crushed the Guard in the Legionary Rebellion of January 1941 and ruled as a military dictatorship. Romania joined Operation Barbarossa and recovered Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina, and he became Marshal of Romania.

His regime's policies were responsible for the deaths of as many as 400,000 people, mostly Bessarabian, Ukrainian and Romanian Jews, and Romani. They combined pogroms and mass murders, among them the Odessa massacre, with ethnic cleansing and deportations to occupied Transnistria. Odessa fell in October 1941 after a two-month siege. The system was inconsistent: it put plunder before killing, treated most Jews of the Old Kingdom with leniency, and in the end refused the Final Solution.

Allied air attacks on Romania and heavy losses on the Eastern Front led Antonescu to open inconclusive peace talks in 1944. On 23 August 1944 King Michael I led a coup against him and had him arrested. Tried by a People's Tribunal in May 1946 for war crimes, crimes against the peace and treason, he was executed on 1 June 1946. The tribunals were comparable to the Nuremberg trials, though the procedures were politicised in favour of the Romanian Communist Party.

Under communist rule the documentation of the massacres came chiefly from Jewish Romanians, such as Matatias Carp's Black Book of 1946–1948. In 2003 an international commission led by Elie Wiesel studied the Holocaust in Romania, and its final report brought official recognition of Antonescu's part in it.
ion-iliescu: Ion Iliescu was born on 3 March 1930 in Oltenița, in the Muntenia region of the Kingdom of Romania. His father Alexandru was a railway worker, trade unionist and member of the then illegal Romanian Communist Party, who was arrested in 1937 and held in prison and labour camps until 1944 and died in 1945, when Ion was fifteen. His grandfather, a Bolshevik who fled the Russian Empire, had settled in Oltenița around 1895 and taken the name Iliescu. Ion was raised by his grandparents and his stepmother and in 1939 was adopted by his aunt Aristița, a cook at the residence of the communist activist Ana Pauker. He studied fluid mechanics at the Bucharest Polytechnic Institute and then at the Moscow Power Engineering Institute.

He joined the Union of Communist Youth in 1944 and the Communist Party in 1953, became secretary of the Youth Union's Central Committee in 1956 and was elected to the party's Central Committee in 1965. He briefly headed the Department of Propaganda and in 1967 became Minister for Youth-related Issues. In 1972 he was pressured to resign, since Nicolae Ceaușescu did not fully trust him and believed that he might be his successor. He was demoted to posts in Timiș and Iași and then ran the Editura Tehnică publishing house. Ceaușescu could not remove him from the Central Committee until 1985, after which the Securitate watched him more closely.

On 22 December 1989, after Ceaușescu fled Bucharest, revolutionaries occupied the Central Committee building, the Ministry of Defence and the television station. Iliescu led a group that included communist dissidents, whose authority the Minister of Defence, Victor Atanasie Stănculescu, recognised that afternoon. The Ceaușescus were captured, tried by a drumhead court-martial and executed on Christmas Day. Iliescu proposed multi-party elections and what he called an original democracy.

The National Salvation Front, led by Iliescu, won the 1990 general election, and in May 1990 he won the presidency with 85 percent of the vote, the first free presidential election in Romania in 53 years. Romania adopted its first post-communist constitution in 1991. In 1992 he won a second term with 61 percent in the second round, and in 1996 he lost to Emil Constantinescu and conceded within hours. In 2000 he defeated Corneliu Vadim Tudor with 66.8 percent in the runoff. In his term ending in December 2004 Romania joined NATO and completed its negotiations to join the European Union.
iona: Iona lies about 2 km from the coast of Mull, off the Ross of Mull. It is about 2 km wide and 6 km long, with few trees, and its highest point is Dùn Ì, at 101 metres. The main settlement, Baile Mòr, stands at St Ronan's Bay on the eastern side. The name has been explained in several ways: the earliest recorded forms may have meant yew-place, and the Gaelic name Ì Chaluim Chille means the island of Columba's monastery. The form Iona arose from a transcription error, attested from about 1274.

In the early historic period Iona lay in the Gaelic kingdom of Dál Riata. Columba, also called Colm Cille, sailed from Ireland and founded the monastery in 563 with twelve companions. It may have helped convert the Picts and Gaels in the late 6th century, and it was central to the conversion of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Northumbria in 635. It became a centre of learning whose scriptorium probably produced the original texts of the Iona Chronicle, and it backed the Celtic calculation of the date of Easter, which Northumbria gave up at the Synod of Whitby in 664. According to Bede, Iona itself adopted the Roman system in 715.

The Book of Kells may have been produced or begun there late in the 8th century, around the time the island's high crosses were sculpted. Viking raids then plundered its treasures many times, and in 849 Columba's relics were divided between Scotland and Ireland as the monastery was abandoned. Iona became part of the Kingdom of the Isles under Norse rule, and after the Treaty of Perth in 1266 the Hebrides passed to Scotland. The Benedictine abbey whose buildings stand today dates from about 1203, and an Augustinian nunnery was founded about 1208. At the Reformation the buildings were demolished and all but three of 360 carved crosses were destroyed.

Iona Abbey, now an ecumenical church, is the best-preserved medieval ecclesiastical building in the Western Isles of Scotland, and the nunnery is the most complete medieval nunnery remnant in Scotland. St Martin's Cross, of the 9th century, stands in front of the abbey. The graveyard is said to hold many early Scottish kings, among them Kenneth I, Duncan I and Macbeth, and an inventory of 1549 recorded 48 Scottish, eight Norwegian and four Irish kings. About 178 people lived there in 2022, and the island is reached by a ten-minute ferry from Fionnphort on Mull.
ionia: Ionia was an ancient region on the central part of the western coast of Anatolia, never a unified state. Ionia proper was a narrow coastal strip from Phocaea in the north to Miletus in the south, and included the islands of Chios and Samos. It was bounded by Aeolia to the north, Lydia to the east and Caria to the south. Three fertile river valleys gave it a reputation as the most fertile region of Asia Minor. A core of twelve cities formed the Ionian League, with a shared sanctuary and festival at the Panionion on Mount Mycale. The League was mainly religious and cultural, and Ionians generally identified themselves by their city; Thales of Miletus's advice to form a political union was rejected.

The Greeks believed the Ionians were descendants of Ion who left the northern Peloponnese, took refuge in Athens, and then sailed to Asia Minor under the sons of Codrus. Greek settlement of Ionia probably took place in the 11th century BCE, though the lack of contemporary sources leaves the sequence unclear. In the Archaic period its cities were among the cultural, intellectual and political leaders of the Greek world, and Miletus founded colonies around the Euxine Sea.

The cities fell fully under Lydian rule under Croesus. After Cyrus the Great defeated Croesus they came under the Persian monarchy, with considerable autonomy under local tyrants loyal to the Persian king. About 500 BCE Histiaeus of Miletus's circle ignited the Ionian Revolt, with help from Athens and Eretria; the rebels burnt Sardis, but the Ionian fleet was beaten off Lade and Miletus was destroyed after a long siege. The Battle of Mycale in 479 BCE secured their freedom, and they became dependent allies of Athens. The Peace of Antalcidas of 387 BCE recognised Persian possession, and Alexander the Great presented his invasion as a liberation. In 133 BCE Ionia became part of the Roman province of Asia, with Ephesus as capital.

From the 7th century BCE Ionia, above all Miletus, was home to the Ionian school of philosophy, founded by Thales and his student Anaximander, which sought explanations of natural phenomena without recourse to myth. A distinct school of art flourished between 700 and 500 BCE. The Persian word Younan for Greek, the Hebrew Yavan and the Sanskrit yavana all derive from Ionia.
ionian-revolt: Greek settlers from three groups, Aeolians, Dorians and Ionians, emigrated to Asia Minor after the fall of Mycenaean civilisation. The Ionians founded twelve cities, including Miletus, Ephesus, Samos and Chios, which were independent but shared a common temple, the Panionion. They were conquered by the Lydian king Croesus around 560 BCE and then passed to Cyrus the Great's Achaemenid Empire, which ruled them through native tyrants. In 499 BCE the tyrant of Miletus, Aristagoras, joined the satrap Artaphernes in an expedition against Naxos that failed after a four-month siege. Unable to repay Artaphernes and expecting to lose his position, he chose to incite the Milesians to revolt against Darius the Great.

In 498 BCE, with twenty triremes from Athens and five from Eretria, the Ionians took the lower city of Sardis, which then burned. Persian troops followed them back to Ephesus and routed them. The Athenians withdrew, but the revolt spread to the Hellespont, Caria and Cyprus. Three Persian armies set out in 497 BCE to recover the rebel lands. Daurises took several cities on the Hellespont and defeated the Carians at the Marsyas River, though his army was later destroyed in an ambush at Pedasus. Aristagoras left Miletus for Thrace.

By 494 BCE the Persians had regrouped and went straight for Miletus. The Ionians gathered 353 triremes at Lade but were decisively beaten after the Samians defected. Miletus was besieged and captured. According to Herodotus most of its men were killed and its women and children enslaved, which archaeology partly confirms. In 493 BCE the Persians took Chios, Lesbos and Tenedos and the remaining cities.

Artaphernes set a workable peace: disputes between cities were to be settled by arbitration, and tribute was set in proportion to the size of each city's land. The next year Mardonius abolished the tyrannies and put democracies in their place. The Ionian cities recovered quickly, except for Miletus, and could equip a large fleet for the second Persian invasion of Greece 13 years later. The revolt was the first major conflict between Greece and Persia. According to Herodotus, Darius resolved to punish Athens and Eretria, and the first Persian invasion of Greece followed in 492 BCE.
ionian-sea: The Ionian Sea is an elongated bay of the Mediterranean. The International Hydrographic Organization bounds it on the east by the mainland coast from the mouth of the Butrinto River in Albania down to Cape Matapan, on the south by a line from Cape Matapan to Cape Passero in Sicily, and on the west by the east coast of Sicily and the south-east coast of Italy. Its ports include Syracuse, Catania, Messina, Reggio Calabria and Taranto in Italy and Patras, Pylos and Kalamata in Greece. The Calypso Deep, at 5,109 metres, is the deepest point in the Mediterranean, and the sea is one of the most seismically active areas in the world.

The name comes from the Greek Ionion, whose etymology is unknown. Ancient Greek writers, especially Aeschylus, linked it to the myth of Io, who swam across it. According to the Oxford Classical Dictionary the name may derive from Ionians who sailed to the west. Other tales name Ionius, son of Adrias, or Ionius, son of Dyrrhachus, whom Heracles killed by mistake, after which the body was cast into the water.

The sea is known for the seafaring adventures of Odysseus, the warrior-king of Ithaca. It was regularly crossed from at least the 8th century BCE by Greek colonisers founding colonies in Italy. In the Roman period it was the site of the Battle of Actium between Octavian and Mark Antony in 31 BCE. Major naval engagements were fought over its eastern section and its islands throughout the modern era, ending in its control by the modern state of Greece, while the western section has been controlled by Italy since 1861.
ionians: The Greeks of the ancient period saw themselves as divided into four major tribes: Dorians, Aeolians, Achaeans and Ionians. The term Ionian had several senses. In the narrowest it meant the region of Ionia in Asia Minor. More broadly it covered all speakers of the Ionic dialect, including the Greek populations of Euboea, the Cyclades and many cities founded by Ionian colonists, and in the broadest sense all speakers of the East Greek group, which included Attic.

The foundation myth current in the Classical period held that the Ionians were named after Ion, son of Xuthus, who lived in Aigialeia in the north Peloponnese. When the Dorians invaded the Peloponnese they expelled the Achaeans from the Argolid and Lacedaemonia, and the displaced Achaeans moved into Aigialeia, thereafter Achaea, expelling the Ionians. The Ionians went to Attica, mingled with its people and later emigrated to the coast of Asia Minor, founding Ionia. Herodotus says that all are Ionians who are of Athenian descent and keep the feast Apaturia.

The name appears in the records of many civilisations. A fragmentary Linear B tablet from Knossos bears the name i-ja-wo-ne, interpreted as possibly an ethnic name, and Homer uses Ἰάονες once, of long-robed Greeks apparently identified with Athenians. Letters of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from the 8th century BCE record attacks by what appear to be Ionians on Phoenician cities, including a raid reported to Tiglath-Pileser III in a letter from the 730s BCE. Old Persian inscriptions of the Achaemenid Empire list the Yaunā among the empire's provinces. In the Book of Genesis, Javan, a son of Japheth, is believed by most Bible scholars to represent the Ionians.

The Edicts of Ashoka refer to the Yonas, in the Thirteenth Edict dated to 260–258 BCE. Ionic Greek, spoken in Euboea, the northern Cyclades and, from about 1000 BCE, Asiatic Ionia, was the base of the literary language of Homer and Hesiod, though it was eventually supplanted by Attic, dominant in the Greek world by the 5th century BCE.

Unlike the austere and militaristic Dorians, the Ionians are known for their love of philosophy, art, democracy and pleasure, traits most clearly expressed by the Athenians. In the 6th century BCE the coastal towns of Miletus and Ephesus became the focus of a revolution in thinking about nature. Thales and his successors, called physiologoi, were sceptical of religious explanations and sought mechanical and physical ones. The physicist Carlo Rovelli regards the work of the Ionian school as the first great scientific revolution.
ipswich: Ipswich is a port town and borough in Suffolk, on the River Orwell, 65 miles (105 km) north-east of London. It is the county town and the largest town in Suffolk. It was first recorded in the medieval period as Gippeswic and has also appeared as Gyppewicus and Yppswyche. The town centre contains the historic town square, the Cornhill, while the waterfront lies south of the centre on a meander of the Orwell.

Ipswich is claimed to be the oldest continuing town established and developed by the English, with continuous settlement since early Anglo-Saxon times. In Roman times a large fort stood at Walton near Felixstowe, and the largest Roman villa in Suffolk, possibly an administrative complex, stood at Castle Hill. The modern town took shape in the 7th and 8th centuries around its port. From the 14th to the 17th centuries Ipswich was a kontor, or trading base, of the Hanseatic League, with the port used for imports and exports to the Baltic.

In 1824 Dr George Birkbeck and local businessmen founded one of the first Mechanics' Institutes, which survives as the Ipswich Institute. In the mid-19th century coprolite, fossilised animal dung, was discovered and mined, and dissolved in acid it formed the basis of the Fisons fertiliser business. Ransomes, Sims and Jefferies, one of the best-known agricultural manufacturers, was based in the town, and Ransomes built the world's first commercial motorised lawnmower in 1902.

Ipswich has no cathedral, and the Bishop of St Edmundsbury and Ipswich is based at Bury St Edmunds. Among its buildings are Christchurch Mansion, given to the town by Felix Thornley Cobbold in 1896, and Ipswich Minster, once St Mary-le-Tower, rebuilt by the Victorians. The church of St Lawrence houses the world's oldest circle of church bells.
ipswich-massachusetts: Ipswich lies in Essex County, on the coast about 45 km northeast of Boston. The Ipswich River and Plum Island Sound join at their mouths and empty into Ipswich Bay through a narrow, navigable channel at the foot of Castle Hill. The town includes the southern part of Plum Island and Castle Neck, and much of its western end is Willowdale State Forest. The Bull Brook archaeological site, dated to about 11,500 years ago, gives some of the oldest signs of human habitation in New England. Early English colonists met an Indigenous settlement near Ipswich Bay that they rendered as Aggawom, Agawam or Angoam.

John Winthrop the Younger, son of the first governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, resolved in 1633 to settle at Agawam with the permission of the General Court, and sailed into the harbour with twelve men. Agawam was incorporated on 5 August 1634 as Ipswich, after Ipswich in Suffolk, in acknowledgment of the kindness shown to colonists who had sailed from there. Nathaniel Ward, assistant pastor from 1634 to 1636, wrote the first code of laws for Massachusetts. In 1638 the chief Masconomet contracted to sell Ipswich to Winthrop for wampum, other goods and twenty pounds. Epidemics had devastated Indigenous people of the area around 1617 and again in 1633.

The settlers became farmers, fishermen, shipbuilders and traders. In 1687 townspeople led by the Reverend John Wise protested a tax imposed by Governor Sir Edmund Andros, arguing that as Englishmen they could not be taxed without representation. Citizens were jailed, but Andros was recalled to England in 1689 and the new sovereigns, William III and Mary II, issued another charter. The town calls itself the Birthplace of American Independence for this reason. In 1868 Amos A. Lawrence established the Ipswich Hosiery Mills, which became the nation's largest stocking mill by the turn of the 20th century; a strike led by the Industrial Workers of the World took place there in 1913.

Ipswich had 13,785 inhabitants at the 2020 census. It has many early buildings, including the John Whipple House of 1642 and 1677 and the Choate Bridge of 1764, and is known for its clams and for Crane Beach. The Castle Hill estate, bought in 1910 by Richard T. Crane Jr., was left in 1949 to The Trustees of Reservations.
iran: Iran has an area of 1,648,195 square kilometres, the sixth-largest country entirely in Asia. It is one of the world's most mountainous countries, consisting mostly of the Iranian Plateau, with ranges such as the Zagros and Alborz in the populous west. Mount Damavand, at 5,610 metres, is the highest point and the highest volcano in Asia. Lush Caspian Hyrcanian forests cover the north, while the east is mostly desert basins such as the Kavir and Lut deserts. The country lies in a seismically active area, where an earthquake of magnitude 7.0 or higher occurs on average once every ten years.

Hominins were present in Iran around 800,000 years ago, and agriculture appeared some 12,000 years ago; Ganj Dareh shows the earliest known domestication of goats, around 10,000 years ago. Susa, later the capital of Elam, was first settled in 4400–4200 BCE, and Elam lasted from 3200 to 539 BCE. The earliest Iranian peoples began to arrive from Central Asia in the 2nd millennium BCE. The Median dynasty ruled the earliest Iranian state, and in 612 BCE Cyaxares and the Babylonian king Nabopolassar destroyed Nineveh. Cyrus the Great then defeated the Medes and founded the Achaemenid Empire, the largest-ever Iranian state, and his son Cambyses II conquered Egypt.

Alexander the Great conquered the empire in the 4th century BCE, the Parthian Empire arose in the 3rd century BCE, and the Sasanian Empire succeeded it in the 3rd century CE. After the 7th-century Muslim conquest Iran underwent Islamization, and during the Iranian Intermezzo Iranian Muslim dynasties ended Arab rule and revived the Persian language. Seljuk and Khwarazmian rule, Mongol conquests and the Timurid Renaissance followed. In the 16th century the Safavid dynasty re-established a unified Iranian state with Twelver Shia Islam as its official religion. Iran was a leading world power under the Afsharid Empire but lost the status after the Qajars took power in the 1790s.

Reza Shah founded the Pahlavi dynasty after ousting the last Qajar Shah in 1925. The Iranian Revolution of 1979 overthrew the monarchy, and Ruhollah Khomeini became the first supreme leader of the Islamic Republic; Iraq invaded in 1980, starting an eight-year war. The supreme leader is head of state and commands the armed forces, while the president has limited power. Tehran, with about 9.4 million people, is the capital and largest city. Persians are estimated at 51% of the population and Azerbaijanis at 24% in a 2003 estimate, although ethnic composition is debated because no state censuses count it. Iran has 30 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
iran-iraq-war: The two states had long disputed the Shatt al-Arab. In 1937 they agreed that Iranian ships would pay tolls on the river, and in 1969 Iran stopped paying. Tension led to bloodshed until the 1975 Algiers Agreement, in which Iraq ceded the eastern bank to Iran. After the Iranian Revolution of 1979, Iraq feared that Ruhollah Khomeini would export Iran's new ideology and rally Iraq's Shia majority against its Sunni Muslim-controlled Baʽathist government, and Saddam Hussein also wished to replace Iran as the main power in the Persian Gulf. Iran's army was weakened: by September 1980 about 12,000 officers had been purged. On 10 September Iraq took territories at Zain al-Qaws and Saif Saad that Iran had not handed over under the 1975 agreement.

Iraq invaded on 22 September 1980 with air strikes on ten Iranian airfields, which failed to destroy Iran's air force. The battle for Khorramshahr left some 7,000 dead on each side and delayed the Iraqis enough for Iran to deploy its forces. The advance had stalled by December, and the war settled into trench warfare. Iran recaptured all its territory by June 1982 and then invaded Iraq. For the next five years Iraq stayed mostly on the defensive while Iran launched more than 70 offensives, often by human wave assaults.

The war also reached shipping and cities. Iraq bombed Iranian tankers, economic targets and cities, and from February 1988 launched over 200 al-Husayn missiles at 37 Iranian cities. Iraq used chemical weapons, and in mid-1988 poison gas bombing of the town of Oshnavieh killed and wounded over 2,000 civilians. Iraq was supported by the United States, the Soviet Union, France and most Arab states, and Iran by Syria, Libya and others.

Iran accepted a ceasefire under United Nations Security Council Resolution 598, effective in August 1988. The fear of chemical attack on its civilians weighed heavily on its leadership. The war caused around 500,000 deaths, not counting the related Anfal campaign. It brought no permanent change of borders, and neither country received reparations. Both sides suffered financially, and low-level conflict continued until relations improved after Saddam Hussein was overthrown in 2003.
iranian-plateau: The plateau spans parts of Central Asia, South Asia, West Asia and the South Caucasus. It is bounded by the Zagros Mountains to the west, the Caspian Sea and the Köpet Dag to the north, the Armenian Highlands to the north-west, the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf to the south, and the Hindu Kush and Sulaiman Mountains to the east. It stretches nearly 2,000 kilometres and covers some 3,700,000 square kilometres, including most of Iran and Afghanistan and the parts of Pakistan west of the Indus.

Despite its name the plateau is far from flat. It holds several mountain ranges, among them the Alborz, whose peak Damavand reaches 5,610 metres, the Zagros, the Kopet Dag and the ranges of Balochistan. If the eastern Hindu Kush is counted, its highest point is Noshaq at 7,492 metres, and its lowest is the Lut Desert east of Kerman, below 300 metres. Geologically it lies along the suture where the northward-moving Arabian plate meets the Eurasian continent.

Studies of ancient and modern populations suggest that the plateau may have served as a population hub in the expansion of modern humans after their migration out of Africa. In the Bronze Age the civilization of Elam stretched across the Zagros and linked Mesopotamia with the plateau. The kingdoms of Aratta, known from cuneiform sources, may have lain on the central plateau. Archaeological sites there include Shahr-e Sukhteh, Konar Sandal, Tepe Yahya and Tappeh Sialk, the first three associated with the so-called Jiroft culture.

In classical antiquity the region was known as Persia, after the Achaemenid dynasty that arose in Fars. The Middle Persian word Erān, from which modern Persian Irān comes, began to be used for the state rather than as an ethnic label in the Sasanian era. Historically the region includes Parthia, Media and Persis, and some of the earlier territories of Greater Iran.

The plateau holds historical oak and poplar forests, notably around Shiraz, and a wide range of wildlife, including leopards, bears, hyenas, ibex, gazelles and mouflons, mostly in its wooded mountains. The plateau produces wheat, barley, millet, cotton and tobacco, and fruits such as pears, apples, apricots, plums and peaches, while almonds and pistachios grow in the warmer areas. Its timber was used for doors, ploughs and baskets.
iranian-revolution: The Shi'a clergy first showed itself a political force in the Tobacco protest of 1891, when a fatwa by Mirza Hasan Shirazi led to boycotts that forced Nasir al-Din Shah to cancel a British tobacco monopoly. The Constitutional Revolution of 1905 to 1911 created a parliament, the Majlis. General Reza Khan seized power in 1921 and was made monarch in 1925 as Reza Shah, founder of the Pahlavi dynasty. British and Soviet troops deposed him in 1941 and installed his son, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. In 1963 the Shah launched the White Revolution, a programme of land reform and the enfranchisement of women, which alienated the clergy in particular. Ruhollah Khomeini, who led opposition to it, was exiled in 1964.

Demonstrations began in October 1977 and grew into a campaign of civil resistance that included communists, socialists and Islamists. Mosques and bazaars became a protest network. On 19 August 1978 a fire at the Cinema Rex killed around 400 people; many in the public blamed the Shah's secret police, SAVAK, and it fuelled outrage. Oil strikes began in the autumn. Khomeini, expelled from Najaf, moved to a village near Paris, from where tapes of his sermons were sent into Iran, and he called on soldiers to defect.

On 16 January 1979 the Shah left Iran, leaving Shapour Bakhtiar as prime minister. Khomeini returned on 1 February, greeted by several million people. By 11 February the monarchy fell as guerrillas and rebel troops overwhelmed loyalists. Historians estimate deaths in the revolution at between 532 and 2,781, while Khomeini claimed 60,000.

A referendum in the spring of 1979 recorded 98.2 per cent in favour of an Islamic republic. On 4 November 1979 students seized the United States embassy in Tehran and held 52 diplomats for 444 days. Khomeini and his followers claimed sole credit for the revolution; by 1982 they had defeated rival factions and consolidated power, banning other groups in succession. The revolution alarmed Iran's neighbours, among them Kuwait, Iraq and Saudi Arabia, since its supporters called for monarchies to be replaced by Islamic republics.
iraq: Iraq lies in West Asia, bordered by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Iran, Kuwait, Jordan and Syria, with a coastline of 58 kilometres on the northern Persian Gulf. The Tigris and Euphrates run south through the country into the Shatt al-Arab and then the Persian Gulf. Fertile alluvial plains lie between and beside the two rivers, which carry about 60,000,000 cubic metres of silt a year to the delta, and marshlands flank the estuary.

Rocky deserts cover about 40 percent of Iraq and another 30 percent is mountainous, with the northwestern end of the Zagros range. Summer temperatures average above 40 °C for most of the country, and most places receive less than 250 millimetres of rain a year.

Iraq largely coincides with ancient Mesopotamia. Sumer emerged between 6000 and 5000 BCE during the Neolithic Ubaid period, and is recognised as the world's earliest civilisation. The territory includes the heartlands of the Akkadian, Neo-Sumerian, Babylonian, Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian empires. After the Achaemenid conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE, Cyrus the Great adopted titles such as King of Babylon and King of Sumer and Akkad, and Aramaic became the lingua franca of the empire.

Babylon surrendered without resistance to Alexander the Great in 331 BCE, and after his death in 323 BCE Seleucia became the imperial capital in Mesopotamia. Cuneiform writing and temple institutions continued under Seleucid rule. After the Arab conquest in the 7th century, Iraq became the centre of the Abbasid Caliphate, and the name Iraq came into use for the region. The Mongols destroyed Baghdad in 1258, and from the 16th century until the 20th Iraq was governed within the Ottoman system.

Iraq became independent in 1932. A military coup led by Abdul Karim Qasim overthrew the monarchy in 1958, and the Ba'ath Party took power in 1968. The country fought a war with Iran from 1980 to 1988, invaded Kuwait in 1990, and was invaded by a U.S.-led coalition in 2003. Iraq is a federal parliamentary republic.

Oil was nationalised in 1972. The 2021 population estimate was 43,533,592, and most Iraqis are Arabs, with Kurds, Turkmens, Assyrians, Yazidis and others. Arabic and Kurdish are the official languages.
irish-sea: The Irish Sea separates the islands of Ireland, the Isle of Man and Great Britain. Scotland lies to the north, England to the east, Wales to the south-east, and Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland to the west. St George's Channel links it to the Celtic Sea in the south, and the North Channel to the Inner Seas off the West Coast of Scotland in the north. Anglesey is its largest island, followed by the Isle of Man.

The western side is a deeper channel about 300 km long and 30 to 50 km wide, with depths from 80 to 275 metres, while the bays to the east are shallow. During the last ice age the central part of the sea was probably a long freshwater lake, which reconnected to the sea as the ice retreated about 10,000 years ago.

The sea was formed in the Neogene era. In the Roman Empire it was called Mare Hibernicus. Several invasions of Ireland from Britain crossed it. The Norman invasion of Ireland took place in stages during the late 12th century, from Porthclais near St Davids in Wales to Wexford Harbour in Leinster. The Tudors crossed it in 1529 in caravels and carracks to invade.

Because no tunnel or bridge joins Ireland to Great Britain, most heavy goods are carried across the sea by ship. Ferries run from Fishguard and Pembroke to Rosslare, from Holyhead to Dublin and Dún Laoghaire, and from Cairnryan to Belfast and Larne. The sea has also seen shipwrecks, among them the SS Mesaba, sunk by the German submarine U-118 in 1918, and HMS Mercury, which sank in 1940.

The sea lies off Scotland, England, Wales, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, and is used for trade, shipping and transport, for fishing and for power generation. Oil and gas fields lie in Liverpool Bay and in the basins of Cardigan Bay and Caernarfon Bay.
irish-war-of-independence: Since the 1870s the Irish Parliamentary Party had demanded home rule, while small groups such as Arthur Griffith's Sinn Féin argued for immediate independence. The Easter Rising of April 1916 proclaimed an Irish Republic and was put down within a week, with over four hundred dead. The execution of its leaders and the arrest of thousands of activists then raised support for Sinn Féin, and the Conscription Crisis of 1918 added to it. In the general election of 1918 Sinn Féin took 73 of the 105 Irish seats, and 91 per cent of those outside Ulster.

Its members met as the First Dáil at the Mansion House in Dublin on 21 January 1919, reaffirmed the 1916 proclamation and issued a declaration of independence. The Irish Volunteers were reconstituted as the Irish Republican Army (IRA).

On the day the Dáil met, Seán Treacy, Séumas Robinson, Seán Hogan and Dan Breen, acting on their own initiative, shot two Royal Irish Constabulary (RIC) constables at Soloheadbeg in County Tipperary. The IRA, organised in flying columns of 20 to 100 men, claimed 70,000 members but only about 3,000 were active fighters. Michael Collins built an intelligence network and a group of gunmen called the Squad.

The British reinforced the RIC with the Black and Tans, about seven thousand mostly ex-soldiers, and the Auxiliaries, who gained a reputation for indiscipline and reprisals against civilians. On Bloody Sunday, 21 November 1920, fourteen British intelligence operatives were killed in Dublin and the RIC fired on a crowd at Croke Park, killing fourteen civilians. A week later the IRA killed seventeen Auxiliaries at Kilmichael. Martial law followed and the centre of Cork was burnt. About 1,000 people died between January and July 1921, and 4,500 republicans were interned. In the north-east the conflict had a sectarian aspect, and in Belfast almost 500 people were killed, most of them Catholics.

A truce began on 11 July 1921 after a stalemate and growing British criticism at home and abroad. The Anglo-Irish Treaty was signed on 6 December 1921 and ratified by the Dáil on 7 January 1922. The Irish Free State was created as a self-governing Dominion on 6 December 1922, while Northern Ireland, created by the Government of Ireland Act in May 1921, remained in the United Kingdom.

One count puts the dead at 2,346: 919 civilians, 523 police, 413 British military personnel and 491 IRA volunteers. Disagreement over the Treaty among republicans led to the eleven-month Irish Civil War from June 1922.
irkutsk: Irkutsk lies on the Angara River, a tributary of the Yenisei, 72 kilometres below its outflow from Lake Baikal, about 850 kilometres south-east of Krasnoyarsk and about 520 kilometres north of Ulaanbaatar. The Irkut River, from which the town takes its name, joins the Angara directly opposite the city. The city stands among rolling hills in the thick taiga typical of Eastern Siberia. The Trans-Siberian Highway and the Trans-Siberian Railway connect it to other regions of Russia and to Mongolia.

In 1652 Ivan Pokhabov built winter quarters near the site for gold trading and for collecting fur taxes from the Buryats. Yakov Pokhabov built an ostrog, a small fort, nearby in 1661, and it gained official town rights in 1686. Its position at the crossroads of colonisation, trade and industrial routes gave it a larger role in the history of Eastern Siberia than its military importance would suggest. It became the administrative centre of the large Irkutsk province in 1731. The first road connection between Moscow and Irkutsk, the Siberian Route, was built in 1760, and goods imported from China via Kyakhta, including silk and tea, became widely available.

In 1821, under Mikhail Speransky's reforms, Siberia was divided at the Yenisei and Irkutsk became the seat of the Governor-General of East Siberia. In the early 19th century many artists, officers and nobles were exiled to Siberia for their part in the Decembrist revolt against Tsar Nicholas I. Irkutsk became the main centre of their intellectual and social life, and they built wooden houses with ornate hand-carved decoration, many of which survive. By the end of the 19th century there was one exiled man for every two locals. A fire in July 1879 destroyed three-quarters of the city, including about 4,000 houses. The first train arrived on 16 August 1898, and by 1900 the city had the nickname of the Paris of Siberia.

During the Russian Civil War Irkutsk saw fierce fighting between the White movement and the Bolsheviks. In 1920 Aleksandr Kolchak, commander of the largest anti-Bolshevik force, was executed there, which effectively ended anti-Bolshevik resistance. The Irkutsk Region KGB estimated that 15,000 to 17,000 victims of the Great Terror were buried on the city outskirts, and the burial area was explored only after 1989.

Irkutsk is the largest city and administrative centre of Irkutsk Oblast, with a population of 587,891 at the 2010 census. Its historic centre is on UNESCO's tentative list of World Heritage Sites. The Savior Church, laid in stone in 1706, and the Epiphany Cathedral are among the oldest stone buildings in Siberia.
iron-age: The Iron Age is the final epoch of the three-age system of technology, after the Stone Age and the Bronze Age. The concept was devised for Iron Age Europe and the ancient Near East. Meteoric iron had been used for thousands of years earlier; the earliest known artifacts are nine small beads dated to 3200 BCE from burials at Gerzeh in Lower Egypt.

The beginning of the Iron Age is defined locally by archaeological convention, when smelted iron, especially steel tools and weapons, replaces bronze in common use. Smelting iron requires temperatures above 1,250 °C, impractical to reach commonly until the end of the second millennium BCE, and it also required procedures for removing impurities and regulating carbon content.

The three-age system was first used for the archaeology of Europe in the first half of the 19th century and was introduced to Scandinavia by Christian Jürgensen Thomsen in the 1830s; its name recalls Hesiod's Ages of Man. The earliest tentative evidence for iron-making is a few iron fragments with suitable carbon content from Proto-Hittite layers at Kaman-Kalehöyük in Turkey, dated to 2200 to 2000 BCE. A long-held view that a Hittite monopoly on ironworking underlay Hittite success no longer represents scholarly consensus.

Modern evidence identifies the start of large-scale global iron production about 1200 BCE, which marks the end of the Bronze Age. Anthony Snodgrass suggests that a shortage of tin and disrupted Mediterranean trade about 1300 BCE forced metalworkers to look for an alternative; once tin returned, iron was cheaper, stronger and lighter.

The Iron Age varies by region. In the ancient Near East it is considered to last from about 1200 BCE, the Bronze Age collapse, to about 550 BCE, with the Achaemenid Empire traditionally the end date. Iron working spread through the Mediterranean and to South Asia between the 12th and 11th centuries BCE. In Central and Western Europe the Iron Age lasted from about 800 BCE to about 1 BCE, ending with Roman conquest, and in Northern Europe it began about the 5th century BCE.

In China, writing developed first, so Bronze Age China passes almost directly into the Qin dynasty. Many parts of Africa passed directly from stone to iron, and some archaeologists believe iron metallurgy developed independently in sub-Saharan Africa; the Nok culture may have smelted iron from about 1000 BCE. Indigenous cultures of the Americas did not develop an iron economy before European contact.
iron-crown-of-lombardy: According to tradition, St. Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, had the crown forged for her son around a beaten nail from the True Cross, which she had found. Pope Gregory the Great is said to have given it to Theodelinda, princess of the Lombards, as a diplomatic gift, although he mentions no such donation among his recorded gifts, and Theodelinda gave it to the church at Monza in 628.

Scholars have long debated its origin, since no contemporary sources record its making. Radiocarbon analysis in the late 20th century identified at least two phases: the oldest components, including organic materials used to set the gemstones, date to between the 5th and 6th centuries, and others to between the late 7th and 10th centuries. The gold plates are consistent with late Roman and Byzantine craftsmanship, and some scholars think the crown was once part of a ceremonial helmet or diadem.

The crown has an outer circlet of six hinged segments of beaten gold, partly enamelled and set with 22 gemstones in relief, in the form of crosses and flowers. Inside is a band about one centimetre wide that is said to have been beaten from a nail of the crucifixion.

In 1993 the University of Milan tested it with X-ray fluorescence and radiocarbon dating. The band was found to be pure silver, with no iron. A note in the Roman Ceremonial of 1159 suggests the name came from a lamina of iron once laid over the crown, probably as an arch, rather than inside it. Beeswax under three enamel plates dated to around 500 and that under the others to around 800, consistent with a more ancient crown decorated under Theoderic and extensively restored under Charlemagne.

The Lombard kings did not use it, being acclaimed by the people in arms with the spear as symbol of royal power. Critical scholarship identifies only a limited number of the coronations that 17th-century writers attributed to it, the first confirmed being that of Otto III in 996 at Pavia, followed by Conrad II in 1026. Later confirmed uses include Charles IV in 1355, Sigismund in 1433 and Charles V in 1530 at Bologna, the last coronation performed by a pope.

On 26 May 1805 Napoleon crowned himself King of Italy in Milan Cathedral with it, saying, God has given it to me, woe to him who touches it. After being taken to Vienna, it was returned to Italy in 1866 and restored to Monza Cathedral. It is kept in the Chapel of Theodelinda there.
iron-curtain: The phrase was used before the Cold War: Queen Elisabeth of Belgium used it in 1914 for a barrier descending between her people and Germany. Perhaps the first recorded application to Soviet Russia is in Vasily Rozanov's 1918 polemic The Apocalypse of Our Time.

Winston Churchill's first recorded use was in a telegram of 12 May 1945 to President Harry S. Truman, expressing concern about Soviet actions, and he repeated it on 4 June and in the House of Commons on 16 August 1945. On 5 March 1946, at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, with Truman attending, he said that from Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic an iron curtain had descended across the continent.

The antagonism behind the term had several origins. The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact of August 1939 contained a secret agreement to split Poland and Eastern Europe between the Soviet Union and Nazi Germany, and the Soviets then occupied eastern Poland, the Baltic states and northern Romania. Between 1945 and 1949 the Soviets converted East Germany, Bulgaria, Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Romania and Albania into satellite states, while Yugoslavia turned away from the Soviet Union in the late 1940s.

The curtain took physical shape as border defences, among the most heavily militarised areas in the world, particularly the inner German border. In Hungary a double barbed-wire fence was set 50 metres from the border with mines between the fences, later replaced by an electric signal fence, guard towers, a sand strip to track violations and patrols authorised to use weapons to stop escapees. Emigration from east to west was effectively halted after 1950, after more than 15 million people, mainly ethnic Germans, had left Soviet-occupied countries in the five years following the war.

Churchill's speech was not well received at the time, and much of the Western public still regarded the Soviet Union as a close ally. The phrase gained popularity as a shorthand for the division of Europe as the Cold War progressed, and the curtain served to keep people in and information out.

Its end began with the fall of communism in Poland, Hungary, East Germany, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia and Romania. East Germany reunited with West Germany on 3 October 1990, the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991 and Czechoslovakia in 1992. The fall of the curtain was accompanied by a large rise in east–west migration.
iron-gates: In the broad sense the Iron Gates are a route of 134 kilometres on the Danube, where the river separates the southern Carpathian Mountains from the north-western foothills of the Balkan Mountains. In the narrow sense the name means only the last barrier, just beyond the Romanian city of Orșova. The first narrowing is the Golubac gorge, 14.5 kilometres long, with a medieval fort on the Serbian bank. Next come Gospodjin Vir, with cliffs rising to 500 metres, and the Great and Small Kazan gorges. The Great Kazan is the narrowest, where the river is 150 metres wide and up to 53 metres deep.

The rapids and rocks in the riverbed made the passage infamous for shipping. Under Ottoman rule local pilots called kalauz guided ships through; under Prince Miloš Obrenović Serbs took over, with a Turkish title, dumendžibaša. The name Đerdap comes from Turkish girdap, meaning whirlpool, and the name Iron Gates translates the Turkish Demir-kapija.

The area has been inhabited for a very long time. The Iron Gates Mesolithic culture, dated about 13,000 to 5,000 years ago, is named after the gorge, and Lepenski Vir, unearthed in the 1960s, is often regarded as the most important Mesolithic site in south-east Europe. The Danube was part of the Roman frontier here, and the emperor Trajan had a bridge built by Apollodorus of Damascus east of the Great Kazan between 103 and 105, before his final conquest of Dacia.

The islet of Ada Kaleh, a Turkish exclave with about 400 to 500 people, changed hands between Austrians and Ottomans several times from 1669; the Treaty of Lausanne gave it to Romania in 1923. In the nineteenth century István Széchenyi drafted a plan in 1831 to make the passage navigable, and Hungarian engineers worked from 1889 on channels through the rocks. The Sip Canal was inaugurated on 17 September 1896 by Franz Joseph, Carol I of Romania and Alexander Obrenovich of Serbia.

A joint Romanian-Yugoslav project began in 1964. The Iron Gate I Dam opened in 1972 and Iron Gate II in 1984, each with a hydroelectric station and navigation locks. The river rose 35 metres near the dam, submerging old Orșova, Ada Kaleh and at least five other villages with 17,000 people, and the dams interrupted the spawning routes of several sturgeon species. The Đerdap National Park in Serbia dates from 1974 and the Porțile de Fier National Park in Romania from 2001.
ironclad: The ironclad became feasible and necessary through three developments of the first half of the nineteenth century: steam propulsion, shell guns and iron construction. Steam became suitable for major warships after the screw propeller was adopted in the 1840s, and the French built the first purpose-built steam battleship, Napoléon, in 1850. Explosive shells, developed by the French general Henri-Joseph Paixhans, were part of standard armament by the 1840s. Iron hulls began in the 1830s with the gunboat Nemesis, built for the East India Company in 1839.

France launched the first ocean-going ironclad, Gloire, in 1859. Her wooden hull was sheathed in iron plates 4.5 inches thick, and she carried thirty-six rifled guns. Britain responded and built the first completely iron-hulled warships, among them HMS Warrior, protected by wrought iron backed by 15 inches of teak.

Ironclads first fought in the American Civil War, notably at the Battle of Hampton Roads in 1862, where the Monitor and the Virginia met. Their performance showed that the ironclad had replaced the unarmoured ship of the line as the most powerful warship afloat. The first fleet battle between ironclads was the Battle of Lissa in 1866, between Austria and Italy, in which the Austrian flagship rammed and sank the Italian Re d'Italia.

The success at Lissa and the scant gun damage at Hampton Roads fuelled a ram craze from the 1860s to the 1880s, though few ships were actually sunk by ramming. Heavier guns, mounted in turrets and barbettes, replaced rows of broadside guns, and the torpedo added a threat from small craft. Early ironclads kept masts and sails, because early steam engines were inefficient and carried only a few days' coal.

Change was so rapid that many ships were obsolete almost as soon as they were finished. There is no clear end to the ironclad period, but in the 1890s navies settled on a standard pattern, the pre-dreadnought, and the terms battleship and armoured cruiser replaced the word ironclad. Ironclads were still in use in the First World War. Several survive as museum ships, among them HMS Warrior at Portsmouth and Huáscar at Talcahuano.
iroquoian-languages: The Iroquoian languages, occasionally called the Ogwehoweh languages, are a family of indigenous languages of North America. The family divides into Northern Iroquoian and Southern Iroquoian, or Cherokee. Northern Iroquoian includes the Iroquois Proper or Five Nations group of Seneca, Cayuga and Onondaga, a Mohawk–Oneida group, the Huronian languages Wendat, Petun and Wyandot, and the Tuscarora–Nottoway group of Tuscarora, Meherrin and Nottoway. Susquehannock, Wenro, Neutral, Erie and Laurentian are unclassified. Cherokee has dialects in South Carolina and Georgia, in North Carolina and in Oklahoma. Several of these languages are extinct or dormant, including Wendat, Petun, Wyandot, Tuscarora, Meherrin and Nottoway.

The Iroquoian languages are polysynthetic and head-marking, and they are known for their general lack of labial consonants. Where labials occur they are largely restricted to borrowings, expressive vocabulary or variant pronunciations. In Cherokee, native vocabulary has them only in the words for water and salt. No member contrasts voicing, and most have oral vowels with no nasal counterparts and nasal vowels with no oral ones. Cherokee has lexical tone, which its relatives lack. Attempts to link Iroquoian, Siouan and Caddoan languages in a Macro-Siouan family are suggestive but remain unproven.

Several of the peoples are poorly documented. The languages of the Wenro, the Susquehannock or Conestoga Confederacy, the Neutral Nation and the Erie Nation are very poorly documented in print, and the Wyandot called the Neutral Atiwandaronk, meaning they who understand the language. By 1660 all of these peoples except the Conestoga and the Haudenosaunee Confederacy had been defeated and scattered, migrating to form new tribes or adopted into others. The Iroquoian peoples adopted valiant enemies, and captive women and children, to replace the dead.

Almost all surviving Iroquoian languages are severely or critically endangered, and some have only a few elderly speakers. The two languages with the most speakers, Mohawk in New York and Canada and Cherokee in Oklahoma and North Carolina, are spoken by fewer than 10 per cent of the populations of their nations. Programmes support revival: Syracuse University has a Certificate in Iroquois Linguistics for Language Learners, Six Nations Polytechnic in Ohsweken, Ontario offers diplomas and degrees in Mohawk or Cayuga, and from September 2017 the University of Waterloo has offered a credit course in Mohawk.
irrawaddy-river: The Irrawaddy rises where the N'mai and Mali rivers meet in Kachin State, both fed by Himalayan glaciers. The N'mai is the larger but cannot be navigated because of its current, while the Mali is navigable despite a few rapids. The drainage basin of about 400,000 square kilometres covers 61 per cent of the land area of Burma. Between Myitkyina and Mandalay the river runs through three defiles, then crosses the central Dry Zone, the ancient cultural heartland of the Bamar people, and is joined by the Chindwin before turning south.

The delta begins about 93 kilometres above Hinthada, with the Pathein River as its westernmost distributary and the Yangon River as its easternmost. Its fine silt is renewed by the river, and the delta surface extends into the Andaman Sea at about 50 metres a year. Monsoon rains between mid-May and mid-October make the flow vary greatly, with the highest water in August and the lowest in February.

The name comes from Pali, Irāvatī or Airāvatī being the name of the elephant mount of Indra. During the Age of Discovery European explorers also called the river the Pegu, after the Hanthawaddy kingdom whose main river it was. As early as the sixth century the river carried trade and transport, and by the twelfth century a developed network of canals supported flourishing rice cultivation. Later it became a key economic tool of British imperial interests, who set up trading ports along its shores.

The Irrawaddy is about 2,170 kilometres long and remains the most important commercial waterway of Myanmar. Commercial transport is maintained for about 1,300 kilometres, from Hinthada to Bhamo throughout the year, and rice from the delta, one of the major rice-growing areas of the world, is among the main goods carried, together with teak floated down in rafts and petroleum from the oil-field district at Chauk. Until the Ava Bridge, built by the British colonial government in 1934, the only way across was by ferry. The river gives its name to the Irrawaddy dolphin, and Rudyard Kipling's poem has led it sometimes to be called the Road to Mandalay.
irredentism: The term was coined from the Italian phrase Italia irredenta, meaning unredeemed Italy. It referred to territory in Austria-Hungary that was mostly or partly inhabited by ethnic Italians, in particular Trentino and Trieste but also Gorizia, Istria, Fiume and Dalmatia, during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. An Italian movement after 1878 claimed parts of Switzerland and the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Irredentism is tied to the rise of modern nationalism and the nation-state, which are often linked to the French Revolution of 1789, and it has been an influential force in world politics since the mid-nineteenth century. Some scholars argue that similar phenomena existed earlier, for example in the claim that the crusades aimed to liberate fellow Christians and redeem the Holy Land, but most see it as a recent development.

Irredentism is the desire of one state to annex territory of another, either because its population is ethnically similar to that of the parent state or because the territory once formed part of it. There is no consensus on its exact definition. Political theorists Naomi Chazan and Donald L. Horowitz distinguish two types: a state seeking to annex territory of a neighbour, as with Nazi Germany's claim on the Sudetenland of Czechoslovakia, and a minority spread across several countries seeking to unite in a new state, as in the proposed Kurdistan. Not all theorists accept the second type.

It differs from secession, in which a territory breaks away to form an independent state, and from revanchism, which seeks territory in revenge for an earlier grievance. The word revanchism comes from the French revanche and was first used after the Franco-Prussian War for nationalists who wished to reclaim Alsace-Lorraine.

Among the cases often discussed are the Megali Idea, the Greek nationalist project that shaped Greek history from the War of Independence in the 1820s through the Balkan Wars and began to fade after the Greco-Turkish War of 1919 to 1922; the annexation of the Sudetenland in 1938, ceded to Germany under the Munich Agreement in an attempt to prevent a major war; Somalia's invasion of Ethiopia in 1977; and Argentina's invasion of the Falkland Islands in 1982.

International law is for the most part hostile to irredentism: the United Nations Charter calls for respect for established borders, as do the Organization of African Unity, the Organization of American States and the Helsinki Final Act. Irredentist movements often fail, and peaceful settlements usually bring mutual recognition of existing borders rather than territorial change.
irtysh: The Irtysh runs through China, Kazakhstan and Russia and is the chief tributary of the Ob and the longest tributary in the world. It rises as the Kara-Irtysh, or Black Irtysh, in the Mongolian Altai in Xinjiang, close to the border with Mongolia. It flows northwest through Lake Zaysan in Kazakhstan, meets the Ishim and Tobol and joins the Ob near Khanty-Mansiysk in western Siberia after 4,248 kilometres. Its name first appears in the epitaphs of the Turkic commanders Tonyukuk and Kul Tigin. Mahmud al-Kashgari derived it from ertishmak, a quick jump, while a legend told by al-Gardizi says a slave of the Kimak founder Prince Shad called out irtysh, meaning stop.

Mongol and Turkic peoples held the banks for many centuries. In 657 the Tang general Su Dingfang defeated Ashina Helu, qaghan of the Western Turkic Khaganate, at the Battle of Irtysh River, which ended the Khaganate. In 1208 the Mongol Empire fought an alliance of Merkit and Naimans near the mouth of the Bukhtarma. In the 15th and 16th centuries the middle and lower river lay within the Tatar Khanate of Sibir, whose capital Qashliq stood a few kilometres upstream from the mouth of the Tobol. The Russians conquered the Khanate in the 1580s and founded Tobolsk in 1587 and Tara in 1594.

In the 17th century the Dzungar Khanate controlled the upper river and became Russia's southern neighbour. Russia founded Omsk in 1716, Semipalatinsk in 1718, Ust-Kamenogorsk in 1720 and Petropavlovsk in 1752. The Qing Empire conquered Dzungaria in the 1750s, and the border between the two empires in the basin was roughly marked by chains of guard posts. The Convention of Peking of 1860 and the Protocol of Chuguchak of 1864 set a line close to China's present border, leaving Lake Zaysan on the Russian side, and the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1881 adjusted it slightly in Russia's favour.

Ships navigate the river in Kazakhstan and Russia from April to October, and Omsk is the largest river port of Western Siberia. Hydroelectric plants stand at Bukhtarma, Ust-Kamenogorsk and Shulbinsk in Kazakhstan, and the lock at Ust-Kamenogorsk has a drop of 42 metres. The Irtysh–Karaganda Canal was built between 1962 and 1974 to supply the Kazakh steppe. Cities on the river include Oskemen, Semey and Pavlodar in Kazakhstan and Omsk, Tobolsk and Khanty-Mansiysk in Russia. The railway bridge at Omsk, opened in 1896 on the Trans-Siberian Railway, is the oldest on the river.
isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa: Isa was born in Jasra to Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa and Mouza bint Hamad Al Khalifa, a member of the House of Khalifa. He succeeded his father as ruler upon his death in November 1961 and was installed on 16 December. On 8 May 1949 he had married his cousin Sheikha Hessa bint Salman Al Khalifa, the daughter of Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa. They had five sons and four daughters, and the eldest son, Hamad, succeeded him.

Isa ruled as Hakim until 1971 and as Emir for the remainder of his reign. In 1968 he visited Mohsin Al Hakim in Najaf to indicate his wish to strengthen relations with the Shia. Bahrain gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1971. The government at first considered joining the United Arab Emirates, but Isa withdrew his country, along with Qatar, because he was dissatisfied with the proposed constitution.

He then attempted to introduce a moderate form of parliamentary democracy, and men, though not women, were given the vote in parliamentary elections in 1973. In August 1975 he dissolved Parliament because it refused to pass the government-sponsored State Security Law of 1974. The parliamentary system was never restored in his lifetime, despite occasional protests from leftist and Islamist groups that reached their peak in 1994. During his reign the Emir had a diplomatic and ceremonial role by arrangement with his brother Sheikh Khalifa bin Salman, who controlled the government and economy as Prime Minister. In 1981 Isa was among the founders of the Dar Al Maal Al Islami Trust, initiated by Mohammed bin Faisal Al Saud, son of King Faisal.

During his 38 years as Emir Bahrain was transformed economically into a modern nation and a key financial centre of the Persian Gulf, though critics note that he also dissolved Parliament and took on absolute power. Isa died of a heart attack on 6 March 1999 at the Government House in Manama, at the age of 65, shortly after a meeting with the United States defense secretary William Cohen. The last function he attended was the funeral of King Hussein of Jordan, less than a month earlier. US President Bill Clinton expressed deep sadness, and UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan described him as a force for stability in the region. He was buried at the Al-Rifa'a cemetery.
isaac-ii-angelos: Isaac Angelos was possibly born in September 1156, the son of Andronikos Angelos Doukas, a general in Asia Minor under Manuel I Komnenos. Through his grandmother Theodora Komnene, a daughter of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, he belonged to the extended imperial clan of the Komnenoi. During the regency of Andronikos I for Alexios II he joined a plot against Andronikos, fled by boat, and reached Damascus and Baghdad before settling at Acre. On 11 September 1185 Andronikos's lieutenant Stephen Hagiochristophorites tried to arrest him. Isaac killed him and took refuge in the Hagia Sophia, where a popular tumult proclaimed him emperor. Andronikos was killed on 12 September 1185.

Isaac began his reign with a victory over the Norman king William II of Sicily at the Battle of Demetritzes on 7 November 1185. He strengthened his position by marriage, wedding Margaret of Hungary, daughter of Béla III, in January 1186. His taxes, raised to pay his armies and finance the marriage, produced a Vlach-Bulgarian uprising late in 1185 and the empire under the Asen dynasty. His fleet failed to recover Cyprus from the rebellious noble Isaac Komnenos. He also faced several usurpers, among them Alexios Branas, who was killed outside Constantinople, and Theodore Mangaphas of Philadelphia.

In 1189 Frederick I Barbarossa asked to lead the Third Crusade through Byzantine territory. Isaac suspected his intentions, Barbarossa's army occupied Philippopolis, and in 1190 Isaac released the German emissaries and exchanged hostages. His campaigns against Bulgaria brought defeats at Tryavna in 1190 and Arcadiopolis in 1194. In April 1195 his older brother Alexios Angelos was proclaimed emperor as Alexios III while Isaac was away hunting, and had him blinded and imprisoned.

Isaac's son Alexis sought help in Venice, and the Fourth Crusade, diverted by Doge Enrico Dandolo, took Constantinople in July 1203. Isaac was freed after eight years of captivity and confirmed the Pact of Zara by chrysobull, and his son was crowned co-emperor as Alexios IV, the effective monarch because blindness and confinement had enfeebled Isaac. At the end of January 1204 Alexios Doukas seized the throne as Alexios V amid riots. Isaac died, allegedly of shock, and Alexios IV was strangled. Isaac has the reputation as one of the most unsuccessful rulers of the Byzantine throne, held responsible for the empire's troubles at the end of the 12th century.
isaac-newton: Isaac Newton was born on 25 December 1642 (4 January 1643 in the modern calendar) at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire. His father, also named Isaac Newton, had died three months before. Born prematurely, he was a small child; his mother, Hannah Ayscough, said that he could have fit inside a quart mug. When he was three she remarried and left him in the care of his grandmother. From about the age of twelve until seventeen he attended The King's School in Grantham. His mother tried to make him a farmer, an occupation he hated, until his uncle and the schoolmaster persuaded her to send him back to school.

Newton was a fellow of Trinity College and the second Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at the University of Cambridge, appointed at the age of 26. He refused to take holy orders in the Church of England. He served two brief terms as Member of Parliament for the University of Cambridge, in 1689 to 1690 and 1701 to 1702.

In 1696 he moved to London as Warden of the Mint, a post obtained through the patronage of Charles Montagu, 1st Earl of Halifax. He took charge of England's great recoining. He became Master of the Mint in 1699, holding the post for the last 30 years of his life. These appointments were intended as sinecures, but Newton took them seriously, reforming the currency and punishing clippers and counterfeiters. He was president of the Royal Society from 1703 and was knighted by Queen Anne in 1705. He died on 31 March 1727, at the age of 84, and was the first scientist to be buried at Westminster Abbey.

Newton began his work on calculus, which he called fluxions, in 1664, and by 1665 had developed a systematic calculus unifying differentiation and integration. He was self-taught in mathematics. He later quarrelled with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz over priority. Both are now credited with developing calculus independently, though Newton came to it much earlier. Leibniz's notation, however, proved the more convenient. The Principia of 1687 set out his laws of motion and universal gravitation, and his Opticks appeared in 1704.

Newton was a devout but heterodox Christian who privately rejected the doctrine of the Trinity, and he devoted much time to biblical chronology and alchemy.
