Of an estimated ten million words in his papers, about one million deal with alchemy. Most of his writing in these fields stayed unpublished until long after his death. His library of 1,752 identified books held 477 on theology and 169 on alchemy.
isaac-watts: Isaac Watts was the eldest of nine children of Sarah Watts and Isaac Watts Senior, a nonconformist who had been imprisoned twice for his views. He was educated at King Edward VI School in Southampton, where he learned Latin, Greek and Hebrew, and he was said to have shown a gift for rhyme at seven. In 1690 he went to the Dissenting Academy at Stoke Newington. He then worked as a private tutor in the household of the Hartopp family and lived for a total of 36 years in the household of Sir Thomas Abney and Lady Mary Abney. He began preaching in 1698.

Watts held more ecumenical opinions than was usual among Congregationalists and cared more for education and scholarship than for any sect. He led a change in worship by adding new poetry on Christian experience to the older tradition of singing the Psalms. In his metrical psalter he adapted the Psalms with a Christian perspective, and he explained that where the Psalmist speaks of sacrificing goats and bullocks, he mentions the sacrifice of Christ. Many later poets followed his path.

His textbook Logick was first published in 1724 in four parts: perception, judgement, reasoning and method. It shows the influence of John Locke, and it treats logic as a practical art useful in any inquiry. It became the standard text at Oxford, Cambridge, Harvard and Yale, and was used at Oxford for well over 100 years. A supplement, The Improvement of the Mind, followed in 1741 and later inspired Michael Faraday.

Edinburgh gave Watts a Doctor of Divinity diploma in 1728. He lived at Abney Hall in Stoke Newington until his death in 1748 and was buried in Bunhill Fields. His papers were given to Yale University. His hymns influenced nonconformists and revivalists such as Philip Doddridge, who dedicated his best-known work to him. King Edward VI School in Southampton named one of its houses Watts and uses Our God, Our Help in Ages Past as its school hymn.
isabeau-of-bavaria: Isabeau was born into the House of Wittelsbach, the only daughter of Duke Stephen III of Bavaria-Ingolstadt and Taddea Visconti, a daughter of Bernabò Visconti, Lord of Milan. She was most likely born in Munich and baptised Elisabeth. In 1383 her uncle Duke Frederick of Bavaria-Landshut proposed her as a bride for King Charles VI of France, and the match was raised again at the Burgundian double wedding at Cambrai in April 1385. At 15 or 16 she was sent to France, and the couple wed three days after their first meeting. Her coronation on 23 August 1389 was marked by a lavish entry into Paris.

In 1392 Charles suffered the first attack of a lifelong mental illness. Although he demanded her removal from his presence during his illness, he consistently allowed her to act for him. She became regent to the Dauphin and sat on the regency council, with far more power than was usual for a queen consort. As rivalry grew between Charles's brother Louis I, Duke of Orléans, and the royal dukes of Burgundy, she acted as a peacekeeper. In 1401 she intervened between Orléans and Burgundy and prevented bloodshed, and in 1402 Charles gave her control of the treasury.

John the Fearless had Orléans assassinated in 1407, and the Armagnac–Burgundian Civil War broke out in 1411. Isabeau shifted her allegiance in the interest of the heir. When she followed the Armagnacs the Burgundians accused her of adultery with Orléans, and when she sided with the Burgundians the Armagnacs removed her from Paris and imprisoned her. After Henry V of England's victory at Agincourt in 1415, she accompanied Charles to sign the Treaty of Troyes in May 1420, standing in for him because of his illness.

Isabeau lived in English-controlled Paris until her death on 24 September 1435. She had twelve children, of whom only her youngest son, Charles VII, reached adulthood among the sons. She was long portrayed as a spendthrift and philanderer and accused of giving away the crown at Troyes. Historians who re-examined the chronicles in the late 20th century concluded that many of these charges stemmed from factionalism and propaganda, in particular the pro-Burgundian writing of Pintoin. She was also a patron of goldsmiths, and in 1404 she gave Charles the gold statuette known as the Little Golden Horse Shrine.
isabel-princess-imperial-of-brazil: Isabel was born on 29 July 1846 at the Paço de São Cristóvão in Rio de Janeiro, eldest daughter of Emperor Pedro II and Empress Teresa Cristina, of the Brazilian branch of the House of Braganza. After the deaths of her two younger brothers in infancy she was recognised as her father's heir presumptive, and the losses led Pedro II to see his position as that of a head of state for his own lifetime only. Her education began in 1854, and in 1856 the Countess of Barral became her aia, a role model for the young princess. In 1864 she entered an arranged marriage with the French prince Gaston, Count of Eu, with whom she had three sons.

Isabel served as regent three times, in 1871-1872, 1876-1877 and 1887-1888, while her father travelled abroad. In her first regency she signed on 27 September 1871 the Law of Free Birth, which freed all children born of slaves after that date. Her second regency was marked by election fraud and violence, tension between the Church and State and a drought in the north-east, and she and Gaston withdrew from public life, which left them isolated.

During the third regency, from 30 June 1887, she became convinced that more action was needed and pressed the Conservative prime minister, Baron of Cotegipe, to free more slaves. After the Rio police mishandled a pro-abolition demonstration in early 1888, she replaced him with João Alfredo Correia de Oliveira.

Isabel sponsored and signed the Lei Áurea, the Golden Law, in 1888, abolishing slavery in Brazil. Emancipation was widely welcomed but intensified opposition among landowners and political elites, and her prospective accession was contested because of gender prejudice, her strong Catholic faith and her marriage to a foreign prince. The military coup of 1889 overthrew the monarchy, and the family went into exile, settling at Cannes after the new government abolished their allowances. On the day after the coup she wrote that if abolition was the cause she did not regret it.

Isabel died in 1921 and was buried at Dreux, and in 1971 her remains and her husband's were interred in the Cathedral of Petrópolis. Historian Roderick J. Barman writes that posterity remembers her for acting decisively once, on the abolition of slavery.
isabella-i-of-castile: Isabella was born on 22 April 1451 at Madrigal de las Altas Torres, the daughter of King John II of Castile and his second wife, Isabella of Portugal. When her father died in 1454, her half-brother became King Henry IV, and she and her brother Alfonso were left in his care. On 19 October 1469 she married Ferdinand of Aragon in secret at Valladolid. Because they were second cousins they needed a papal dispensation, and the bull produced was supposedly Pope Pius II's, though he had died in 1464.

Henry IV denounced the marriage and in October 1470 declared his daughter Joanna his true heir. When he died on 11 December 1474, Isabella took refuge in the Alcázar of Segovia and was proclaimed Queen of Castile and León the next day. Supporters of Joanna planned to marry her to King Afonso V of Portugal. The war ended in a Castilian victory on land and a Portuguese victory at sea, and by the treaties of Alcáçovas, signed on 4 September 1479, Portugal gave up the Castilian throne and kept most of the disputed Atlantic territories, apart from the Canary Islands.

Isabella tackled the disorder left by her brother's reign and in 1476 created a police force, the Santa Hermandad. With Ferdinand she completed the Reconquista, ordered the expulsion of the Jews from Spain in the Alhambra Decree, began the Spanish Inquisition and financed Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage. The Granada War began in 1482, and it took ten years to conquer the Emirate of Granada. After a Muslim uprising in 1499, the monarchs broke the Treaty of Granada in 1502 and ordered Muslims to convert or leave.

Isabella withdrew from government on 14 September 1504 and died on 26 November at Medina del Campo. She is buried in the Capilla Real in Granada beside Ferdinand. Of her seven children five survived to adulthood, among them Joanna, Queen of Castile, and Catherine of Aragon. A cause for her beatification was opened in 1958 and she was named a Servant of God in 1974, but John Paul II suspended the cause in 1991 because of the expulsion of the Jews.
isabella-ii-of-jerusalem: Isabella II was born in late 1212 in the Kingdom of Jerusalem, then a rump state without the city of Jerusalem. She was the only child of Queen Maria of Montferrat, who died of complications of childbirth, and so inherited the kingdom within days. The situation was unprecedented, because her father, John of Brienne, had become king by marrying Maria and expected to keep the crown for life. A faction around the Ibelin family held that he could rule only as regent for his daughter. Pope Innocent III promised support to John and Isabella.

In 1223, at a conference in Ferentino, Hermann of Salza, grand master of the Teutonic Knights, proposed her as a bride for Emperor Frederick II, recently widowed and preparing to lead a crusade. John, who wanted a powerful leader to summon Western aid, accepted once Hermann promised him the government of the kingdom for life.

In August 1225 Isabella was married by proxy at Acre and crowned queen of Jerusalem at Tyre. She sailed to Brindisi, where she married Frederick in person on 9 November 1225, becoming empress and queen of Sicily. Frederick then summoned John and declared that he would take his wife's rights and the kingdom, in breach of his agreement. The leading men who had come with her accepted him as king. The pope refused to call him king of Jerusalem for six years.

Frederick kept Isabella in relative seclusion at Palermo and did not take her on his crusade in 1227. Chroniclers close to her father said he mistreated her; the historians Guy Perry and David Abulafia doubt such stories. Isabella issued a charter in which she is principal grantor, the first by a queen of Jerusalem since Melisende, and her consent appears in another. A daughter, Margaret, born in November 1226, died in August 1227.

Isabella gave birth to her son Conrad II on 25 April 1228 and died a few days later at the age of fifteen. She was buried in the Cathedral of Saint Peter in Andria. Rumours that Frederick had killed her, probably encouraged by her father, are dismissed by Abulafia as nonsense. Through her marriage the Kingdom of Jerusalem passed to largely absentee kings until its fall sixty-six years later, and Perry argues that she simply did not live long enough to have much impact.
isabella-ii-of-spain: Isabella was born in the Royal Palace of Madrid on 10 October 1830, the elder daughter of King Ferdinand VII and Maria Christina of the Two Sicilies. Ferdinand had induced the Cortes Generales to set aside the Salic law, brought in by the Bourbons in the early 18th century, so that his daughter could inherit.

Her uncle, Infante Carlos, Count of Molina, disputed her title, and his supporters, the Carlists, fought over the succession for seven years during her minority. Maria Christina acted as regent, and Baldomero Espartero succeeded her until a pronunciamiento led by Leopoldo O'Donnell and Ramón María Narváez removed him in 1843. Isabella was then declared of age at thirteen.

On 10 October 1846 she was married to her double first cousin Francisco de Asís, Duke of Cádiz, in a union that was unhappy and the subject of persistent rumour. Marshal Narváez dominated the Moderate decade from 1844. On 2 February 1852 a priest, Martín Merino y Gómez, stabbed her; her embroidered dress and corset limited the wound, and he was executed. A pronunciamiento at Vicálvaro on 28 June 1854 led to a popular revolution and the return of Espartero for the progressive biennium. Her later reign saw a war against Morocco in 1859–1860 and the Chincha Islands War of 1865–1866.

In August 1866 Democratic and Progressive exiles signed the Pact of Ostend in Belgium. On 18 September 1868 a pronunciamiento at Cádiz led by Marshal Prim and Admiral Topete began the Glorious Revolution. Historians point to the alienation of both moderates and progressives, the queen's conduct, corruption and an economic crisis. Isabella's forces under Manuel Pavía y Lacy were beaten by Marshal Serrano at the Battle of Alcolea on 28 September, and she crossed into France on 30 September.

She settled in Paris and renounced her dynastic rights in favour of her son Alfonso on 25 June 1870. A coup begun at Sagunto on 29 December 1874 overthrew the First Spanish Republic and proclaimed Alfonso XII. Isabella returned to Spain in July 1876 but was soon back in France. She died in Paris on 9 April 1904 and her body was taken to El Escorial, where she had wished to be entombed. She is the only queen regnant in the history of unified Spain, and was nicknamed the Traditional Queen and the Queen of Sad Mischance.
isabella-jagiellon: Isabella was born in Kraków on 18 January 1519, the oldest child of Sigismund I the Old and Bona Sforza. She grew up at Wawel Castle, received a good education and could speak and write Polish, Latin, German and Italian. Her mother favoured her and arranged her marriage early: a French match with a son of Francis I was proposed when she was two months old and failed after the Battle of Pavia, and several Italian, Habsburg and Savoy matches came to nothing. Around 1531 a plan emerged to wed her to John Zápolya, whom Bona backed as an opponent of the Habsburgs. Sigismund relented on condition of a peace between Zápolya and the Habsburgs, which came as the Treaty of Nagyvárad of February 1538.

She married Zápolya in 1539 and was crowned Queen of Hungary at Székesfehérvár. Her son John Sigismund was born on 7 July 1540, and Zápolya died on 22 July. Nobles led by Bishop George Martinuzzi elected the infant king in September 1540, with Isabella as regent, against the treaty's provision for Ferdinand to succeed. Ferdinand besieged Buda, and Sultan Suleiman lifted the second siege in 1541, annexed most of Hungary and left Transylvania and the lands east of the Tisza to Isabella and her son. She settled at Gyulafehérvár and began rebuilding the bishop's palace in Alba Iulia.

Ferdinand and Martinuzzi agreed in 1549 that she would give up Transylvania. After fighting near Cenad, she signed the Treaty of Weissenburg in July 1551, exchanging Transylvania for the Duchy of Opole and Racibórz and other territories, and gave up the Holy Crown of Hungary. She lived in Poland for five years. Invited back by Suleiman and local nobles, she entered Kolozsvár in October 1556 with Ottoman troops, and on 25 November the Transylvanian Diet gave her a five-year regency. In 1557 she signed an edict granting freedom of religion to Catholics, Lutherans, Calvinists and Unitarians, a step towards the Edict of Torda of 1568.

Isabella died of a long illness in September 1559, three years after her return. She is noted as the first European ruler to issue laws on religious tolerance. According to a legend, she carved the letters SFV, for Sic fata volunt, meaning it is the will of fate, on an oak at Meszes in 1551; the motto also appears on her coins and jewellery.
isabella-of-angouleme: Isabella was the only child of Aymer Taillefer, Count of Angoulême, and Alice of Courtenay, a sister of Peter II of Courtenay, Latin Emperor of Constantinople. She was originally betrothed to Hugh IX le Brun, Count of Lusignan, grandson and heir of the Count of La Marche. On 24 August 1200, at the age of 12 or 14, she married King John at Angoulême, a year after he had annulled his first marriage to Isabel, Countess of Gloucester. She was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 8 October. King Philip II of France confiscated John's French lands over the match, and armed conflict followed. She became Countess of Angoulême in her own right on 16 June 1202.

Contemporaries admired her beauty, and historians have sometimes called her the Helen of the Middle Ages. The common people termed her a siren. Stories that John neglected state affairs to remain in bed with her were rumours spread by his enemies. On 1 October 1207 she bore the future Henry III at Winchester Castle, followed by Richard and three daughters, Joan, Isabella and Eleanor; all five children survived to adulthood.

After John died in October 1216 she arranged the coronation of her nine-year-old son at Gloucester on 28 October, supplying her own golden circlet because the crown had been lost in the Wash. In the following July she left him with the regent William Marshal and returned to France. In spring 1220 she married Hugh X of Lusignan, son of her former fiancé, who had been promised her daughter Joan. Joan wed Alexander II of Scotland in 1221. Because Isabella had not sought the English council's consent, it confiscated her dower lands and stopped her pension, then settled by granting her the Devon stannaries, the revenue of Aylesbury for four years and £3,000 of arrears.

Isabella bore Hugh nine more children, and the eldest, Hugh XI, succeeded his father in 1249. Some contemporaries called her 'vain, capricious and troublesome'. Summoned with Hugh to the French court to swear fealty to Alphonse, the new Count of Poitou, she was publicly snubbed by the queen dowager Blanche of Castile, and she is said to have joined a confederacy with Raymond VII of Toulouse against King Louis IX. After it failed, two royal cooks arrested in 1244 for attempting to poison the king confessed that they were in her pay. She fled to Fontevraud Abbey and died there on 4 June 1246; none of this can be confirmed.

She was first buried in the churchyard as an act of repentance. Henry III, visiting, had her moved inside, beside Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine. Most of her Lusignan children went to Henry's court in England.
isabella-of-hainaut: Isabella was born in Valenciennes on 5 April 1170, the daughter of Baldwin V, Count of Hainaut, and Margaret I, Countess of Flanders. When she was one year old her father betrothed her to Henry, the future Count of Champagne, a nephew of Adèle of Champagne, the queen of France. In 1179 both fathers swore that the marriage would go ahead, but her father later agreed to her marrying King Philip II instead.

Isabella married the fifteen-year-old Philip on 28 April 1180 at Bapaume and brought the county of Artois as her dowry. The match was arranged by her maternal uncle Philip, Count of Flanders, an adviser to the king. The queen dowager disliked it, since it rejected her nephew and lessened her brothers' influence. Isabella was crowned at Saint Denis on 28 May 1180. As a descendant of Charlemagne, she was seen by chroniclers as uniting the Carolingian and Capetian dynasties, a union represented in her son Louis VIII. She was also formally countess of Artois de jure from 1180 to 1190.

At first she failed to win Philip's affection, since she had given him no heir. In 1184 Philip was at war with Flanders and, angry at her father's support for his enemies, threatened to divorce her. According to Gislebert of Mons, she went barefoot and dressed as a penitent through the town's churches and won the sympathy of the people, and the king's uncle Robert intervened. No repudiation followed; it would also have meant losing Artois. The marriage grew stronger, and on 5 September 1187 she gave birth to a son, Louis.

Her second pregnancy was extremely difficult. On 14 March 1190 she gave birth to twin boys, Robert, who died the same day, and Philip, who died three days later. Owing to complications she died in Paris on 15 March, not quite twenty years old, and was buried in the cathedral of Notre-Dame. Philip was in Normandy campaigning against Richard I of England; on learning of her death he signed a truce, returned to Paris and spent several days in mourning. Her son Louis succeeded her as count of Artois, and the county returned to the crown when he became king. In 1858 her body was exhumed, and a silver seal found in her coffin is now in the British Museum.
isaiah: The name Isaiah is Hebrew, Yəšaʿyāhū, meaning Yahweh is salvation. The first verse of the Book of Isaiah says that he prophesied during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. Uzziah reigned for 52 years in the middle of the 8th century BCE, so Isaiah probably began his ministry in the 740s BCE, a few years before Uzziah's death, and may have been a contemporary of Manasseh for some years. On this reckoning he prophesied for as long as 64 years.

According to some modern interpretations, his wife was called the prophetess, either because she had the prophetic gift or simply as the wife of the prophet. They had two sons, Shear-Jashub, meaning A remnant shall return, and Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz, meaning Quickly to spoils, plunder speedily.

In the time of Ahaz the kingdom of Judah was untouched by Assyria, while Shalmaneser V destroyed Samaria in the northern kingdom of Israel. Hezekiah, once on the throne, was encouraged to rebel against the king of Assyria and allied himself with the king of Egypt. Sennacherib then invaded Judah, and Hezekiah submitted. When war broke out again and an Assyrian detachment threatened Jerusalem, Isaiah urged Hezekiah to resist.

According to 2 Kings 19 and the derived account in 2 Chronicles 32, an angel of God killed 185,000 men of the Assyrian army in one night. The remaining years of Hezekiah's reign were peaceful, and Isaiah probably lived to its close. The Book of Isaiah calls him the prophet, but how far the book is the work of the historical prophet is disputed. The traditional view assigns all 66 chapters to him, while another widely held view holds that chapters 1 to 39 in part come from him and that the rest dates from around the end of the exile in Babylon in the 6th century BCE.

Neither the Hebrew Bible nor other primary sources state the time or manner of his death. The Talmud says that Manasseh had him sawn in two, and in one version Isaiah hid in a cedar tree that was then sawn in half. The story passed to Christian and Muslim writers. The Ascension of Isaiah, a Christian text of between the end of the 1st century and the beginning of the 3rd, tells of his martyrdom.

Christian writers such as Jerome valued the book highly, and New Testament writers quote it many times. In Islam he is not named in the Quran but appears as a prophet in works such as those of al-Tabari. In 2018 the archaeologist Eilat Mazar announced a seal impression reading belonging to Isaiah nvy, found near a bulla of King Hezekiah, though damage leaves it doubtful whether it names the prophet.
isaiah-berlin: Isaiah Berlin was born in Riga on 6 June 1909, the only son of Mendel Berlin, a timber trader whose family firm was one of the largest in the Baltics, and Marie Volshonok. He witnessed the February and October Revolutions of 1917 in Petrograd, and a memory of a man dragged from a rooftop by a crowd left him, he said, with a permanent horror of violence. The family left Petrograd in October 1920 and moved to Britain in early 1921, when he was 11. His English was virtually nonexistent at first, but he reached proficiency within a year.

Berlin was educated at St Paul's School in London and at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and took first-class honours in literae humaniores in 1928. In 1932, aged 23, he became the first unconverted Jew elected to a prize fellowship at All Souls College. During the Second World War he worked for British Information Services in New York and then at the British embassies in Washington and Moscow until 1946.

From 1957 to 1967 he was Chichele Professor of Social and Political Theory at Oxford. In 1966 he helped create Wolfson College, becoming its founding president, and he was president of the British Academy from 1974 to 1978. He disliked writing, and much of his published work comes from recorded lectures, edited from 1974 chiefly by Henry Hardy.

His inaugural lecture, Two Concepts of Liberty (1958), defined negative liberty as the absence of coercion by an external body, and positive liberty as self-mastery. He argued that positive liberty had been used in the 19th century to defend nationalism, paternalism and social engineering at the expense of negative liberty. His value pluralism held that moral values may be equally valid and yet incompatible, so that liberty may clash with social justice.

The Hedgehog and the Fox, his best-known essay for the general public, divides thinkers into hedgehogs, who see the world through one idea, and foxes, who draw on many; he later said he meant it as an enjoyable game. He died in Oxford on 5 November 1997, aged 88.
isar: The Isar has its official source in the Hinterau valley east of the village of Scharnitz, in the Karwendel mountains, at 1,160 metres above sea level. Its longest headstream is the Lavatschbach, and the Birkkarbach, which rises on the Birkkarspitze, feeds the young river as well. It enters Germany near Mittenwald and reaches Upper Bavaria after about 22 kilometres. The river is 295 km long and drains a basin of some 9,000 square kilometres, and at its mouth its average discharge is 174 cubic metres a second. Snowmelt raises the flow each spring.

At Bad Tölz the Isar leaves the Bavarian Alps and passes from its upper to its middle course. It crosses a glacial moraine landscape towards Wolfratshausen, where the Loisach joins it, and then the Munich gravel plain. At Moosburg its most important tributary, the Amper, flows in, and the lower course begins. Beyond Landshut the river runs through the Tertiary Hills of Lower Bavaria and descends some 848 metres in all before it enters the Danube about five kilometres from Deggendorf.

The name is first recorded in 763 as Isura. One theory derives it from an Indo-European root meaning flowing water, which in Proto-Germanic narrowed to the sense of frozen water, as in English ice and German Eis. The river was a prehistoric trade route, and in the Bronze Age Munich was among the largest raft ports in Europe. Between Moosburg and Plattling gold was washed from the river's sediments in the 16th and 17th centuries, though the small amounts found brought little profit.

Industrialisation made the Isar a river of many uses. Since the 1920s its water has generated electricity, and over forty hydropower plants were built on it to electrify Bavaria. In 1923 all the water north of Mittenwald was diverted to the Walchensee for the Walchensee Hydroelectric Power Station. The Sylvenstein reservoir was built between 1954 and 1959 to support power generation and to prevent floods, and it has kept the river from overflowing at Munich in years such as 1979, 1999 and 2005.

The upper Isar is now protected from development. Since 1990 a small share of the water, 4 cubic metres a second, has been left in the river to prevent drought. Under the Isar-plan, carried out between 2000 and 2011, embankments were removed in Munich, the bed was widened, connections to the flood plains were restored and rock ramps were built so that fish can again move upstream. The Isartalverein, founded in 1902 by Gabriel von Seidl, bought 90 hectares of land and maintains more than 330 km of hiking trails.
ischia: Ischia is a volcanic island at the northern end of the Gulf of Naples, about 30 kilometres from the city of Naples. It is the largest of the Phlegrean Islands, measures about 10 kilometres from east to west and 7 from north to south, and has an area of 47 square kilometres. It is almost entirely mountainous; the highest point is Mount Epomeo, at 788 metres. An eruption about 56,000 years ago was followed by the formation of a caldera that covers almost the whole island.

The acropolis site of Monte Vico was inhabited from the Bronze Age. In the 8th century BCE Euboean Greeks from Eretria and Chalcis established a trading post there for dealing with the Etruscans, with a mixed population of Greeks, Etruscans and Phoenicians. The Greeks called it Pithekoussai; Pliny the Elder derived the name from the Greek word for an amphora, which fits the finds of local pottery. Around 700 BCE it held 5,000 to 10,000 people.

A Euboean cup found in a grave in 1953 and dated to about 730 BCE carries lines in the Greek alphabet and refers to Nestor's Cup. It is one of the most important witnesses to the early Greek alphabet, and some scholars think it may be the oldest written reference to the Iliad.

In 6 CE Augustus restored the island to Naples in exchange for Capri. Saracens devastated it in 813 and 847, and Roger II of Sicily took it in 1130. In 1543 and 1544 Hayreddin Barbarossa laid it waste and took 4,000 prisoners. The Bourbons took it in March 1734, and the French occupied it on 13 February 1806.

Ischia is divided into six municipalities and is densely populated. Its volcanic soils support a wine industry with its own DOC, in which white wines predominate. The Aragonese Castle stands on a rock joined to the island by a stone bridge built by Alfonso V of Aragon in 1441, and the gardens of La Mortella at Forio were laid out for the composer William Walton.
ise-grand-shrine: According to the Nihon Shoki, about 2000 years ago Yamatohime-no-mikoto, daughter of Emperor Suinin, set out from Mount Miwa to find a permanent place to worship the sun goddess Amaterasu, and wandered for 20 years before reaching Ise, where she heard Amaterasu say that she wished to dwell in that secluded and pleasant land. The Gekū was founded after Emperor Yūryaku dreamt of Amaterasu, who said she could not get food and asked him to bring Toyouke-hime from Tanba.

The traditional date of establishment is 4 BCE, but other dates in the 3rd and 5th centuries have been proposed. The first shrine building at the Naikū was erected under Emperor Tenmu (678–686), and the first ceremonial rebuilding was carried out by his wife Empress Jitō in 692.

The shrine is Shinto's holiest site. The Naikū is built of Japanese cypress, joined without nails, and the Gekū stands some kilometres away. The style is called shinmei-zukuri, characterised by simplicity and antiquity, and its principles date back to the Kofun period. Every twenty years the shrines and the Uji Bridge are rebuilt on an adjacent site, in a process called Shikinen Sengū, as part of the belief in tokowaka, the renewal of objects to preserve their divine prestige. The buildings of 2013 are the 62nd iteration.

The empty site of the previous shrine, the kodenchi, is strewn with white pebbles and holds a small hut, the oi-ya, sheltering the sacred central pole, which a new shrine is built around so that the pole is never seen. Access to both sites is strictly limited, and visitors cannot go beyond sight of the thatched roofs of the central buildings.

From the late 7th century until the 14th, the chief priestess of Ise, the Saiō, was a female member of the Imperial House. The shrine became an object of imperial patronage in the early Heian period; in 965 Emperor Murakami ordered messengers to report important events to the guardian kami of Japan, and Ise was among the first 16 shrines to receive offerings. Annual festivals follow the agricultural year, and the most important, the Kannamesai in October, offers the first harvest to Amaterasu, with food offerings made daily.

In the Edo period it is estimated that one in ten Japanese made the Okage mairi pilgrimage. Historical documents record 3.62 million visitors in 50 days in 1625, and 1.18 million in three days in 1829, when the festival held every twenty years took place.
isere-river: The Isère rises in a glacier known as the Sources de l'Isère, in the Vanoise National Park in the Graian Alps of Savoie, near Val-d'Isère on the border with Italy. Its course measures 286 kilometres. From the Alps it crosses the Pays de Savoie and the Tarentaise valley, cuts between the Chartreuse and Belledonne ranges, follows the Vercors Massif, passes through the Dauphiné and meets the Rhône at the foot of the Vivarais, a few kilometres north of Valence. Its main tributaries include the Arc, 127.5 kilometres long, the Drac, 130.3 kilometres, and the Romanche, 78.4 kilometres. Its drainage basin covers 11,890 square kilometres.

The upper valley is called the Tarentaise and the middle valley the Grésivaudan. The lower valley forms part of the Plain of Valence and is narrow, no more than 2 kilometres wide. Towns on its banks include Bourg-Saint-Maurice, Moûtiers, Albertville, Grenoble and Romans-sur-Isère. Many communes have taken the river's name, and the department of Isère is named after it.

The name was first recorded as Isara, meaning the impetuous one, the swift one. It was not originally a Celtic word but was very likely taken over by the Celts in ancient times. It is related to the Indo-European root *isərós, meaning impetuous, quick, vigorous, which is similar to the Sanskrit isiráḥ. The same word figures in many other river names of ancient Gaul and neighbouring lands, among them the Isar in Germany, the Franco-Belgian Yser, the ancient name of the Oise, the Isarco in Italy and the Jizera in the Czech Republic.

The lower valley's shape comes from the Quaternary glaciations. Alluvium laid down during glaciations, and deepening of the channel in the warmer periods between them, produced stepped terraces on a bed of Miocene molasse, such as the one on which Saint-Marcel-lès-Valence stands. The terraces still define the geography of the Plain of Valence. The river is fed largely by snowmelt, with spring floods and low water in autumn and winter. Its highest recorded instantaneous discharge was 2,050 cubic metres per second on 16 September 1960.
iserlohn: Iserlohn lies at the northern end of the Sauerland, near the Ruhr, in the Märkischer Kreis district of North Rhine-Westphalia. It is the largest town of the district and of the Sauerland by both population and area. In 1975 it absorbed the surrounding former municipalities of Letmathe, Hennen, Sümmern and Kesbern. Although part of the district, it keeps a special status and performs tasks usually left to the district, such as social and youth affairs, so that it is comparable to an urban district.

The Pancratius church, also called the Bauernkirche, is believed to have been founded around 985. The first written document that mentions the place dates only from 1150. In 1237 the Count of the Mark gave Iserlohn municipal rights, and the checked band in the town's coat of arms comes from the arms of the Counts of the Mark. Above it stands Saint Pancras, patron of the oldest church, between two towers of the historic town wall.

In the 18th century the town became known for Iserlohn boxes, a form of tobacco or snuff box with an engraved or embossed lid that often showed an image of the former Prussian king Frederick the Great. In the Second World War, the tank ace Albert Ernst, born in 1912, is recorded as having saved the town by surrendering it peacefully to US troops.

The Dechenhöhle caves, discovered in 1868 during the building of the railway between Hagen and Iserlohn, have 360 metres open to visitors, with many stalactites and stalagmites. The Danzturm, a tower on the southern hill above the old town, is a landmark and appears on the logo of the local brewery. The Schützenfest, a shooting festival held every year at the Parkhalle, is central to the town's cultural life and identity, and since 1991 a free peace festival has run beside it around the Bauernkirche.

The town is home to the headquarters of the South Westphalia University of Applied Sciences and to the ice hockey club Iserlohn Roosters, which joined the top German league in 2000. Among its twin towns are Almelo in the Netherlands, Biel/Bienne in Switzerland and Hall in Tirol in Austria.
isfahan: Isfahan stands on the plain of the Zayandeh River and the foothills of the Zagros Mountains, about 1,590 metres above sea level and 440 kilometres south of Tehran. It lies at the intersection of the two principal routes across Iran, north to south and east to west. The name derives from Middle Persian Spahān, attested on seals and inscriptions, including that of the Zoroastrian magus Kartir. A Persian proverb holds that Isfahan is half the world.

Human habitation in the region goes back to the Palaeolithic period. Under Median rule it became a regional centre, helped by the Zayandeh River. In the Parthian era Arsacid governors administered provinces from Isfahan, and in the Sassanid era the city was governed by the Espoohrans, descended from seven noble Iranian families. The Arabs captured it in 642 CE and made it the capital of al-Jabal province. It prospered under the Buyid dynasty in the tenth century, and Toghril Beg, founder of the Seljuq dynasty, made it his capital in the mid-eleventh century.

When Ibn Battuta visited in 1327 he found it largely in ruins. In 1387 Isfahan surrendered to Timur. After the city killed his tax collectors and some of his soldiers, Timur ordered a massacre in which his soldiers reportedly killed 70,000 citizens.

The city's golden age began in 1598, when the Safavid ruler Abbas the Great moved his capital from Qazvin to the more central Isfahan. He increased Iranian involvement in the Silk Road trade and forcibly resettled Turkish, Armenian and Persian craftsmen in the city. Industrialisation came under the Pahlavi period, and textile mills earned it the nickname Manchester of Persia.

Isfahan is the capital of Isfahan Province. Naqsh-e Jahan Square, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, lies at the centre of the Safavid city, with the Ali Qapu and Chehel Sotoun palaces and the Shah Mosque of 1629. The Khaju Bridge, built by Shah Abbas II in 1650, is 123 metres long with 24 arches. The New Julfa quarter holds the Armenian churches, among them the Vank Cathedral of 1664.
ish-bosheth: The Books of Samuel call the king Ish-bosheth, which in Hebrew means man of shame, while the Books of Chronicles call him Eshbaal, meaning Baal exists or fire of Baal. Critical scholarship suggests that Bosheth was a substitute for Baal, made when that word became unspeakable, in the way that Adonai came to stand in for the divine name. His sister Michal had been married to David until Saul fell out with David and gave her to another man.

According to the Hebrew Bible, Abner, the captain of Saul's army, proclaimed Ish-bosheth king at Mahanaim in Transjordan after Saul and his other sons had been killed in the battle of Gilboa. Ish-bosheth was forty years old and is said to have reigned for two years. Abner made him king over Gilead, the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin and all Israel.

The tribe of Judah had meanwhile proclaimed David as its own king, and war followed between the two houses. David's side gradually gained the upper hand, and the fighting lasted until Abner went over to David. David's terms for peace required the return of Michal, and Ish-bosheth complied. After Abner's death he seems to have given up hope of keeping power.

Two of his own army captains, Rechab and Baanah, came to his house at midday while he rested, stabbed him and carried his head to David at Hebron, expecting a reward. David instead had both men executed and their hands and feet cut off, and his supporters buried the head in Abner's grave at Hebron. Ish-bosheth's death left David as king over the whole kingdom.

In 2012 the Israel Antiquities Authority reported a jar inscription of about 3,000 years ago from Khirbet Qeiyafa that bears the name Eshbaal ben Beda. It names a different man, but it was the first time the name had been found in an ancient inscription. David Rohl has identified Ish-bosheth with Mutbaal, son of Labaya, but the chronology this requires is not accepted by most scholars.
ishango-bone: The bone was found by the Belgian Jean de Heinzelin de Braucourt while he was exploring what was then the Belgian Congo. He excavated at Ishango, near the Semliki River, which carries water from Lake Edward towards the headwaters of the Nile. He found a bone about the size of a pencil among human remains and many stone tools in a small community that fished and gathered. De Heinzelin brought the bone to Belgium, where it was kept in the treasure room of the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences in Brussels, and moulds and copies were made to protect the fragile original.

The bone is dark brown and curved. It has been narrowed, scraped, polished and engraved, so the animal it came from cannot be told, though it was a mammal. The first estimate placed it between 9,000 BCE and 6,500 BCE, while other analyses suggested an age of up to 44,000 years. The site was dated again, and the bone is now believed to be from between 18,000 BCE and 20,000 BCE. The date remains debated because nearby volcanic activity upset the ratio of carbon isotopes.

The 168 engravings run in three parallel columns along the bone, each mark differing in length and orientation. The central column on the most curved side is called M, from the French milieu, and the left and right columns are G and D, for gauche and droite. De Heinzelin held that the marks showed knowledge of simple arithmetic, or at least were deliberately planned. Some readers have taken column G as a table of prime numbers between 10 and 20, but this may be coincidence. Peter S. Rudman argues that prime numbers were probably not understood before about 500 BCE.

Later interpretations differ. Dirk Huylebrouck and Vladimir Pletser propose a counting tool using base 12 with sub-bases 3 and 4, but find the evidence insufficient to show an understanding of primes. Caleb Everett holds that the quantities in the groups of marks are not random and may reflect prehistoric numerals. The archaeologist Alexander Marshack proposed a six-month lunar calendar, since the first two columns sum to 60; critics reply that he only searched for a pattern.

Others urge caution. A second bone from the same layer has marks that are not mathematically suggestive, and Olivier Keller warns against projecting modern ideas of number onto the object. George Gheverghese Joseph wrote that a single bone with suggestive markings does not give conclusive evidence. Older engraved bones are known, such as the Lebombo bone, about 42,000 years old.
ishida-mitsunari: Mitsunari was born in northern Ōmi Province, in what is now Nagahama in Shiga Prefecture, the second son of Ishida Masatsugu, a retainer of the Azai clan. His childhood name was Sakichi. The Ishida withdrew from service after the Azai were defeated at the Siege of Odani Castle in 1573. A legend that he was a Buddhist monk before entering the service of Toyotomi Hideyoshi is of doubtful accuracy, since it was first recorded in the Edo period. In 1577 he met Hideyoshi, then daimyō of Nagahama.

Mitsunari assisted Hideyoshi at the sieges of Tottori Castle and Takamatsu Castle and fought at Shizugatake in 1583. In 1585 he became administrator of Sakai with his elder brother, and was one of the five bugyō, the top administrators of Hideyoshi's government, with Asano Nagamasa, Maeda Gen'i, Mashita Nagamori and Natsuka Masaie. He became daimyō of Sawayama and in 1588 took charge of Hideyoshi's sword hunt to disarm the non-military population. In 1590 he commanded the Siege of Oshi, where his plan to flood the castle failed; other records say Hideyoshi himself ordered it.

He was one of the Three Bureaucrats in the invasions of Korea from 1592. In 1598 several generals, dissatisfied with his assessments of their achievements in Korea, marched on his mansion in Osaka. He fled to Fushimi Castle, where Tokugawa Ieyasu mediated. Some historians call the incident the generals' lawsuit against Mitsunari rather than a plot to kill him.

After the deaths of Hideyoshi and Maeda Toshiie in 1599, Mitsunari formed an alliance of Toyotomi loyalists against Ieyasu. His army was defeated at Sekigahara on 21 October 1600. Ōtani Yoshitsugu had warned him that the daimyō disliked him. Mitsunari was caught by villagers while trying to escape, beheaded in Kyoto and his head displayed.

Stephen Turnbull writes that traditional historiography neglected him because he lost, often portraying him as a weak bureaucrat, and that later historians note his planning skill and think Sekigahara could have gone his way had a few more lords stayed loyal.
ishikawa-prefecture: Ishikawa lies on the Sea of Japan coast of Honshu, in the historic Hokuriku region. It covers about 4,191 square kilometres and borders Toyama Prefecture to the east, Gifu to the south-east and Fukui to the south. Its northern part is the narrow Noto Peninsula, which forms Toyama Bay, one of the largest bays in Japan. The southern part is wider and mostly mountainous, and Kanazawa, the capital and largest city, stands on the coastal plain. Other major cities are Hakusan, Komatsu and Kaga.

Ishikawa was formed in 1872 from the merger of Kaga Province and the smaller Noto Province, with its government at first at Mikawa. The seat moved to Kanazawa in 1873. In 1878 six shizoku, former samurai dissatisfied with the Meiji government, assassinated the statesman Ōkubo Toshimichi in the Kioizaka Incident. The national government feared that a Hokuriku bloc might form in support of the Freedom and People's Rights Movement and wished to weaken the former Kaga lords, so it divided the prefecture in two stages. Fukui Prefecture was formed in 1881 and Toyama Prefecture in 1883.

Ishikawa was formerly an important populated centre that held some of the wealthiest han of the feudal period. Noh was introduced under the fifth Maeda lord, Tsunanori, and the tea ceremony came in 1666 when Maeda Toshitsune invited Senbiki Soshitsu of Urasenke to Kanazawa. Kutani ware, Kaga silk, Kanazawa lacquerware decorated with gold dust and Kanazawa gold leaf are among its best-known products. Kanazawa Castle and Kenroku-en, one of the Three Great Gardens of Japan, stand in the capital. Industry is dominated by textiles, particularly artificial fabrics, and by machinery, particularly construction machinery.
ishtar-gate: The Ishtar Gate was the eighth gate in the inner city wall of Babylon, on the north side of the city, near present-day Hillah in Iraq. Nebuchadnezzar II, who reigned from 604 to 562 BCE at the peak of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, ordered its construction around 569 BCE and dedicated it to the goddess Ishtar. His inscription, in Akkadian cuneiform on white and blue glazed bricks, says that the earlier gates had become lower as the street was filled, so he pulled them down, laid new foundations at the water table with asphalt and bricks, and roofed them with cedar beams. The gate was part of a grand walled processional way leading into the city.

The original was a double gate with a smaller frontal gate and a larger, more grandiose rear section, about 15 metres high with foundations reaching a further 14 metres underground. Its walls were faced in glazed bricks, mostly vivid blue to imitate lapis lazuli, with animals in low relief in alternating rows: the mušḫuššu dragon of Marduk, the aurochs of the storm god Adad, and the lion of Ishtar. The bricks were pressed in moulds, fired, glazed and fired again, and the seams were sealed with bitumen. Rosettes, often seen as symbols of fertility, run in the borders.

Once a year the gate and the Processional Way formed the route of a New Year procession, part of a twelve-day festival at the start of the agricultural year, held at the spring equinox in the month of Nisan. Statues of the deities were carried through the gate and down the street. The purpose of the festival was to affirm the supremacy of Marduk and the king as his representative, and to give thanks for the fertility of the land. The Processional Way, traced to over 800 metres, was lined with friezes of lions, bulls and dragons and paved in stone set in bitumen.

Claudius Rich published the first topographical records of the ruins of Babylon in 1815. The German archaeologist Robert Koldewey, who began work at Babylon in 1899, led the excavation that uncovered the gate and the palaces of Nebuchadnezzar, and it continued until 1914. The glazed bricks were numbered, packed in barrels and shipped to Berlin, where after 1918 the smaller frontal gate was reconstructed at the Pergamon Museum, 14 metres high and 30 metres wide. The larger rear gate is in storage. Panels and animals from the Processional Way are also in museums in Istanbul, Copenhagen, the Louvre, New York and elsewhere. Iraq petitioned Germany for the gate's return in 2002 and again in 2009.
isidore-of-seville: Isidore was born in Cartago Spartaria, now Cartagena, to a notable family of Roman Hispania. His family was influential in the political and religious manoeuvring that converted the Arian Visigothic kings to Catholicism. His elder brother Leander of Seville preceded him as archbishop and opposed King Liuvigild, and his younger brother Fulgentius of Cartagena became Bishop of Astigi. Isidore was educated at the cathedral school of Seville, where learned men including Leander taught the trivium and quadrivium. He mastered classical Latin and acquired some Greek and Hebrew.

After the death of Leander on 13 March 600 or 601 Isidore succeeded to the See of Seville, and made himself protector of monks. He tried to unite the peoples of the Visigothic kingdom into one nation. He presided over the Second Council of Seville, begun on 13 November 619 in the reign of King Sisebut, which set out the nature of Christ against the Acephali. At the Fourth National Council of Toledo, begun on 5 December 633, the aged archbishop presided and originated most of its enactments. It ordered every bishop to found a seminary in his cathedral city on the model of Seville's school, teaching Greek, Hebrew and the liberal arts.

Isidore's most important work, the Etymologiae, is the first Christian attempt at a summa of universal knowledge, in 448 chapters and 20 volumes. It is largely a digest of Roman handbooks and compendia and preserves many fragments of classical learning that would otherwise have been lost. His contemporary Braulio of Zaragoza called it practically everything that it is necessary to know, and because it was so highly regarded it superseded the copying of many classical works, which were then lost.

It was the most popular compendium in medieval libraries and was printed in at least ten editions between 1470 and 1530. He also wrote a history of the Gothic, Vandal and Suebi kings and De natura rerum, dedicated to King Sisebut. He died on 4 April 636, after more than 32 years as archbishop, and was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church in 1722.
isis: Neither Isis nor her husband Osiris is mentioned by name before the Fifth Dynasty, about 2494 to 2345 BCE. An inscription that may refer to her dates from the reign of Nyuserre Ini, and she appears prominently in the Pyramid Texts. Several passages link her with the Nile Delta near Behbeit el-Hagar and Sebennytos, and her cult may have originated there. In the Osiris myth she belongs to the Ennead of Heliopolis, born to Geb and Nut with Osiris, Set and Nephthys. As sister and wife of Osiris she is his queen, and she resurrects him after he is slain and bears and protects their heir, Horus.

Isis was believed to help the dead enter the afterlife as she had helped Osiris, and she was the divine mother of the pharaoh, who was likened to Horus. Her maternal aid was invoked in healing spells for ordinary people. She was usually shown as a woman with a throne-like hieroglyph on her head. In the New Kingdom she took on traits of Hathor and wore her headdress of a sun disk between cow horns.

She was at first a minor figure in rituals concerning the living king. In the first millennium BCE the triad of Osiris, Isis and Horus gained emphasis and her popularity grew greatly. Nectanebo I of the Thirtieth Dynasty claimed her as his patron in the fourth century BCE, and the Kingdom of Kush equated her with the kandake, the queen or queen mother. Her temple at Philae was a religious centre for Egyptians and Nubians alike.

Greeks knew of Isis by the Archaic Period, and her first known temple in Greece was built by Egyptians living in Athens. Spread by merchants, the cults of Isis and Serapis took root in Greek port cities from the end of the fourth century BCE. Greek devotees ascribed to her the invention of marriage and the protection of ships. Her devotees were a small proportion of the Roman Empire's population but came from every level of society, and women were more strongly represented than in most Greco-Roman cults. Plutarch's On Isis and Osiris and Apuleius's novel The Golden Ass are the main literary witnesses.

Christianity ended her worship between the fourth and sixth centuries CE. Whether her cult shaped Christian belief, for example the veneration of Mary, is contested. She appears in Western esotericism and in Mozart's opera The Magic Flute of 1791.
iskandar-muda: Iskandar Muda, whose name means young Alexander, was born about 1583, the son of Mansur Syah, a grandson of Sultan Abdul Jalil, and of Puteri Raja Inderabangsa, a daughter of the tenth sultan. He thus joined the two branches of the Acehnese dynasty. The Hikayat Aceh, which extols his qualities, describes his youth at length.

Known first as Perkasa Alam, he fell out about 1605 with his uncle Sultan Ali Ri'ayat Syah III and was imprisoned after a failed plan to rebel. When the Portuguese invaded Aceh in 1606 he was released and distinguished himself in beating them back. Sultan Ali died suddenly on 4 April 1607, and Perkasa Alam secured the throne the same day, later having his other uncle Husain killed.

His power rested on a navy of heavy galleys each carrying 600 to 800 men, a cavalry using Persian horses, an elephant corps, conscript infantry and more than 2,000 cannons and guns. He took Deli in 1612, and in 1613 Aru and Johor, bringing the sultan of Johor and his family to Aceh, though Johor expelled the garrison later that year.

He defeated a Portuguese fleet at Bintan in 1614, conquered Pahang in 1617, Kedah in 1619, where the capital was laid waste, and Perak in 1620, and took Nias in 1624/5. In 1629 he sent several hundred ships against Portuguese Melaka; according to Portuguese sources, all were destroyed with 19,000 men. His sultanate kept northern Sumatra but never gained supremacy in the strait.

The economy rested on the spice trade, above all pepper, and he made the court the sole contact with foreign merchants. He suppressed the Acehnese elite, the orang kaya, by forcing them to attend court and barring them from building independent houses, and set up war leaders, hulubalang, and royal officials, panglima, in their place. He created courts using Islamic jurisprudence, and a palace guard of 3,000 women. His rule was brutal: a French visitor of the 1620s reported mutilations almost daily, and he had his own son Meurah Pupok executed, naming his son-in-law Iskandar Thani heir.

Iskandar Muda died on 27 December 1636. He was the last sultan of Aceh to descend in the male line from the founder, Ali Mughayat Syah. Under him Aceh became a centre of Islamic learning, drawing the Sufi writers Hamzah Pansuri and Syamsuddin of Pasai, and the Hikayat Aceh probably dates from his reign. Among the Acehnese he is revered as a symbol of Aceh's past greatness, with the posthumous title Po Teuh Meureuhom, Our Beloved Late Lord.
iskander-mirza: Iskander Ali Mirza was born in Murshidabad, Bengal, on 13 November 1899, into the family of the Nawab of Murshidabad, and was a descendant of Mir Jafar. His mother belonged to the Tyabji family of Cambay. He was educated at Elphinstone College in Bombay and then at the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, from which he was the first Indian graduate. He was commissioned in the British Indian Army in July 1920 and fought in Waziristan. In August 1926 he joined the Indian Political Service, serving mostly on the North-West Frontier, where he learned Pashto, and in 1946 he became Joint Secretary at the Ministry of Defence in New Delhi.

After independence in 1947 Prime Minister Liaquat Ali Khan made him Pakistan's first Defence Secretary. In that post he oversaw the military effort in the first war with India and the failed secession in Balochistan, and in 1951 he argued for promoting the junior-most major-general, Ayub Khan, as the first native commander-in-chief of the army. As governor of East Bengal from June 1954 he dismissed the provincial assembly and the United Front government and had arrests reach 1,051 by mid-June, including 33 assembly members. In October 1954 he became Interior Minister.

Mirza dismissed Governor-General Malik Ghulam Muhammad in October 1955 and took the post himself. When the first constitution was promulgated on 23 March 1956 the electoral college unanimously elected him president. During his presidency four prime ministers were dismissed in about two years: Muhammad Ali, Huseyn Suhrawardy, I. I. Chundrigar and then Feroz Khan, who was his own party's. Faced with pressure over his re-election, he declared martial law in October 1958, abrogated the constitution and dissolved the assemblies, and appointed Ayub Khan chief martial law administrator.

Within three weeks, on the night of 26–27 October 1958, Ayub Khan sent troops to the presidential palace and had Mirza flown into exile in England. He lived in London on a pension of £3,000 and ran a small hotel. He died of a heart attack on 13 November 1969, his 70th birthday. Pakistan's president Yahya Khan denied him burial in East Pakistan, and the Shah of Iran sent a plane for his body, which was given a state funeral in Tehran. Pakistani historians often criticise him for imposing martial law, and he is held responsible for the instability that brought the armed forces into politics. He held that democracy could not flourish amid low literacy.
isla-mujeres: Isla Mujeres, Spanish for Women Island, lies where the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea meet, about 13 kilometres off the coast of the Yucatán Peninsula in the state of Quintana Roo. It is approximately 7 kilometres long and 650 metres wide. The eastern shore faces the Caribbean with strong surf and a rocky coast, and across the water to the west the skyline of Cancún can be seen. The western coast is part of the Costa Occidental de Isla Mujeres National Park, and the southeast tip is the easternmost point in Mexico. The town on the island is the seat of Isla Mujeres Municipality and had 12,642 inhabitants in the census of 2010.

In pre-Columbian times the island was sacred to Ixchel, the Maya goddess of childbirth and medicine, and the newcomers of the sixteenth century named it after the many images of goddesses. The earliest available information places it between 564 and 1516 in the Maya province of Ekab, one of four Maya provinces in the area of the modern state of Quintana Roo. The Maya exploited the salt of its salinas, small interior lagoons, using it to preserve food, in medicine and as a currency. A temple to Ixchel stood where the Hacienda Mundaca now stands, and a small Maya temple at the southern tip was badly damaged by Hurricane Gilbert in 1988, leaving most of its foundation.

In the early 1800s the island was a favourite stopping place for pirates, because the shallow lagoon on the mainland side was a good place to sit out storms, clean hulls and trade for salt. Jean Lafitte and Hernán Mundaca are named among those who spent time there. Mundaca built a large hacienda in the hope of winning Martiniana Gómez Pantoja, who married someone else.

Since the 1970s, along with nearby Cancún, the island has seen substantial tourist development, with ferries from Puerto Juárez and Cancún, restaurants, beaches such as Playa Norte, and coral reefs such as the one at Garrafon Park. The Cancún Underwater Museum, made by the English sculptor Jason deCaires Taylor, lies off the western coast. The island is the home of the Mexican naval base Quinta Región Naval. Hurricanes, among them Carmen and Wilma, have caused devastating damage there.
islam: According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad was born in Mecca in 570 CE and was orphaned early. He grew up as a trader, became known as the 'trusted one' and later married his employer, the businesswoman Khadija. In 610 CE he retreated to the Cave of Hira near Mecca, where he is said to have received the first revelation of the Quran from the angel Gabriel, an event known as the Night of Power. Over the next 22 years he continued to receive revelations.

In Mecca he preached first in secret and then in public, urging his listeners to abandon polytheism. Many early converts were women, the poor, foreigners and slaves such as the first muezzin, Bilal ibn Rabah al-Habashi. The Meccan elite felt he was destabilizing their social order, and they profited from pilgrimages to the idols of the Kaaba. By the time of his death most of the Arabian Peninsula had converted, and Muslim rule then expanded outside Arabia under the Rashidun Caliphate.

The Islamic creed requires belief in six articles: God, angels, revelation, prophets, the Day of Resurrection and divine predestination. The central concept is tawhid, the oneness of God, and associating anything with God is idolatry, called shirk. Muslims consider the Quran the verbatim word of God and hold Muhammad to be the final prophet. His teachings and example, the Sunnah, are documented in hadith. Islam has no clergy in the sacerdotal sense, and no intermediaries are needed to reach God.

Five acts of worship are duties: the shahada, the declaration of faith; the five daily prayers, recited in Arabic and performed toward the Kaaba; almsgiving (zakat); fasting during Ramadan; and the pilgrimage (hajj) to Mecca. The two main festivals are Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.

The two main branches are Sunni Islam, 87–90% of Muslims, and Shia Islam, 10–13%. The divide began in disagreement over the succession to Muhammad and grew to cover theology and law. Sunnis follow one of four schools of jurisprudence: Hanafi, Hanbali, Maliki or Shafi'i. Sharia, the body of religious law, is studied through fiqh. Sufism, a mystical approach seeking direct personal experience of God, is not a sect, and its adherents belong to various denominations. About 25.6% of the global population, roughly 2 billion people, are Muslims. They are a majority in 53 countries, and about 12% live in Indonesia.
islam-karimov: Islam Karimov was born in Samarkand to Uzbek parents who were civil servants. In 1960 he graduated in mechanical engineering from the Central Asian Polytechnic Institute and began work as an engineer, later taking a degree in economics. From 1966 to 1986 he rose through the Uzbek State Planning Committee, becoming Minister of Finance of the Uzbek SSR and deputy chairman of its Council of Ministers. In 1989 he became first secretary of the republic's Communist Party, after his predecessor failed to quell inter-ethnic clashes in the Fergana Region.

On 24 March 1990 the Uzbek Supreme Soviet elected Karimov the republic's first president. On 31 August 1991, ten days after the attempted coup in Moscow, he declared Uzbekistan independent, the second Central Asian republic to do so after Kyrgyzstan. In the presidential election of December 1991 he received 86 per cent of the vote against 12.3 per cent for Muhammad Salih of the Erk Party; foreign observers and the opposition alleged irregularities. A referendum in 1995 extended his term until 2000, and he was re-elected in 2000, 2007 and 2015, each time with over 90 per cent.

In 1999 the Oliy Majlis imposed new restrictions on religious groups, and after an assassination attempt that year the government pressed harder against Islamist movements such as the Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan and Hizb ut-Tahrir. After the attacks of 11 September 2001 Uzbekistan hosted about 800 United States troops at Karshi-Khanabad, which supported the invasion of Afghanistan. On 13 May 2005 troops fired on demonstrators at Andijan, and detailed accounts put the dead at some 400 of 500 protesters. After Western criticism, Karimov expelled United States forces from the base in July 2005.

Western states repeatedly criticised his administration's record on human rights and press freedom, and the United Nations found torture in the judicial system to be institutionalised, systematic and rampant. Karimov died on 2 September 2016, after 25 years as president, following a stroke. He was buried in his native Samarkand, and Shavkat Mirziyoyev, the prime minister, headed the funeral committee and later succeeded him as president.
islamabad: Islamabad lies about 540 metres above sea level at the northern edge of the Pothohar Plateau, at the foot of the Margalla Hills, in the northern part of the Punjab region. It forms a conurbation with the older Gakhar city of Rawalpindi, to its south; the two are commonly called the Twin Cities. The city is 120 km southwest of Muzaffarabad, 185 km east of Peshawar and 295 km northwest of Lahore. It covers 906 square kilometres, and a further Specified Area of 2,717 square kilometres runs into the hills. The southern part is an undulating plain drained by the Kurang River, on which the Rawal Dam stands.

The Pothohar Plateau is considered one of the earliest sites of human settlement in Asia. Stone Age artefacts dating from 100,000 to 500,000 years ago have been found there, among them rudimentary stones from the terraces of the Soan River. Excavations by Abdul Ghafoor Lone found relics and human skulls dating back to 5000 BCE, which indicate Neolithic peoples on the banks of the Soan, who later formed small communities around 3000 BCE. Remnants of Aryan, Soanian and Indus Valley cultures, and Buddhist remains, can still be found in the region.

Later buildings include Pharwala Fort, built by the Gakhars in the 15th century, and Rawat Fort of the 16th century, which holds the grave of their chief Sultan Sarang Khan. The Mughal commander Raja Man Singh turned the village of Saidpur into a place of Hindu worship and built ponds there, and the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb built the shrine of Bari Imam. The modern city was built as a planned capital in the 1960s and established in 1967, replacing Karachi. The Greek architect Constantinos Apostolou Doxiadis drew up its master plan, which divided the city into eight zones: administrative, commercial, educational, industrial, diplomatic, residential, rural and green.

The name means City of Islam, from the Arabic Islam and the Persian suffix -abad. Residential sectors are each identified by a letter and a number and cover about 2 km by 2 km. The city is administered federally as the Islamabad Capital Territory, and its parks and forests include Margalla Hills National Park and Shakarparian. The Faisal Mosque, completed in 1986 to a design by the Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay, was named after King Faisal bin Abdul Aziz of Saudi Arabia, who financed it, and can hold up to 74,000 worshippers. The Islamabad Museum holds relics of the Gandhara period.
islamic-calendar: The Hijri era has its epoch at the Islamic New Year of 622 CE, the year in which Muhammad and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina and established the first Muslim community, an event commemorated as the Hijrah. Dates in the era are denoted AH, from the Latin Anno Hegirae. In pre-Islamic Arabia a year was named after a major event, and tradition names the Year of the Elephant, in which Muhammad was born, as the year most often equated with 570 CE. The first ten years of the Hijra were not numbered but were named after events, such as the year of permission and the year of farewell.

Muslim authors of the Abbasid era record that the ancient Arabs distinguished permitted months from four forbidden months in which fighting was prohibited: Rajab and the three around the pilgrimage. The Qur'an links these to nasi', 'postponement', which is interpreted as either postponing the month of the pilgrimage or intercalating an extra month. Muslims believe its prohibition was revealed in the tenth year of the Hijra.

The calendar has twelve lunar months and a year of 354 or 355 days. A month begins with the first sighting of the new crescent moon, so it has 29 or 30 days depending on visibility, and the day traditionally begins at sunset. Because the lunar year is about eleven days shorter than the solar year, the months move about eleven days earlier each year against the seasons and pass through them in about 33 solar years.

Twelver Shia Muslims hold that the year's first month is Rabi' al-Awwal, the month of the Hijrah, so that Shias place the battle of Karbala in 60 AH and Sunnis in 61 AH. Saudi Arabia has used the astronomical Umm al-Qura calendar, and the Tabular Islamic calendar follows a 30-year cycle with 11 leap years of 355 days. Most theologians oppose calculation instead of sighting, though jurists such as Yusuf al-Qaradawi have endorsed it.

The calendar fixes the dates of Islamic holidays and rituals: 1 Ramadan, the first day of fasting, 1 Shawwal, Eid ul-Fitr, the Hajj on 8 to 13 Dhu'l-Hijja, and 10 Dhu'l-Hijja, Eid al-Adha. The tenth of Muharram is Ashura, observed by Shias and Sunnis for the death of Husayn ibn Ali. Being purely lunar, it cannot serve agriculture, so farming communities used other calendars, such as the Egyptian and the Iranian.
islamic-golden-age: The period is dated from the 8th century CE to the 14th century and is understood to have begun under the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid (786–809), with the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, one of the world's largest cities at the time. The institution drew scholars from across the Muslim world to translate the classical knowledge of the known world into Arabic.

Several causes are proposed. Quranic injunctions valuing education and knowledge may have encouraged the search for learning, and a hadith attributed to Muhammad states that seeking knowledge is obligatory upon every Muslim. The state patronised scholars heavily. Paper spread from China into Muslim regions in the eighth century through mass production in Samarkand and Khorasan, which made it possible for the first time to make a living from writing and selling books.

Intellectual and cultural activity flourished in many centres besides Baghdad, among them Cairo, Umayyad Córdoba, Damascus, Nishapur, Samarkand, Ghazni, Kairouan and Fez, and later Nasrid Granada. The period is said to have ended with the collapse of the Abbasid caliphate after the Mongol invasions and the Siege of Baghdad in 1258, though some scholars extend it to around 1350, to the 15th century or even the 16th.

Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī contributed to algebra, arithmetic and Hindu–Arabic numerals, and Omar Khayyam found the general geometric solution of the cubic equation. Ibn al-Haytham, known as Alhazen, argued correctly that vision occurs when light travelling in straight lines reflects off an object into the eyes. Al-Biruni (973–1050) estimated the radius of the earth at 6339.6 km, the best estimate of his time. Calligraphy, geometric ornament and the poetry of Rumi, Hafez, Saadi and Ferdowsi flourished.

The metaphor of a golden age was applied to Islamic history in 19th-century literature, in the context of the western fashion known as Orientalism. Translations of philosophical texts from Arabic into Latin led, according to the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, to the transformation of almost all philosophical disciplines in the medieval Latin world.

Explanations of the decline differ. The economic historian Joel Mokyr has argued that al-Ghazali was a key figure in the decline of Islamic science, while George Saliba points out that the golden age did not slow after al-Ghazali and places the golden age of astronomy in the period after him. Ahmad Y. al-Hassan holds that science declined only after the 16th century and explains the decline by economic and political factors.
islamic-movement-of-uzbekistan: Islam in Soviet Central Asia was officially suppressed until the Soviet–Afghan War (1979–1989), when conscripts sent to fight the Afghan mujahedin came home impressed by their opponents' zeal. One of them, the paratrooper Juma Namangani, returned to Namangan in the Fergana Valley and became associated with the Islamic ideologue Tohir Yuldashev. After Uzbekistan's independence in 1991 they founded a Salafi group, Adolat, which took civil authority in Namangan and enforced Sharia. President Islam Karimov at first tolerated it, but by 1992 he had outlawed it.

Yuldashev and Namangani fled to Tajikistan, where Namangani commanded units of the United Tajik Opposition in the civil war. Yuldashev toured Afghanistan, Turkey and the Middle East and from 1995 to 1998 was based in Peshawar, where he met Osama bin Laden. After the 1997 peace agreement in Tajikistan, the two men, disillusioned with the political concessions made by the Tajik Islamists, formed the Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan in 1998 to oppose Karimov.

After explosions in Tashkent in 1999, Karimov blamed the movement, though that attribution remains disputed. Later that year it made its first verifiable raid, into the Batken region of Kyrgyzstan, seizing the Mayor of Osh and obtaining a ransom and a helicopter. Under pressure, Namangani left Tajikistan for northern Afghanistan in late 1999. In 2000 the movement, then estimated at about 2,000 strong, supplied around 600 fighters to the Taliban's offensive against Ahmad Shah Massoud, and raided Kyrgyzstan and northern Uzbekistan again. In August 2000 it kidnapped four American climbers, who escaped on 12 August, and the United States designated it a Foreign Terrorist Organization.

After the American-led invasion of Afghanistan the movement was largely destroyed. Namangani was killed in November 2001 by a United States airstrike, and Yuldashev withdrew to the tribal areas of Pakistan, where he was killed in a drone strike on 27 August 2009. Fighting broke out with local Taliban leader Maulvi Nazir in early 2007, and the group worked with Baitullah Mehsud and the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan. In April 2012 about 150 fighters of the movement and the Tehrik-i-Taliban attacked Bannu Prison, freeing nearly 400 prisoners. Its leader Usman Ghazi declared support for ISIS in September 2014, and videos in 2015 announced allegiance to Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi. In June 2016 a new faction denounced ISIS and declared loyalty to the Taliban and al-Qaeda.

Though founded as an ethnic Uzbek movement, it later recruited Afghans, Tajiks, Uyghurs, Turkmens, Arabs, Chechens and others. Of 87 martyrs listed on its website in 2011, only four were Uzbeks from Uzbekistan. Its media arm was Jundallah Studio, which produced videos and statements in many languages. The movement's leaders after Yuldashev were Abu Usman Adil, killed in a drone strike in April 2012, and then Usman Ghazi.
islamic-revolutionary-guard-corps: The Corps is also known as Sepah or Pasdaran, from Persian words meaning corps and guardians. It was established by Ruhollah Khomeini as a military branch in May 1979, in the aftermath of the Iranian Revolution, and was formed on 5 May 1979 by Abbas Duzduzani. Its purpose was to consolidate several paramilitary forces into a single force loyal to the new government and to serve as a counter to the regular military, which was at first seen as a possible source of opposition because of its traditional loyalty to the Shah. The Constitution of the Islamic Republic entrusted the defence of Iran's territorial integrity and political independence to the regular army, the Artesh, and gave the Pasdaran the task of preserving the Revolution itself.

The Corps emerged from the Iran-Iraq War of 1980 to 1988 as a largely independent organisation on which the clerical leadership relied. Its share of the Iranian military budget was 7.3 per cent in 1980, rose to 20.3 per cent by 1982 and reached almost 50 per cent by 1987. During the war it also built a large apparatus for cultural and media production. Early 1980s reports credit it with establishing over 2,400 libraries, producing some 440,000 publications and holding 4,049 film screenings and 1,620 exhibitions.

During the Lebanese Civil War it allegedly sent troops to train fighters after the Israeli invasion of 1982, and Christian militias such as the Lebanese Forces declared war on it, claiming it violated Lebanese sovereignty. In September 2008 it reorganised from a centralised to a decentralised force, with 31 provincial corps and an autonomous missile command. A command for cyber security was set up within it in 2007.

The Corps is a multi-service force with ground, aerospace and naval branches, the Quds Force and the Basij, a volunteer militia that serves as its auxiliary. Its commander-in-chief is appointed by the supreme leader. Its operations are geared to asymmetric warfare and less traditional duties such as control of smuggling and of the Strait of Hormuz, and it is responsible for internal and border security and for Iran's missile forces. Its aerospace branch controls the strategic-missile force, and its Quds Force trains, arms and advises allied non-state groups abroad.

Its members have taken part in politics: Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, president from 2005 to 2013, joined it in 1985, and a majority of his first cabinet were veterans. It first moved into commerce through networks of veterans and former officials, and grew into a conglomerate with interests across the Iranian economy, including contracts in oil, gas and petrochemicals and in major infrastructure.
islay: Islay lies in Argyll and Bute just south-west of Jura and about 40 kilometres north of the Northern Irish coast. It is the fifth-largest Scottish island, with an area of almost 620 square kilometres, 40 kilometres long from north to south and 24 kilometres broad. The east coast is rugged and mountainous, rising steeply from the Sound of Islay, while the fertile south-western arm is called The Rinns and a rocky peninsula, The Oa, is the closest point in the Hebrides to Ireland. The Gulf Stream keeps the climate mild, though winter gales off the Atlantic can gust up to 185 kilometres per hour. Its capital is Bowmore and its main port is Port Ellen.

The earliest settlers were hunter-gatherers who arrived after the retreat of the ice caps. A flint arrowhead found near Bridgend in 1993, dated to 10,800 BCE, is among the earliest evidence of human presence yet found in Scotland, and Mesolithic finds date to 7000 BCE. By the Neolithic settlement was more permanent and communal monuments were built. Ptolemy probably recorded the island as Epidion, and in the 7th century Adomnán called it Ilea. The root of the name is not Gaelic and is of unknown origin.

By the sixth century CE Islay lay within the Gaelic kingdom of Dál Riata, which had strong links to Ireland. According to the Senchus fer n-Alban, the Cenél nÓengusa controlled Islay and Jura. The arrival of Scandinavian settlers in the ninth century began with the destruction of Dál Riata, and place names suggest a complete break from the past, although Gaelic survived as a spoken language of low status. The Norse set up the Kingdom of the Isles, which became part of the crown of Norway, and its rulers were mostly of Norse origin for four centuries and more.
