The transfer of the Hebrides to the Kingdom of Scotland was followed by the emergence of the Clan Donald Lordship of the Isles, originally centred at Finlaggan, a period described as a cultural high point. At the end of the 13th century the MacDougalls backed John Balliol against Robert the Bruce, and when Robert won, he declared their lands forfeit and gave them to the MacDonalds and the Macruari. In the 17th century the power of Clan Donald waned. Improvements to agriculture and transport raised the population to a peak in the mid-19th century, followed by substantial forced displacements and falling numbers.

Islay has over 3,000 inhabitants, and about a quarter of them speak Scottish Gaelic. Its main activities are agriculture, malt whisky distilling, fishing and tourism. Wintering populations of Greenland white-fronted and barnacle geese make it a destination for birdwatchers.
isle-of-lewis: Lewis is the northern part of Lewis and Harris, the largest island of the Western Isles, and covers 683 square miles (1,770 square kilometres). It is the lower-lying part of the island, while Harris is more mountainous. Its west coast is mostly sandy beaches backed by dunes and machair, and the centre is an expansive peat-covered plateau. The east coast is more rugged, with rocky cliffs broken by small coves, and its more fertile land drew most of the population, including the only town, Stornoway. The moorland of heather explains the Gaelic name Eilean an Fhraoich, the Heather Isle.

Peat samples indicate that about 8,000 years ago much of the native woodland was burned to make way for plants on which deer could browse. The earliest archaeological remains date from about 5,000 years ago, when people began to settle in permanent farms rather than following their herds. Their small houses have been found across the Western Isles, notably at Dail Mòr, Carloway, and the temples and communal burial cairns of the period include Calanais (Callanish). There are also the remains of several brochs.

Scandinavian settlers established communities in the Outer Hebrides from the 9th century, and one explanation of the name Lewis derives it from the Old Norse Ljóðhús, interpreted as song house. The island was once part of the Norse Kingdom of the Isles. Later landmarks include Dùn Èistean, the ancestral home of the Morrisons of Ness.

Stornoway, from which ferries sail to Ullapool on the mainland, is the commercial centre and has about 8,000 people. Lewis holds three quarters of the population of the Western Isles, and the island is administered by Comhairle nan Eilean Siar, based in Stornoway. Crofting, fishing and weaving are the traditional industries. Scottish Gaelic remains the daily language of around 60 per cent of islanders. Much of the population belongs to the Free Church or the Church of Scotland, both Presbyterian in tradition, and the Sabbath is generally observed.
isle-of-mull: Mull covers 875.35 square kilometres, making it the fourth-largest island in Scotland, and has a coastline of 480 km moderated by the Gulf Stream. Three large peninsulas jut west from a mountainous south-eastern core, whose highest peak, Ben More at 966 m, is the only Munro in the Scottish islands outside Skye. The Aros peninsula in the north holds the main town of Tobermory, a planned fishing town that was a burgh until 1973. Ardmeanach lies in the middle, and the Ross of Mull to the south-west, where the ferry to Iona leaves from Fionnphort. Off the west coast lie many smaller islands, among them Iona, Staffa, the island of Fingal's Cave, and Ulva.

Mull has probably been inhabited since shortly after the last Ice Age, about 11,000 years ago, as radiocarbon dating of a Mesolithic hut at Crieth Dubh shows. Bronze Age and Iron Age people built brochs at Dun Nan Gall and An Sean Chaisteal, a stone circle at Lochbuie and numerous burial cairns. In the 6th century CE Irish migrants established the kingdom of Dál Riata, in which the Cenél Loairn controlled Mull and the adjacent mainland.

In the 9th century Viking invasions destroyed Dál Riata and replaced it with the Norse Kingdom of the Isles, which became part of the kingdom of Norway after its unification, around 872. After Robert I defeated his enemies, among them the MacDougalls, he gave Mull and other lands to Angus Og Macdonald, Lord of the Isles, who had fought beside him at Bannockburn. The descendants of the Cenél Loairn kept their identity as the MacLeans. When John MacDonald was exiled, James IV restored their authority over Mull. Duart Castle, received as a dowry by an earlier chief, became their stronghold, and a cadet branch built a tower house at Moy.

After the Jacobite risings the Heritable Jurisdictions Act abolished comital authority in Mull, and the Campbells could only assert influence as landlords. Many MacLean castles had been slighted by the Campbells or fallen into disrepair. Gaelic, the traditional language since the early Middle Ages, declined in the 20th century, with a fall of 20 percent in Mull after the Second World War.

The island's population was 3,063 in 2022, and much of it lives in Tobermory. Tourism is the mainstay of the economy, which began to revive when Craignure Pier was built in 1964. The reintroduction of white-tailed eagles in 2005 became an ecotourist attraction. Four castles stand on the island, among them Duart and the keep of Moy Castle, and there are two distilleries, at Tobermory and Tiroran. The most-used ferry runs from Oban to Craignure.
isle-of-skye: Skye covers 1,656 square kilometres and is the second-largest island in Scotland after Lewis and Harris. Its coast is a series of peninsulas and bays radiating from a centre dominated by the Cuillin hills. The origin of its name is uncertain: one proposal derives it from an early Celtic word for winged, but no definitive solution has been found, and the name may come from an earlier, non-Gaelic language. The climate is mild, wet and windy.

The oldest evidence of people on Skye is a set of late Upper Palaeolithic stone tools from South Cuidrach, probably 12,500 to 11,000 years old. The late Iron Age inhabitants were probably Pictish, and three Pictish symbol stones have been found. Adomnán's life of Columba, written shortly before 697, shows the saint visiting Skye and baptising a pagan leader through an interpreter. The Norse held sway throughout the Hebrides from the 9th century until after the Treaty of Perth in 1266. Apart from placenames little of their presence survives, and the name Skye itself is the only pre-Norse place name that seems to have lasted.

After the Norse period the most powerful clans were the MacLeods, originally based in Trotternish, and the Macdonalds of Sleat. In 1401 the island was declared part of Ross, and it passed with Ross to the Lords of the Isles. After the Lordship of the Isles broke up in the late 15th century Clan Mackinnon also emerged as independent. The rivalry between the MacLeods and the MacDonalds of South Uist produced the Battle of the Spoiling Dyke in 1578.

Harvesting of kelp grew important in the late 18th century but collapsed from 1822. Thirty thousand people were evicted from the island between 1840 and 1880, many forced to emigrate to the New World. The Battle of the Braes, a protest against evictions, led to the Napier Commission, which reported in 1884, and disturbances continued until the Crofters' Act of 1886.

Skye is part of the Highland Council area and lies wholly within the historic county of Inverness-shire. Portree is the largest settlement and the capital. Since 1995 the Skye Bridge has linked the island to the mainland at Kyle of Lochalsh, and ferries serve nearby islands. Dunvegan Castle is a principal visitor attraction. The population peaked in 1841 and by 2011 was 10,008. About a third of residents spoke Gaelic in 2001, and the language remains important to island culture.
isle-of-wight: The Isle of Wight is separated from the mainland by the Solent strait, which lies between 2 and 5 miles wide, and is otherwise surrounded by the English Channel. It covers about 380 square kilometres, making it the largest island in England, and has 57 miles of coastline. A large monocline tilts the chalk beds to almost 90 degrees at the Needles. The climate is milder and sunnier than most of Britain's, and the island is one of the few places in England where the European red squirrel still flourishes, since no grey squirrels live there.

Early Bronze Age occupation is shown by bell beaker pots, flint tools and the Arreton hoard of bronze, and by barrows on the chalk downland, such as the cemetery of Five Barrows near Brook. Julius Caesar reported that the Belgae took the island in about 85 BCE, and the historian Suetonius says that Vespasian captured it. The Romans built no towns there, but the remains of at least seven villas show a prosperous agriculture, with exports of hides, enslaved people, hunting dogs, grain, cattle and metals.

After the Norman Conquest of 1066 William the Conqueror gave the island to his kinsman William FitzOsbern, and Carisbrooke Priory and Carisbrooke Castle were founded. Allegiance was sworn to FitzOsbern rather than to the king. Henry I granted the lordship to the de Redvers family after he succeeded in 1100. John Keats worked on Endymion at Carisbrooke and Shanklin in 1817. In the mid-1840s potato blight was first found in the United Kingdom on the island. During the Second World War it was bombed often and hosted the RAF radar station at Ventnor.

The island is a ceremonial county and a unitary authority, with Newport as its administrative centre and Ryde, in the north-east, as its largest town. Until 1 April 1890, when the Isle of Wight County Council was formed, it was administered as part of Hampshire, and it became a full ceremonial county in 1974. Queen Victoria built Osborne House at East Cowes as her summer residence and final home, and the poets Tennyson and Swinburne lived on the island. It has a tradition of boat-building, and Cowes hosts the annual Cowes Week. Tourism is its largest industry.
isma-il-pasha: Isma'il was the second of the three sons of Ibrahim Pasha and a grandson of Muhammad Ali Pasha, a family of Albanian descent. He was born in Cairo; his mother, Hoshiyar Qadin, was Circassian. He received a European education in Paris, where he attended the École d'état-major. After the death of his elder brother he became heir to his uncle Sa'id, the wali of Egypt and Sudan, who sent him on missions abroad, to the Pope, to Napoleon III and to the Ottoman sultan. In 1861 he led an army of 18,000 to put down an insurrection in Sudan.

Isma'il was proclaimed khedive on 19 January 1863, although the Ottoman Empire and the other powers at first recognised him only as wali. In 1867 Sultan Abdülaziz granted a firman recognising the title of khedive in exchange for a larger tribute, in return for Egyptian help in the Cretan revolt. Another firman made the succession pass from father to son, and a decree of 1873 confirmed Egypt's virtual independence. He also replaced Ottoman Turkish with Arabic as the language of administration and in November 1866 opened an advisory assembly of delegates.

His spending built over 900 miles of railways, 5,000 miles of telegraph lines, 400 bridges, harbour works at Alexandria and 4,500 schools, and a national library was founded in 1871. He annexed Darfur in 1874, but his army was beaten by Emperor Yohannes IV of Ethiopia at Gundet on 16 November 1875 and again at Gura in March 1876. The costs, and the lavish festival for the opening of the Suez Canal, left Egypt deeply in debt to European creditors.

In 1875 Isma'il sold the Egyptian shares in the Suez Canal Company to the British government for £3,976,582, and direct intervention by the great powers followed. The Caisse de la Dette was set up in 1876, and Britain and France took joint control of much of the government's finances. In June 1879 they pressed Sultan Abdülhamid II to depose him, which was done on 26 June, and his eldest son Tewfik Pasha succeeded him.

Isma'il went into exile near Naples and from 1885 lived in his palace at Emirgan on the Bosporus, more or less a state prisoner, until his death on 2 March 1895. He was later buried in Cairo. The historian Eugene Rogan observed that Egypt had begun its development schemes to secure independence, yet with each new concession made itself more open to European encroachment. The city of Ismailia is named after him.
ismail-al-jazari: Al-Jazari was born in 1136 in Upper Mesopotamia, perhaps in Jazirat ibn Umar, from which the name Jazari may come. The only biographical information known about him is in his own book. Like his father before him he served as chief engineer at the Artuklu Palace, residence of the Mardin branch of the Artuqids, who ruled Upper Mesopotamia as vassals first of the Zengid dynasty of Mosul and later of Saladin. Little is known of his ethnic background, and he has been described as Arab, Kurdish or Persian.

His Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, also known as Automata, describes 50 mechanical devices with instructions for building them. The Artuqid ruler Nasr al-Din Mahmud commissioned the first edition in April 1206, and that manuscript, now in the Topkapı Sarayı Library, is the earliest known. Al-Jazari describes only devices he had built himself, and the book reads in style like a modern do-it-yourself manual. It survives in many manuscript copies. He was a practical engineer who appears to have been more interested in the craftsmanship than in theory, and his machines were usually assembled by trial and error.

He drew on earlier makers: a Pseudo-Archimedes for a water clock, the Banū Mūsā brothers for fountains and al-Saghani for a candle clock. His own contributions include an early crankshaft and crank-slider mechanism in a twin-cylinder pump, a camshaft and an escapement for controlling the speed of a wheel. His five water-raising machines include saqiya chain pumps, one of them driven by hydropower. The historian Donald Hill notes that his work shows for the first time the lamination of timber to minimise warping, the use of paper models to establish designs and the casting of metals in closed mould boxes with sand.

The elephant clock he described in 1206 was the first clock in which an automaton reacted after certain intervals of time, a figure striking a cymbal and a mechanical bird chirping, and the first water clock to record the temporal hours that match the uneven length of days through the year. He also built a portable water-powered scribe clock and a castle clock driven by water and weights. Lynn Townsend White observed that segmental gears first clearly appear in al-Jazari, and that conical valves, once thought to appear first in Leonardo's drawings, are shown in his pictures. He has been called the father of robotics.
ismail-i: Ismail was born on 17 July 1487 in Ardabil, the son of Shaykh Haydar, head of the Safavid Sufi order, and Halima Begum, a daughter of Uzun Hasan of the Aq Qoyunlu. His father was killed in 1488 in a battle at Tabasaran. In 1494 the Aq Qoyunlu captured Ardabil and killed his eldest brother, Ali Mirza, and the seven-year-old Ismail went into hiding in Gilan, where scholars educated him. He came out of hiding at twelve with his followers. His rise was made possible by the Turkoman tribes of Anatolia and Azerbaijan who formed the Qizilbash movement, and a group of seven advisers, the ahl-i ikhtisas, directed the Safavid revolution.

In the summer of 1500 Ismail rallied about 7,000 Qizilbash troops at Erzincan, defeated the Shirvanshah Farrukh Yassar and took Baku. After he conquered Tabriz, the Aq Qoyunlu capital, he was crowned shah in 1501. One of his first acts was to proclaim Twelver Shia Islam the official religion, which began Iran's transformation from a mostly Sunni to a mostly Shia country, partly through forced conversion. In 1508 he destroyed the tombs of the Abbasid caliphs, of the Sunni Imam Abu Hanifa and of the Sufi Abdul Qadir Gilani, causing sectarian tension. He also wrote poetry in Turkic and Persian under the pen name Khaṭāʾī.

His recruiting among Turkoman tribes of Eastern Anatolia brought him into conflict with the Ottomans. After a pro-Safavid rebellion in 1511 and Selim I's accession in 1512, Selim invaded two years later. At Chaldiran in 1514 Ismail rejected his commanders' proposal for a quick attack, saying, "I am not a caravan-thief; whatever is decreed by God, will occur." The Ottomans decisively defeated the Safavids, ending Ismail's conquests.

After Chaldiran Ismail lost his aura of invincibility and fell into heavy drinking. He never again took part in a campaign and left the affairs of state to his vizier Mirza Shah Husayn, who was assassinated in 1523 by a group of Qizilbash officers. Ismail died on 23 May 1524, aged 36, and was buried in Ardabil. His son Tahmasp I succeeded him. The dynasty he founded ruled for over two centuries, and Iran was unified under native rule for the first time since the Islamic conquest.
ismail-ibn-ahmad: Ismail was born in Farghana in May 849, the son of Ahmad ibn Asad and a descendant of Saman Khuda, the ancestor of the Samanids. The Samanids were native to Balkh. The family claimed descent from the Parthian Mihran family, possibly to enhance its lineage, and spoke and advocated Persian and used pre-Islamic bureaucratic titles, probably to suggest that its rule continued the Sasanian Empire. His brother Nasr I ascended the throne in 864/5 and sent Ismail to take control of Bukhara, which had been devastated by looting by forces from Khwarezm. The citizens welcomed him as someone who could bring stability.

A disagreement over the distribution of tax money led to a struggle between the brothers, which Ismail won. He did not formally overthrow Nasr, since the caliph had given Nasr the investiture of Transoxiana and the Saffarids of Sistan had claims there. He recognised Nasr until his death in August 892 and then took power officially. In 893 he took Taraz, the capital of the Karluk Turks, with many slaves and livestock, and a Nestorian church there was converted into a mosque. He also ended the Principality of Ushrusana and partitioned Khwarezm.

The caliph al-Mu'tadid urged Ismail to fight the Saffarid ruler Amr-i Laith, whom he considered a usurper. The armies met at Balkh in the spring of 900. Ismail came out with 20,000 horsemen against Amr's 70,000, many of them poorly equipped, but Amr was captured after some of his troops switched sides. The caliph invested Ismail with Khorasan, Tabaristan, Ray and Isfahan. A Samanid army defeated the Zaydid ruler Muhammad ibn Zayd at Gurgan in 900, and the Samanids took over Tabaristan, restoring Sunni Islam there. Ismail sent gifts to the caliph but paid no tribute and never took a title higher than amir.

After a long sickness Ismail died on 24 November 907 and was succeeded by his son Ahmad Samani. He gave away enormous booty and kept nothing. Because of his campaigns in the north, his realm was so safe from incursions that the defences of Bukhara and Samarkand went unused, which was regretted when the Karakhanids and others later attacked. A historian of Bukhara writing in 943 and Nizam al-Mulk, in the Siyasatnama, both praised his justice. After the end of Soviet rule in Tajikistan his legacy was revived: the currency, the somoni, is named after him, and the highest mountain of Tajikistan, once called Stalin Peak and Communism Peak, is now Ismoil Somoni Peak.
ismail-qemali: Ismail Qemali was born on 16 January 1844 in Vlorë, then part of the Ottoman Empire, into an Albanian Muslim family. He attended the Zosimaia School in Ioannina and graduated from the Ottoman law school in Istanbul. He married a Greek woman, Kleoniki Sourmeli, and sent his children to be educated in Greece. After moving to Istanbul in May 1860 he became a civil servant, reaching high positions in the European and Asian parts of the empire.

He belonged to the reform wing of Midhat Pasha and served as governor of several Balkan towns. When Sultan Abdulhamid II dismissed Midhat, Qemali was exiled to western Anatolia, later recalled and made governor of Beirut, and finally sent to Tripoli, a post he saw as exile. In May 1900 he boarded the British ambassador's yacht, claimed asylum and spent eight years abroad. In Paris he took part in the Congress of Ottoman Opposition of 1902. After the Young Turk Revolution of 1908 he returned as deputy for Berat and then turned to Albanian nationalism, joining the leaders of the revolt of 1911 in drawing up the Greçë Memorandum.

In November 1912 Qemali sailed from Trieste to Durrës and reached Vlorë on 26 November. He was the principal figure in the Albanian Declaration of Independence of 28 November 1912, which ended more than 400 years of Ottoman rule in Albania. Together with Luigj Gurakuqi he raised the Albanian flag on the balcony of the building in Vlorë where the declaration had been signed.

The All-Albanian Congress elected him leader of the Provisional Government, and he served as prime minister and foreign minister. Aware that Ottoman power in the Balkans was collapsing, he asked the Great Powers to recognise and support an independent Albania. In January 1914 the International Control Commission, which administered Albania for the Great Powers, raided Vlorë on 7 and 8 January and found more than 200 Ottoman troops in a plot to restore Ottoman influence. Qemali and his cabinet resigned.

During the First World War Qemali lived in exile in Paris, where he worked with the journalist Somerville Story on memoirs published after his death. In 1918 he travelled to Italy to seek support for his movement but was kept there and stayed in a hotel in Perugia. He died of an apparent heart attack on 26 January 1919, and his body was taken to Vlorë and buried in the local tekke of the Bektashi Order. He is commemorated in Albania as Babai Kombit, the Father of the Nation.
ismailism: Ismailism arose from the succession crisis that divided the early Shia after the death of the imam Ja'far al-Sadiq. One group accepted his younger son Musa al-Kazim and became the Twelvers, the much larger group. The other held that the imam was his eldest son Isma'il, who had died before his father, and became known as the Ismailis. The Ismailis were historically called Batiniyya, from the word for the esoteric, since they stress the inner meaning (batin) of Islam alongside its outward form (zahir).

In the years after Muhammad ibn Isma'il the imams lived hidden from the Abbasid Caliphate, which had overthrown the Umayyads in 750, and the teacher-missionaries called dais organised the community. This period ended with the imam Abdullah al-Mahdi Billah, born in 873, who taught that the imams had not been literally secluded but had been directing the dais.

Ismaili thought is heavily influenced by Neoplatonism. It holds that all things proceed from one source, and that knowledge of God comes through the Universal Intellect. Ismailis believe the Arabic Quran is God's Speech in a secondary sense, since Muhammad expressed in Arabic words a nonverbal inspiration received through the archangel Gabriel. Classical doctrine teaches that revelation was given in six periods to six prophets, each called a Natiq or Speaker, and that the imam is the manifestation of truth and the path of salvation.

Beyond the five pillars of Islam, Ismailis observe two more, purity (taharah) and walayah, a guardianship that means love of and devotion to God, the prophets, the imams and the dais. Jihad is understood as a struggle against one's own soul.

Not all movements that grew from Ismaili teaching were accepted by the wider community. The Qarmatians, based in Bahrain, rampaged across the Middle East in the tenth century and stole the Black Stone from the Kaaba in 930. They returned it in 951 and were defeated by the Abbasids in 976, after which the group dwindled and has no adherents today.

Under the Fatimids missionaries such as Hassan-i Sabbah, born at Qom in 1056, spread the faith and became important to the survival of the Nizari branch. After the Fatimid Caliphate fell, the three living branches developed in isolation. The Musta'li moved their mission to India after 1197, where they are known as Bohras. The Nizaris, the largest branch, today follow the Aga Khan as hereditary imam. Smaller communities live in Yemen, Syria and Central Asia.
ismet-inonu: İsmet İnönü was born Mustafa İsmet in 1884 in Smyrna (İzmir), the second child of Hacı Reşid, a retired official of the War Ministry, and Cevriye. He graduated from the Imperial School of Military Engineering in 1904 as a lieutenant gunnery officer and from the Military Academy in 1906 as a staff captain. In the First World War he rose to colonel and was chief of staff of the Second Army. He was a member of the Special Organization, and on the Caucasus front he requested that Armenians be extradited to Russia or deported to inner Anatolia, weeks before the government ordered the deportation of the Armenians of the eastern border areas.

After the occupation of Constantinople on 16 March 1920 he escaped to Anatolia and joined the Grand National Assembly at Ankara as deputy of Edirne. He became chief of the general staff and then commander of the Western Front, and was promoted to Mirliva after the First and Second Battles of İnönü. He was chief negotiator at the Armistice of Mudanya and at the Lausanne conference, which convened in late 1922 to replace the Treaty of Sèvres; he became known for his stubborn resolve, and is said to have switched off his hearing aid during the speeches of Lord Curzon.

As prime minister under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk he helped carry out the reforms: the Hat Law in 1925, the Latin alphabet in 1928 and the Surname Law of 1934. After the Sheikh Said rebellion he banned the opposition parties and the press, and the Report for Reform in the East recommended forbidding non-Turkish languages. His economic policy was heavily statist, inspired by the Soviet Five Year Plan. Atatürk dismissed his government in 1937 and appointed Celâl Bayar.

Elected second president on Atatürk's death in 1938, İnönü received the title Millî Şef, or National Chief. He annexed the Hatay State in 1939 and kept Turkey neutral through most of the Second World War. In 1945 he openly called for an opposition party, and the Democrat Party, founded by Bayar, took power in the elections of 1950. İnönü led the opposition, was prime minister again after the 1961 election and led the Republican People's Party until 1972. He died on 25 December 1973, aged 89, and is buried at Anıtkabir in Ankara opposite Atatürk's mausoleum.
isocrates: Isocrates was born into a prosperous Athenian family shortly before the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War. According to the Suda, a Byzantine encyclopedia, his father Theodorus owned a workshop that made auloi, a type of musical instrument, and his mother was named Heduto. Accounts including his own say that the war wiped out his father's estate and forced him to earn a living.

His career is said to have begun with logography, the writing of courtroom speeches for others, since Athenian citizens had to represent themselves and hired writers instead of lawyers. He had great talent for it and amassed a considerable fortune; A weak voice kept him from speaking in public himself, and he took no direct part in state affairs, but he published pamphlets that influenced opinion. After founding his school he abandoned judicial work and disparaged speech-writing.

The school took no more than nine pupils at a time, usually for three or four years. Isocrates encouraged them to observe public behaviour in the city and to learn by imitation, with the aim of serving the city. His pupils included Isaeus, Lycurgus, Hypereides, Ephorus, Theopompus, Speusippus and Timotheus, who set up a statue of him at Eleusis. He called his teaching philosophia, meaning the practical study of ethics, politics and public speaking rather than the abstract dialectic that Plato marked out as philosophy. He stressed natural ability, training and practice over fixed rules, and fitness for the occasion, kairos.

Of 60 orations in his name known in Roman times, 21 survived the medieval period. His surviving works include the autobiographical Antidosis and the polemic Against the Sophists, which explains his educational principles. In On the Peace, written at the end of the Social War in 355 BCE, he asked that both sides be heard fairly.

The Panegyricus of 380 BCE had called for an all-Greek campaign against Persia under Athenian leadership. In 346 BCE he addressed Philip II of Macedon. He called for a league of Greek cities, not an empire of Macedon. Reports say he starved himself to death soon after the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, out of disappointment at the loss of Greek freedom, a report that J. F. Dobson doubts.
His works were popular in Renaissance Europe, and translations of To Nicocles were given to rulers as a mirror of princes. His influence reached the Roman rhetoricians Cicero and Quintilian.
isparta: Isparta is a Turkish form of the Greek name Sparta. The ancient city of Baris in the Roman province of Pisidia was once said to correspond to it, a later theory identified it with the Eastern Roman fortress Saporda, and Muslim sources call it Sabarta. The archaeologist G. E. Bean found these shifting conceptions bewildering, and modern scholars place Baris near Kılıç in the Keçiborlu district of the province. At an early stage the city became a Christian bishopric, suffragan of the metropolitan see of Antioch of Pisidia. Two bishops are known with certainty: Heraclius, who took part in the First Council of Nicaea in 325, and Leo, at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787.

The Seljuk Turks conquered the area in 1071, and in the late 13th century it became part of the Hamidids. In 1381 the Hamidid emir sold Isparta to the Ottoman sultan Murad I. Muslim refugees from the Balkans settled around Isparta in the late 19th century, and Bulgarian refugees brought the knowledge of kazanlik rosewater production, which led to its nickname, the city of roses. According to the Ottoman statistics of 1914 most of the district's people were Muslims, with Greek and Armenian minorities. In the middle of the 19th century the city had around 1,000 Greek Orthodox Christian families, and in 1923 its Greek inhabitants were moved to Greece under the Greco-Turkish population exchange.

Isparta is the seat of Isparta Province, at an elevation of 1,035 metres, with 247,580 inhabitants in 2022. Its main economic activities are the production of rosewater and handmade carpets, which were a major industry in the early 20th century. The lakes around the city moderate a hot-summer Mediterranean climate, and Süleyman Demirel University is based there.

The city lies close to a fault line, and an earthquake in 1914 destroyed most of the old city, leaving few historical buildings. The oldest is the Kutlu Bey Mosque, or Ulu Camii, built in 1429 by Kutlu Bey, a general of Sultan Murad II, which was badly damaged in 1914 and restored in 1922. The Firdevs Paşa Mosque of 1561 and its neighbouring bedesten are attributed to the architect Sinan. The Greek Orthodox church of Aya Baniya, built in 1750, houses a museum of scents.
issyk-kul: Issyk-Kul, in Kyrgyz Ysyk-Köl, meaning Hot Lake, is an endorheic saline lake in the western Tian Shan, just south of a range dividing Kyrgyzstan from Kazakhstan. It lies at 1,607 metres, is 182 kilometres long and up to 60 kilometres wide, and covers 6,236 square kilometres. Its depth reaches 668 metres. Despite its elevation and cold winters it rarely freezes, because of its salinity, about 0.6% compared with 3.5% for typical seawater.

About 118 rivers and streams flow into the lake, the largest being the Jyrgalang and Tüp. It has no current outlet, though some hydrologists hypothesise that its water filters deep underground into the Chu River. The Teskey Ala-Too Range dominates the southern shore and the Kungey Alatau runs parallel to the north shore.

Issyk-Kul was a stopover on the Silk Road. The Chinese Buddhist monk Xuanzang passed by the lake in the 7th century and noted it in his Great Tang Records on the Western Regions. In Manchu and Mongol records it was called Temurtu-Nor, Iron Lake. It was once part of the territory of the Qing dynasty and was ceded to Russia, together with the surrounding territory, after the Treaty of Tarbagatai.

Many historians believe the lake was the point of origin of the Black Death of the 14th century. In 2022 researchers reported on genetic material from seven individuals buried in two cemeteries near Issyk-Kul, which showed that the plague was present there in 1338 or 1339, eight years before it devastated Eurasia. It first infected people in a settlement of traders and spread along trade routes.

The lake level is some 8 metres higher than in medieval times, and divers have found the remains of submerged settlements in shallow areas. Toru-Aygyr, near the north-west shore, was founded in the 13th century and submerged by earthquakes in the 15th century. In the Soviet period the lake became a popular resort, with sanatoria and vacation homes along the northern shore, mostly around Cholpon-Ata.

The lake and the adjacent land form the Issyk-Kul Region of Kyrgyzstan, whose administrative seat is Karakol, near the eastern tip, where a wooden mosque built without metal nails by the Dungan people stands. Issyk-Kul State Reserve, the first nature reserve in Kyrgyzstan, was established in 1948, the lake became a Ramsar site in 1975, and the Issyk-Kul Biosphere Reserve was set up in 2000. The lake supports a rich endemic fish fauna and large numbers of wintering waterfowl.
istakhr: Istakhr stood in Fars, about 5 km north of Persepolis, in the valley of the Polvar River between the Kuh-e Rahmat and Naqsh-e Rostam, where the valley opens onto the plain of Marvdasht. The name is the New Persian form of the Middle Persian Stakhr, believed to mean stronghold. Istakhr was probably first part of the settlements around the Achaemenid royal residences, and became a separate city soon after Alexander the Great brought down Persepolis; much of Persepolis's rubble seems to have been used to build it.

After Seleucus I died in 280 BCE, the Persians of Persis began to reassert their independence, and Istakhr, better protected by its hills than Persepolis and on the road to Isfahan, appears to have been the centre of resistance. It flourished as the capital of the Frataraka governors and Kings of Persis until the early 3rd century CE. Sasan, ancestor of the Sasanian dynasty, came from Istakhr and was warden of its Anahid fire-temple. His son Papak dethroned the local ruler Gochihr in about 205, and Papak's sons Shapur and Ardashir were the last two Kings of Persis.

In 224 Ardashir founded the Sasanian Empire, and Istakhr briefly served as its first capital, then as the principal city and religious centre of the province of Pars. It held an important mint and the royal treasury, which kept one of the limited copies of the Great Avesta.
Istakhr resisted the Arab conquest fiercely. A campaign in 640 failed, the city surrendered in 643 and then revolted, and further campaigns in 648 or 649 and 649 caused the death of many inhabitants.

It remained a stronghold of Zoroastrianism and a fairly important place in the early Islamic period, and its mint struck Umayyad and Abbasid coins. On 11 April 890 Amr ibn al-Layth defeated a caliphal governor there. The Buyid Abu Kalijar later sent an army under Qutulmish that destroyed and pillaged the city, which never recovered and became a village of no more than a hundred inhabitants. Its castle held out until Shah Abbas besieged it, and Pietro della Valle saw it in ruins in 1621.

Eugène Flandin and Pascal Coste made the most detailed account of the ruins before the 20th century, in late 1840. Ernst Herzfeld and a University of Chicago team led by Erich Schmidt explored the site only cursorily in the first half of the 20th century, and Sasanian Istakhr remains largely unexcavated.
istanbul: Istanbul straddles the Bosporus Strait in north-western Turkey, between the Sea of Marmara and the Black Sea. The strait is the only passage from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean. About two-thirds of the population live on the European side and the rest in Asia. The meeting of the Sea of Marmara, the Bosporus and the Golden Horn gave the city both a defence against attack and a natural toll-gate for trade. The belief that seven hills make up the city is a myth: there are more than 50 hills within its limits.

Neolithic artefacts show that the historic peninsula was settled as far back as the 6th millennium BCE. Megarian colonists founded Byzantium around 657 BCE, claiming descent from its founder Byzas, said to be the son of the god Poseidon and the nymph Ceroëssa. The Roman emperor Constantine the Great refounded the city in 324 CE, at first calling it New Rome, and it became Constantinople in 330.

For nearly 16 centuries it served as the capital of four empires: the Roman Empire from 330 to 395, the Byzantine Empire from 395 to 1204 and from 1261 to 1453, the Latin Empire from 1204 to 1261, and the Ottoman Empire from 1453 to 1922. It was important in the advance of Christianity in Roman and Byzantine times. The Ottomans conquered it in 1453 and made it the seat of their caliphate. By 500 CE it had 400,000 to 500,000 people, more than Rome, and it was the largest city in Europe from 1500 to 1750, when London surpassed it. Constantinople remained the usual Western name until the 1930s. The Republic of Turkey made Ankara its capital in 1923.

Istanbul is the largest city in Turkey, with a population of over 15 million. The historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and palaces and imperial mosques still line its hills. The Galata Tower is the one survivor of the medieval Genoese fortifications of Galata. The first Turkish newspaper, Takvim-i Vekayi, was published there in 1831.
isthmian-games: The games were reputed to have begun as funeral games for Melicertes, instituted by Sisyphus, the legendary king of Corinth, who found the body and buried it on the Isthmus. Another myth, probably later, held that Theseus, the legendary king of Athens, enlarged a closed night rite into athletic games dedicated to Poseidon and open to all Greeks. A further version credits Kypselos, tyrant of Corinth in the 7th century BCE, with restoring the games to their old splendour. According to Solinus they were constituted in the 49th Olympiad; 582 BCE is the date generally accepted, though one recent study places the first games in 581 BCE.

The festival was held in spring, in the second and fourth years of each Olympiad, the year before and the year after the Olympic Games, at the rural sanctuary of Poseidon on the Isthmus of Corinth, a place easily reached by land and by sea. The contests were the same as at Olympia, among them wrestling, boxing, pankration and horse and chariot racing, and there were musical and poetical contests in which women were allowed to compete.

Until at least the 5th century BCE, the time of Pindar, the victor's wreath was of celery; later it was made of pine. A victor might also be honoured with a statue or an ode, and Athens paid its own victors 100 drachmas. Before the games Corinth declared a truce that gave athletes safe passage through Greece: in 412 BCE the Athenians were invited as usual although Athens and Corinth were at war. The games were especially popular with Athenians, while the Eleans boycotted them.

The festival served many as a forum for political propaganda, and from 228 or 229 BCE Romans were allowed to take part. Corinth, rebuilt by Caesar in 44 BCE, recovered the games shortly afterwards, but they were then held in the city itself and did not return to the Isthmus until 42 or 43 CE. Libanius mentions cult activity at the Isthmus into the middle of the 4th century, and the games probably continued at least until the end of that century. The circumstances of their end are unknown; imperial pressure against pagan rites grew at that time, though some polytheistic cult practices continued at Corinth into the 6th century.
isthmus-of-corinth: The isthmus lies near the city of Corinth, between the Gulf of Corinth to the west and the Saronic Gulf to the east, and is 6.3 kilometres wide. In antiquity it was the landmark that separated the Peloponnese from mainland Greece. The geographer Strabo, in the first century CE, recorded a stele on the isthmus with two inscriptions: the one facing east towards Megara read "Here is not Peloponnesus, but Ionia", and the one facing west read "Here is Peloponnesus, not Ionia". Plutarch ascribed its erection to the Attic hero Theseus, on his way to Athens.

The Greeks long considered a shortcut that would spare ships the voyage around the Peloponnese. The tyrant Periander tried to cut a canal in the 7th century BCE but gave it up because of technical difficulties, and built instead a stone ramp, the Diolkos, along which ships were dragged overland. Remains of the Diolkos survive beside the modern canal. Under Roman rule, Julius Caesar saw the value of a link for his new colony, Colonia Laus Iulia Corinthiensis.

Engineers under Tiberius tried to dig a canal but lacked the equipment, and boats were rolled across on logs instead, a method in use by 32 CE. In 67 CE the emperor Nero ordered 6,000 slaves to dig a canal with spades; Flavius Josephus says they were Jewish captives taken by Vespasian. According to Pliny the Elder the work advanced about 0.8 kilometres. Nero died the next year and his successor Galba abandoned the project as too costly.
The Romans also built the Hexamilion, a defensive wall across the isthmus that guarded the only land route into the Peloponnese and is the largest single archaeological structure in Greece.

The idea of a canal was seriously proposed again in 1830, soon after Greek independence from the Ottoman Empire, and the Corinth Canal was completed in 1893 after eleven years' work. It effectively makes the Peloponnese an island, and road, railway and submersible bridges cross it. Campaigners call for better protection of the Diolkos.
isthmus-of-panama: The Isthmus of Panama, historically known as the Isthmus of Darien, is the narrow strip of land between the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean that links North and South America. The country of Panama and the Panama Canal lie on it. It is generally thought to have formed around 3 million years ago, separating the Atlantic and Pacific and, in the view first put forward by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1910, giving rise to the Gulf Stream. Its closing allowed animals and plants to cross between the continents in what is called the Great American Interchange.

Vasco Núñez de Balboa, a Spanish conquistador, was the first European to reach the Pacific from the isthmus, on 25 September 1513. The town of Panamá was founded in 1519 on the Pacific coast, and in 1671 the Welsh privateer Henry Morgan crossed from the Caribbean side and destroyed it. The ruins of Panamá Viejo were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.

Spanish conquest was ruinous for the local Cueva people. A regional slave trade, deadly working conditions, wars of conquest and the destruction of communities led to their dispersal, and by 1550 fewer than 300 indigenous people were counted in the towns of Panama, Nombre de Dios and Nata combined. Silver and gold from Peru crossed the isthmus overland to Porto Bello.

In 1698 Scotland tried to found a colony called New Caledonia on the Gulf of Darién; the scheme was unsuccessful. The California gold rush from 1849 sent travellers across the isthmus. Ferdinand de Lesseps started a canal company in 1880 that went bankrupt in 1889. In 1902–1904 the United States forced Colombia to grant independence to the Department of the Isthmus, bought the company's assets and finished the canal in 1914.
isthmus-of-tehuantepec: The isthmus lies in south-eastern Veracruz and Oaxaca, with small areas of Chiapas and Tabasco. At its narrowest it is 200 km across from gulf to gulf. The Sierra Madre del Sur breaks down there into a broad ridge, and the highest point reached by the railway, at Chivela Pass, is 224 m. The northern side is swampy and densely covered with jungle, which has been a greater obstacle to railway builders than the grades over the mountains. The name comes from the town of Santo Domingo Tehuantepec, from the Nahuatl Tecuantepec, meaning jaguar mountain.

Since the conquest the Spanish monarchy sought a passage between the Gulf of Mexico and the Pacific. In 1520 Hernán Cortés used the isthmus to move equipment and supplies from the gulf to his shipyard on the Pacific coast, going part of the way by river. Later in the 16th century materials and artillery for shipbuilding were taken up the Coatzacoalcos River in canoes and carried on the backs of indigenous people to the Pacific. The Panama route eventually eclipsed Tehuantepec as the favoured site for a canal.

The Gadsden Purchase treaty of 1854 allowed the United States to carry mail and trade goods across the isthmus. The McLane-Ocampo Treaty of 1859, signed by Benito Juárez but never ratified by the United States Congress, would have given extensive transit rights. The London contractors S. Pearson and Son began work on 10 December 1899 to rebuild the railway and construct ports at Coatzacoalcos and Salina Cruz, and the line was ready for formal opening in January 1907.

The Tehuantepec railway, now the Ferrocarril Transístmico, is 308 km long and runs from Coatzacoalcos on the Gulf of Mexico to Salina Cruz on the Pacific. In the Oaxaca half of the isthmus the people are mostly Zapotec, and the women known as Tehuanas are noted throughout Mexico for their colourful dress. The Selva Zoque in the east-central part is the largest remaining area of tropical rainforest in Mexico.
istvan-bethlen: Bethlen was born on 8 October 1874, the only son of Count István Bethlen de Bethlen and Countess Ilona Teleki de Szék, with two elder sisters. His family was an old noble house of Transylvania. He was elected to the Hungarian Parliament as a liberal in 1901 and married his distant cousin, the author Countess Margarete Bethlen de Bethlen, on 27 June 1901. They had three sons.

The British historian C. A. Macartney described him as a poor public speaker, very reserved, with the assurance of a man whose family had been obeyed for centuries. He spoke Hungarian, English, French, German and Romanian. Macartney called him a conservative in the truest sense, who believed in the right of Hungary to rule the Danube basin through his own class.

After the attempt of King Charles IV to return to the throne in 1921, Horthy asked Bethlen to form a strong government. Bethlen disliked the House of Habsburg and, though he wanted Hungary to remain a monarchy, opposed a Habsburg restoration. Horthy appointed him as a compromise: as a Calvinist from Transylvania he was expected to follow a revisionist foreign policy, which suited the radicals, while his standing among the great aristocratic families satisfied the conservatives. He was prime minister until 1931.

From 11 October 1932 anti-Jewish demonstrations broke out at Hungarian universities, with Christian students complaining that Jewish students exceeded the quota of the numerus clausus law of 1920. Gömbös and his education minister Bálint Hóman supported the protests, and Gömbös used them to charge that Bethlen had failed to enforce the law during his decade in office.

Bethlen was increasingly sidelined, but he stood out as one of the few Hungarian voices opposed to an alliance with Nazi Germany. He objected that the Germans wanted Hungary to remain agrarian and supply them with cheap food and raw materials, and expected Britain to win the Second World War.
istvan-szechenyi: István Széchenyi was born in Vienna to Count Ferenc Széchényi and Countess Juliána Festetics de Tolna. The Széchenyis were an old and influential Hungarian noble family, traditionally loyal to the House of Habsburg. His father, an enlightened aristocrat, founded the Hungarian National Museum and the Hungarian National Library.

At seventeen he joined the Austrian army and fought in the Napoleonic Wars, distinguishing himself at the Battle of Raab on 14 June 1809 and carrying messages through enemy lines before the Battle of Leipzig in October 1813. He left the service as a captain in 1826, after a promotion to major was turned down, and from September 1815 to 1821 he had travelled in France, England, Italy, Greece and the Levant. The rapid modernisation of Britain fascinated him most.

Széchenyi organised the National Casino in 1827 as a forum for the patriotic nobility. His political writings, Hitel (Credit, 1830), Világ (Light, 1831) and Stádium (1833), condemned the nobility's conservatism and urged it to give up feudal privileges such as freedom from taxation and to lead modernisation. He envisioned reform within the Habsburg monarchy, opposed radicalism, and thought nationalism particularly dangerous in the multi-ethnic Kingdom of Hungary. In 1835 he established the Óbuda Shipyard, the first industrial-scale steamship builder in the Habsburg Empire. He led the Danube Navigation Committee, which finished its work in ten years, and was the first to promote steamboats on the Danube, the Tisza and Lake Balaton.

He backed the Chain Bridge, the first permanent bridge between Buda and Pest, as a symbol of their later union. He disagreed with Lajos Kossuth, whom he thought an agitator: in his pamphlet People of the East (1841) he argued for slow, careful reform to avoid Habsburg intervention, favouring laissez-faire and agriculture where Kossuth favoured protective tariffs and rapid industrialisation. In March 1848 he accepted the portfolio of ways and communications under Lajos Batthyány.

As the revolution of 1848 moved towards an attempt to break from Habsburg rule, contrary to his vision, Széchenyi suffered a breakdown in early September and was placed in Dr Gustav Görgen's asylum at Oberdöbling. He recovered enough to write Önismeret and Ein Blick, but never returned to politics. Still depressed, he shot himself on 8 April 1860, aged 68. All Hungary mourned, and more than 50,000 people visited his grave at Nagycenk in the three days after his funeral. A statue was unveiled in Budapest on 23 May 1880, and in 1898 the Chain Bridge was named the Széchenyi Chain Bridge in his honour.
istvan-tisza: Tisza was the son of Kálmán Tisza de Borosjenő, prime minister of Hungary from 1875 to 1890, and of Countess Helene von Degenfeld-Schonburg, a Hungarian-German aristocrat from Baden-Württemberg. He was raised in a puritanical and authoritarian Calvinist household, studied at home until the age of twelve and then attended the Calvinist Gymnasium of Debrecen. He studied law in Budapest, then international law at Heidelberg, economics in Berlin and political science at Oxford. After a year as a volunteer hussar he settled in Bihar County, and after five years overseeing the family estates he turned to politics, winning his first seat for the Liberal Party in 1886.

In the 1890s Tisza presided over the Hungarian Industrial and Commercial Bank and sat on many company boards. He resigned from all of them before his first term as prime minister, in 1903-1905, in which he had the remains of Prince Francis II Rákóczi brought back from Turkey and interred in Kassa, today Košice. When a railway workers' strike paralysed the economy on 19 April 1904, he had the organisers arrested and the strikers conscripted into the army. In Bihar the police dealt harshly with peasants at a Socialist gathering, leaving 33 dead and several hundred wounded.

He became prime minister again on 7 June 1913. His cabinet introduced the legal categories of defamation, libel and scare-mongering, which made the press actionable in the courts, and newspapers and journalists regarded this as a violation of freedom of the press. He promised to re-establish the Croatian Constitution, suspended in May 1912, and Croatian constitutional government was restored in November 1913. He supported industrialisation, opposed antisemitism as economically counterproductive, resisted breaking up the large estates and opposed extending the vote to soldiers on active duty; before 1918 only 10 per cent of the citizens of the Kingdom of Hungary could vote.

Tisza was seen by many as the representative of the war policy of the Monarchy, and he survived three attempts on his life, the first in the Hungarian parliament in 1912. On 31 October 1918 soldiers broke into his home, the Róheim Villa in Budapest, in front of his wife and grandniece and killed him. Some sources suggest that they were deserters who blamed him for starting the war. His son István died of Spanish flu five days later. A trial that ended on 6 October 1921 found six men guilty, among them József Pogány and Pál Kéri.
itaipu-dam: The plan for a power plant on the Paraná grew out of negotiations between Brazil and Paraguay in the 1960s. The Iguaçu Act, signed on 22 July 1966 by the foreign ministers Juracy Magalhães and Raúl Sapena Pastor, declared a shared interest in studying the use of the river's water from the Salto de Sete Quedas to the Iguaçu River watershed. The Itaipu Treaty followed on 26 April 1973, and the body Itaipu Binacional was created on 17 May 1974 to manage construction, which began in January of the following year. The name comes from an island near the site, called in Guarani after the idea of a sounding stone.

Argentina first contested the project. The dispute ended with the Tripartite Agreement of 19 October 1979, which set the permitted river levels and became the basis of later Argentine–Brazilian integration. The river was diverted on 14 October 1978 to dry the section of bed where the dam was built.

The dam is 7,235 metres long and 196 metres high, and is really four dams joined: an earth fill dam, a rock fill dam, a concrete buttress main dam and a concrete wing dam. The reservoir began to fill on 13 October 1982, and the first generating unit started on 5 May 1984. The last two of the twenty units, each of 700 MW, began work in September 2006 and March 2007, bringing the capacity to 14 GW.

Ten units generate at 50 Hz for Paraguay and ten at 60 Hz for Brazil. Paraguay's output exceeds its own demand, so most of it goes directly to the Brazilian side, and two 600 kV direct-current lines about 800 kilometres long carry the bulk of the power to south-eastern Brazil. Around forty thousand people worked on the construction, which shifted 50 million tonnes of earth and rock.

The project displaced about 10,000 families and flooded the Guaíra Falls, the waterfall largest by volume in the world; some 80 people died when a crowded bridge over the falls collapsed shortly before the reservoir was filled. The falls had separated two freshwater ecoregions, and after they vanished more than 30 fish species from below them spread above. In 1994 the American Society of Civil Engineers named Itaipu one of the seven modern wonders of the world. The composer Philip Glass wrote a symphonic cantata called Itaipu.
italian-east-africa: Italy colonized Eritrea in 1890 and Italian Somaliland in 1905, and its invasion of Ethiopia in the First Italo-Ethiopian War of 1895–1896 failed. After the First World War, nationalist feeling grew from the belief that Italy had been denied its due, a sentiment called the Mutilated Victory, and it contributed to the rise of Benito Mussolini in 1922. A border clash at Ual-Ual in 1934 gave Mussolini a pretext for war. The Second Italo-Ethiopian War began without a declaration in October 1935. Italian troops used mustard gas in aerial bombardments against combatants and civilians, and Emperor Haile Selassie fled to England. Italian forces entered Addis Ababa on 5 May 1936, and Mussolini proclaimed the Italian Empire on 9 May.

A decree of 1 June 1936 united Ethiopia, Eritrea and Somalia as Italian East Africa. It was ruled by a Governo Generale from Addis Ababa under a viceroy appointed by the Italian king, who took the title Emperor of Ethiopia, and it was divided into six governorates. The League of Nations ended its sanctions in July 1936, and by November 1938 47 countries had recognized the king's new title. The administration divided inhabitants into citizens, meaning Italians and other Europeans, and subjects, and racial legislation of 1939 prohibited mixed marriages. It marginalized the Amhara elite and often treated the Oromo and Muslim communities more favourably.

Roads were the main public works, linking Addis Ababa with Massawa, Mogadishu and Assab. By 1939 about 165,270 Italian colonists lived there, though by 1940 only 3,200 farmers had reached Ethiopia, less than ten percent of the regime's goal. The population in 1939 was estimated at 12.1 million. Ethiopian resistance never ceased. After an attempt on Rodolfo Graziani's life on 19 February 1937, Italian troops and Blackshirts massacred thousands of civilians in Addis Ababa, with estimates from 1,400 to 19,000 deaths.

British forces attacked Italian East Africa in the East African campaign of the Second World War, and after the Battle of Gondar in November 1941 all its territories came under British military administration. Haile Selassie was restored, and Ethiopia's full sovereignty returned in 1944. British-occupied Somalia became a Trust Territory under Italian administration in 1950 until independence in 1960, and Eritrea became an autonomous part of Ethiopia in 1952. Italian archaeologists began studying the obelisks of Axum and the churches of Lalibela in 1938.
italian-empire: Italy, unified as a nation-state in the late 19th century, wished to compete with the other European powers and saw its interests in the Mediterranean and the Horn of Africa. It arrived late and depended on the acquiescence of Britain, France and Germany. When France imposed a protectorate over Tunisia in May 1881, what the Italian press called the Slap of Tunis left Italy isolated and led it to sign the Triple Alliance in 1882 with Germany and Austria-Hungary.

The genesis of the empire was the purchase in 1869 of Assab Bay on the Red Sea by an Italian navigation company wanting a coaling station as the Suez Canal opened. The government took it over in 1882, making it modern Italy's first overseas territory.

Italy joined the Allies in 1915 after being promised territorial spoils, mainly from Austria and Turkey. Albania and Dalmatia saw Italian occupations during the First World War. In 1923 the Treaty of Lausanne formalised Italian administration of Libya and the Dodecanese. Mussolini, in power from 1922, sought to enlarge the empire, and in 1939 drew up a document, The March to the Oceans, arguing that countries without free access to the high seas were not independent. By 1939 Italian settlers numbered 120,000 to 150,000 in Libya and 165,000 in Italian East Africa, where the government encouraged systematic demographic colonisation.

At its peak, between 1936 and 1941, the colonial possessions in Africa covered present-day Libya, Eritrea, Somalia and Ethiopia, the last three grouped as Africa Orientale Italiana. Outside Africa Italy held the Dodecanese Islands and Albania and had a concession at Tianjin in China. In the World War II it allied with Germany in 1940 and occupied British Somaliland, western Egypt, much of Yugoslavia and most of Greece.

The Italian Army was expelled from East Africa by British and Commonwealth forces in 1941, and by the autumn of 1943 the empire had effectively ended. Mussolini was deposed on 25 July 1943, and an armistice with the Allies was made public on 8 September, after which German forces ended Italian rule in Albania, Croatia and the Dodecanese. In 1947 Italy relinquished its claims on its former colonies. In 1950 the former Italian Somaliland became a UN trust territory under Italian administration, which lasted until its independence in 1960.
italian-riviera: The Italian Riviera, or Ligurian Riviera, is the narrow coastal strip between the Ligurian Sea and the mountain chain formed by the Maritime Alps and the Apennines. It runs from the French border near Ventimiglia, a former customs post, eastwards to Capo Corvo, also called Punta Bianca, at the eastern end of the Gulf of La Spezia. It includes nearly all the coastline of Liguria, about 350 km long, and crosses all four Ligurian provinces: Genoa, Savona, Imperia and La Spezia.

The point of division between the Riviera di Ponente, 'the coast of the setting sun', and the Riviera di Levante, 'the coast of the rising sun', is the apex of the Ligurian arc at Voltri. The Ponente's part centred on Savona is called the Riviera delle Palme, and the part centred on Sanremo the Riviera dei Fiori, after its long-established flower growing.

The history of the Italian Riviera is chiefly that of the Liguria region. Historically the name Riviera extended further west, through what is now French territory as far as Marseille. The coast has been a destination for travellers since the time of Lord Byron and Percy Bysshe Shelley, and Ezra Pound and Ernest Hemingway were among the writers inspired by it. The musician Niccolò Paganini (1782-1840) and the poet Eugenio Montale (1896-1981) are among the figures linked with the region.

About 1.6 million people live on the Riviera, most of them in the coastal area. Its mild climate supports a tourist trade in resorts such as Alassio, Bordighera, Camogli, Portofino, Sanremo and Santa Margherita Ligure, and in the Cinque Terre. Industry is concentrated around Genoa, Savona and the Gulf of La Spezia: Genoa and La Spezia are leading Italian shipyards, La Spezia is Italy's major naval base, and Savona is a major centre of the iron industry.

Two World Heritage Sites lie on the coast: the Strade Nuove and the system of the Palazzi dei Rolli in Genoa, and Portovenere, the Cinque Terre and the islands of Palmaria, Tino and Tinetto. Local foods include pesto, focaccia and farinata, and the Sanremo Music Festival and the Milan-Sanremo cycling race are held on the coast.
italian-somaliland: Italian interest began with exploring societies founded from 1876. In 1889 two Somali rulers sought protection from Italy by treaty: Sultan Yusuf Ali Kenadid of Hobyo, who signed on 8 February, and Boqor Osman Mahamuud of the Majeerteen Sultanate, who signed on 7 April. Each hoped for Italian support against rivals. The treaties promised that Italy would not interfere in their administration, in return for arms and an annual subsidy.

In the south the consul at Zanzibar, Vincenzo Filonardi, was charged with creating outposts on the Banaadir coast. The port of Adale was occupied in February 1891 and renamed Itala. In 1893 Filonardi and the Italian navy occupied Merca, Mogadishu, Barawa and Warsheekh, and Giumbo followed in 1895.

Somali resistance marked the whole period. In November 1896 Antonio Cecchi, administrator for the Benadir Company, and thirteen others were killed in an ambush at Lafoole by Biimaal and Wa'daan fighters. A punitive expedition under Giorgio Sorrentino in 1897 destroyed villages and seized livestock. Further wars against the Biimaal and their allies in 1905 to 1908 extended Italian control over the whole Lower Shabelle region. The Dervish movement of Mohammed Abdullah Hassan defeated an Italian advance at Hiraan in 1913.

After the First World War Britain ceded Jubaland to Italy in 1925, and by the end of 1927 the sultanates of Hobyo and the Majeerteen had been annexed after a two-year campaign under Governor Cesare Maria De Vecchi. The colony saw railways, dams, farms and villages, among them an agricultural settlement at Jowhar. By 1935 more than 50,000 Italians lived there, about 5 per cent of the population. In October 1935 the southern front of the invasion of Ethiopia was launched from the colony, and in June 1936 it became the Somalia Governorate of Italian East Africa.

British forces defeated the Italians in 1941 and administered the territory until 1950. The Somali Youth Club, the first modern Somali political party, was founded in Mogadishu in 1943 and became the Somali Youth League. In November 1949 the United Nations granted Italy trusteeship on condition that Somalia become independent within ten years, and Italian administration began on 1 April 1950. The Somali Youth League won 75.58 per cent of the vote in the parliamentary election of 1959. On 1 July 1960 the Trust Territory united with former British Somaliland to form the Somali Republic, with Mogadishu as its capital.
italian-war-of-1521-1526: After Maximilian I died on 12 January 1519, Charles I of Spain and Francis I of France competed for the imperial crown. Charles bought the votes of the electors with money borrowed from the Fugger banking family, and he was crowned King of the Romans on 23 October 1520. Pope Leo X needed his support against Martin Luther, and Charles issued the Edict of Worms in May 1521. Leo promised to help expel the French from Lombardy, which left Francis with only the Republic of Venice as an ally. Francis tried to divert Charles by attacking Luxembourg and Navarre in 1521, but both offensives failed.

Imperial troops invaded northeastern France in August 1521, and Charles and Henry VIII signed the secret Treaty of Bruges in November. On 27 April 1522 the Imperial and Papal army defeated the French at the Battle of Bicocca, and Lombardy was abandoned. England declared war on France on 29 May 1522. Charles de Bourbon, angered by Francis's attempt to seize his inheritance, entered the Emperor's service, and Venice changed sides by the Treaty of Worms of 29 July 1523. A French attack in 1524 failed at the Battle of the Sesia, where Bayard was killed, and Bourbon invaded Provence. Francis then crossed the Alps and besieged Pavia.

On the night of 23 February 1525 the Imperial army moved against his camp, and in the four-hour battle that followed arquebusiers cut down the French cavalry. Francis was captured by Charles de Lannoy.

Francis was held at Pizzighettone and then in Madrid. His mother, Louise of Savoy, sent a mission to Suleiman, which brought an Ottoman ultimatum to Charles and laid the foundation of the Franco-Ottoman alliance, a scandal in the Christian world. Suleiman defeated Charles's allies at the Battle of Mohács in 1526. Francis signed the Treaty of Madrid, giving up his claims to Italy, Artois, Flanders and Burgundy, but repudiated it a few weeks after his release, which began the War of the League of Cognac. The Italian Wars went on for three more decades.
italian-wars: The Treaty of Lodi of 1454 ended the long Wars in Lombardy, and a non-aggression pact, the Italic League, followed shortly afterwards. It brought forty years of stability and economic expansion. The League's main supporter was the Florentine ruler Lorenzo de' Medici, who tried to keep France and the Holy Roman Empire out of the peninsula. His death in April 1492 weakened it just as France was seeking to expand in Italy. Louis XI of France had inherited the County of Provence in 1481 together with the Angevin claim to the Kingdom of Naples, and his son Charles VIII became king of France.

The first war began when Ludovico Sforza, regent of Milan, encouraged Charles VIII to invade Italy on the strength of the Angevin claim. Charles crossed into the peninsula in September 1494, saying he meant to use Naples as a base for a crusade against the Ottoman Turks. The French marched through Italy almost unopposed, entering Florence on 17 November and Rome on 31 December, and Charles withdrew in 1495. After 1503 most of the fighting began with French invasions of Lombardy and Piedmont.

The League of Cambrai, signed on 10 December 1508, turned against Venice, and the French largely destroyed a Venetian army at Agnadello on 14 May 1509. Charles I of Spain was elected Emperor Charles V on 28 June 1519, which left France surrounded by what was called the Habsburg ring, and his rivalry with Francis I of France became one of the fundamental conflicts of the sixteenth century. A Franco-Ottoman alliance followed in 1536, and a Franco-Ottoman fleet captured Nice on 22 August 1543, an attack on a Christian town that was regarded as shocking.

The growth of Protestantism meant that by 1557 the main belligerents faced internal conflict over religion and had to turn to domestic affairs. Under the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis, France was largely expelled from Italy but gained Calais from England and the Three Bishoprics from Lorraine. Spain acquired sovereignty over the Kingdoms of Naples and Sicily and the Duchy of Milan.

The wars were fought with considerable brutality. Some historians see them as the dividing point between medieval and modern warfare. Charles VIII brought in 1494 the first truly mobile siege train, with guns on wheeled carriages drawn by horses and iron cannonballs, and Francesco Guicciardini wrote that a city could be taken in days and hours rather than months. A skirmish in 1503 first showed the use of the arquebus.
italica: Italica was an ancient Roman city in Hispania, close to the town of Santiponce in the province of Seville. It stood near the Guadalquivir, close enough to control the area, and near the larger native and Roman city of Hispalis, modern Seville, which would remain the greater of the two. The original old city, the vetus urbs, lies under present-day Santiponce, while the archaeological site covers mainly the new city that Hadrian added to the north.

Italica was the first Roman settlement in Spain. It was founded in 206 BCE by Publius Cornelius Scipio during the Second Punic War, close to a native Iberian town of the Turdetani, as a settlement for his Italic veterans, a mixture of allies and Roman citizens, and was named after them. It grew by drawing migrants from the Italian peninsula and the children of Roman soldiers and native women. Among the settlers were a branch of the gens Ulpia from Tuder in Umbria and a branch of the gens Aelia from Hadria, the families of the emperors Trajan and Hadrian. According to some authors it was also the birthplace of Theodosius I.

The old city was laid out on a Hippodamian street plan with a forum at the centre, linked to a busy river port. Italica thrived under the patronage of Hadrian, who expanded it northwards as the new city and, at its request, raised it to the status of colonia, although it already held the rights of municipium. He added temples, including the enormous Traianeum, which honoured his predecessor and adoptive father, and rebuilt public buildings. The city began to dwindle as early as the 3rd century, when a shift in the bed of the Guadalquivir left its port high and dry. In late antiquity it had a bishop and, in the Visigothic age, a garrison, and its walls were restored by Leovigild in 583.

Because no modern city covers much of the new city, Italica is an unusually well preserved Roman site, with cobbled streets and mosaic floors still in place. Its amphitheatre, the third largest in the Roman Empire at the time, seated 25,000 spectators in a city whose population is estimated at only 8,000. The Traianeum measured 108 by 80 metres and was decorated with over a hundred columns of Cipollino marble, and an aqueduct of 37 kilometres fed a huge cistern that remains intact. Houses of the elite quarter keep splendid mosaics, among them the House of the Birds and the House of the Neptune Mosaic.

The ruins were long used as a quarry: in 1740 Seville ordered the amphitheatre's walls demolished to build a dam. A first law of protection took effect in 1810, and Italica was declared a National Monument by Royal Order of 1912.
italo-balbo: Italo Balbo was born on 6 June 1896 in Quartesana, part of Ferrara. He supported Italy's entry into the First World War, served with the Alpini, and by the end of the war had earned one bronze and two silver medals for valour and the rank of captain. He then took a law degree and a degree in Social Sciences, with a thesis on the thought of Giuseppe Mazzini, and worked as a bank clerk in Ferrara. In 1921 he joined the National Fascist Party and soon became secretary of the Ferrara Fascist organization.

Balbo formed his own group, nicknamed Celibano, which broke strikes for landowners and attacked communists and socialists. At twenty-six he was the youngest of the four Quadrumvirs who planned the March on Rome in 1922, and in 1923 he became a founding member of the Grand Council of Fascism. In 1926 he became Secretary of State for Air and began building the Italian Royal Air Force. He organized air cruises over the Mediterranean in 1928 and 1929, and led twelve flying boats from Orbetello to Rio de Janeiro between 17 December 1930 and 15 January 1931, in which some aircraft were lost.

From 1 July to 12 August 1933 twenty-four seaplanes flew from Rome to the Century of Progress exposition in Chicago and back. Chicago renamed a street Balbo Drive, and President Franklin Roosevelt presented him with the Distinguished Flying Cross. Back in Italy he was made Marshal of the Air Force.

Balbo governed the new colony of Libya, formed on 1 January 1934, and was in effect removed from Roman politics, where Mussolini saw him as a threat. He built the Via Balbia and the Marble Arch, unveiled on 16 March 1937, and tried to attract Italian immigrants. He was the only leading Fascist to oppose strongly the Racial Laws of 1938 and to criticize publicly the alliance with Nazi Germany.

On 28 June 1940, shortly after British aircraft had attacked Tobruk, Italian anti-aircraft batteries misidentified his Savoia-Marchetti SM.79 and shot it down, killing everyone aboard. Rumours that Mussolini ordered his assassination have been debunked. The RAF dropped a wreath with a note of condolence. He was buried outside Tripoli on 4 July 1940, and in 1970 his remains were brought to Orbetello and reburied by his family.
italo-turkish-war: Italian claims to Libya date back to the Ottoman defeat by Russia in the war of 1877–1878. At the Congress of Berlin in 1878 France and the United Kingdom agreed to a French occupation of Tunisia and British control over Cyprus, and the French told Italian diplomats that Tripoli would be a counterpart for Italy. Italy made a secret agreement with Britain in February 1887, and in 1902 signed a secret treaty with France giving freedom of intervention in Tripolitania and Morocco. In the 1909 Racconigi Bargain Russia acknowledged Italy's interest in Tripoli and Cyrenaica.

Italy published a declaration of its direct interest in Libya on 29 September 1911, and military operations began with the bombardment of Tripoli on 3 October. The Ottomans had sent their Libyan battalions to Yemen and had no full army in Tripolitania; their officers travelled there secretly through Egypt, and local Libyans were organised for the defence. Italian forces captured Tripoli, Tobruk, Derna, Bengasi and Homs between 3 and 21 October, but suffered a defeat at Shar al-Shatt. The corps was then enlarged to 100,000 men, and the war became one of position, with the Italians unable to advance far inland.

The war saw early uses of new technology. On 23 October 1911 Capitano Carlo Piazza flew the first aerial reconnaissance mission, and on 1 November Sottotenente Giulio Gavotti dropped the first aerial bomb on Ottoman troops. At sea the Italian Navy, with seven times the tonnage of the Ottoman, sank Ottoman gunboats at Kunfuda Bay in January 1912 and ships at Beirut on 24 February. On land the Ottomans turned to guerrilla tactics, and the Italians answered with repressive measures including public hangings; in October 1911 Italian troops killed thousands of civilians in the Tripoli massacre.

The Treaty of Ouchy, signed on 18 October 1912, gave Italy possession of Libya, and Italy agreed to return the Dodecanese. The vagueness of its text, the Balkan Wars and the First World War kept the islands under Italian administration, and in 1923 Turkey recognised the Italian annexation at the Treaty of Lausanne. The islands became part of Greece by treaty in 1947.

The war cost Italy 1.3 billion lire, nearly a billion more than Giovanni Giolitti had estimated. Resistance by the Senussi continued, and Italian control of the interior was ineffective until the late 1920s, when Pietro Badoglio and Rodolfo Graziani waged pacification campaigns. Resistance ended after the execution of Omar Mukhtar on 15 September 1931. The war is considered a precursor of the First World War: the Balkan League attacked the Ottoman Empire in October 1912, starting the First Balkan War days before the treaty.
italy: Italy consists of the Italian Peninsula, which extends into the Mediterranean Sea, together with Sicily, Sardinia and nearly 800 islands. It covers 301,340 square kilometres, with the Alps along most of its northern boundary and the Apennine Mountains forming the backbone of the peninsula. Over 35% of its territory is mountainous, and the highest point is the summit of Mont Blanc at 4,810 metres. Many parts are of volcanic origin, and active volcanoes include Mount Etna in Sicily, the largest in Europe, as well as Vulcano, Stromboli and Vesuvius. The sovereign states of San Marino and Vatican City are enclaves within Italy.

Lower Paleolithic artefacts dating back 850,000 years have been recovered from Monte Poggiolo. Pre-Roman Italy was inhabited mostly by Italic peoples, along with the Etruscans, the Elymians and Sicani of Sicily, and the prehistoric Sardinians who gave rise to the Nuragic civilisation. Phoenicians established emporiums on the coasts of Sicily and Sardinia, and during the 8th and 7th centuries BCE Greek colonies were founded, an area later known as Magna Graecia. Rome, a settlement on the River Tiber traditionally founded in 753 BCE, was ruled by monarchs for 244 years, and in 509 BCE the Romans expelled the monarchy and established a republic.

Roman expansion consolidated the peninsula, named Italia, and Rome grew into an empire stretching from Britain to the borders of Persia. Augustus, the first emperor, began an age of peace and prosperity. Barbarian invasions led to the decline and fall of the Western Roman Empire, after which the Ostrogothic Kingdom of Italy was created.

By the 11th century Italian city-states and maritime republics expanded, and the Italian Renaissance flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries. After centuries of political division the Kingdom of Italy was established in 1861, following wars of independence and the Expedition of the Thousand. The fascist dictatorship was established in 1922, and in 1946 a republic replaced the monarchy.

Italy has 58,915,561 inhabitants, and Rome is the capital. It has been a unitary parliamentary republic since 1946, with a president elected for a single seven-year term and a perfectly bicameral Parliament made up of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate of the Republic.
From the late 19th century to the 1960s Italy was a country of mass emigration, and the diaspora included more than 25 million Italians. Italy has 62 World Heritage Sites.
itchan-kala: Khiva is divided in the traditional way into two parts: the Inner City, Itchan Kala, enclosed by an inner defensive wall, and the outer city, Dishan-Qal'a, enclosed by an outer wall. Both walls are of mud brick. The walls of Itchan Kala are 8 to 10 metres high and 5 to 6 metres thick, with a perimeter of 6,250 metres. Watchtowers project outward every 30 metres, and the top of the wall is crenellated for defenders to shoot from.
