Water-filled moats were part of the defence, and remnants can still be seen in the south, while in the north and west old clay pipes cover them. Four gates remain: Bogcha Gate in the north, Polvon Gate in the east, Tosh Gate in the south and Ota Gate in the west. They have towers on both sides of the passage and galleries above, and a long passage may have several domes.

The building of the monuments falls into four periods. The first runs from ancient Khorezm to the Mongol invasion, and from it come the western wall of the Konya Ark, an ancient tower in the north-eastern corner of the castle wall and remains of the castle wall. The second is the restoration after the Mongol invasion of 1220, when the Said Alovuddin Mausoleum was built.

In the third period, in the 16th and 17th centuries under Abulgazi Khan and Asfandiyar Khan, Anusha Khan's bathhouse (1657), the Ak Mosque (1675) and the madrasa of Khojamberdibi (1688) were raised, and the khan's reception hall was built in 1686-1688. In the first half of the 18th century the war between Bukhara and Iran for the Khanate of Khiva badly damaged the town.

The fourth period runs from the 18th to the 20th century. The Juma Mosque, established in the 10th century, was rebuilt in 1788-1789 and kept a hypostyle hall with 112 columns taken from ancient structures. A main road was laid between two gates and the ruined walls were restored. Building quickened under Muhammad Rahim Khan I (1806-1825), Alla-Kulli-Khan (1825-1842) and Muhammad Amin Bahadur Khan (1845-1855): the palace in the Konya Ark was finished, the Toshhovli Palace was built, and a caravanserai, madrasa and tim went up near the Polvan Gate. The Pahlavon Mahmud Mausoleum was also built in this period.

The old town keeps more than 50 historic monuments and 250 old houses, mostly of the 18th or 19th century. Among the notable buildings are the Konya Ark, the Juma Mosque, the Ak Mosque, the Hasanmurod Qushbegi Mosque, the madrasas of Alla-Kulli-Khan, Muhammad Aminkhon and Muhammad Rakhimkhon, the mausoleums of Pahlavon Mahmoud and Sayid Allavuddin, and caravanserais and markets. Local legend holds that the water channel of Khiva was dug by Shem, the son of Noah.
ito-hirobumi: Itō Hirobumi was born Hayashi Risuke on 16 October 1841 in Tsukari village in Suō Province, within the Chōshū Domain, the son of a farmer of humble origins. His father entered the service of a low-ranking samurai, Itō Naoemon, and was adopted with his household into the Itō family, which gave them samurai status at the lowest rank. His name became Itō Shunsuke in 1858 and Hirobumi around 1869. In 1863 he was one of the Chōshū Five who secretly travelled to Britain, against the shogunate's ban on overseas travel, and studied at University College London.

After the Meiji Restoration of 1868 his knowledge of the West advanced him. He became the first governor of Hyōgo Prefecture, and in 1870 and 1871 he toured the United States to study finance, which influenced the New Currency Regulation of 1871 that put Japan on the gold standard. From late 1871 to 1873 he was one of four deputy ambassadors of the Iwakura Mission to the United States and Europe, where his ability to speak English made him useful. On his return he sided with those who opposed a military expedition to Korea, and was appointed councilor and minister of public works.

In the Political Crisis of 1881 he used Ōkuma Shigenobu's proposal for a British-style parliament to force Ōkuma's resignation and secured agreement on a gradual, Prussian-influenced course, emerging as first among equals in the Meiji oligarchy. He then travelled in Europe and from 1884 headed the bureau drafting the constitution. In 1885 he replaced the Daijō-kan with a cabinet and became the first prime minister. He led the Privy Council that reviewed the constitution before its promulgation in 1889.

His pragmatism earned him the nickname Round Itō. He accepted reluctantly that a government party was needed, an idea Yamagata and the other elder statesmen vetoed in 1892, and he founded the Rikken Seiyūkai in 1900.

Itō oversaw the First Sino-Japanese War and negotiated the Qing dynasty's surrender on terms that included the annexation of Taiwan. After the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1905 he became the first Resident-General of Korea. He first supported a protectorate rather than annexation, but pressure from the army leadership and the failure of his gradualist approach contributed to his support for annexation. He resigned in June 1909 and four months later was assassinated at Harbin in Manchuria by the independence activist An Jung-geun.
itsukushima: Itsukushima, popularly known as Miyajima, which means Shrine Island, lies in the western part of the Inland Sea of Japan, in the north-west of Hiroshima Bay. It is one of Hayashi Gahō's Three Views of Japan, specified in 1643, and belongs to the city of Hatsukaichi in Hiroshima Prefecture; before a merger in 2005 it was the town of Miyajima. The island and the waters around it lie within Setonaikai National Park. Strong tides expose the sea bottom beyond the shrine's torii at low tide, and at high tide the sea fills the areas under the shrine boardwalk.

The island is mountainous and sparsely settled, with an area of only 30.39 square kilometres and a population of about 2,000. Its highest point is the peak of Mount Misen, at 535 metres. Because the island is seen as sacred, trees may not be cut for lumber, and sika deer roam freely; in Shinto they are thought of as messengers of the gods. Its maple trees are known throughout Japan, and momiji manjū, pastries with maple-leaf emblems, are a popular souvenir.

The site was considered sacred for a long time, and locals may have built a simple shrine there before the complex was built in 593. In 1168 Taira no Kiyomori, a warrior-courtier, contributed greatly to giving the shrine its present form. The existence of the shrine is confirmed by early 9th century texts, and the Nihon Shoki confirms the sacredness of these structures during the Heian period. Daiganji Temple was reconstructed around 1200, in the Kamakura period. The Five-storied Pagoda was built in 1407.

In the 16th century Toyotomi Hideyoshi began the Senjōkaku, a pavilion of a thousand mats and the largest structure on the island, as a Buddhist library where sutras could be chanted for fallen soldiers. He died in 1598 and it was never fully completed. Until the Meiji Restoration forbade the mixing of Shinto and Buddhism in 1868, Daishō-in temple administered the Itsukushima Shrine. The Senjōkaku was then converted into a Shinto shrine dedicated to Hideyoshi.

The Itsukushima Shrine, a Shinto shrine known for its floating torii gate, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the National Treasures of Japan. Next to it stands Daiganji Temple, dedicated to the goddess Benzaiten, one of the three best-known Benzaiten temples in Japan, which opens its Benzaiten to the public only on 17 June. Daishō-in on Mount Misen is the headquarters of the Omuro branch of Shingon Buddhism and the 14th temple of the Chūgoku 33 Kannon Pilgrimage. A ferry of about ten minutes crosses to the mainland at Miyajimaguchi.
itzcoatl: Itzcoatl, whose name in Classical Nahuatl, Itzcōhuātl, means "Obsidian Serpent", was born around 1380. He was the natural son of the tlatoani Acamapichtli and an unknown Tepanec woman from Azcapotzalco. His half-brother was Huitzilihuitl, and he was an uncle of Chimalpopoca and of Moctezuma I. He married the princess Huacaltzintli, and they had a son, Tezozomoc.

Itzcoatl was elected king of Tenochtitlan, the fourth to hold the office, after his nephew and predecessor Chimalpopoca was killed by Maxtla of the neighbouring Tepanec city-state of Azcapotzalco. Allied with Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco, he defeated Maxtla and ended Tepanec domination of central Mexico. Itzcoatl, Nezahualcoyotl and Totoquilhuaztli, king of Tlacopan, then formed the Triple Alliance, the basis of the later Aztec Empire.

Itzcoatl next turned to the chinampas districts on the south shores of Lakes Xochimilco and Chalco, where fresh water springs had allowed extensive raised gardens to be built on the shallow lake floors. Campaigns against Xochimilco in 1430, Mixquic in 1432, Cuitlahuac in 1433 and Tezompa secured agricultural resources for Tenochtitlan. With the conquest of Culhuacan and Coyoacán, they cemented the Triple Alliance's control over the southern half of the Valley of Mexico. In 1439 he led a campaign outside the valley, against Cuauhnahuac, now Cuernavaca.

According to the Florentine Codex, Itzcoatl ordered the burning of all historical codices because it was "not wise that all the people should know the paintings". Among other purposes, this allowed the Aztec state to develop an official history and mythology that honoured Huitzilopochtli. During his reign temples, roads and a causeway were built at Tenochtitlan.
Itzcoatl also set up the religious and governmental hierarchy that his nephew Moctezuma I took over when Itzcoatl died in 1440. He is regarded as the founder of the Aztec Empire.
ivan-alexander-of-bulgaria: Ivan Alexander was the son of Despot Sratsimir of Kran and of Petrica, a sister of Michael Asen III of Bulgaria, and so a nephew of Michael Asen III and a descendant of the Asen dynasty. The date of his birth is unknown. By 1330 he was a despot governing the city of Lovech. That year he fought the Serbs at the Battle of Velbazhd alongside his father and his father-in-law Basarab of Wallachia, and Bulgaria was defeated. The defeat and worsening relations with the Byzantine Empire brought an internal crisis, and in 1331 a coup drove Ivan Stefan out of Tarnovo and the conspirators placed Ivan Alexander on the throne.

In 1331 he reconquered north-eastern Thrace from the Byzantines. Relations with Serbia eased under Stefan Uroš IV Dušan, who allied with him and married his sister Helena of Bulgaria in 1332. In the summer of 1332 the Byzantine emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos advanced while a rebellion by Belaur broke out at Vidin. Ivan Alexander defeated the Byzantines at the Battle of Rusokastro and made peace on the status quo. In 1344 the regency of John V Palaiologos ceded him Philippopolis and nine fortresses in the Rhodope Mountains for his support in the Byzantine civil war, his last major foreign success.

Afterwards the empire suffered Turkish raids on Thrace, the Black Death and the loss of his sons Ivan Asen IV in 1349 and Michael Asen IV by 1355. Louis I of Hungary conquered Vidin in 1365 and took Ivan Sratsimir captive, but Ivan Alexander, with money paid by John V after Count Amadeus VI of Savoy had seized Bulgarian coastal cities, induced Dobrotica of Dobruja and Vladislav I of Wallachia to reconquer it in 1369. He also crowned sons of his second marriage, Ivan Shishman and Ivan Asen V, as co-emperors, while Ivan Sratsimir became effectively independent around 1356.

Ivan Alexander died on 17 February 1371 and was succeeded by Ivan Sratsimir at Vidin and Ivan Shishman at Tarnovo. His reign saw a cultural flowering, sometimes called the Second Golden Age of Bulgarian culture. He ordered many monasteries and churches built or renovated, and portraits of him as a donor survive at the Bachkovo Monastery and the Rock-hewn Churches of Ivanovo.

Works of the period include the Middle Bulgarian translation of the Manasses Chronicle of 1344 to 1345, the Tetraevangelia of Ivan Alexander of 1355 to 1356, now in the British Library, and the Tomić Psalter of 1360. He convened councils in 1350 and 1359 to 1360 that condemned heresies such as the Bogomils, and the writer Ivan Vazov made him the hero of a novelette and a drama.
ivan-asen-i: Ivan Asen came from the Byzantine theme of Paristrion; his exact place and date of birth are unknown. Chronicles of the late 12th and early 13th centuries describe him and his brothers Theodor, later called Peter, and Kaloyan as Vlachs, but they were most likely of mixed Bulgarian, Cuman and Vlach ancestry, a question that remains controversial. Ivan was his baptismal name; Asen and Belgun are Turkic, meaning sound, safe, healthy and wise. Robert of Clari wrote that Asen had charge of one of the emperor's horse farms, which may show that he was a pastoralist rather than a landowner.

In autumn 1185 Asen and Theodor met the Byzantine emperor Isaac II Angelos at Kypsela in Thrace to ask for a grant. The emperor refused, and on the order of his uncle John Doukas Asen was struck across the face for impudence. A special tax for the emperor's marriage to Margaret of Hungary had already brought the Bulgarian and Vlach population to the edge of revolt. The brothers had shamans declare that Saint Demetrius of Thessalonica would come over to their side, and Theodor was crowned as Peter. After Isaac II defeated them in early 1186 they fled across the Danube, and returned in the autumn with Cuman reinforcements, seizing Paristrion.

Asen became his brother's co-ruler in 1187 or 1188; seals call him Ivan, basileus of the Bulgarians. In 1188 Isaac II besieged Lovech and captured Asen's wife Helen and his brother Kaloyan. When Frederick Barbarossa's crusaders crossed the Balkans in 1189 the brothers occupied Dobruja and parts of Thrace. Around 1192 they divided the realm, Asen keeping Tarnovo and its region. After Isaac II was blinded by his brother Alexios in April 1195, Asen defeated Alexios Aspietes, took the fortresses along the Struma River, and surrounded and defeated a Byzantine army under Isaac Komnenos near Serres.

In 1196 the boyar Ivanko stabbed Asen to death. Niketas Choniates gave two versions: that the captive Isaac Komnenos persuaded Ivanko by promising him his daughter, or that Ivanko's affair with the sister of Asen's wife had been discovered. Choniates also stated that Ivanko wished to rule more justly than Asen, who had governed everything by the sword; Paul Stephenson concludes that Asen had introduced a reign of terror with the help of Cuman mercenaries, while Vásáry says the Byzantines encouraged the killing. Peter forced Ivanko to flee to the Byzantine Empire and put Kaloyan in charge of Asen's realm. Asen's son Ivan Asen became emperor in 1218.
ivan-asen-ii: Ivan Asen II was born in the 1190s, the son of Ivan Asen I and Elena. His father was killed in 1196 and his uncle Kaloyan succeeded. After Kaloyan was murdered in 1207, Ivan Asen had a strong claim, but Kaloyan's Cuman widow married Boril, the son of one of Kaloyan's sisters, who was proclaimed emperor. According to George Akropolites, Ivan Asen fled to the lands of the Russians. He returned with hired soldiers, probably after Boril's ally Andrew II of Hungary left for the Fifth Crusade in 1217, besieged Boril in Tarnovo, and captured and blinded him in 1218.

Andrew II, returning from the Fifth Crusade in late 1218, was not allowed to cross Bulgaria until he promised his daughter Maria to Ivan Asen. Early in 1230 Theodore Komnenos Doukas invaded along the Maritsa, and the armies met at Klokotnitsa in March or April. Ivan Asen marched into battle holding a copy of his peace treaty with Theodore high in the air, a reference to Theodore's betrayal. The Bulgarians captured Theodore and his principal officials; Ivan Asen released the common soldiers and later, after a plot, had Theodore blinded. His troops took Ohrid, Prilep, Serres, Adrianople and Plovdiv, and his son-in-law Manuel Doukas took control of the Empire of Thessaloniki.

Control of the Via Egnatia, the trade route between Thessaloniki and Durazzo, brought revenue; he struck gold coins at a new mint in Ohrid and built in Tarnovo, including the Church of the Holy Forty Martyrs, which commemorated Klokotnitsa. In 1235 he met John III Vatatzes of Nicaea at Lampsacus, where Patriarch Germanus II recognised Joachim I as patriarch of the Bulgarian Church, acknowledging its autocephaly. The allies besieged Constantinople unsuccessfully in 1235 and again the next year. In 1237 Ivan Asen broke the alliance, fearing that Vatatzes would gain most from the fall of the Latin Empire.

In 1237 Mongol invasions drove thousands of Cumans across the Danube into Bulgaria. Ivan Asen later married Irene, who had been captured with her father Theodore in 1230. The date of his death is unknown; Alexandru Madgearu writes that he most probably died in May or June 1241. Historian Jean W. Sedlar described him as the last really powerful ruler of Bulgaria. His reign ended during the Mongol invasion of Europe; the Mongols invaded Bulgaria in 1242 and forced it to pay yearly tribute, and his successor's minority gave rise to boyar factions. His seal is shown on the reverse of the Bulgarian 2 lev banknote.
ivan-gundulic: Ivan Gundulić, baptised Dživo Franov Gundulić, was born in Dubrovnik on 8 January 1589 into a wealthy Ragusan noble family. His father Frano was a senator and diplomat. Ivan received an excellent education, probably studying the humanities with the Jesuit Silvestro Muzio, and then Roman law. In 1608, at nineteen, he became a member of the Great Council, and he was twice, in 1615 and 1619, knez of Konavle, an area southeast of the city.

From 1621 he held various offices in the city government. He became a senator in 1636, a judge in 1637 and a member of the Small Council in 1638. He died of a fever on 8 December 1638 and was buried in the Franciscan church of Dubrovnik. Had he lived longer, he would probably have been elected knez himself.

Gundulić began with poems and melodramas staged in Dubrovnik, but he published only his larger works, and his early writing, which he called a brood of darkness, is lost. In 1621 he published reworkings of Psalms of David and religious poems. His Tears of the Prodigal Son of 1622, in three cries named Sin, Insight and Humility, sets out sin, repentance and redemption through contrasts of life and death, purity and sin, Heaven and Hell. His pastoral play Dubravka of 1628 recalls the former glory of Dubrovnik and contains some of the best-known verses in Croatian literature, among them the lines on sweet liberty.

His main work is the epic Osman. It opens with the Sultan reckoning with the Ottoman defeat at Chocim in 1621 and follows the envoys he sends to the Kingdom of Poland, the battle itself and the Slavs enslaved under Ottoman rule. The army finally captures and executes Osman and installs Mustafa. The poem contrasts Christianity and Islam, Europe and the Turks, and what the poet saw as freedom and slavery, continues Marko Marulić's celebration of the fight against the invading Ottoman Turks, and reminds the reader constantly of fortune's wheel and the transience of the world. The 14th and 15th of its twenty cantos were never found.

Osman was first printed in Dubrovnik in 1826 with the two missing cantos replaced by verses of a descendant, Petar Ignjat Sorkočević-Crijević. The Illyrian movement chose Gundulić's work as a model of Croatian, and Ivan Mažuranić composed two chapters to complete the poem. Gundulić is regarded as the Croatian national poet, and his influence on the final standardisation of the language was great.
ivan-i-of-moscow: Ivan was the fourth son of Daniel of Moscow, the first prince of Moscow and the youngest son of Alexander Nevsky. Chroniclers did not record his birth, and the date c. 1288 is inferred from his father's appointing him to represent him in Novgorod in 1296. Because Daniel died before becoming grand prince, his descendants were excluded from the title under collateral succession. His brother Yury, who succeeded in 1303, was made grand prince by Özbeg Khan in 1318 but lost the title four years later, and was murdered in 1325 by Dmitry of Tver. Ivan then inherited the principality of Moscow.

In 1327 the people of Tver killed the deputy Özbeg had sent to test the loyalty of Aleksandr of Tver. Ivan went to the khan expecting the grand princely patent but was instead given a Tatar army and ordered, with Aleksandr of Suzdal, to sack Tver. Aleksandr of Tver fled to Pskov, and because Ivan could not bring him back, Özbeg divided the grand principality in 1328 between Ivan and Aleksandr of Suzdal. Ivan later became sole grand prince. He then collected tribute from the other princes, and used the funds to develop Moscow.

He allied with Metropolitan Peter, who chose Moscow as his residence and died there on 20 December 1326. Ivan laid the foundation of the Dormition Cathedral, Moscow's first stone church, on 4 August 1326, and under Peter's successor Theognostus four further stone churches were built. Ivan also brought the princes of the lower lands, including Rostov, into his orbit, partly by dynastic marriages, and in 1333 he led an army into Novgorod territory when Novgorod's archbishop-elect appeared to be agreeing a defensive alliance with Gediminas of Lithuania.

Ivan drew up his will, probably in 1339, dividing Moscow between his three sons, and took a copy to Sarai, where the khan approved it. He died in Moscow on 31 March 1340 and was buried in the Church of the Archangel, which he had built. Aleksandr of Tver was executed at the Horde in 1339, ending a struggle of 35 years.

The name Kalita, 'money bag', is explained by some sources as a sign of his generosity to the poor and by Vasily Klyuchevsky as ironic, a reference to stinginess. The Trinity Chronicle credits his policy towards the Mongols with forty years of peace, and Nikolay Karamzin called him gatherer of the Russian lands. Soviet-era historians, following Karl Marx, were more critical.
ivan-iii: Ivan Vasilyevich was born on 22 January 1440, the son of Vasily II, grand prince of Moscow, and Maria of Borovsk. He served as co-ruler and regent for his blind father before he officially ascended the throne in 1462. Vasily II's will gave him the grand principality.

Ivan's rule was marked by a vast expansion of Muscovite territory. After a war with the Novgorod Republic in 1471, when his army defeated the Novgorodians at the Battle of Shelon on 14 July, Novgorod ceded much of its northern territory and paid an indemnity of 15,500 rubles. In 1478 it recognised his direct rule, and he abolished its veche. Its acquisition nearly doubled the size of his realm. Other principalities were absorbed by conquest, purchase or marriage contract: Yaroslavl in 1463, Rostov in 1474, Tver in 1485 and Vyatka in 1489. His last will ordered that the domains of all his kinsfolk pass to the reigning grand prince after their deaths instead of to their heirs.

In 1476 Ivan refused to pay the customary tribute to Ahmed Khan of the Great Horde. In 1480 Ahmed invaded, and the Muscovite and Tatar armies faced each other across the Ugra River until Ahmed retreated into the steppe on 11 November. Russian historiography marks this as the end of the Tatar yoke. In 1500 Ivan defeated Lithuania at the Battle of Vedrosha, and in 1503 Grand Duke Alexander ceded Chernigov, Starodub, Novgorod-Seversky and sixteen other towns for peace.

After the death of Maria of Tver in 1467 he married Sophia Palaiologina in 1472, a niece of the last Byzantine emperor Constantine XI. The marriage was sponsored by Pope Paul II in the hope of binding Moscow to Rome, but she endorsed Orthodoxy. Under her influence the double-headed eagle was adopted in Moscow. From 1484 Ivan used the title tsar in foreign correspondence. He reduced the boyars' powers, granted estates called pomestie in return for military service, and had a new law code, the sudebnik, compiled; it restricted the movement of peasants and so laid the groundwork for serfdom.

Ivan died on 27 October 1505 and was succeeded by his son Vasily III. Moscow's territory had grown from under 600 square miles under Ivan II to more than 15,000 at the end of Vasily II's reign, and Ivan III absorbed its old rivals. Russian historians call him the gatherer of the Russian lands.
ivan-mazepa: Mazepa was born on 30 March 1639 (20 March in the old style) in the village of Mazepyntsi near Bila Tserkva, then in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, into a noble family. He studied at the Kyiv Mohyla Collegium and in 1659 entered the service of King John II Casimir, who sent him on diplomatic missions to Ukraine. From 1669 to 1673 he served under Hetman Petro Doroshenko, as a squadron commander and chancellor on missions to Poland, Crimea and the Ottoman Empire. Captured in 1674 by the Kosh Otaman Ivan Sirko, he then spent seven years as a courtier of Doroshenko's rival Ivan Samoylovych.

In 1687 Mazepa accused Samoylovych of conspiring to secede from Russia and was elected hetman of Left-bank Ukraine at Kolomak. By supporting the removal of the regent Sophia in 1689 he won the trust of Tsar Peter I, who valued his education. His new strategy against the Tatars and their Ottoman overlords brought him the Order of St Andrew, and in 1707 Emperor Joseph I made him a prince of the Holy Roman Empire. His long rule is described as a period of recovery from the Ruin, and he patronised churches, learning and the arts.

In the Great Northern War he supplied Peter with troops from 1700, and in 1704 the tsar allowed him to incorporate Right-bank territories into the Hetmanate. Peter's reforms steadily reduced the Hetmanate's autonomy, and in 1708, after the tsar refused to protect it against the advancing Swedes, Mazepa abandoned the alliance and sided with Charles XII of Sweden.

Charles did not allow Mazepa's forces to take part at Poltava in 1709. Mazepa retreated with the king to Bendery in the Ottoman Empire and died there on 2 October 1709 (21 September in the old style), of a stroke following gout. The Russian Orthodox Church pronounced an anathema on his name in 1708, which the Ecumenical Patriarchate considers uncanonical. Russian authorities removed his crest from churches and blacked out his name in books. His life has inspired many literary, artistic and musical works.
ivan-mazuranic: Ivan Mažuranić was born on 11 August 1814 in Novi Vinodolski on the northern Croatian coast, the third of four sons of a well-to-do yeoman family. His brother Anton became a jurist and philologist, and Matija wrote a travel book, A Look at Bosnia (1842). Ivan was said to speak nine languages. He studied law at the University of Zagreb from 1835 to 1837 and philosophy at the University of West Hungary, then taught at a gymnasium in Zagreb and worked as a lawyer in Karlovac. He married Aleksandra Demeter, sister of the poet Dimitrija Demeter.

Mažuranić was a member of the People's Party and held the office of ban from 20 September 1873 until 21 February 1880. As the first ban not of old nobility he was known as Ban pučanin, the commoner ban. He saw Croatia caught between the hammer of Austrian bureaucracy and the anvil of Hungarian expansionist nationalism.

During his rule the Sabor passed 60 laws on liberal principles stressing the constitution, individual rights, education and laissez faire, to move Croatia from a semi-feudal system to a modern civil society. He formed a network of public schools and reduced the weight of denominational schools. That was one of the issues behind his resignation in 1880; the Catholic Church and ethnic Serb politicians in the Sabor criticised it, while others thought it a necessary step in secularisation.

In his native land Mažuranić is best known for the epic poem The Death of Smail-aga Čengić, based on an ambush in Montenegro in which a local Muslim tyrant was killed in a vendetta. He turned an act of tribal revenge into a hymn to the struggle for freedom. Following Kačić and Ivan Gundulić, whose epic Osman he completed, he closed the era of Romanticism and classic epic poetry in Croatian literature.
With Josip Užarević he published a German-Illyrian dictionary in 1842, and he coined words that became commonplace in standard Croatian. His portrait was on the 100 kuna banknote of 1993 and 2002.
ivan-mestrovic: Ivan Meštrović was born on 15 August 1883 in Vrpolje, Slavonia, and grew up in the Dalmatian village of Otavice, where his father was a poor peasant and sheep-breeder. At sixteen he became an apprentice to the stonemason Pavle Bilinić in Split. A mine owner from Vienna paid for him to study at the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna, where his teachers were Edmund von Hellmer and Otto Wagner. In 1905 he first exhibited with the Secession Group. In 1908 he moved to Paris, and in 1911 his work for the Serbian Pavilion at the Rome International Exhibition won the grand prix.

After a journey to Serbia, Meštrović became a supporter of Yugoslav unity and was called the Prophet of Yugoslavism. His Kosovo cycle of 1908 to 1910 revived national myth, and he was a founding member of the Yugoslav Committee during the First World War. After the war he settled in Zagreb in 1922 and became professor and later director of its Academy of Fine Arts. His monuments of the 1920s and 1930s include Gregory of Nin in Split, the Victor on the Kalemegdan fortress and the Monument to the Unknown Hero on Avala, and he designed the Račić family mausoleum at Cavtat.

On 7 November 1941 the Ustaše arrested him in Zagreb, and he spent three and a half months in prison. With the help of Archbishop Aloysius Stepinac and the Vatican he was released and left for Rome, then Switzerland in 1943. After the war he refused Tito's government's invitation to return, and in 1946 Syracuse University gave him a professorship; he taught at the University of Notre Dame from 1955.

In 1952 he signed his Croatian estates over to the people of Croatia, with more than 400 sculptures. He died on 16 January 1962 in South Bend, Indiana, and was buried in the family mausoleum at Otavice. The Ivan Meštrović Gallery in Split holds 86 statues given in 1950. Alonzo Lansford wrote after his 1947 exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art that American sculptors of all schools revered him. He also wrote essays, short stories and memoirs.
ivan-paskevich: Ivan Paskevich was born in Poltava on 19 May 1782, the son of a Zaporozhian Cossack gentry family and a Belarusian noblewoman. He was educated at the Page Corps and in 1800 received a commission in the Guards and the post of aide-de-camp to the tsar. His first active service was at Austerlitz in 1805. From 1807 to 1812 he fought the Ottomans and became a general officer in his thirtieth year. In 1812–1814 he commanded the 26th infantry division and fought at Borodino, Dresden, Leipzig and Paris.

Before the Russo-Persian War of 1826–1828 Paskevich commanded the 1st Guard Infantry, in which the future Nicholas I served, and Nicholas came to call him father-commander. In the spring after the war began he replaced Aleksey Petrovich Yermolov as chief commander. Under him the Erivan and Nakhichevan Khanates were conquered from the Persians, and the tsar gave him the title Count of Erivan, a million rubles and a diamond-mounted sword. He then led the Caucasus front in the Russo-Turkish War and was made field marshal at forty-seven.

In June 1831, after Field Marshal von Diebitsch died, Paskevich took command of the Russian troops crushing the Polish November Uprising. After a slow advance he redeemed his reputation at the Battle of Warsaw, which ended Polish hopes of independence. He was created Prince of Warsaw and namestnik of the Kingdom of Poland. In 1848 he commanded the Russian troops sent to aid Austria in the Hungarian Revolution and forced the Hungarians to surrender at Világos.

In Poland the period under Paskevich is known as the Paskevich Night and remembered for political repressions, economic sanctions and Russification, though he also promoted industry, highways, railways and fortresses. A decree prepared with his participation in 1846 barred landlords from removing peasants holding more than three morgen from the land. In 1854 he took command of the Army of the Danube in the opening phase of the Crimean War, laid siege to Silistria and advised abandoning the campaign because Austria threatened to intervene. Wounded on 9 June, he returned to Russia. He died in Warsaw on 1 February 1856, and his titles ended with his only son in 1903.
ivan-shishman: Ivan Shishman was born in 1350 or 1351, the eldest son of Emperor Ivan Alexander of Bulgaria and his second wife Sarah-Theodora, a Jewish convert to the Eastern Orthodox Church. Ivan Alexander's eldest son by his first marriage, Michael Asen IV, died in battle against the Ottomans in 1355, and the succession was settled in Ivan Shishman's favour because he had been born after his father's coronation. By the end of 1355 he had been proclaimed heir and co-emperor. His half-brother Ivan Sratsimir was given Vidin, probably as compensation, and in 1356 proclaimed himself emperor there.

Ivan Shishman was proclaimed emperor on 17 February 1371, when he was in his early twenties. He inherited only part of his father's realm, the lands between the Iskar River and Silistra, the valley of Sofia, parts of the Rhodope Mountains and northern Thrace. Ivan Sratsimir ruled around Vidin, and the Principality of Karvuna under the despot Dobrotitsa also refused to recognise him. After the Ottoman victory at the Battle of Maritsa on 26 September 1371, Sultan Murad I conquered northern Thrace and the Rhodopes. In 1373 Ivan Shishman became an Ottoman vassal and gave his sister Kera Tamara in marriage to Murad, regaining some towns. Sofia fell to the Ottomans in 1385.

After the victory of the Serbs and Bosniaks at the Battle of Pločnik in 1387, he renounced his vassalage. An Ottoman army of 30,000 under the Grand Vizier Çandarlızade Ali Pasha took Shumen and other fortresses in 1388 and besieged him at Nikopol, and he had to accept harsher terms, including Ottoman garrisons in several towns. In the spring of 1393 Sultan Bayezid I besieged Tarnovo, whose defence was led by Patriarch Evtimiy while the emperor was at Nikopol. The city fell on 17 July 1393. According to the cleric Gregory Tsamblak, it fell through treason. Ivan Shishman's lands were reduced to Nikopol and a few Danube towns.

Bayezid captured Nikopol after returning from Wallachia in 1395. According to the Anonymous Bulgarian Chronicle, Ivan Shishman was killed there, a Byzantine chronicle gives a different date, and some sources suggest he died in prison. Bulgarian historians have often judged him harshly, as a ruler who took the throne through his mother's intrigues and divided the country on the eve of the invasion. Under him Tarnovo remained a cultural centre, where Patriarch Evtimiy carried out an orthographic reform.

In Bulgarian folklore he is the most prominent medieval ruler, remembered as a hero who fought and died against overwhelming forces, and many fortresses, caves and places are named after him. Rebels at Tarnovo in 1598 proclaimed a claimed descendant as Shishman III.
ivan-sratsimir: Ivan Sratsimir was born in Lovech, the second son of Theodora and Ivan Alexander, who was then despot of Lovech. In 1337 his father proclaimed him co-emperor with his brothers, without defining their authority, which led to rivalry, and gave him Vidin as an apanage. Relations with his father soured after Ivan Alexander divorced his first wife and married Sarah-Theodora, whose son Ivan Shishman was born in 1350 or 1351. When the heir Michael Asen IV died in battle against the Ottomans in 1355 or 1356, Ivan Shishman, born in the purple, was declared heir.

Ivan Sratsimir was proclaimed emperor in Vidin in 1356 and took the title Emperor of Bulgarians and Greeks. He married his cousin Anna, daughter of the Wallachian voivode Nicholas Alexander, to secure an alliance with Wallachia. In 1365 King Louis I of Hungary demanded his vassalage; when he refused, Louis took Vidin on 2 June after a brief siege. Ivan Sratsimir and his family spent four years in honorary captivity in Croatia and were made to accept Catholicism. After a popular uprising and an Orthodox coalition organised by his father, he was restored in the autumn of 1369.

After his father died on 17 February 1371 he ruled without acknowledging Tarnovo, and in 1381 he placed the archbishopric of Vidin under the Patriarchate of Constantinople. The Ottoman invasion of 1388 made him a vassal with an Ottoman garrison in Vidin. He stayed inactive while Tarnovo fell in 1393 and Ivan Shishman was killed in 1395. Vidin became a literary centre, and he minted his own coinage from the 1360s.

In 1396 Ivan Sratsimir joined the crusade of King Sigismund of Hungary and opened the gates of Vidin to it. After the crusaders' defeat at Nicopolis on 25 September, Sultan Bayezid I seized Vidin by the end of 1396 or early 1397. Ivan Sratsimir was imprisoned in Bursa, where he was probably strangled. His son Constantine II claimed the title of emperor, but historians generally regard Ivan Sratsimir as the last ruler of medieval Bulgaria.
ivangorod: Ivangorod stands on the east bank of the Narva River, which flows along the border between Estonia and Russia, 159 kilometres west of Saint Petersburg and 218 kilometres east of Tallinn. It lies in Kingiseppsky District of Leningrad Oblast, directly opposite the Estonian town of Narva. The Tallinn to Saint Petersburg railway passes through it, and the Friendship Bridge, built in 1960, carries the road across the river.

Chronicles first mention a New Village on the Narova River in 1470, and in 1473 the First Pskov Chronicle records Pskov and Novgorod envoys sent there to meet the Livonians opposite Rugodiv, as Narva was then called. The fortress was built in 1492, during the reign of Ivan III, as one of a series of fortifications on the border with Livonia. The site was chosen deliberately: the Grand Prince had asked about Baltic harbours in the 1480s, since the Baltic route allowed trade independent of foreign control. The town was meant to become the first seaport of the Russian state. Ivan was said to have blinded the architect so that he could build such a fortress for no one else.

The Swedes besieged and destroyed the first fortress in 1496, after which the Russians restored and enlarged it. With ten towers and mighty stone walls, it was the first Russian defensive work with a regular rectangular plan. German documents of the late 15th century called it a counter-Narva. After Sweden took the area, Ivangorod received town privileges and was administered as a Russian township until 1649, when its burghers were ordered to move to a suburb of Narva. The Treaty of Stolbovo of 1617 placed the area under Swedish sovereignty, and Russia reconquered it in the Great Northern War in 1704.

Its military importance then waned, and from 1649 until 1945 it was administratively part of Narva, remembered in the 19th century as the Ivanov side of Narva. After the Estonian War of Independence, Estonia took control of the whole of Narva, Ivangorod included, in January 1919; Soviet Russia recognised this in the Treaty of Tartu of 1920. In 1922 the district had 7,000 inhabitants, of whom 42 percent were Estonians. It was occupied by Germany from 1941 to 1944. In January 1945 the Soviet authorities made the Narva River the border between the Estonian and Russian republics, and Ivangorod passed to Leningrad Oblast. It gained town status on 28 October 1954.

Ivangorod had a recorded population of 9,854 in the census of 2010. Its industries include textiles, food and timber, and the Narva Hydroelectric Station lies within its limits. It has thirty-three cultural heritage monuments of federal significance, all of them related to the fortress, which serves as a museum.
ivano-frankivsk: Ivano-Frankivsk lies northeast of the Carpathian Mountains, about 120 metres above sea level, in the Stanislav Basin. Vovchynets Hill, 300 to 350 metres high and part of the Pokuttya Highland, rises just outside the city. The nearest city is Tysmenytsia, less than 10 kilometres to the east. The climate is moderate continental, with warm summers and fairly cold winters.

Stanisławów was founded as a fortress to protect the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth from Tatar invasions. Andrzej Potocki bought the village of Zabolotiv and the land around it and issued a declaration establishing the city with Magdeburg rights on 7 May 1662. The Polish Crown did not recognise it until 14 August 1663. By 1672 the fortress had been rebuilt in stone and brick, and Jews were granted the right to settle permanently. The name is generally traced to the hetman Stanisław Potocki, though some sources name his grandson.

Habsburg Austria took the town in the First Partition of Poland in 1772, and it lay in the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria. After the collapse of Austria-Hungary in October 1918 the West Ukrainian People's Republic was proclaimed, and from January to May 1919 the city was its temporary capital. The Unification Act with the Ukrainian People's Republic was signed there on 22 January 1919. Poland annexed the city, and it became the seat of the Stanisławów Voivodeship.

The Soviet Union took it in September 1939, and the city was under German occupation from 2 July 1941 to 27 July 1944. More than 40,000 Jews lived there when it was occupied, a ghetto was formed, and most of the Jewish population and more than 600 educated Poles were murdered. After 1944 most of the Polish population was forced to leave. The city was renamed Ivano-Frankivsk on 9 November 1962, after the writer Ivan Franko.

Ivano-Frankivsk is the administrative centre of Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast in western Ukraine and one of the principal cities of the Carpathian Euroregion. It has been part of independent Ukraine since 1991. Its architecture combines the Polish city hall, the Austro-Hungarian business centre and Soviet apartment blocks on the edge of the city.
iviron-monastery: The monastery was founded by two Georgian monks, John the Iberian and John Tornike, to serve as a centre of scholarship for Georgian clergy. John the Iberian was appointed abbot of the new foundation in 980, and Euthymius the Iberian became a second abbot in 1005. In Greek, Iviron means "of the Iberians", a term used in historical and literary contexts for the core Georgian kingdom. The monastery is home to the Panagia Portaitissa icon of the Virgin Mary.

In the Middle Ages Iviron became a centre of Georgian religious culture. A large group of Georgian scholars and calligraphers worked there, among them George the Hagiorite, and original works were composed while major Byzantine theological texts were translated into Georgian. Georgian monarchs and other donors supported it so generously that it reportedly distributed some of its funds to other Athonite monasteries to ease any resentment. As the Kingdom of Georgia weakened, Greeks gradually took possession of the monastery, and Georgians became a minority after 1357. It still relied on Georgian patronage beyond the 17th century.

After the Russian Empire annexed Georgia, Georgians sought to strengthen their presence at Iviron. In the 1860s a donation of 35,000 rubles and the arrival of 40 new Georgian monks met resistance from the Greeks, who ultimately demolished the buildings and gardens the Georgians had built and refused them re-entry, although Russians from the St Panteleimon Monastery had supplied building materials. In 1879 Georgian nobles petitioned the Russian government to restore the monastery's Georgian character, but the authorities declined official help, not wishing to strain relations with the Greeks. A Georgian minority survived at Iviron until the middle of the 20th century.

The monastery remains the historic Georgian monastery on Mount Athos, inhabited by Georgian Orthodox monks for nearly a millennium. Russian officials in the 19th century preferred to build the New Athos Monastery on the Black Sea coast of Georgia for Russian monks who feared expulsion from Mount Athos. A few Georgian monks live elsewhere on Mount Athos, but none lived at Iviron according to data from 2011.
ivo-andric: Ivan Andrić was born on 9 October 1892 in the village of Dolac, near Travnik, while his mother, Katarina, was visiting relatives. His father, Antun, a silversmith who worked as a school janitor in Sarajevo, died of tuberculosis when Andrić was two, and the boy was raised in Višegrad by an aunt and uncle. A scholarship took him in 1902 to the Great Sarajevo Gymnasium, whose curriculum aimed to produce supporters of the Habsburg Monarchy, which he disliked. After Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1908 he became involved in South Slav youth movements. In late 1911 he was elected first president of the Serbo-Croat Progressive Movement, and he joined Young Bosnia.

When Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip, a friend of Andrić, he was in Split, and he was arrested in late July or early August for anti-state activities. Held in several prisons, he spent much of the war under house arrest and was released under an amnesty in July 1917. He studied South Slavic history and literature at Zagreb and took his doctorate at Graz in 1924, with a dissertation on spiritual life in Bosnia under Ottoman rule, which characterised the Ottoman occupation as negative. He entered the diplomatic service of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia, working in it from 1920 to 1923 and again from 1924 to 1941, and in 1939 became ambassador to Germany.

His tenure ended in April 1941 with the German-led invasion. He returned to occupied Belgrade and lived quietly in a friend's apartment for the rest of the war, in conditions some biographers liken to house arrest, writing some of his most important works. Na Drini ćuprija (The Bridge on the Drina) appeared in March 1945, followed by Travnička hronika that September and Gospođica that November. The first chronicles the Mehmed Paša Sokolović Bridge and the town of Višegrad from the 16th century until the outbreak of the First World War; the second follows a French diplomat in Bosnia during the Napoleonic Wars.

On 26 October 1961 the Swedish Academy awarded Andrić the Nobel Prize in Literature, citing the epic force with which he traced themes and depicted human destinies drawn from his country's history. He gave all the prize money, some 30 million dinars, to buy library books in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He died in Belgrade on 13 March 1975. The apartment where he spent the war became a museum, and the Ivo Andrić Foundation supports study of his work. As Yugoslavia's only Nobel laureate in literature he was widely respected there, and Serbia regards him highly, while Bosniak critics have disparaged his works for their supposed anti-Muslim bias.
ivory-coast: Portuguese merchant-explorers of the 15th and 16th centuries divided the west coast of Africa into four coasts named for the trade each offered. The Costa do Marfim, translated into French as Côte d'Ivoire, took its name from the export of ivory, as the Gold Coast and the Slave Coast did from theirs. Other names for the stretch included the Côte de Dents, the Coast of Teeth, and the Windward Coast. In the 19th century usage settled on Côte d'Ivoire, a name kept through French rule and independence in 1960.

The first human presence is hard to determine, since remains are poorly preserved in the humid climate, though polished axes and tool fragments suggest a large presence in the Upper Paleolithic period or at least the Neolithic. Historians believe the earliest inhabitants were displaced or absorbed by the ancestors of the present peoples, who migrated south into the area before the 16th century.

The first recorded history comes from the chronicles of Berber traders, who ran a caravan trade across the Sahara in salt, slaves and gold. Around the southern terminals of those routes, Djenné, Gao and Timbuktu, the great Sudanic empires developed, and they also became centres of Islamic education. From the 11th century Islam spread south into the north of what is now Ivory Coast. The Ghana Empire flourished between the 4th and 13th centuries, and the Mali Empire that followed held only the northwest corner of Ivory Coast, around Odienné.

The country was traditionally home to several states, including Gyaaman, the Kong Empire and Baoulé. It became a protectorate of France in 1843 and was consolidated as a French colony in 1893 during the Scramble for Africa. It achieved independence in 1960 under Félix Houphouët-Boigny, who ruled until 1993. Through coffee and cocoa production it became an economic powerhouse in West Africa in the 1960s and 1970s. The capital has been Yamoussoukro since 1983.

Ivory Coast is a republic with strong executive power vested in its president, and its parliament consists of a Senate and a National Assembly. Since 2011 it has been organised into 12 districts and two autonomous cities. French is the official language and about 78 languages are spoken, among them Baoulé, Dyula and Bété. The citizen population falls into macroethnic groupings, chiefly the Akan, Voltaic or Gur peoples, Northern Mandés, Kru-speaking peoples and Southern Mandés. Each ethnic group has its own music, mostly with strong vocal polyphony, and talking drums and polyrhythms are common.
ivrea: Ivrea stands at about 267 metres above sea level on the Dora Baltea, a tributary of the Po, not far from the entrance to the Aosta Valley, on a road that formed part of the medieval Via Francigena. It is regarded as the capital of the Canavese area. The surrounding country was shaped by a large Pleistocene glacier, which left moraine hills known as the Ivrea Morainic Amphitheatre and, after the last glaciation retreated about 9700 BCE, a ring of lakes. The Latin name Eporedia is probably Celtic, perhaps from the Gaulish epo, horse, and reda, a four-wheeled cart.

Before the Roman colony, the main settlement of the Salassi in the area was at Brich Appareglio, about 3 km south of the old centre, occupied from the Final Bronze Age until the fifth century BCE and briefly again in the later second century BCE. The colony of Eporedia was founded in 100 BCE, in the sixth consulship of Gaius Marius, as a colony of Roman citizens on the left bank of the Dora Baltea. It was meant to control the Salassi, whom Rome finally subjugated in 25 BCE. Remains include an amphitheatre and a theatre.

In the Lombard period Ivrea was the seat of a duchy. Under the Franks in the 9th century it was a county capital. In 1001, after disputes with Bishop Warmund, who ruled the city, Arduin conquered the March of Ivrea, later became King of Italy and began a dynasty that lasted until the 11th century, when the city fell again under the bishops. Ivrea became a free comune in the 12th century, fell to Emperor Frederick II early in the 13th and was then disputed between the bishops, the marquisate of Monferrato and the House of Savoy.

Amadeus VI of Savoy acquired Ivrea in 1356. Apart from a brief French conquest at the end of the 16th century it remained under the House of Savoy until 1800, when Napoleon Bonaparte entered the city on 26 May; his control ended in 1814. In the 20th century it was the base of Olivetti, a maker of typewriters, mechanical calculators and later computers.

Ivrea had 22,604 inhabitants in 2021. UNESCO listed the Olivetti site, Ivrea, Industrial City of the 20th Century, as a World Heritage Site on 1 July 2018, saying that it expresses a modern vision of the relationship between industrial production and architecture. The Ivrea Carnival is known for the Battle of the Oranges, thrown over three days by townspeople divided into teams at carriages that represent a duke's guard.
iwan: An iwan is a rectangular hall or space, usually vaulted, walled on three sides, with one end entirely open. Its formal gateway is called a pishtaq, a portal projecting from the facade and usually decorated with calligraphy bands, glazed tilework and geometric designs. The definition allows some interpretation, so scale, material and decoration vary greatly. The form is not confined to any one function and appears in secular and religious buildings, public and residential. The New Persian word eyvān is borrowed from Persian into Arabic and Turkish, and its etymology is unclear. Scholars once derived it from Old Persian apadāna, a word Darius I used for a structure at Persepolis, but this is no longer taken for granted.

The iwan is pre-Islamic and Iranian in origin. Many scholars discuss its invention in Mesopotamia, and there is a general consensus that it evolved locally rather than being imported. What made it a landmark development was the incorporation of a vaulted ceiling, though vaults already existed in Elamite Susa, Assyrian Nineveh, Egypt and the Mycenaeans. Most scholars now credit the Parthians with its invention. One of the earliest Parthian iwans stood at Seleucia on the Tigris, where the shift from post-and-lintel construction to vaulting occurred around the 1st century CE, and others have been found at Ashur, Hatra, Dura Europos and Uruk.

The Sasanian Empire also favoured the form but changed its function. A Parthian iwan was a room in itself, while a Sasanian one served as a grand entranceway to a larger, usually domed space. The chief Sasanian example is the Taq Kasra at Ctesiphon, begun under Khosrau I after a campaign against the Eastern Romans in 540. Its hall was about 37 m high, 26 m across and 50 m long, the largest vault built to that time. It was later largely demolished by al-Mansur, who reused its bricks.

Islamic architecture borrowed the iwan from the Sasanians. Before the 12th century it appeared mostly in houses, civic structures and palaces, and from the 12th century it became common in religious buildings. It was especially important in Central Asia and Greater Iran, and was adopted elsewhere, as at the Taj Mahal and other Mughal mausoleums.

The four-iwan plan places four iwans around a central courtyard, one often facing the qibla with a mihrab. It was already used in Parthian and Sasanian palaces and temples. Its earliest known Islamic appearance is at the governor's palace in Kufa, as rebuilt in the late 7th century. It became common in mosques only in the 12th century, when the Seljuks used it, probably first in their changes to the Great Mosque of Isfahan. It then spread with the madrasa, and was prominent in the Ayyubid and Mamluk madrasas of Egypt and Syria.
iwate-prefecture: Iwate faces the Pacific Ocean on the east, with sheer rocky cliffs along most of the shore. The Ōu Mountains on the west, where Mount Iwate, at 2,038 metres the highest point of the prefecture, is still an active volcano, form the border with Akita Prefecture. The older Kitakami Mountains run through the middle from north to south, and between the two ranges flows the Kitakami River, the longest river in Tōhoku. Its large, fertile basin holds the prefecture's biggest cities and farms. In the past Iwate was known for gold, iron, coal and sulfur, which are no longer produced.

Jōmon people inhabited the area, leaving burial pits at Nishida and clay figurines, masks and stone tools at sites such as Tateishi, Makumae and Kunenbashi. The Yamato government claimed all of Honshu from the earliest times, but its forces could not occupy any part of what became Iwate until 802. In March 787 the Emishi leaders, among them Aterui, trapped the Yamato infantry at Sufuse Village and pushed them into the Kitakami River, where more than 1,000 soldiers drowned in their heavy armour.

When battle failed, the Japanese made the Emishi dependent on trade for iron wares and sake, bribed leaders with rank and citizenship, and burned crops and relocated Emishi women and children to western Japan. On 15 April 802 More and Aterui surrendered with about 500 warriors. They were taken to Kyoto and beheaded against the wishes of the general Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, and the Emishi fought on for twenty years or more. Forts on the Chinese model were built along the Kitakami. In the latter part of the Heian period Hiraizumi became the capital of the Northern Fujiwara, and Minamoto no Yoshitsune fled there after the Genpei War. Until the Meiji Restoration the area belonged to Mutsu Province.

Iwate is the second-largest prefecture of Japan after Hokkaido, and its capital and largest city is Morioka. It has the lowest population density of any prefecture outside Hokkaido. Its sights include Morioka Castle and the Buddhist temples of Hiraizumi, among them Chūson-ji and Mōtsū-ji. The poet Matsuo Bashō visited Hiraizumi and wrote of it in Oku no Hosomichi. The coast has suffered repeated earthquakes and tsunamis, among them the tsunami of 15 June 1896, whose waves reached 24 metres at Yoshihama and killed 18,158 people in Iwate.
iyasu-v: Lij Iyasu, baptised Kifle Yaqob, was born on 4 February 1895 at Dessie in Wollo. His father was Ras Mikael, governor of Wollo, who had been born Mohammed Ali and was a Muslim until 1875, when he converted to Christianity by order of Emperor Yohannes IV. His mother, Shoaregga, was the eldest daughter of Emperor Menelik II. Because he was never crowned he took no regnal name, and Lij, meaning child, especially one of royal blood, is the title by which he is usually known.

Menelik, weakened by a stroke in 1908, told his ministers on 15 May 1909 that Iyasu would succeed him, with Ras Tessema Nadew as regent. After Tessema died on 10 April 1911, Iyasu is reported to have answered the council's question about a successor with "Myself!", and on 11 May his seal replaced his grandfather's.

Menelik died on the night of 12 to 13 December 1913. Iyasu took little interest in daily government, insulted his grandfather's ministers, led by the Minister of War Fitawrari Habte Giyorgis, and was often away from the capital. In 1915 he spent Easter at Harar among Muslims, and in August he went in disguise to French Somaliland. Allied and Italian reports claimed he had declared himself a Muslim and meant to join the Central Powers. The historian Bahru Zewde doubts these reports and notes that forged pictures and documents were used against him.

On 27 September 1916 the nobles charged him with apostasy, Archbishop Mattewos released them from their oath, and he was excommunicated. Zewditu was named empress and Tafari Makonnen made Ras and heir.

His father, Negus Mikael, was defeated at the Battle of Segale on 27 October 1916. Iyasu was besieged at Maqdala, raised a revolt in Wollo in 1917 that was crushed, and roamed the Afar desert until he was captured on 11 January 1921. He escaped in 1931, was recaptured and held at Mount Gara Muleta. During the Italian invasion of 1935 Italian aircraft dropped leaflets calling for support of the "true Emperor Iyasu V". His death was announced in November 1935, and its circumstances and burial place remain unclear.

Bahru Zewde calls his reign one of the most enigmatic in Ethiopian history, crediting it with a revised criminal code and a municipal police force. Paul Henze credits him with good intentions but judges his performance inept.
izborsk: Izborsk is a village in Pechorsky District of Pskov Oblast, Russia, 30 kilometres west of Pskov and just east of the Russian-Estonian border. It contains one of the most ancient and impressive fortresses of western Russia. Truvor's gorodishche, a settlement about half a kilometre north of the present fortress, grew to twice its size in the 10th and 11th centuries and was the predecessor of the fortress.

According to the Russian Primary Chronicle, Izborsk was the seat of Rurik's brother Truvor from 862 to 864. The historian Valentin Yanin, writing in 2008, found the existence of the Rurik brothers doubtful, and noted that excavations at Izborsk have found no trace of a Scandinavian presence in the 9th century, which indicates an important centre of the early Krivichs. Izborsk later became the main settlement on the western frontier of the Novgorod Republic.

In 1233 the fortress was captured by the Livonian Brothers of the Sword and their ally Yaroslav of Pskov, who wanted to regain control of the Pskov principality, but they soon withdrew. In 1240 the Livonian Knights took it, and it was freed two years later; the Livonians burned it in 1269. Pskov's posadnik Sheloga later built a new fortress on higher ground at the top of Zheravya hill, and it withstood several sieges. In 1348 the Pskov Republic, which included Izborsk, separated from the Novgorod Republic, and in 1399 it became a viceroyalty of the Grand Principality of Moscow.

In 1569 a small Lithuanian regiment seized the fortress, to the shock of Ivan the Terrible: a Russian turncoat named Teterin, disguised as an oprichnik, ordered the gates opened in the name of the oprichnina. Ivan retook it with little difficulty and, fearing that other cities would follow, ordered the executions of the assistant crown secretaries of Izborsk and of the surrounding fortresses. Lithuanian troops took Izborsk again during the Siege of Pskov in 1581, but it was handed back to Russia after the Truce of Yam-Zapolsky in 1582.

In 1920 the Treaty of Tartu put the boundary east of Izborsk, so the town became part of Estonia. In 1945 the border was redrawn along the pre-1918 line between Livonia and the Pskov Governorate, leaving Izborsk in the Pskov Oblast of the Russian SFSR. The oldest surviving structure of the fortress is the Lukovka tower. The walls were thickened in the 15th and 16th centuries to take cannon, and the Nativity church inside dates from the 16th century. In 2002 the fortress was nominated to Russia's World Heritage Tentative List.
iziaslav-i-of-kiev: Iziaslav was the oldest son of Yaroslav I the Wise by his second wife Ingigerd Olafsdottir and was baptised Demetrius. He succeeded his father after Yaroslav's eldest child Vladimir died before him. In 1043 Yaroslav agreed with King Casimir I of Poland that Cherven belonged to Kiev, and the agreement was sealed by a double marriage: Casimir married Yaroslav's sister Dobronega, and Iziaslav married Casimir's sister Gertrude. From 1045 to 1052 he was Prince of Turov. He is credited as one of the authors of the Pravda of Yaroslav's Descendants, part of the Russkaya Pravda, and with founding the Kiev Pechersk Monastery.

On Yaroslav's death in 1054 the realm was divided between Iziaslav, Sviatoslav and Vsevolod, who ruled as a triumvirate for twenty years. They defeated Vseslav of Polotsk at the Battle on the Nemiga River on 3 March 1067. In 1068 the Cumans defeated them at the Alta river. A veche in Kiev urged Iziaslav to fight, but he refused even to negotiate, and the Kievans rose against him, freed Vseslav and acclaimed him prince. Iziaslav fled to Poland and returned with the help of Boleslaw II, and was received back in Kiev by 2 May 1069.

By 1073 he had alienated so many people that Sviatoslav and Vsevolod drove him out of Kiev on 22 March in a seemingly bloodless coup. Boleslaw took his bribes and gave no aid, and in January 1075 he appealed to King Henry IV of Germany at Mainz, while his son Yaropolk went to Rome to ask Pope Gregory VII for support. Sviatoslav died in 1076, and Iziaslav returned to Kiev on 15 July 1077.

A dispute over the succession to Chernigov followed Sviatoslav's death. Iziaslav and Vsevolod drove out Sviatoslav's son Oleg in April 1078. Oleg returned with Cuman support and his cousin Boris and defeated Vsevolod in August. Iziaslav agreed to help and died in battle against Oleg on 3 October 1078. He was the only incumbent Grand Prince of Kiev to be killed in battle. His children Yaropolk and Sviatopolk ruled the Turov Principality, and Sviatopolk II became grand prince of Kiev.
izium: The area around Izium has been inhabited since ancient times, and archaeologists have found Mesolithic and Neolithic settlements. The land belonged to Kievan Rus, and in 1111 the Battle of the Salnytsia River was fought on it, in which East Slavs led by Vladimir II Monomakh and Sviatopolk II defeated a Cuman army. The Mongol Empire devastated the area in the 1240s. Muscovy built the Belgorod line (1635–1658) and the Izium line (1679–80) against Crimean Tatar raids, and in 1681 Colonel Donets of the Kharkiv Sloboda Cossack Regiment built a fortress named Izium on the site, generally regarded as the city's foundation.

From 1685 until 1765 Izium was the seat of the Izium Regiment of Sloboda Ukraine, and its residents took part in the Bulavin Rebellion of 1707–1708. After the Cossack system was abolished in 1765 Izium received city status, and from 1780 it was the centre of Izyumsky Uyezd. By the 1880s it had factories making bricks, vodka, butter and wax and a population of 14,761. The Kharkiv–Donbas railway reached it in 1910, and in 1916 work began on the first optical glass plant in the Russian Empire.

Izium became part of the Ukrainian SSR after the Russian Civil War. In the Holodomor of 1932–1933, 2,761 people from Izium are documented as having died. German forces occupied it from 24 June 1942, and the Red Army liberated it on 5 February 1943. Its population grew from about 12,000 in 1926 to 64,334 in January 1989, as a junction between Kharkiv and the Donbas.

Izium lies on the Siverskyi Donets about 120 kilometres south-east of Kharkiv and is the administrative centre of Izium Raion, with 44,979 inhabitants in 2022. Its position on the rail and road link between Kharkiv and the Donbas has long given it economic importance. Russian forces took the city on 1 April 2022, and Ukrainian forces recaptured it in September of that year.
izmail: The fortress was built by Genoese merchants in the 12th century, when it was known in Greek as Licovrissi. It belonged briefly to Wallachia in the 14th century and from the end of that century was under the rule of Moldavia. In 1484 the Ottoman state conquered the territory, which came under direct rule in 1538. From the early 16th century Izmail was the main Ottoman fortress of the Budjak region. In 1569 Sultan Selim II settled it with Nogai subjects, and in 1609 Cossacks destroyed the fortress.

After the Russian general Nicholas Repnin took it in 1770, the Turks refortified it heavily so that it would never be captured again. During the Russo-Turkish War of 1787–1792, Alexander Suvorov stormed it on 22 December 1790. The garrison had orders to hold to the end and had rejected a Russian ultimatum. The defeat was a catastrophe in the Ottoman Empire, while in Russia it was glorified in the country's first national anthem. One account says that nearly every Muslim inhabitant was killed in three days of massacre, with some 40,000 dead.

The town was returned to the Ottoman Empire at the end of the war, and Russian forces took it again on 14 September 1809. It passed to Russia with the rest of Bessarabia under the Treaty of Bucharest of 1812 and was rebuilt; the Intercession Cathedral (1822–36) dates from then. After Russia lost the Crimean War it returned to Moldavia, and Russia regained it after the war of 1877–1878. Romanian troops occupied it on 22 January 1918. In August 1940, under the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, it was included in the Ukrainian SSR, and it has been part of independent Ukraine since 24 August 1991.

Izmail lies on the left bank of the Chilia branch of the Danube, about 80 kilometres from the Black Sea, and is the largest Ukrainian port in the Danube Delta. Its oldest building, a small Turkish mosque of the 15th or 16th century, was converted into a church in 1810 and is now a museum of the storming of 1790. The port, ship repair and food canning form the basis of its economy.
izmit: İzmit is the capital district of Kocaeli Province, on the Gulf of İzmit in the Sea of Marmara, about 100 km east of Istanbul, in the north-western part of Anatolia. The city is mostly built on hill slopes because of the cramped area, while flat plains surround the gulf. In antiquity it was known as Nicomedia and Ólbia, and the name İzmit derives from Nicomedia prefixed with the Greek word meaning to or into.

In antiquity the city was called Astacus or Olbia, said to be founded in 712 BCE. After its destruction it was rebuilt by Nicomedes I of Bithynia in 264 BCE as Nicomedia, and it remained one of the most important cities of north-western Asia Minor. Hannibal came to Nicomedia in his final years and killed himself at nearby Libyssa, modern Gebze, between 183 and 181 BCE. The historian Arrian was born there, and it was the metropolis of Bithynia under the Roman Empire.

In 286 CE the emperor Diocletian made Nicomedia the eastern capital when he introduced the Tetrarchy, and it remained the eastern and most senior capital until Constantine the Great defeated Licinius in 324. Constantine resided mainly in Nicomedia for the next six years, until in 330 he declared nearby Byzantium to be Nova Roma, later Constantinople. He died at an imperial villa near Nicomedia on 22 May 337.

Seljuk Turks captured Nicomedia in the late 11th century, but the successes of the First Crusade returned it to Byzantine rule. After the sack of Constantinople in 1204 it became part of the Latin Empire, and the Byzantines recaptured it around 1235. The Ottoman Turks conquered it in 1337, and it became the capital of the Sanjak of Kocaeli. British forces occupied İzmit on 6 July 1920 during the Turkish War of Independence, handed it to Greece on 27 October 1920, and the Turks retook it on 28 June 1921; atrocities against Greek civilians took place around the city in 1920–1921. The earthquake of 17 August 1999 devastated the region and killed more than 17,000 people.

İzmit had 376,056 inhabitants in 2022. It lies on the main road and rail lines between Istanbul and Ankara and has a major port, and the Istanbul–İzmit area is one of the main industrial regions of Turkey, with an oil refinery and paper and cement factories. Remains of the ancient city include the acropolis, agora and amphitheatre, Roman walls and aqueducts, and the Orhan Gazi Mosque of 1333.
iztaccihuatl: Iztaccíhuatl lies within Izta-Popo Zoquiapan National Park. It stands north of its twin Popocatépetl, to which it is joined by the high-altitude Paso de Cortés. It is exceeded in height only by Pico de Orizaba and Popocatépetl. Depending on atmospheric conditions it is visible much of the year from Mexico City, about 70 kilometres away. Four individual snow-capped peaks depict the head, chest, knees and feet of a sleeping woman when seen from east or west, and the mountain is sometimes nicknamed La Mujer Dormida, the Sleeping Woman. It is the lowest peak in Mexico that holds permanent snow and glaciers.

The massive volcano has a volume of about 450 cubic kilometres. Its summit ridge is a series of overlapping cones built along a north-north-west to south-south-east line south of the Pleistocene Llano Grande caldera. Andesitic and dacitic eruptions of the Pleistocene and Holocene came from vents at or near the summit. The most recent vents are at El Pecho and in a depression on the ridge midway between El Pecho and Los Pies.

The first recorded ascent was made in 1889, though archaeological evidence suggests that the Mexica and earlier cultures had climbed it before. In Tlaxcaltecan mythology Iztaccíhuatl was a princess who fell in love with one of her father's warriors, Popocatépetl. The emperor sent him to war in Oaxaca and promised him Iztaccíhuatl as his wife on his return, which her father presumed he would not make.

She was falsely told that Popocatépetl had died in battle and died of grief. When he returned and found her dead, he carried her body to a spot outside Tenochtitlan and knelt by her grave. The gods covered them with snow and turned them into mountains. Popocatépetl became an active volcano, raining fire in rage at the loss of his beloved.
izu-province: Izu Province, known in its abbreviated form as Zushu, bordered Sagami and Suruga Provinces. Its mainland part, the Izu Peninsula, is today the eastern portion of Shizuoka Prefecture, while the Izu Islands belong to Tokyo. The province was created in 680 CE, when two districts of Suruga Province, Tagata and Kamo, were separated to form it. Naka District was added at some point between 701 and 710. The capital was at Mishima, which also held the province's Kokubun-ji and its Ichinomiya, the Mishima Taisha. Under the Engishiki classification Izu ranked as a lesser country.

Under the ritsuryo legal system Izu was one of the preferred places of exile for those convicted of political crimes by the Heian period court. In the Kamakura period it was ruled by the Hojo clan. In the Muromachi period the Uesugi clan held it nominally through their post as Kanto Kanrei, but in practice it came under whoever ruled Sagami and Musashi, which by the Sengoku period meant the Later Hojo clan based at Odawara. After the Battle of Odawara, Toyotomi Hideyoshi moved Tokugawa Ieyasu from the Tokai region to the Kanto, and Izu came under Tokugawa rule.

Under the Tokugawa shogunate Izu stayed a tenryo territory administered directly by the shogun, much of it by a daikan at Nirayama, with portions given to hatamoto and to Odawara Domain. Kimisawa District was added to the three ancient districts. The Tokaido road between Edo and Kyoto crossed northern Izu, with a post station at Mishima-shuku, and the port of Shimoda in the south was a required port of call for vessels approaching Edo from the east.

Shimoda was chosen by the Tokugawa government as a port to be opened to American trade under the Convention of Kanagawa, signed by Commodore Matthew Perry on 31 March 1854. Yoshida Shoin made an unsuccessful attempt there in 1854 to board Perry's Black Ships. The first American consulate in Japan opened at the temple of Gyokusen-ji in Shimoda under Townsend Harris, who negotiated the Treaty of Amity and Commerce, signed at Ryosen-ji in 1858. The Treaty of Shimoda with Russia was signed at Choraku-ji in 1855.

After the start of the Meiji period Izu was merged into the short-lived Ashigaru Prefecture in 1871. That prefecture was divided between Shizuoka Prefecture and Kanagawa Prefecture on 18 April 1876, and the Izu Islands passed from Shizuoka to Tokyo in 1878.
